Written  by a team of experts, this updated handbook offers the latest information on advanced failure  analysis tools and techniques, buttressed with numerous real-life examples. Relevant and widely used articles on classic techniques have also been updated to include recent developments. xi


With the development of new multilevel packages, sophisticated application circuits, and ever-shrinking integrated circuit feature sizes, identifying the  root cause of a failure is becoming more challenging. Failure analysis support is needed through the  product life cycle, from technology development, design debug, fabrication, packaging, and reliability  qualification, to production failures and customer  returns. Identifying root cause requires knowledge of  advanced failure analysis tools and newly developed  techniques as well as strategic planning to determine  which method to use and when. To continue to succeed, an analyst’s skills and knowledge must continue to grow as the defects and features we investigate  relentlessly shrink.

Overview of Wafer-level Electrical Failure Analysis Process  for Accelerated Yield Engineering

Introduction


A typical product yield ramp cycle usually consists of the  following stages: technology development, qualification and  production. The technology development phase is usually  considered the most intense as a result of increasing pressure  to constantly improve time-to-market. As today’s integrated  circuits (ICs) become more complex at all levels in terms of  design marginality, integration, functionality and storage  capacity, failure analysis (FA) is becoming more challenging. This also makes it difficult to pinpoint the underlying root  cause that has the most impact on yield.  A 100% failure  analysis success based on a couple of worse failing dies is no  longer meaningful to yield.  To ensure a fast product yield  ramp-up, a prompt, conclusive, defect-learning approach is  necessary in order to devise a precise corrective action.


Wafer-level testing is the process of evaluating the quality of  fabricated integrated circuits before they are diced and  packaged. Packaged or system-level testing takes the critical  role as a secondary screen for test escapes. Although the  trigger to any FA process can be initiated by a fail encounter  from either evaluation methods (wafer or packaged), it is most  time-effective to perform FA directly on a wafer.


Since typical test coverage on wafer-level testing is close to  99% [1] especially in the digital cores, the chance of  discovering critical defects is high. Therefore, a wafer-level  failure analysis process can contribute to accelerate the  technology development yield ramp-up.


Traditional Failure Analysis Process


Traditionally, the FA process for root cause determination  involved 5 main steps: 1) failure validation, 2) fault  localization, 3) deprocessing, 4) defect localization (or  characterization), and 5) physical inspection (or  characterization) [2, 3]. Failure validation refers to the  electrical verification of the failure mode on an industrial  system-on-chip (SoC) tester, preferably on the exact tool that  indicates the fail. Sometimes, depending on the defect type, common laboratory bench analyzers is sufficient to reveal the  anomaly as well. Fault localization (FI) then interrogates the  device using localization techniques, typically using photon or  laser-based techniques, to isolate possible fail sites. Once the  suspected locations are identified, deprocessing sequentially


delayers, employing both mechanical and chemical means. The metallization and thin films are inspected using scanning  electron microscopy until the defect site is revealed. Depending on the nature of the failure, a secondary  localization step using nanoprobing may be required to further  pinpoint the exact fail location or characterize the defect.  The  final step involves inspecting the defect using high-resolution  scanning electron microscopes and spectroscopy to determine  the failure root cause. Although this FA process flow works  well in general, it does not differentiate between the  approaches to analyze complex or simple failures, leaving it to  the analyst’s discretion based upon his experience.


As an improvement, Ferrier [4] explains the need for an  enhanced FA process that inspires a thought process; it centers  on solving the issue instead of over-emphasizing on the tools  and techniques that is employed in each of 5 generic steps. Upon validating the failure, FI should not proceed without  further rigorous probing into the possible causes of the failure  mode to guide a hypothesis-driven next course of action. More  measurements should be taken if necessary.  In fact, this best  practice is already widely adopted today in most laboratories.


Wafer-level Failure Analysis Process


Thus far, all refinements to the FA process workflow apply to  both die and package-level analysis, with a common target to  achieve 100% defect learning success. To emphasize, this is  not sufficient to realize an accelerated yield ramp-up. Oftentimes, the defect found is inconclusive to devise a  corrective action or any action undertaken does not recover the  bin yield loss significantly. These are indications that only  random defects are found and the root cause of the specific  issue is not identified.


To address this challenge, we propose a wafer-level failure  analysis process approach. The crucial differentiator lies in the  dies selection process leading to FI. Before presenting the  workflow, it is appropriate to take reference from some  established workflows in a different domain of FI.


In general, FI can be broadly classified into software and  hardware-based (commonly referring to FA) techniques. Software-based techniques rely on a combination of test  pattern, design input, and test failing log (containing failing  cycles and output pins information) to simulate possible


suspected fail locations. The main applications are memory  bitmapping [5, 6] and scan diagnosis [7]. Scan diagnosis, as  the name suggests, is effective to locate digital logic defects. Table 1, for example, shows a typical list of the number of  possible suspects, their corresponding confidence score and  failing net length. Although this information is sufficient to  guide decision for physical FA, they do not reflect the  criticality of the suspects. Volume scan diagnosis [8, 9] which  involves additional analysis steps is developed to provide this  insight. Figure 1 illustrates a simple example of stacking the  suspected failing nets from all dies to generate a pareto chart. Net 17043 is assessed to be more critical since most dies fail  the same path. Therefore, they should be prioritized for FA [10, 11]. In this way, valuable FA resources are invested to  achieve optimum yield learning.


In fact, such methodology can be applied to hardware-based  FI with the adoption of a wafer-level analysis flow as shown  in Figure 2. The flow includes a volume electrical  characterization on the failing signatures and systematic  analysis to identify critical fail dies for FI. A hypothesis to  guide subsequent FI approach is then formulated. This process  iterates until a reasonable confidence level to proceed is  achieved. The rest of the flow follows convention.

Static and Dynamic Fault Isolation


Both static and dynamic FI approaches work in  complementary. Because of its setup and application  simplicity, the static approach generally has a shorter  turnaround time. Static FI, however, is not as effective in the  debug of functional and soft failures.  Dynamic FI fills this  gap with its suite of techniques such as dynamic photon  emission microscopy, soft defect localization and laser voltage  probing. However, these techniques require significantly  longer execution time. Considering the strengths and  shortcomings in both approaches, outcomes from the volume  electrical characterization and hypothesis steps play a  secondary role to guide decision making on the approach to  adopt.


Overview


In this article, we introduce the wafer-level FI FA process  flow. The primary design considerations of a wafer-level FI  system are discussed in-depth with an emphasis on complex  tester-based applications. Examples that demonstrate the  benefits of the enhanced wafer-level FA process will be also  be presented. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In  the next section, the setup of the wafer-level FI system is  introduced. Some common design limitations and their  implications are discussed in section 3. An exemplary case  study is presented in section 4 and section 5 introduces a  different value-add application flow capitalizing on the waferlevel FI system before section 6 concludes.


Wafer-level Dynamic FI Setup


The current state-of-the-art scanning optical microscope (SOM) tool enables both static and dynamic fault isolation to  be performed on the same tool. Figure 3 shows a wafer-level  FI setup that involves docking a standard production tester to  an inverted scanning optical microscope (SOM).


Figure 3: Prober configuration for wafer-level testing and  dynamic fault isolation.


It is apparent that the test setup remains unchanged; the only  difference lies in the prober. The probe pins on the probe card  electrically couples the devices through the wafer top-side  while the upward-looking optics image through the back  substrate in the SOM prober.  Figure 4 illustrates a mobile  probing kit that can be installed on top of the prober for static  FI. The concept of operation is similar to a typical inverted  static FI tool.


Figure 4: Static fault isolation setup on a wafer-level


scanning optical microscope.


Hard and Soft Docking


In general, a tester interfaces a wafer-level FI prober in two  ways, namely hard dock (also known as pogo tower-based) and soft dock (also known as cable-based) as shown in Figure  5(a) and (b) respectively. The electrical coupling between the  tester and device is made possible by a probe stack which  comprises the probe card, pogo tower and prober interface  board (PIB). The main difference between hard and soft  docking is the presence of additional cable connections  between tester interface board and PIB for the latter. Currently, in the industry, both types of wafer-level SOM  probers exist.


Although it might seem trivial, their differences affect the  conduct of dynamic FI. Table 2 compares the advantages and  disadvantages of both docking methods. Firstly, an additional  cost is involved to fabricate the tester interface boards and PIB  in the case of soft docking. Oftentimes, they have to be  customized to different tester platforms such as the Verigy (Advantest) and Flex (Teradyne). Second, cable delay and  attenuation increases with the length of the cables. This limits  the maximum test clock speed which, in turn, limits the type  of failures that can be investigated on dynamic FA.  Based on  experience, a 40-50 cm long cable constrains the test to  approximately 40 MHz A cable length with few tens of  millimeters and a transmission line propagation calibration  step are usually preferred. Since additional hardware is  introduced at the dynamic FA stage, a correlation step is also  required to ensure failure mode consistency. This adds to the  overall turnaround time for FA. Despite these disadvantages, soft docking has the advantage in decoupling tester vibrations. In general, a tester requires to be cooled and it can be  accomplished by using an integrated fan or an external water  chiller, both of which causes vibrations. The situation is worse  on fan-cooled testers. Such vibrations result in optical image  distortions.

A direct dock configuration has also been developed to  eliminate unnecessary packaging cost and shorten the  turnaround time for the debug on at-speed failures (usually up  till a few GHz range) that occur during system-level testing  Figure 6 shows the actual implementation with the test head


(a) removed and (b) docked. In comparison to Figure 3, Figure  6(b) shows a smaller gap between the test head and SOM. This is because a direct dock probe stack does not require a  probe card and pogo tower. The probe head which holds the  probe pins are built directly on the prober interface board. In  this way, the signal path is much shortened, hence enabling  higher test clocking. This is the current state-of-the-art  docking mechanism.


Figure 6: Photo illustration of a (a) mounted interface headplate and (b) test direct docked to SOM system.


Wafer Area Coverage


In making electrical connections, the probe pins on the probe  card are aligned to the die pads. There are two ways to achieve  this alignment and they are related to the docking mechanism  and how the wafer is held in place.


Table 3: List of testers which can be docked to a wafer-level  SOM.


In the case of soft docking, the wafer rest on the top surface  or platen of the wafer-level FI tool and a manipulator ring ‘pushes’ it around with the help of an air cushion which  reduces friction between the wafer and platen, as shown in  Figure 7(a). The air flow is removed and vacuum activated  once the die of interest arrives at the position for optical  analysis. Since the tester is decoupled from the probe card via  the cables, the probe card rotates to align the pins to the pads  on the wafer [12].


For hard docking, the wafer is not directly in contact to the  platen as shown in figure 7(b). The wafer sits on three wafer  holder rings which secures the wafer and navigates it around  the platen. A wafer support ring that resides at the optics  clearance opening provides the vacuum when the wafer is in  place [13]. For alignment, the wafer holder ring rotates since  the entire probe stack is secured to the test head. Unlike soft  docking, the use of wafer holder and support rings have an  adverse effect on the area of the wafer that can be assessed, hence limiting the number of dice that can be analyzed. Figure  8 illustrates this constraint. First, dice below the holder ring is  clearly inaccessible. In addition, objective lens clearance from  the opening and thickness of the support ring contributes to a  keep-out zone. Overall, there is a dead zone of radius of  approximately 14-15 mm about the point of contact between  the wafer and holder ring.


Test Pin Signal Extraction


In soft defect localization (SDL), laser-assisted device  alteration (LADA), or their derivatives, laser scanning is  synchronized to test. Selected test pins’ signals are required to  be extracted for monitoring from the probe card as shown in  Figure 9(a). To achieve this, connections can be made at the  plated through-hole which is basically an annular plated ring  on the board. The front-side of these plated through-holes  contacts the pogo tower pins which eventually contacts to the  tester channels (reside in test head) directly. Therefore, instead  of tracing from the PC, the appropriate connection points to be  extracted can be determined based on a trace from the tester  channel and pogo pins. Figure 9(b) shows how the wires can  be routed through existing gaps in between the probe stack to  the top-side of the setup.

It is evident that the induced current is at least an order higher  without SIL under the same 1064 nm laser intensity. One  solution to circumvent is to use laser source with a high  power, at least 1 watt (output from source).


Image Quality


Test head cooling mechanism is another factor that can impact  the quality of wafer-level FI analysis. Vibrations are induced  as a result of the cooling process and couples into the SOM  system. In general, there are two types of coolers, namely  water- and fan-cooled. A water-cooled tester uses an external  chiller and therefore, any vibration is usually minimal. A  challenge arises when the tester is fan-cooled or utilizes a  combination of both. In the worst case of hard docking, the fan  vibrations are coupled to the probe stack. Although it does not  impact contact quality (no concern on probe continuity), the  vibrations are coupled and affects imaging. Figure 13(a) and


(b) show a reflected laser and frequency map (also commonly  known as laser voltage imaging, LVI) signal image on random  digital scan chain of a 28 nm technology device. The results  are obtained on a water-cooled tester. It is observed that  frequency signals clearly differentiated from each other. However, this is not the case for a fan-cooled tester as shown  by the results in Figure 13(c) and (d).  Figure 13(d) shows the  frequency signal image with the scan cells bounding boxes  overlaid. The signals appear to be merged. Although this does  not affect localization at 28 nm [16] (missing signals from  bounding boxes can still be observed clearly in Figure 13(d)),

it could pose a problem at sub-20 nm, especially for  techniques that require high resolution like laser voltage  probing.


Case Study


The application of the wafer-level FA process on a 22 nm  technology device failing memory test is studied. The  SEMICAPS SOM 5000 tool was used in this work.


Wafer Sort Result


Figure 14(a) shows the sort bin map of the wafer of interest. A  wafer edge with an obvious 9 o’clock failing signature on bin  3 was observed. Instead of following the custom workflow to  analyze dies within the abnormal region, wafer-level FA  process ensues. Volume electrical failure characterization on  bin 3 was conducted.


Volume Electrical Failure Characterization


Dynamic current measurements on three different power  supplies are characterized on the failing bin 3 dice and the  results are shown in Figure 14(b). By comparing both wafer  maps, it is apparent that bin 3 fails can be re-classified into 4  different sub-bins, namely 33, 22, 11 and 66, according to the  number of power supplies that exhibit abnormal currents. For  instance, sub-bin 33 indicates anomalies in all three power  supplies and sub-bin 66 indicates that the fail has no  relationship to the power supply current. Table 4 summarizes


all the sub-bins description and their corresponding yield loss  impact. It is observed that wafer edge fails are contributed  mainly from sub-bin 66. For the 9 o’clock failing signature, it  involves dice with abnormal currents on 2 of the power  supplies (sub-bin 22). However, its impact on yield is not the  highest. This is a classic example to illustrate the importance  of volume failure characterization: in order to ensure the  highest bin 3 yield recovery, bin 66 should be selected for FI, instead of randomly picking a couple of bin 3 dice for FI

Wafer-level Fault Localization


More than 10 dice were selected for analysis on dynamic  photon emission microscopy. It was discovered that the  signals suggest two further groups of classification among  sub-bin 66, labelled as group A and B in Figure 14(b). Figures


15(a) and Fig. 15(b) show the emission images from group A  while Fig. 15 (c) and Fig. 15(d) show the images from group  B.


Physical FA was performed on both groups of dice at the  signal locations. Figure 16(a) shows a void in the second  interconnect layers for group A and Figure 16(b) shows a void  in the third metal layer for group B dice. This finding reveals  another benefit of the wafer-level FI process. With the semiautomated stepping capability of wafer-level FI tool, more  dies can be analyzed for further characterization. This presents  a more extensive FI analysis. In retrospect, following the  conventional FA process of randomly picking fail dice for  analysis at the 9 o’clock region, these defects would not have  been identified.

List of fail suspects correlation


Besides mapping scan chains, more importantly, this  phenomenon can be extended to devise a fast approach to  validate the accuracy of software-based scan diagnosis. In  brief, scan diagnosis is a tool that simulates design  information and tester failing pins/cycles data collectively to  suggest suspected problematic locations in digital scan-based  logic [7, 18]. It is a common practice that after the diagnosis is  accomplished, a validation step follows to confirm its  accuracy before it is released to production. Successful defect  finding based on at least three dice on physical FA is used as  criteria.


We propose a more efficient approach that leverages a waferlevel FI tool. A 1064 nm laser interrogates a good part using a  point mode on a scan cell, for instance cell 21 as shown in  Figure 17, while the tester (which is electrically coupled to the  wafer) executes the scan test in a loop manner. The laser  power is increased gradually until a soft stuck-at fail occurs. The laser stops after the fail log is acquired. A post diagnosis  on the log pinpoints the location of the soft defect. In this way, the accuracy or inaccuracy of the scan diagnosis tool can be  determined. Figure 18 depicts the workflow [19].

Conclusion


In accordance to the industry drive towards 100% success in  finding defects that really matters to yield, we propose an  enhanced wafer-level FI process flow. It offers a time-efficient  methodology to resolve yield issues conclusively, thus  accelerating yield ramp-up. The systematic approach behind  this flow pinpoints the failure root cause that contributes to the  highest yield loss. This is demonstrated by the case study  presented. More importantly, this article also aims to create  awareness on the design considerations and implications of the  wafer-level FI tool when interacting with the testers. This will  enable a better leverage on the strengths and management of  the limitations to ensure an optimum implementation.

Package Failure Analysis: Flow and Technique


Maxim Integrated, San Jose, CA


Tejinder.gandhi@maximintegrated.com, Jason.silva@maximintegrated.com


Abstract


A systematic approach is needed to uncover the root cause of a  modern package failure.  Opens and shorts sound easy, when  compared to functional or a leakage failure, but when the  problem can be anywhere inside a complex hybrid package or  buried inside an embedded IC, things can get tough.


The first step in analyzing contact failures is to investigate  possible package root causes as the package needs to be at least  partially removed before the integrated circuits can be  observed.  To avoid missing a package defect, a thorough, stepby-step approach to open and short failures is critical.   Although a single process can never be 100% effective, in most  cases, the generic procedures outline in this article will lead to  a better success rate.


As semiconductor feature sizes have shrunk, the technology  needed to encapsulate modern ICs (integrated circuits) has  expanded.  Although DIP (dual in-line package) and QFN (quad-flat no-leads) packages are still widely used; they are  being replaced in most high-volume applications with WLPs (wafer level packages).  Board space limitations are driving  complex sensor and 3D package development as consumers  demand smaller products with more functionality and increased  battery life.  Due to these industry changes, package failure  analyses are becoming much more challenging; a systematic  approach is therefore critical.


The proposed flow begins with a data review; how did the  device fail and how was it processed?   Next step is to perform  non-destructive techniques to document the condition of the asreceived units.  With the background understood and the  condition of the devices well documented, the reported ATE (automated test equipment) failures need to be duplicated in the  lab.


Using the failure signature, the iterative fault isolation process  begins; techniques vary depending on the electrical signature. Package failures commonly involve open and shorts; as  functional failures are likely associated with the semiconductor, their analysis in not covered in this article.


All possible failure sites are evaluated with the package  drawing and device specifications. Could a defect at this  location cause the observed malfunction?  When the answer is  finally yes, step-by-step deprocessing begins.


Investigations continue after a defect is found.  What caused it  and how can it be prevented in the future?  A strong process


understanding, and a team approach are needed to answer these  questions and to ensure the corrective action responses (CARs) are effective.  With the problem and proposed solutions  identified, a report can be written and shared.


Package Failure Analysis Flow


History and Background


The initial history and data review is time well spent; although  it is the most critical step, it is also the most overlooked as  engineers often mistakenly rush to the lab before understanding  the whole issue.


 How was the failure created?


 What is the lot history?


 Have similar failures been seen in the past?


 What information do other team members have?


Good answers are needed to avoid starting down the wrong  path; take the time and do it right from the start.


Incoming Inspection


Because FA (failure analysis) handling and electrical testing  can damage a device, a complete suite of non-destructive


investigations is performed on the as-received units.


External Optical Inspection:


A thorough optical inspection is always the first procedure  performed on the devices; results can be reviewed later in the  investigation if FA handling damage is subsequently suspected. Top and bottom images are needed to record the markings and  condition of the pins or solder balls.  Side inspections are also  recommended as package edges are frequently damaged, especially with WLPs.


Figure 1 is an example of external optical inspection on the  device reported failing short between bumps A2 and A3 after  THB (Temperature Humidity Bias) stress [1]. Even though it  was mounted to a board, all four package edges were carefully   imaged.  Contamination between the shorted Pins A2 and A3  was uncovered on the PCB (printed circuit board) surface.  Subsequent investigations identified the contamination as tin  dendrites.  Working with the CAR and Reliability teams, it was  determined that unremoved solder residue from the board  mounting process was the root cause of the failure.


Figure 1:  Red circle highlights the residue observed between  Pins A2 and A3 after THB stress.


X-Ray Inspection [2]:


Defects embedded into the package which cannot be seen  optically can be seen with 2D and 3D X-ray imaging. X-ray  inspections are performed on all packages without a thick metal  covering. Even WLP devices are checked as the RDL layers can  be imaged with a high-resolution system.  Top down images  and side view images are recommended on package to look for  RDL issues, bond wire issues, die attach issues, poorly formed  solder joints and metal bridging.


Figure 2 is an example of 2D X-ray image captured on a device  failing short after package Reflow [3] stress.  No obvious defect  was observed during optical inspection on this unit.


Figure 2:  Red circle highlights the residue observed between  bumps after reflow stress.


Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM) [4]:


Sound waves are also used to non-destructively investigate  semiconductor packages.  Reflected and transmitted signals  highlight internal differences in the package’s acoustic density.  Because even the tiniest gap will cause a phase shift in the  reflected signal, the phase of the reflected signal is monitored


to detect package voids.  Cracks and foreign material are also  typically uncovered with this technique.


This technique is also helpful at uncovering issues with wafer  level packages.  For example, a crack under a WLP solder ball  was revealed with this technique, Figure 3.  Further  investigations confirmed that the crack propagated in the  semiconductor and was therefore the root cause of the failure.  Root cause identification in the above example was likely not  possible without the SAM data, as internal cracks are often  attributed to mechanical cross-sectioning techniques.


Figure 3: Red circle highlights the defect observed using  scanning acoustic microscopy.  With further analysis the  defect was identified to be a crack under the bump.


Infrared Microscopy:


As low doped silicon is transparent to IR, during the incoming  inspections, infrared inspections are always performed on


packages with exposed substrates.  While electrical overstress  induced open and short failures are typically found with this  technique, IR is also very effective at imaging internal cracks. Figure 4.


Figure 4: Red arrows highlight the die crack observed using  backside infrared inspection.

Electrical Verification


As tester contact issues and intermittency are very common, the  failing electrical signature must be confirmed in the lab, even  for the “simple” opens and shorts associated with package  failures.  IV curves should be collected as they provide much  more insight into what is wrong with the device.


Figure 5 shows curve trace data between bumps A2 and A3 on  device shown in Figure 1. Curve trace confirmed short between  the bumps, as reported by failure analysis requestor.

Fault Isolation


Unless an analyst has collected an image of a defect that will  cause the electrical failure signature, fault isolation is  recommended. While there are several fault isolation  techniques to tackle the wide array of failure signatures, only a  few are routinely used for opens and shorts and are discussed.


Open and Short Failures


IR Lock-In Thermography [5]:


This technique is commonly used for short failures.  The failure  is typically stimulated by applying a bias between the shorted  pins; spurious heat is generated at the defect site and is  conducted to the package surfaces and is detected by the  thermal camera. To improve the signal to noise ratio, a lock-in  signal is used to simultaneously toggle the failure and the  thermograph’s heat signature collecting hardware.  This  technique allows the detection of temperature modulation of  few uK.


Figure 6 is an example of the image captured using IR Lock-In  Thermography on the unit reported failing short between pins 6  and 7. Heat source was observed to be in the package as shown  by superimposition of X-ray and IR- thermography image in  Figure 7.

Figure 7: Super imposition of X-Ray image with IR lock-in  Thermography image identified the location of heat source to  be in the package; between bond wires.


Magnetic Current Imaging [6]:


Using sensitive magnetic sensors, currents flowing through a  sample can be imaged through the magnetic fields they  produce.  To improve the signal-to-noise ratio, a lock-in  amplifier is used to modulate the sample current and sensor  operation.  Two types of sensors are typically used, magneto  resistive and SQUIDs (superconducting quantum interference  devices); their sensitivity and resolution are affected by the size  of the current and proximity of the sensor to the device.  As they  are the most sensitive, SQUIDs are typically used for package  investigations; in a typical application, if it is placed within 400 μm of the source, 500 nA of current can be imaged.

Magnetic current imaging can be used to investigate both high  and low resistances shorts or any other failure that involves  current flow.   Figure 7 shows an example; where location of  short was isolated using current imaging technique.


Figure 7: X-ray image of packaged lead frame superimposed  with current density image shows the location of short (red  arrow).  [7]


Time Domain Reflectometry [8] and EOTPR [9]:


Time domain reflectometry is the primary fault isolation tool  for open failures.  TDR instrument is basically a very wide  bandwidth sampling oscilloscope (18-20Ghz or higher) with an  internal step generator. A fast rise step signal is delivered to pin  failing open and the reflected signal waveform is captured and  compared to the incident signal to perform fault isolation.


Figure 8 shows TDR waveforms captured to isolate location of  open. Figure 9 shows the optical image captured of the open.


00m w50.002日QQ10000s39.540m日1:20PM 3/11/04  Figure 8:  TDR result showing an open in package substrate.


Figure 9: Optical image showing broken trace in package  substrate


Using the package material propagation velocity, the TDR time  measurements can also be equated to distance in the sample and  location of open can be identified. With 30-40ps rise time of the  TDR instrument and with dielectric constant 4 of FR4 material, spatial resolution of TDR is about 1mm.


While this distance is acceptable for cables and printed circuitry  board failures, it is too large to be useful for most package  applications.  In response, an electro-optical terahertz pulse  reflectometer (EOTPR) was developed.  During operation, electrical pulses are launched into the failing device and  reflected signal waveform is captured in time by a fastphotoconductive switch. Spatial resolutions of less than 10 µm  have been obtained with this innovative TDR refinement.


Destructive Analysis


Scanning Electron Microscopy [10] and Material Analysis


If the defect has been imaged or its location established with  high confidence, step-by-step inspection and deprocessing can  begin.  Optical inspections are most commonly used as they are

Material identification is most commonly performed through  EDS, energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy [11].  The incident  electron beam creates inner shell vacancies; the electrons  arranging themselves into a lower energy state, resulting in the  emission of elemental specific x-rays.  As radiation peaks can  overlap, using multiple characteristic x-rays for elemental  identification is recommended, especially if the material is not  commonly found in integrated circuits.

Mechanical/FIB Cross Section


In cases where defect is embedded in the package, sample may  need to be cross sectioned to get to the defect before SEM and  EDS analysis can be performed.


Cross sectioning methods are carried out using various  polishing media specific to the application.  In general, this is  done by starting with rough polishing media to approach the  area of interest and progressing through finer polishing media  until the area of interest.  Sandpaper, diamond lapping films, diamond slurries and various abrasive suspensions are  employed depending on the application.  In order to prevent  samples from acquiring artifacts such as cracks or delamination  caused by the polishing process, the samples can be potted in  some form of epoxy or resin.


A focused ion beam (FIB) tool is routinely used to cross section  failure analysis units.  High energy gallium, iodine, or xenon  ions are generated and rastered across a grounded sample to  very accurately remove small amounts of material.  While  routinely used for semiconductor, with the invention of plasmaassisted FIBs that cut up to twenty times faster, this technique  has been extended to IC packages.  As it doesn’t not induce  large die stresses, a pFIB is extremely useful for WLP open  failures as the solder ball and die pad can be cross sectioned  without fear of inducing artifacts. This is especially beneficial  when materials such as solder or gold being cross sectioned are  smeared by manual cross section methods (Figure 12).

The root cause identification of open and short failures in  modern IC packages is often considered easy; reality, though, is often unkind. Chip-Scale Packaging and Its Failure Analysis Challenges


Cypress Semiconductor, San Jose, California, USA


The adoption of Chip Scale Packages (CSPs) has been  one of the most significant and successful trends in the  electronics industry since their introduction in the early 90s.  CSPs are well accepted by the electronic industry due to their  many benefits. They have the advantage of smaller size and  low package profile, lesser weight, relatively easier assembly  process, lower overall manufacturing costs and improved  electrical performance [1][2].  With their reduced package size  compared to traditional leaded packages, CSPs are ideal for  the applications of cell phones, smart devices, laptops and  digital cameras that require better use of real estate on the PC  boards.


However, the reduced package size of CSPs has created  challenges for this type of package during failure analysis  process [4].  For CSPs in a FBGA (Fine Ball Grid Array) package, precision chemical decapsulation of these near-diesize packages is required in order to keep the device functional  for subsequent fault isolation work.  For the more recent CSPs  in WLCSP (Wafer Level CSP) form, handling of these baredie-like devices creates new difficulties for the failure analysts  in performing routine failure analysis work using conventional  FA tools. These are just a few examples of challenges that can  be encountered during failure analysis on CSPs devices.  In  this paper, an overview of CSPs and their applications will be  provided, and some challenges in performing failure analysis  on CSPs will be revealed, particularly for CSPs in special  package configurations such as stacked die Multi-ChipPackages (MCP) and Wafer Level CSPs.  Finally, solutions  and best practices will be shared on how to overcome these  challenges.  A few case studies will be presented at the end of  paper to demonstrate how failure analysis work on CSPs can  be successfully completed.


A Chip Scale Package (based on IPC/JEDEC J-STD-012  definition) is a category of IC packages that is surface  mountable and whose area is no more than 1.2x the original  die area.  Originally the CSP term stood for “Chip Size


Package” but very few packages are in fact the size of the  chip.   The IPC/JEDEC definition does not define how a chip  scale package is to be constructed, so any package that meets  the surface mount-ability and dimensional requirement is a  CSP, regardless of structure.  Since the introduction of Chip  Scale Packages in early 90s, CSPs have evolved rapidly and  there are more than 50 different types of CSPs currently  available in the market.


There are many reasons why CSPs have been so well  accepted within the industry.  The biggest advantage of CSPs  is the size reduction of the package.  Most CSPs use a Ball  Grid Array (BGA) design which has all the interconnects  under the package (Figure 1).  In such a BGA style, you can  increase the number of interconnects while saving PCB  routing spacing.   In recent WLCSP devices [3], such BGA  designs have been used directly onto the wafer-level Si device  by having an array of bumps or solder balls attached at an I/O  pitch that is compatible with traditional circuit board assembly  process (Figure 1).  WLCSP is a true chip scale package since  the resulting package is of the same size of the die as the CSP  was originally defined.


Figure 1: A typical CSP in FBGA Package (left) and in  WLCSP form (right).  The cross-sectional images are shown  below the corresponding package type.


To further increase silicon density with small CSPs, Stacked Chip Scale Packages (SCSPs) or Multi-Chip Packages (MCPs) have emerged in the market and are becoming one of  the most rapidly growing sectors for CSPs.  Packaging for  MCPs begins by stacking two or more dice on top of a BGA  substrate with an insulating strip between them.  Leads are  bonded to the substrate, and molding around the stack  completes the device.  Since an MCP is a package that may  even be smaller than the enclosed die area (counting area from  the stacked dice), the definition of a CSP no longer holds.  The  MCP example in Figure 2 shows paired Flash memory and  SRAM in a FBGA package.


Figure 2: A two die stacked MCP package with SRAM on top  of Flash configuration: (a) top view of the MCP package (b) cross-sectional view of the MCP package


Another MCP example is memory to support logic.  Package-on-Package (PoP) stacking is often used to make the  assembly process high yield, low cost and more flexible for  the integration of memory to logic devices.  Figure 3 shows an  example of PoP stacking.  These stacked packages are so thin (1.4mm) that wafers must be thinned to 150-200um prior to  wafer saw for die separation in order to fit into the MCPs.


Figure3: PoP stacking provides high yield, low cost and more  flexible assembly process for the integration of memory to  logic devices


With so many different types of CSPs developed over the  years, an effort was made to systematically characterize the  CSPs as a package group.  Bases on their structures and  building materials, there are 4 categories or classifications for  CSPs as shown in table 1.  These are:


1) The flex circuit interposer type


2) The rigid substrate interposer type


3) The custom leadframe type


4) The wafer-level assembly type

Chip Scale Packaging combines the strengths of various  packaging technologies.  It has the size and performance  advantage of bare die assembly while maintaining the  reliability of encapsulated devices.  The significant size and  weight reduction make CSPs the ideal solution for  applications in mobile devices like cell phones, smart devices, laptops and digital cameras.  Some CSPs use a fortified BGA  design, which allows less dense routing on PCB and bigger  sized solder balls.  Such CSPs in fortified BGA can have  superior board level reliability, and are often used in  applications of telecommunication, network, automotive  engine controls and navigation systems.


Failure Analysis Challenges


The advantages of reduced package size for CSPs creates  challenges when performing failure analysis if there is a  device failure at the package level or die level.  Since they are


Frontside Emission


in packages that are near the die size, it is difficult to expose  the die entirely through chemical decapsulation while keeping  the device functional for subsequent testing and further fault  isolation work; therefore, precision decapsulation is required  for CSP devices. It becomes even more challenging when Cu  bond wires are used when compared to traditional Au wires.  Cu wires can be easily damaged after long exposure to the  sulfuric and nitric acid mixture used for chemical  decapsulation, potentially causing the device to no longer be  electrically functional after decapsulation [6][7][8].  A special  decapsulation procedure must be established to ensure device  functionality.


For CSPs in MCP form, precision decapsulation becomes  even more challenging.  With multiple thin dice (as thin as  40um) stacked on top of each other in a very small package, exposing the failing die for further electrical testing and fault  isolation is not a trial task.  Top die removal or backside  milling may be required if the failing die happens to be in the  middle or at the bottom of the stacked dice.  For CSPs in  WLCSP form, different challenges arise.  These bare-die-like  devices are not intended to be manually handled after

Corresponding Solutions and Best Practices


Precision Decapsulation


For CSP devices precision decapsulation is required, particularly for Si devices in FBGA packages.  An automated  Jet Etcher is often used for chemical decapsulation (Figure 5).  A device subjected to decapsulation is placed facing down on  a rubber gasket with a pre-defined etching window to create a  vacuum-sealed environment during the chemical etch.  A  mixture of strong chemical acid of sulfuric and nitric is pulsed  up to etch the package area through the open etching window  in the gasket.  Depending on the die size and package  thickness, the etch time and chemical acid flow can be  adjusted to achieve the best results of decapsulation.


Figure 5: An automated Jet Etching system used for regular  chemical decapsulation


For CSP devices the package is very thin, and die size is  near the package size, so the etching window on the gasket  needs to be well defined to avoid over-etching.  Rubber  gaskets erode after exposure to the strong acid, so the etching


window edges become rough and their shape and size change  slightly after multiple use.  To make the etching window  precise it is recommended to use a new gasket for each  decapsulation job to ensure the precision decapsulation results.


For FBGA packages using Cu bond wires, laser milling is  required prior to the chemical decapsulation.  Cu wires cannot  withstand a long chemical exposure compared to Au wires; therefore, shortening the chemical exposure time is crucial.  Laser milling can thin down the mold compound to about  100um remaining on the die surface with a full thickness rim  around the package to keep the package edge stronger.  The  created reservoir-like trench on the package will hold up the  chemical acid better during the following chemical  decapsulation. It is worth pointing out that the laser milling  should not be getting too close to the die surface.  Due to the  spherical-shaped silica fillers used in mold compound, they  can act as optical lenses, refocusing the laser beam to cause  physical damage at deeper locations in the Si device.  Therefore, an 100um-thick layer of mold compound should  remain on the die surface after laser milling.  The final  chemical decapsulation will clear the remaining mold  compound to exposure the Si device fully.


Access to the Failing Die in Multi-Chip Package


One of the biggest challenges in CSPs failure analysis is to  access the failing die in MCP devices.  Multiple very thin dice  are stacked on top of each other within a small FBGA  package.  Electrical testing can help isolate the possible failing  die except for those devices with high Icc failures.  Most  likely all power pins for the device are shared among the dice  within the MCP, and the Icc leakage could come from any die  in the package.  In the past, removing wires from one die at a  time was done to confirm the source of the ICC leakage; but it  was so time consuming and tedious that the failure analysts  tried to avoid such a process as much as possible.  Fortunately, in the recent years, thermal emission tools that are capable of  detecting the emission site of the possible failing die among  the stacked dice through the package have become available, making the fault isolation relatively easier (Figure 6).


Figure 6: SAM inspection showed 4 groups of 2-die stacking  devices in this MCP device (left), and thermal emission  showed the high Icc leakage is from the upper left stack (right)


Once the failing die has been isolated through the stacked  dice, physically access to that failing die can be quite  challenging if the failing die happens to be the middle die or  the bottom die.  There are many methods that can be used to  successfully reach the failing die, depending on the tool sets  available and skill sets among the failure analysts. Two  examples that have been utilized are as follows:


Extraction and Repackaging


This method retrieves the failing device from the MCP  package by mechanical polishing and chemically dissolving  the plastic package.  After the dice are extracted from the  dissolved package, the failing die can be repackaged into  another new package for electrical testing and further failure  analysis work.  The risk of using this method is that the bond  pads of the failing Si die could be etched so significantly that  re-wire bonding of the failing device into a new package  becomes impossible.  There are many papers published  regarding how to successfully extract the die from an existing  package [5].    Figure 7 shows an example of a Flash device  was extracted from a FBGA package, and then successfully  re-wire bonded into a TSOP package.


Figure 7: A Flash memory device was extracted from the  FBGA package, and then wire-bonded into a new TSOP  package.


Milling and Re-Wire Bonding


For MCP devices with many thin stacked dice it is difficult to  extract and repackage the failing die into a new package since  such a thin die (<100um in thickness) is easily damaged  during the process.  To avoid handling very thin devices, the  MCP device can be polished from the backside of the package  via milling until the backside of the desired failing die is  reached.  The lead frames can also be exposed by local  milling.  The polished MCP device then can be placed and  wire bonded into another open top package, such as a PGA (Pin Grid Array) package for backside emission analysis work (Figure 8).  By doing so, the fragile failing die will not be  individually handled during sample preparation.  This method  is particularly ideal for the devices that requires backside  emission analysis.

Figure 8: Milling and repackaging process for backside  emission analysis on the failing die in MCP devices.


IR Inspection on Wafer Level CSPs


WLCSP is the fastest growing CSP in recent years.  With  its bare-die-like packaging structure it is ideal for cell phones, smart watches, and wearable devices.  However, this package  form is not meant to be manually handled after singulation in  the manufacturing process.  Any “improper” handling, such as  using a tweezer to pick up the device and place it under the  microscope could create die edge or die corner chipping, causing additional device failures.  How to handle WLCSP  devices (many of which are as small as 1mm x 1mm) during  the failure analysis process becomes a big challenge for the  failure analysts.


Frequent checking of the WLCSP device after each failure  analysis step (such as electrical testing, emission analysis, or  micro-probing) is needed to carefully inspect to ensure no  additional damage was introduced during the failure analysis  process.  Traditional inspection tools, such as optical  microscope or SEM can be used for the device inspection.  However, WLCSP is a flip-chip like device so IR inspection  through the backside Si is a suitable way to exam the entire  device at the active circuit level.  IR imaging capability is  available on most Photon/Thermal emission tools and laser  confocal imaging exists on most TIVA/OBIRCH systems. A

The take-away for this case study is that die cracking is  one of the most commonly seen failure mechanisms for MCP  devices, particularly for devices with multiple very thin dice  stacked within the package.  Initial package level analysis may  not detect the failure site; therefore, it is crucial to collect and  retain all information from the SAM and X-ray analysis that  can be re-visited later when potential defects are found during  subsequent analysis steps.  Die cracking on very thin stack  dice is very common and it is important to find the real root  cause for the problem.  Extra effort must be made to perform  fracture analysis on the cracked die if possible, to find the  potential cause and to take corrective actions.

New Challenges


With new technology continuously scaling down of the  transistor size to sub-10nm, and more and more 3D packaging  being used to increase the Si density within the package, the  failure analysis of these IC devices will become more difficult  and challenging.  Introduction of the WLCSP devices changes  the way how FA analysts handle the failing devices  throughout the failure analysis process.   The combination of  different types of ICs into one MCP device forces FA analysts  to acquire new skillsets in repackaging work in order to  reclaim the failing device successfully for failure analysis  work.


Many traditional failure analysis tools may not be adequate  for handling the new products with advanced process and  packaging technologies.  IR microscope, for example, has  replaced the traditional optical microscope for WLCSP visual  inspections.  Board level analysis instead of component level  analysis is much more suitable for analyzing WLCSP devices  compared to the traditional packaged IC devices.   CSP  devices will continue evolve as they have in the past two  decades, and a failure analyst will have to   be more agile and  adaptable in determining the best methods to discover the  cause of failures.


Summary


Since CSPs introduction in the early 90s, they have  continuously increased their market share due to their  advantages of small form factor, cost effectiveness and PCB


Optical Mispection


Inspection


optimization.  The reduced package size also brings challenges  in performing failure analysis work.  For the CSPs special  requirements such as precision decapsulation for FBGA  packages, accessing the failing die for MCP packages, and  careful handling for WLCSP, must be addressed in order to  successfully perform electrical and physical failure analysis.  Some of the challenges and their corresponding solutions and  best practices have been discussed in this paper to increase the  awareness of the issues associated with CSP devices.

Following ongoing trends of miniaturization and increased  functionality, printed circuit boards (PCB) have to cope with  increased solder joint densities, smaller feature sizes and an  adaption to a larger variety of semiconductor package


Systems can be


assembly. This trend includes the integration of 3D device build


Costly, low I/Os and thick


2D,2.5D and 3D

ups, such as stacked-die devices and package-on-packages (PoP). The resulting design realizations are setting a new  standard to quality and reliability and in consequence the  related failure analysis. Physical root causes for defective  behavior can be buried deep within the device build up and  increase in their variety due to the 3-dimensional device  structure. Local electrical probing is increasingly limited and  the complexity of the system requires overall functionality to  remain intact during most of the analysis process. As a result, non-destructive testing is desired and leads to a significant  variation of the overall FA process flow. Methods like X-Ray  microscopy, thermal & ultrasound imaging or time-domain  reflectometry are fitting alternatives that are further developed  and adapted to close the gap between past, present and future  board level FA. The paper will discuss an example of the FA  flow for advanced board level failure analysis and introduces  the techniques that can enable non-destructive testing. The  paper will also give two examples where these techniques have  been applied to localize and analyze defects with high  efficiency and success yield.


Advanced semiconductor products are experiencing a constant  change towards miniaturization, increased functionality density  and growing complexity [1]. Figure 1 shows the developing  PCB roadmap from the initial distinction between component & board level towards the further and further integration of both  technologies. Past systems allowed a clear separation of the  board design and manufacturing and its individual components. Silicon dies were encapsulated in individual packages and  assembled to their position on the board surface. Optical and  electrical measurements were able to find most board related  defects on these technologies and additional component  analysis can be done in a separate failure analysis flow.


Figure 1: Trend overview for semiconductor packaging  integration on board and system level. [2]


In present system designs, high density multi-chip packages, such as multi-chip modules (MCM) and 2.5/3D packages, are  consistently emerging as an alternative to pure silicon scaling. As these packaging solutions are gaining advantage over  System on Chip (SoC) designs, new challenges are arising for  technology integration and failure analysis. Different packaging  technologies, such as TSV, Cu-pillar microbumps and C4  bumps are used to realize the interconnection [3]. The  localization of potential defects in this sample, such as electrical  shorts, voids or electrical opens, is challenging since the  buildup contains a high complexity of layers and a multitude of  materials. This limits access to the defect site, making it  difficult to determine a failure’s root cause. Figure 1 also  demonstrates the trends within packaging technologies towards  shrinking dimensions. The integration of individual  components into the board layer will continue and further  increase in the future design of system level packaging. Embedded systems are on the rise and allow thin, flexible and  high-density packaging solutions [4]. Here, the separation  between system level, board level and individual component  level failure analysis is slowly disappearing. In order to localize  the initial defect area, prepare the sample for root cause analysis  and image the exact root cause, the overall functionality has to  be maintained during the process. This leads to the requirement  of adding additional techniques that help isolate and image  defects that are buried deeply within the board structure. Progress has been made in the field of analysis tools to offer  new opportunities and bring solutions for integrated designs. This article will demonstrate an approach of advanced board  level failure analysis by using several non-destructive  localization techniques. The individual methods and their  operational principles are introduced briefly in this paper along  with case studies that will show the value of using them on  board level defect analysis.


Advanced Board Level Analysis Workflow


In order to maintain high quality failure analysis and ensure  high success rates in determining the physical root cause, an  advanced FA flow on board level is required. A general work  flow proposal for this task is shown in figure 2.


Root cause determination


Figure 2: Failure Analysis flow chart for advanced board level


1271


analysis using non-destructive testing methods. [5]


3271 TED


After initial optical inspection of the failing device, the  electrical characterization (EFA) is conducted and an initial


fault isolation is performed. If the failure is related to a


functional failure of the system, the defect is likely to be related  to the silicon die of one individual component (e.g. CPU, GPU) and will be analyzed accordingly. In case of a physical failure, such as electrical open, short or leakage, the root cause can be  more diverse and requires additional fault isolation on board  level. For such advanced fault isolation, several techniques can  be considered:


 Magnetic current imaging for shorts and opens


 IR Thermography for electrical shorts


 Time-domain-reflectometry for shorts and opens  Scanning Acoustic Microscopy


 2D/3D X-Ray Microscopy


Based on the measurement results of one of several of these  techniques, the defect can be further isolated and physically  analyzed (PFA) if needed. The following section will give a  brief overview over the operational principle of these  techniques.


Operational principle of Non-Destructive Failure  Analysis Techniques


Magnetic Current Imaging (MCI)


Magnetic current imaging is a unique technique that allows to  visualize current flows within a board or individual  components. It is based on the principle of using a hightemperature (72K) superconducting quantum interference


device (SQUID) to measure the vertical components of the  magnetic fields surrounding conductors carrying current  through short circuits or current arising from standing wave  reflections due to opens [6]. Magnetic field images are then  transformed into current density images which typically show  higher gradients inherent in localized narrow current paths or  dissolution of current density where narrower paths dissipate to


EFA


Optical inspection


much broader conductors or power planes at short circuit sites.


An example is given in figure 3, showing the current density

flow across the individual components of a PCB.

Figure 3: Demonstration of magnetic current imaging on PCB  level. The method allows the tracing of the current across the  board and several components [7]. In the picture a sub-surface  short at the top end is visualized where the current dissipates  into the ground plane.


The method, in principle, can detect both electrical shorts and  opens in different measurement modes. For imaging shorts, a  small AC bias is utilized on the sample to enable lock-in  amplification for noise reduction. For opens, an RF waveform (60-200 MHz) is applied to generate a reflected standing wave  current – a method known as space domain reflectometry (SDR) [8]. The current density rapidly decreases toward the  open approaching zero at the actual end of the conductive path. For 3D MCI applications, depth estimations are possible by  analysing the relationship between magnetic field strength, current and geometrical distance between peaks in the zcomponent of the magnetic field intensity normal to the surface  of the sample (current direction is also easily determined as the  fields surrounding active conductors are bipolar). In this  manner it is possible to estimate both absolute current depth and  relative distance between two or more conductors.


Infrared Thermography (IR)


Infrared Thermography is widely used within the  semiconductor packaging failure analysis due to its thermal  imaging capability. Its application ranges from absolute  temperature measurements to the detection of local heat sources  due to electrical shorting. In the past decade, Thermography has  been further adapted by using Lock-in techniques that enable a  highly improved spatial resolution down to single micrometer


and a sensitivity within microwatt range [9]. The general setup  consists of a mid-wave IR camera that is focused on the device  surface while the device is electrically stimulated. If the  electrical stimulation is applied constantly, the resulting  thermal image is representing the heat distribution over the  device and can be used to determine absolute temperatures  under different conditions (e.g. different voltages). In Lock-in  mode, the electrical stimulation is frequency-based, simulating  an on/off switching of the device. Depending on the lock-in  frequency in use, the heat conduction across the device is  strongly damped [10] allowing the precise localization of the  heat origin and is mostly used for short localization within  individual components. The use of this methodology can be  extended to hot spot detection on board level FA. Leakage  current between conductive features like PCB inner and outer  traces or embedded/assembled components generate local heat  during biasing that will be detected as a hot spot by thermal  imaging. An example is given in figure 4 that shows the heat  distribution across a PCB under operation as well as the  contribution of its individual components.


Figure 4: Thermal imaging on board level illustrating the  individual hot spot areas during operation [11].


While the technique is state-of-the art for electrical short  detection, it is strongly limited for detecting electrical opens.


Time-Domain Reflectometry (TDR) and Electro-Optical  Terahertz Reflectometry (EOTPR)


Although in principle based on different signal generation, TDR  and EOTPR use a similar operating principle to detect electrical  opens, leakages and shorts [12]. An electrical pulse is launched  into the defective device and transmitted or partially reflected  at each internal interconnection. The response is measured as a  voltage vs. time function and shows the signal travel through  the device. In the presence of an electrical open, the graph will  show a signal peak at an early time while an electrical short  leads to a negative peak within the measurements. The main  difference between TDR and EOTPR lies within the pulse  frequency that defines both the maximum signal path as well as  the time resolution of the response. As for TDR, which is using


MHz frequencies, it is often used for long current paths of  several hundreds of millimeters. Its resolution is limited to  about 1mm. This limits the major application of TDR to gross  defect localization on board level. EOTPR, developed to  overcome this limitation, is using a shorter pulse length in  Terahertz range. As a result, the spatial resolution is  significantly increased to a few micrometers. This allows the  technique to be used for defect localization (primarily opens) within component to board interconnects and internal die-to-die  connections such as TSV or micro bumps [13]. The use of a  higher frequency leads to a stronger damping over distance and  limits the technique application to netlist lengths that are shorter  than 300mm.


Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM)


Scanning Acoustic Microscopy is often used to detect voids and  delamination within material layers and interfaces. Therefore, it is considered a critical tool to localize electrical opens due to  cold solder joints, cracks within solder bumps and delamination  at component edges or corners. SAM bases on the operational


"℃


principle of inducing an acoustic wave through a transducer into  the device under test top surface that travels through the


50


individual material layers [14]. Each material interface  interaction leads to a partial or total wave reflection that is


45


measured by the transducer based on differences in acoustic  impedances. This procedure is done in scanning mode, enabling


40


an imaging of the individual material layers. Voids such as air  gaps, cracks and delamination lead to a strong reflectance of the


35


wave and are in image contrast to their environment. Scanning  a failed sample and comparing the resulting SAM images to the  ones of a good unit, allows isolation of defect-related signals.


30


SAM applications are limited by two main factors. In order to  induce the acoustic wave into the device with minimum signal


25


loss, the sample is required to be immersed in a water bath. It is  therefore usually used after most electrical tests are completed


20


in order to avoid the generation of electrical shorts and  corrosion. The second limitation of this technique is the  compromise of spatial imaging resolution and total sample  thickness. The resolution of SAM is best with high frequencies  while the maximum travel range is better at low frequencies as  the wave is heavily damped over distance. As a consequence, SAM requires an optimization based on the individual sample  under test. Typical frequencies for PCB inspection are within  the 30 – 50 MHz range and are used to find large delamination  with larger than 1mm. For individual components, such as  stacked dies or bare silicon devices, the frequency can be  increased to 100 MHz – 300MHz. This allows an increase in  resolution in the single micrometer range.


An example of a typical SAM image on board level is given in  figure 5. The image shows the successful imaging through a


1.1mm thick PCB unit based on a 4-2-4 construction. Stacked  filled micro-vias are used for internal connections [15].

2D & 3D X-Ray Tomography


X-ray imaging efficiently provides direct visualization of  devices’ superficial and internal structures, typically with little  need of sample preparation or modification. Compared with  imaging techniques based on electron and visible light, X-rays  offer several favorable traits that makes them uniquely well  suited for non-destructive evaluation and testing. These  characteristics have made X-ray inspection systems a critical  non-destructive imaging and analysis tool in the failure analysis  laboratories. Most of the commercial X-ray equipment are  projection based systems that place the sample in the X-ray  beam path, emitted from micro-focus or nano-focus sources and  record the images. The resolution of such systems depends on  the X-ray source spot size, magnification, and detector pixel  size [16-19]. Approximately 1-um resolution is achievable in  most practical applications. These systems also provide high  imaging speed so that operator can manipulate samples’ position and view multiple angles to make real-time  observations. Some manufacturers have also provided  integration to CAD design data to allow live overlay on 3D Xray images for direct comparison and defect analysis [20].

This is an advantage for  advanced board level analysis with multiple levels of solder  joints to be observed (SiP, POP) or numerous stacked filled  micro-vias or even embedded components. To achieve the  resolution needed in FA analysis, several aspects of the X-ray  system have been recently improved (for instance: resolution of  the X-ray source, sensitivity of the flat panel detector, and  accuracy of manipulator).


Case studies


Case study I: Root cause analysis on board level


The first case study demonstrates the successful defect  localization of an electrical short and electrical open on-board  level by using magnetic current imaging and Terahertz Time  Domain Reflectometry [22]. The sample, a 6-layer PCB of  23mm by 23mm dimensions, shows an electrical short between  two adjacent nets that are located at the bottom left corner of  the device. By performing the current imaging technique and  overlaying the results with the board design layout, the defect  position can be determined, figure 7. Near infrared imaging (NIR) is used for inspecting the localized area and an extra  pattern was found that causes a bridge between the two current  paths. The full FA process is non-destructive and additional  physical failure analysis is only optional.


Figure 7: Magnetic current imaging illustrates the current flow  within the net list (left) and pin point the location of the  electrical short within the circuit path. NIR imaging at different  magnification confirm the root cause due to extra pattern (right) [22].


The second defect localization is done on a similar sample


setup, this time showing an electrical open at the top right


corner of the device. Terahertz imaging is used and the timeamplitude signals are compared to a good unit. Figure 8 top


right shows the comparison. By calculating the time the signal 0OOooo travels through the individual current paths, a rough localization


of the defect position can be made in X and Y. (figure 8, left).


Using NIR imaging, this estimate is confirmed and an open of


the related current path was detected. As in the previous sample,


the measurement is non-destructive and renders additional PFA


obsolete.

Case study II: Root cause analysis from board to component  level


The second case study demonstrates the application of  advanced failure analysis from board level to the individual  failing component. The board, a GPU PCB, showed a failing  behavior and system level testing determined an electrical short  within the 12V power rail as potential root cause. However, due  to the long length of the tested netlist, several dozen of  components and interconnects are in consideration and  additional defect isolation is required. Lock-in thermography is  used by stimulating the defective netlist at 250mV/500mA and  a single hot spot is observed, figure 9.
