Imaging Flip Chip Devices


The development of flip chip technology introduced the need  for high frequency non-destructive imaging of flip chip bump  interconnects and underfill defects. Transducers with improved  lens designs and center frequencies above 200 MHz have been  developed specifically for flip chip applications. These  transducers allow excellent imaging of flip chip bumps and  have detected defects such as non-wets of solder, missing  bumps, solder bridging, and damaged die-level interconnect  cracks.


Data Gate Set-up: For ultra-high frequency PE-SAM on flip  chips, choosing the appropriate data gate length and placement  is critical.  Even when the gate encompasses the echo of  interest, if the gate is not set correctly, the resulting images may  lack the physical defects of interest within the sample.


Figure 33 illustrates the effects that can occur in an image as the  gate position is slightly changed or the gate is lengthened.


Typically, the interface between the die and the underfill does  not produce a single echo, but produces multiple echoes which  are overlapping, even with frequencies >200 MHz.  The echoes  are produced at each interconnect layer within the die, which  typically all blend together to form interference patterns of the  die circuitry.  There is another echo produced at the interface of  the die’s protective overcoat (PO) and the typical polyimide  coatings applied to flip chips at relatively thick dimensions (on  the order of 3 µm or more).  Lastly, an echo is produced by the  interface of the polyimide to the underfill layer that is used to  help neutralize stresses produced by CTE mismatches between  the die and the package substrate.


In flip chip inspection, since the die is mounted upside down  with the circuitry facing the substrate, the earliest signals in the  packet of echoes that first emerges after the signal passes  through the bulk Si of the die contain information from the die  circuitry, and the latest echoes contain the information from the  underfill level.


### Imaging Flip Chip Devices


In Fig. 33, SAM images are shown of a flip chip gated at  different locations, with the A-scan presented beneath to  indicate the gate positions.  A narrow gate placed early in the  echo packet shows interconnect defects caused by a bump that  broke off, damaging the underlying interconnect layers in the  process.  The image from this gate position shows no other  defect.  However, a narrow gate placed late in the echo packet  shows the absence of a solder bump at the location the bump  broke off and reveals a large area of excessive solder bridging  several bumps. If an analyst attempted to use a wide gate  encompassing the entire echo packet, as is often done for lower  frequency imaging of molded packages, the resulting image  shows indications of both defects, but the image clarity is  degraded, and the nature of the defect is not clear.


Figure 33: The effect of gate size and placement on the


resulting image is demonstrated: A) image acquired with wide  gate B) image with “late” narrow gate C) image with “early” narrow gate.


If the echoes from these interfaces were perfectly separated and  isolated from each other, gate placement could easily be  determined based on calculations that incorporate the structure  of the die and package, and the velocity of sound in the various  layers.  However, since the echoes are overlapping, gate  placement is qualitatively determined.  Computer and software  improvements have enabled multiple-gate scanning capability, which greatly aids the determination of proper gating for flip  chips.


This concept operates on the principle that an initial data gate  can be sized and placed at the beginning of the echo train.  Then, the gate is automatically duplicated and placed at set intervals  across the entire echo signal.  When the sample is scanned, multiple images are simultaneously produced from the many  gates.  The gate position used for a particular image can easily  be visualized so there is no guessing as to which gating  conditions produce which type of image.  The only drawback  to this application is that typically, all images produced by a  multiple-gate scan are saved in a single file, which results in  larger file sizes.


Thus, in practice, a multiple-gate scan is extremely effective to  establish the proper single gate set-up condition for each new  flip chip device, which is then applied to all subsequent samples  of the same type. This is easily done for example, if one is  working on process development for underfill, where the only  information desired is how well the underfill flowed, whether  filler particle settling occurs, and whether capture voids are  present. In some instances, however, the use of multiple-gate  scanning must be performed on every sample.  This is typically  the case if one is trying to discriminate between defects in the  interconnect (especially a concern with Cu/low-k dielectric  devices), failures at the PO to polyimide interface, and failures  between the polyimide and underfill.  For example, Fig. 34  shows images from a multiple gate scan that differentiate  defects between the PO and polyimide, and the polyimide and  underfill. With the proper imaging conditions, many types of  defects in flip chips can be detected.  Unless specifically stated  otherwise, all high-resolution flip chip imaging discussed  throughout this section was performed using a transducer  having a 150 MHz center frequency.


Figure 34: Use of a multiple gate scan aids in diagnosing two  types of fail modes. (A) device level defects are found at an early  gate placement (B) underfill to die surface delamination is  visible at a later gate placement.


Setting the Focus:  Normally, the pulse-echo focus is set by  watching the echo of interest and varying the distance between  the transducer and the sample such that the maximum amplitude  of the echo is reached.  With the high frequencies used for flip  chips, this focusing mechanism may not always work.  This is  because water strongly attenuates the high frequency signal. As  the transducer is moved closer to the sample, the water path  shrinks, so there is less absorption and the signal increases in  amplitude.  Depending on the focusing of the transducer,  it is  possible to move the transducer past the focal point, and there  will be no indication of a decreasing signal amplitude, because


O00


the signal intensity continues to increase due to decreasing  attenuation .This effect is illustrated in Fig. 35.  Here two A-


。0


scans captured from the same x-y location at a device are  shown, but with the 180 MHz transducer placed either at the  focal point (yellow) or moved closer towards the sample and  past the focal point (red). The signal strength from the out-offocus placement is significantly increased compared with the  in-focus setting, at both the front surface and sub-surface  echoes.


Figure 35: Using signal amplitude for focus determination of  high frequency transducers can be misleading. A 180 MHz  transducer was positioned over a flip chip at the proper pulseecho focus position. It was then moved through the focus, closer  to the die.  The out-of-focus position produces signals of the  highest amplitude.


Usually, high frequency transducers are designed to target a  water path length of minimum working distance from the  sample, to minimize the water absorption effects.  The typical  die thickness is considered during this calculation.  So, for a  given transducer and given die thickness, once the focus setting  is known, it can be applied uniformly to all flip chip die of the  same thickness.  Sometimes, however, the focus must be  determined empirically.  This may be necessary for example, if  an analyst receives a flip chip for SAM analysis that has been  thinned to facilitate other failure analysis procedures such as  photoemission microscopy.  The thinner the die, the further  away the transducer will be from the sample at focus, and thus, the weaker the signal amplitude.  To identify the proper focus  setting, it is best to run a series of high digital resolution focus  scans, where the transducer position is varied by set intervals.  An example of images from such a series is shown in Fig. 36.


Figure 36: Using signal amplitude for focus determination of  high frequency transducers can be misleading. One  workaround is to perform a high digital resolution focus series  such as shown here. In this case, focus increments of 0.5 µs work very well.  A focus  series should always be obtained by starting with the transducer  in the lowest position (closest to the sample), and then moving  it away from the sample.


Case 1 – Solder Bridging: Figure 37 shows acoustic detection  of solder bridging in a delidded flip chip. While the bridging is  detected acoustically, it is difficult to conclusively say bridging  is the cause of the light and dark stripes connecting the bumps. This is because other defects can cause a similar appearance, such as corroded metal in the die-level interconnect. The  bridging is confirmed by X-ray analysis. The contrast variation  in the SAM-detected solder bridging is caused by variation in  the solder thickness. X-ray is not as sensitive to the thickness  variation, and all bridging bumps have a uniform appearance.  X-ray is a powerful non-destructive imaging tool that is  complementary to SAM.


Case 2 – Non-wet Bumps: In many cases, it is possible to  detect flip chip bumps that have not properly wet to the die  surface. Figure 38 shows such an example.  The high frequency  PE-SAM inspection produces an image where some of the  bumps take on a “snowman” appearance.


500 um


Figure 37: SAM imaging shows shorted flip chip bumps (A). The contrast variation of white or dark in the bridging area in  the SAM image is caused by solder thickness variations. X-ray  confirms the shorting defect (B).


The cause of this appearance is determined by a physical crosssection of the bumps in question.  Incomplete wetting of solder  to the bump pads on the die has occurred.  In this specific  instance, underfill flowed into the space that should have been  occupied by solder. If air were present instead, a largeamplitude reflection would have been received, similar in  brightness to the large white circular underfill delamination  visible in the SAM image.


Case 3 – Defects in Die Interconnect: In addition to revealing  bump defects, acoustic analysis of flip chips can detect largescale damage that has occurred within the die circuitry layers. This is demonstrated within Fig. 39. A device failing for shorts  at a specific bump was submitted for analysis. One of the  images produced by a multi-gate SAM scan shows a bright  reflection associated with a specific bump.  This indicates a  likelihood of delamination and/or cracking beneath the bump.


One of the other images produced by the multi-gate scan clearly  shows a crack surrounding a portion of the bump periphery. A  cross-section into this periphery region of the bump shows  cracking in the dielectric layers, which has now been filled in  with Cu, causing the short. The subsequent failure of the same  bump on two other devices allowed the identification of a bad  socket on a burn-in board as being the root cause of the failures.

Case 4 – Delamination of Low-k Dielectric Layers: In the  late 1990s, the semiconductor industry began working on  converting material sets, replacing aluminum and silicon  dioxides with Cu metal and either polymer or C-doped oxide (CDO) low-k dielectrics.  The initial introduction of low-k  dielectrics posed new challenges for developing robust devices.  Typically, the adhesion of these dielectrics to other materials of  the die was suboptimal during early learning cycles.  The


polyimide


underfill


industry proved that with the appropriate process  improvements, strong adhesion could be obtained.  This is  critical to enable packaging and good reliability for Cu/low-k  products.


One assembly step that highlighted weak adhesion was the saw  process. Mechanical sawing initiates cracks within the scribe


street of all devices manufactured today.  With good adhesion, the cracks do not pose a problem and crack growth is


sufficiently arrested by optimally designed scribe seals. When  suboptimal adhesion exists, the cracks grow into delaminations  that propagate through the scribe seal when subjected to  conditions that stress CTE mismatches, such as temperature  cycles.


Figure 40 shows the PE-SAM result when this type of defect is  present in a flip chip. Depending on gate settings, whether water  enters the crack, and other factors, the delaminated area may or  may not be bright.  It is typically located at the die edge and  propagates into several rows of bumps. One noticeable feature  that frequently occurs and helps distinguish the low-k dielectric  delamination from underfill adhesion issues is that typically, if  underfill delamination occurs, the bumps are still clearly  observable.  On the other hand, as Fig. 40 shows, low-k  delamination often results in the disappearance of the bumps  from the image.


PE-SAM analysis has proven an extremely valuable tool during  Cu/low-k device development, enabling optimization of  assembly processes for low-k devices, and enabling the  development of process improvements for better adhesion in  low-k die.


Figure 40: SAM image of a flip chip with cracking in the lowk dielectric layers. Often, a defect in the low-k layers results in  the loss of bumps from the image.


Case 5 – Bump Size Variations: Although SAM is excellent  for detecting non-wet bumps, solder bridging, and cracking  beneath the bump, some types of bump defects are not readily  observable with SAM. This fact is highlighted by Fig. 41.  SAM  easily detects broken bumps and massive solder bridging, as  discussed previously and again shown in this figure.  However, this figure also highlights a weakness of SAM as applied to flip  chip inspection. The SAM image does not produce an image of  the whole bump, but mostly just the bump to die contact area. This can be partly explained by the spherical shape of the  bumps, which reflects sound away from the transducer.  The  result is that bumps with inadequate solder volumes appear the  same size in a SAM image as perfectly normally shaped bumps,


leading to the conclusion that SAM does not work as well for  showing bump–size related defects.


Figure 41: Optical (A) and high frequency PE-SAM (B) image  comparison shows SAM capability for three types of defects. A  Broken bump (1) and massive solder bridging (3) are clear in  the SAM image. Solder bumps of reduced size (2) are not


detected by SAM. The “edge effect” phenomenon, which


interferes with imaging the outermost row of bumps, is


observed in this SAM image.


Figure 41 is also a good example of the “edge effect” phenomenon, which limits the ability to image features that are  along the edge of a sample.  This is caused by the reflection of  a portion of the conical signal away from the focus near the  edge.  The thicker the die, or the larger the numerical aperture  of the lens, the worse the edge effect.  For flip chips, bumps  within 200 µm of the edge are difficult to image using most high  frequency transducers available commercially.  The  development of higher power transducers that maintain high  resolution at longer working distances may enable better edge  imaging.


Case 6 – Lidded Flip Chip Packages: To allow acoustic  inspection of flip chip bumps and underfill, the backside of the  die must be exposed. This reduces the absorption of the high  frequency sound waves in the lid, which would degrade the  resolution that is needed for bump inspection.  For over-molded  flip chips, the mold compound above the die must be removed, usually by grinding and polishing. For lidded flip chips, there  are various methods available for lid removal. All methods, however, pose the risk of inducing damage during handling. This is especially a concern for devices containing low-k  dielectric materials, which require careful handling to avoid  artifacts. By performing TT-SAM analysis prior to any sample  preparation, one can ensure detected defects are real and not a  result of handling. Figure 42 shows a portion of a flip chip  package imaged with TT-SAM prior to delidding, and with high  frequency PE-SAM after lid removal.


Three points can be made with this figure. First, one must  remember TT-SAM provides information from all interfaces. Taking lid attach analysis as an example, an observed defect in  a TT-SAM image could in fact come from another deeper layer  like underfill, as demonstrated in this case. Second, the TTSAM image provides convincing evidence that the underfill  defect is not an artifact of the de-lidding process. This tactic is  especially valuable when evaluating packages containing  Cu/low-k die. Third, the TT-SAM resolution is much worse


than the resolution obtained in the PE-SAM image. Thus, very  small defects will not be detected by TT-SAM. Note that  although a defect is identified from TT-SAM alone, its location  is not truly revealed until the PE-SAM is applied.

## Complementary Nondestructive Techniques


Complementary Nondestructive Techniques


SAM is one of three complementary techniques used in the  nondestructive inspection of packaged ICs. X-ray radiography  and a transmission acoustic technique called scanning laser


acoustic microscopy (SLAM) and are also used for this  application (Fig. 44). These two techniques can each produce  images of packaged ICs, and therefore have partially  overlapping capabilities. However, unique capabilities of each  technique make them complementary for the nondestructive  inspection of IC packages.


Figure 44: X-ray radiographic inspection (A) and scanning  laser acoustic microscopy (SLAM) (B) of IC packages.


Real-time x-ray inspection offers excellent lateral resolution  and is unsurpassed for nondestructive wire sweep inspection. Images are produced at TV rates and the sample is easily  manipulated. Although commonly used for die attach  inspection, x-ray imaging shows only the location of voids in  the die attach layer, and not the total area of attachment as  delaminations typically do not produce sufficient absorption  contrast to the surrounding material. Likewise, x-ray inspection  often exhibits limited contrast for low mass thickness die attach


layers on metal heat sinks (see Fig. 22). Similarly, detection of  package voids can be limited by lead frame shadowing [32]. Real-time x-ray is an excellent technique for detecting voids in  flip chip bumps, but generally is not useful for detecting  underfill voiding or delamination in flip chips.  However recent  reports indicate high-resolution 3D X-ray microscopy can  detect underfill voids in flip chips assembled using nonconductive film (NCF) (unpublished information).


BC


X-ray laminography is a low-resolution tomographic technique  that produces a 3D image based on x-ray attenuation at a  specific plane within the sample. X-ray laminography has seen  limited use for component level inspection due to its low  resolution, although it has been applied to the inspection of  solder joint quality for surface mount process control [50, 51]. X-ray microscopy (XRM) is a tomographic technique using an  architecture combining geometric magnification with optical  magnification to achieve high-resolution 3D tomography on  intact samples as large as a 300 mm wafer. With the latest  systems having 0.5 µm spatial resolution under optimal  conditions and 1 µm resolution at a 50 mm working distance, 3D x-ray microscopy has become a key package FA technique  that not only detects solder joint problems in flip chip, stacked


die and advanced 2.5/3D packages, but can also image nonA


conductive film (NCF) underfill voids as small as 10 µm with  scans as fast as 30 minutes [personal communication]. Like any  high-resolution technique, it has a limited field of view at high  resolution.  Because of the limited field of view, it is unsuitable  as a full-package screening technique for micron-sized defects, although it can be used for high-resolution feedback from a  small volume of interest with scan times ranging from 10  minutes to hours depending on the resolution required and the  amount of image noise that can be tolerated. Applications are  emerging for its use in measurements of package structures to  aid package development [52].


SLAM is a transmission acoustic technique developed in the  early 1970’s at Zenith and later transferred to Sonoscan in 1974


[53]. SLAM incorporates concepts similar to those presented by  Sokolov in 1936 for his proposed acoustic microscope [54]. In  SLAM, a planar sound wave is transmitted through the sample  onto a mirrored coverslip. The disturbances produced in the  coverslip by the transmitted wave are imaged with a scanned  laser beam. The technique produces either an acoustic shadow  image or an interference pattern by comparison of the signal to  a phase reference. SLAM offers the advantage of real time  imaging which is more suitable for 100% inspection than a  technique involving mechanical scanning. SLAM has been  successfully applied to situations where real time imaging is  critical, and in applications involving samples with irregular  shapes and very thin multi-layer construction that cannot be  imaged well by reflected sound due to the “dead zone” and  reverberation effects described earlier. SLAM applications  have included the inspection of tape automated bonding (TAB) packages, and thin film ceramic chip capacitors [9]. In practical  application the spatial resolution of SAM images of IC  packages is typically superior to that of SLAM images at the  same frequency [55]. SLAM cannot be applied to die attach  inspection in packages with air cavities, such as ceramic DIPs  and pin grid arrays, unless the lid is removed. Similar  information as provided by SLAM can be obtained from a SAM  operating in through-transmission mode.


Current Challenges and New Developments


Stacked Die Packages and Increasing 3D Structures


Form factor considerations and the need for increasing  functionality have driven the development of stacked die  packages for certain markets.  In particular, stacked die  packages are increasingly used in hand-held wireless  communications, such as cell phones, and in the highperformance computer market. These packages stack two or  more functional dies on top of each other. Package  interconnects may be mixed, using both wirebond and flip chip  die in the same package. The packages are required to be thin, so the die are regularly background to very thin dimensions (<150 µm each). Some of the more integrated packages  currently use six or more stacked functional die, each 60 µm  thick. At least one major semiconductor manufacturer can  create 8-die stacks, each only 50 µm thick.


Stacked die packages are difficult to image using SAM if one is  interested in obtaining information beyond the top die surface. In addition to the large number of thin layers, the Si die itself is


### Stacked Die Packages and Increasing 3D Structures


thin, and the velocity of sound is quite high in Si (~8500 m/s). The higher the acoustic velocity, or the thinner the layer, the  closer the echoes will be and thus, the larger the overlap of  adjacent pulses. When both happen together, the echoes  between the die cannot be resolved. Given the acoustic velocity  of Si above, the first sub-surface echo from a 100 µm thick die  should appear 20 ns after the front surface echo. At this close  spacing, typically it is difficult to resolve both sides of a single  thinned die, because the die backside echo partially overlaps the  front-side echo. To overcome this limitation, sophisticated  techniques such as numerical deconvolution analysis is  required.


To better understand the imaging challenges of stacked die  packages, consider the simplest structure available.  Figure 45  shows the general structure of a two-die stacked package, with  die adhered by epoxy and no silicon spacers present. In order to  non-destructively evaluate adhesion between the two die, SAM  needs to be able to resolve the echo from the surface of the  lower die.


Figure 45: A general diagram of a simple stacked die package  having only two stacked die. Total package thickness is <1 mm. Each die is <150 µm thick.


A stacked die package similar to the cartoon in Fig. 45 was  analyzed by SAM. Since the mold compound strongly  attenuates the signal, high frequency inspection could not be  applied. A high numerical aperture 50 MHz transducer was  used to record the image. To obtain as much information as  possible, three types of PE-SAM images were obtained (peak

GHz-SAM Imaging of Wirebond Interfaces and Bond Pads


The inspection of wirebond pads for cracking and cratering of  inter-metal dielectrics and metal layers is challenging for most  non-destructive techniques. The features of interest are  commonly below the resolution capabilities of conventional  SAM. The variation of the absorption contrast required for Xray imaging is extremely low. Cratering is commonly  approached by destructive techniques involving elaborate  etching processes.  This potentially introduces artifacts leading  to a high degree of uncertainty of the investigative results. GHzSAM has been applied for the detection of cratering-related  cracks in bond pads. Due to the reduced penetration depth of  the acoustic aperture in the GHz band, thinning of the sample  to approximately 1-5 µm is required. Even though the effort of  sample preparation is rather high, it avoids the introduction of  artifacts directly into the interfaces, and it leaves the sample  electrically functional. Figure 57 shows the results of a GHzSAM based cratering test for the inspection of the BEOL  system underneath a bonded wirebond pad. Acoustic imaging  was performed through 1 – 2 µm of Si. Figure 57(A) shows a  schematic of the structure underneath the bond pad.


Figure 57 shows GHz-SAM images in B and C that reveal  cracks starting at the center of two different pads of the same  sample that propagate outwards. The electron micrograph in  Fig. 57(D) shows a FIB-prepared cross section along the red  marker in C. The presence of two “gaps” can be seen that have  different diameters. The crack with the 400 nm diameter can be  clearly seen in the acoustic image. This may be caused by the  acoustic waves having to propagate through the BEOL stack  and the fact that the wave field is already defocused at the  location of the crack. In any case, the presence of microcracks  underneath the bond has been observed, and the acoustic  findings were verified by SEM imaging of a cross section  through the site.

In recent years, monometallic Cu-Cu wirebond systems raised  interest due to their potential to drastically reduce  manufacturing costs. The inspection of such monometallic  systems for voids and interfacial integrity is of great interest. Since the pad and the wire consists of the same material, selective etching approaches are not an option. Characterization  of such Cu-Cu wirebonds would rely on purely destructive  methods, like shear testing, that only provide integral values  over the entire pad like e.g.  the analysis of required forces. For  technology development of the bonding process, test structures  containing Cu pads on a Si substrate were inspected and  analyzed by GHz-SAM. Figure 58 summarizes the results  obtained by acoustic inspection. The image on the left in Fig. 58 shows the acoustic image recorded using a 300 MHz  transducer in a conventional SAM. The center image shows the  GHz-SAM image for comparison. Subsequent FIB preparation  and SEM imaging revealed that the three bright wire bonds on  the left were delaminated across most of the bonding area. The  dark appearing wire bonds, on the contrary, adhered well. However, while conventional SAM allowed the identification  of fully delaminated versus mainly intact wire bonds, it did not  provide any detail from across the bonding area. GHz-SAM for the Inspection of Bonding Interfaces in  Wafer Bonding


Several novel interconnect approaches have evolved with 3Dintegration strategies, resulting in package feature shrinkage  and increased integration complexity that are moving beyond  the sensitivity of established inspection techniques. Figure 59  shows a schematic and an electron micrograph of two bonded  Si wafers containing CuSn pillars for realizing electrical  connection. The structure shown is a daisy chain of 10 µm and  15 µm pitch for evaluation of the mechanical strength and  bonding properties. For alignment a mechanical BCB key was  employed and defined the localization accuracy. The layout of  the test vehicle was designed for a 540 x 612 infrared imaging  array and provided 256 individual channels of 1272 bumps  each, to identify and localize any non-conductive bump. GHz  SAM was applied through 5 µm of remaining Si for imaging  the lamination condition between the BCB/underfill and the  electrical routings. Figure 60 contains a SEM image at the top  and an acoustic GHz-image at the bottom.


Both images were recorded at the same location of the sample. The red arrows in the SEM image indicate electrical routings  that are delaminated from the BCB/underfill. At these locations, the intensity in the acoustic GHz-image is elevated indicating  an increased reflectivity. The routing that remains darker in the  acoustic image shows also no indication of delamination in the  electron micrograph. Besides the interfaces of the electrical


routings, the interior of the Cu-bumps can be seen in the  acoustic image in Fig. 60.

In wafer level packaging (WLP), a direct hybrid bonding  scheme has recently been adopted for the realization of 3D  interconnects. The image on the left of Fig. 61 illustrates the  bonding scheme. Two Si wafers are patterned and structured  containing Cu-pads and pillars together with dielectric  materials. During wafer bonding, the patterned wafers are


joined forming a hybrid bonding interface consisting of Cu-Cu, Cu-dielectric and dielectric-dielectric areas. For technology  reasons, the bottom and top pads can differ in size. With respect

to reliability and robustness, the presence of delaminated  regions is a major concern in wafer bonding. In this zone, a circular  delamination would form around the Cu-pillar, stopping at the  dielectric-dielectric interface. With a top-Si thickness of 5 µm, the structure is suitable for GHz-SAM. GHz-SAM Inspection for Void Formation in Metallization  Lines for Automotive Applications


In safety-relevant applications, microelectronic components  and systems are required to exhibit extraordinary reliability  even if they are operated in harsh environments. To ensure  robustness and reliability, the chemical and mechanical  interaction of the applied materials with one another, particularly under harsh thermal and atmospheric conditions, needs to be investigated and their behavior understood. The  case study presented in Fig. 63 to Fig. 66 addresses electrical  power lines consisting of AlCu that have been extensively  investigated and analyzed. Figure 63 shows two schematics of  cross sections through different sample types. Both types  differed in their composition. Although both types consist  primarily of AlCu, the image on the right illustrates the  presence of a 40 nm TiN interlayer in between two 1.5 µm thick  AlCu layers.


Figure 63: Schematic of the structure of the metallization layers  in cross section. Left: Line consisted only of AlCu. Right: Sandwich structure. In the vertical center the line contained a  40 nm TiN interlayer.


The acoustic investigation included three inspection conditions: A) a set of reference samples containing no TiN in the  metallization and not exposed to any environmental stressing, B) samples that also did not contain a TiN interlayer, but were  exposed to a temperature cycling test according to “JESD22-A104E: Temperature Cycling” with the temperature range  adapted according to “AEC-Q100 Rev. C” (the temperature  ranged from -65°C to +175°C and was repeated for 1000  cycles), and C)  samples contained a TiN interlayer as  illustrated in the image on the right in Fig. 63 and were exposed  to the TCT, described above.


For evaluating the general sensitivity of the GHz-SAM towards  the detection of voids in the described structure a sample from  set “B” was investigated. Figure 64 shows the resulting image  obtained by GHz-SAM from this preliminary analysis in the left  image. The graph on the right in Fig. 64 shows an electron  micrograph of the sample after FIB-trenching. This preparation  step removed the upper Si and oxide layer and provided direct  access to the metallization lines for verification of the  acoustically obtained results. Although there have been several  discharges of the ion beam through the AlCu lines, the  correlation between the voids and the “bright spots” in the GHz95


#### GHz-SAM Inspection for Void Formation in Metallization Lines for Automotive Applications


SAM images is evident. The markers with equal color indicate  the same features in the GHz-SAM and the electron  micrograph. These results verify the applicability of the GHzSAM technique for the detection of voids induced upon stress  testing in these samples. Figure 64 contains acoustic GHzimages recorded from the sample sets A, B and C as described  above.


Figure 64: Verification of the contrast in the GHz-SAM images  to be voids. Left: acoustic GHz-image. Right: Electron  micrograph of a FIB-trench parallel to the sample surface.


The intention of this study was the to investigate the effect of  thermal stressing on the reliability behavior of the AlCu lines, as well as to investigate the introduction of a TiN interlayer into  the vertical center of the metallization lines. The GHz-SAM  image at the top in Fig. 65 was recorded from an unstressed  sample that did not contain the TiN interlayer. In this GHzSAM image no voids can be observed. In the center image in  Fig. 65, the result of GHz-SAM inspection of the sample type  without TiN interlayer, but after thermal cycling test (TCT) is  shown. The presence of many voids can be observed. The  bottom graph in Fig. 65  shows the acoustic GHz-SAM image  of a sample that contained a TiN interlayer and was exposed to  the TCT. Here the number of voids is substantially smaller than  observed in the sample that did not contain the TiN. During the  study several samples have been investigated and voids were  characterized in number and size by object recognition to allow  for a statistical analysis. The hypothesis for the observed  substantial reduction in the occurrence of voids is based on the  getter properties of Ti and TiN for hydrogen remnants that are  likely introduced during the processing of the structure. The  hydrogen is expected to act as a seed for the formation of voids  which agglomerate and grow during thermal cycling due to  mechanical forces. A detailed description of this study is  available [58]. In most GHz-SAM inspections, a series of  frames is recorded at decreasing distances between the  transducer and the sample. This is primarily because these  highly focused acoustic transducers can exploit several wave  modes used for imaging by defocusing.


Another effect of the defocusing is that the acoustic focus is  moved from the sample surface to inside the sample while  keeping the narrow axial intensity distribution. In the case of  the samples investigated here, it provided the ability to  distinguish between voids from the upper and the lower AlCu  layer.

Inspection of TSVs Using Acoustic GHz-Microscopy


no TiN post TCT


Routing of electrical interconnects directly through the silicon  wafer using Through Silicon Vias (TSV) is one of the most  promising interconnect technologies for 3D-system integration. However, conventional inspection by either SAM or x-ray for  the presence of filling voids or the delamination of the oxide


80 μm


liner is highly compromised. In this regard, GHz-SAM was  evaluated for its applicability.


TSVs can have largely differing diameters and depths,


with TiN post TCT


depending on the application and the technology. With  diameters in the lower µm range and large differences in the  acoustic properties between the Si matrix and the Cu or W of  the filling, even GHz-SAM inspection is highly challenged. The


10Dμm


penetration depth is limited to single digits in micrometers  underneath the surface. In addition, due to its microstructure, Cu is highly attenuating to acoustic waves and last but not least, lateral feature sizes on the order of the wavelength will increase  the complexity of the acoustic wave propagation. However, this  can also cause phenomena that may help overcome the physical  limitations of purely compressional wave imaging. With its  cylindrical shape, a TSV may act as a wave guide allowing for  acoustic energy to penetrate deeper inside the sample than  would be possible by the compressional wave. In several  studies, imaging contrast correlating to physical structures  exceeding the expected penetration depth inside the TSVs has  been observed [58-60].


Results of a GHz-SAM based inspection of TSVs are provided  in Fig. 67. Due to the rough surfaces that occur from the etching  process, it was quite difficult to get consistent results when  inspecting TSVs by GHz-SAM. Since GHz-SAM is highly  sensitive to the surface and sub-surface region, features in these  areas will dominate the contrast. Therefore, the GHz-SAM has  been adapted and extended to allow for the acquisition of the  unprocessed rf-data. The captured transients recorded with  sufficient defocus were subjected to a Split Spectrum Analysis  as described earlier and parametric images were computed at  individual frequencies. This approach reduced the impact of the  surface region and emphasized the signal features that arise  from larger sample depths.


In Fig. 67 the results of the SSP at 910 MHz and 955 MHz are


6 N


superimposed on the acoustic GHz-image. At these two  frequencies, increased intensity can be observed at the TSV  third from the left. All other TSVs show similar intensities on a  first approximation. The SEM images in the center and bottom  images in Fig. 67 show FIB-prepared cross sections through the  TSVs. The correspondence is indicated by the line style and  color of the markers. It can be observed that the green-marked  TSV contains a medium-sized void at a depth of 3 – 8 µm below  the surface. In the spectral images this TSV exhibits the highest


intensity among the TSVs inspected here. Although the  correspondence between the presence of the defect and the  intensity of the spectrally analyzed acoustic signal is observed  here, TSV inspection by GHz-SAM is not generally applicable  with sufficient certainty. Even though the technique appears  promising it will require further adaptions and extension of the  tool to be reliably applicable for this inspection task.

Photo-acoustic GHz-microscopy: an emerging technique?


Since acoustic waves are highly sensitive towards structural and  elastic properties and property-gradients, they appear promising


### Photo-acoustic GHz-microscopy: an emerging technique?


for inspection of TSVs. However, it seems the penetration depth  of GHz-SAM limits the applicability. Therefore, an alternative  approach for acoustic wave excitation was evaluated with  respect to TSV inspection. Figure 68 contains a schematic of a  photo-acoustic GHz-microscope (GHz-PAM) that was  employed for TSV inspection.


Figure 68: Schematic of the Photo-acoustic GHz-microscopy  setup. The optical excitation is performed through the backside. Acoustic waves then propagate to the surface and are


detected by the acoustic lens.


In this setup, a laser source with optical access to the backside  of the sample excites acoustic waves based on the photoacoustic effect. Here a locally restricted volume is transiently  heated, which results in a thermal expansion that causes an  acoustic wave. This wave then propagates as a spherical wave  through the sample. An acoustic lens which is coaxially aligned  with the laser, but located on the opposite side, receives the  acoustic wave after interacting with the sample’s internal  structure. Since the pulse width of the laser excitation is  extremely short, compared to relaxation times in acoustics, the  excited wave covers a broad spectral range, allowing for the  extraction of energy at harmonics and super-harmonics of the  original signal.


Figure 69 contains the GHz-PAM results obtained from two  TSVs. From top to bottom in Fig. 69, the analysis frequency  increases from 825 MHz to above 4 GHz computed by  spectrally analyzing the photo-acoustic signals. The TSV on the  left was defect-free while the TSV on the right contained a  delamination of the oxide liner as subsequent FIB-SEM  analysis revealed.


The corresponding results are shown in Fig. 70. In the respect  of the intended inspection task GHz-PAM seems promising, however, the required access from the backside may not be  appropriate for most inspections. The application of an optical  excitation in any case allowed extending the inspection depth  from a few µm to the thickness of a full wafer, which  demonstrates a significant potential for upcoming inspection  tasks.


Figure 69: Images of two TSVs reconstructed from the photoacoustic signals. Prior to image reconstruction signals were  subjected to an SSP to allow for harmonic and superharmonic imaging. TSV on the left was defect free while the  TSV on the right contained a delamination of the oxide liner  as confirmed by FIB-SEM.


Figure 70: SEM image of a FIB-cross section through the


TSV. The oxide liner between the filling and the Si shows a  delamination where pointed to by arrows.


## Summary


The SAM used today for IC inspection is a hybrid instrument  with characteristics of both the Stanford SAM and the C-scan  recorder [9,10]. For inspection in layered IC packages both  amplitude and phase are measured and used to produce images  of the internal structure and locations of interfacial  delamination. Precise scanning and high frequencies are used  for optimum lateral resolution. In addition, the depth of the  primary sub-surface reflection is recorded for pseudo-threedimensional representations of the package.


Acoustic microscopy is well suited to plastic package  inspection. Although the plastic mold compound strongly  attenuates sound and thereby limits resolution, the planar, layered design of IC packages is ideal for acoustic inspection. The typically featureless and planar front surface facilitates  sub-surface imaging.


The acoustic microscope has been a key factor in the  understanding of the moisture sensitivity problem in surface  mount plastic IC packages. Polarity analysis of reflected  acoustic pulses is extremely useful in the detection of  delaminations in plastic IC packages and is an important  advantage of inspection with reflected sound. By quantifying  limits on the amount of delamination that is acceptable from a  reliability standpoint, SAM inspection can be incorporated into  standard test methods and is preferred over destructive cross  sectioning and electrical test methods.


The non-destructive nature of acoustic inspection means that in  reliability evaluations involving a dense matrix of variables, fewer devices are required. Previously, a fraction of the  remaining devices would have to be sacrificed for destructive  analysis at each inspection interval. Also, the data of reliability  evaluations using SAM are more valuable because the initiation  and propagation of damage can be tracked on individual ICs  throughout the test.


As packages have continued to evolve with time, adjustments  to the application of acoustic microscopy and improvements in  resolution have successfully overcome analysis challenges and  ensured that SAM continues to be a non-destructive technique  of significant importance for the development and evaluation of  IC packages. Specifically, analysis of BGA packages in  through-transmission mode bypasses two potential problems  that exist for pulse-echo mode: echo interferences from the  multi-layered substrates and reduced acoustic impedances of  the substrates that make phase inversion identification of  delamination invalid. Transducers with center frequencies  above 150 MHz deliver the resolution necessary for flip chip  bump inspection.


Due to frequency-dependent attenuation, the desired feature  size of interest has become smaller than SAM can resolve with  available transducer technology. Frequency-domain analysis  may partially overcome this limitation and is currently being  developed [44, 61]. A one-dimensional or two-dimensional  scanned array technology for acoustic imaging of IC packages  would have a dramatic impact on the effectiveness of SAM for


real-time applications such as process control by eliminating  the need for mechanical scanning.  Such an “acoustic camera” would not have to offer the same analytical capabilities of a  modern SAM to be effective as an on-line screening tool [62].

In this article we explore the world of diagnosis of  digital semiconductors devices. After shortly  outlining the technology behind diagnosis, the main  part of this article describes key improvements to  the basic diagnosis tools we knew from previous  years. These improvements enable the failure  analysis engineer as well as the yield analysis  engineer to use diagnosis as a powerful software  instrument supplementing his portfolio of tools. Throughout this article, we summarize several  successful industrial applications of diagnosis. For  example we recap applications where diagnoses  helped reducing the search area for defect down to  3% of the original search area size; and in another  case, diagnosis was used to improve at-speed tests, increasing the speed by 300MHz, plus several other  cases.


1. Introduction


Scan diagnosis is an established technique  identifying and localizing defects in digital  semiconductor devices that fail manufacturing test. Traditionally, scan diagnosis tools relied on the  stuck-at fault model and could diagnose down to a  logic net in the design. Although this approach is  useful for localization, it has some limitations. Stuckat patterns typically detect a vast variety of defect  types, including bridges and opens, but this fault  model is not always sufficient for effective diagnosis, since an actual defect may not behave as a stuck-at  fault. This typically results in a large number of  candidates, typically referred to as suspects. Even  with a single suspect net, that net could cover a large  area of the die. Early literature references are [1-3].


Over the last few years, these limitations have been  addressed through technologies such as

Figure 47: A B-scan of a stacked die package reveals the  acoustic signal pattern when only 2 die are present. Significant  ringing occurs beneath die 1, which prevents identification of  the die 1 to die 2 interfaces.


However, there is no obvious signal that corresponds to the  interface between die 1 and die 2. The die 2 signal visible in the  B-scan occurs away from the center, where the signal goes  straight through mold compound to die 2. However, in the  center of the package, the sound must travel through mold  compound and then through die 1 before it reaches die 2. Because the acoustic velocity of Si is much higher than in mold  compound, this means that over the center of the package, the  echo corresponding to die 2 should occur sooner than it occurs  in the regions where only mold compound is above die 2. The


absence of a distinct signal in this expected location indicates  that either the echo from die 2 is overlapping with the die 1  echo, or it has been severely attenuated. The subsequent echoes  below the die 1 surface are due to ringing of the signal between  the package surface and die 1, and also due to mode-converted  shear waves from the die 1 surface. It would be easy to view  this B-scan and assume many die were in this package, had it  not been known previously that only 2 die are present.

Frequency Domain Imaging


For features smaller than 20 µm, another method to temporally  resolve echoes is required. With the availability of streamlined  algorithms, fast PCs, and dedicated digital signal processor  chips (DSPs), it becomes feasible to apply frequency-domain


Package surface

Also, at present bondline thicknesses beneath lids  on flip chip packages cannot be measured acoustically due to  absorption of the high frequencies required for resolution by the  thick copper lid. Real-time frequency-domain signal analysis  may offer a non-destructive way to obtain these measurements. The availability of high-speed processors, inexpensive DRAM, and large capacity hard drives also enables the acquisition of  the raw and unprocessed rf-data for subsequent signal analysis  methods based on the acquired time-domain.  Here, the size and  position of data gates can be re-set and through software  analysis, the image can be adjusted accordingly. This “virtual  scanning” enables re-examination of devices after they are no  longer available (i.e. time zero data can be revisited after  devices have been put through environmental testing), allows

Signal Analysis in Acoustic Microscopy for Enhanced  Defect Detection Capabilities


In most acoustic imaging applications, image formation is  based on the peak amplitude of the acoustic signal within a  specified time gate. Even though this allows for imaging  without the need of extended interpretation, the approach  neglects the entire spectral content. The following examples  illustrate the potential of extracted signal characteristics for  enhanced parametric imaging to support interpretation and (defect) classification.


Spectral Analysis and Split-Spectrum Imaging (SSP)


The interpretation of ultrasonic echo signals can be quite  challenging, due to the complexity in the propagation behavior  of the underlying acoustic waves. The incident acoustic signal  interacts with all structures in the propagation path according to  their mechanical properties, leading to challenging  interpretations of the signal when inspection is performed in the  time domain. An example is a transient signal containing a high  number of oscillations in the time domain, caused by the  superposition of echo signals from adjacent structures, that  obscures the desired signal-pattern from the underlying  structure. Another example may be signals that are caused by  mode conversion at interfaces and interference at the detector. However, when inspecting signals in the spectral domain, features can be revealed that are hard to derive from the time  domain. Even though the identical information is contained in  the signal, the presentation makes a significant difference. Figure 49 illustrates the signal analysis approach that splits the  power spectrum of a signal (SSP). Here the acoustic signal in  the time domain is transformed into the spectral domain using  Fourier transformation. From the obtained spectrum, the power  spectrum is computed and separated into several frequency  containers with a specified band width. Figure 50 contains the  results of a split spectrum analysis of a flip-chip (FC) device. The device consisted of a Si chip of 800 µm thickness. The echo  signals from the interface between the Si die to the bottom side  of the bumps were analyzed. It was observed that the spectral  distribution of the signal energy was different when the FC  bumps contained cracks compared to defect free interconnects.


Figure 49: Split Spectrum Analysis: The power spectrum (right) of the time domain signal within the red gate (left) is  converted by Fast Fourier Transform into the spectral


domain. The power spectrum is then split into spectral


containers (orange bars) and integrated values are used to  form a parametric image.

Separating the acoustic signal into individual narrow bands also  allows for increasing the acoustic imaging resolution. This can  be explained by the fact that in acoustic microscopy, the probe  is commonly stimulated by a broad band pulse resulting in the  presence of lower and higher frequencies.


However, the imaging resolution strongly depends on the  wavelength of the acoustic signal. Therefore, imaging at a  higher spectral band will lead to an increased lateral resolution.  This fact is also highlighted in Fig. 51, which overlays a false  color spectrally-imaged area with an acoustic image, enabling  visualization of the improved resolution.

#### Automated Bump Inspection


Automated Bump Inspection


Figure 52 shows another example for supplementing acoustic  imaging with signal analysis. Multiple parameters were  extracted from the acoustic signals, weighted and combined  into a classifier for supporting signal interpretation and feature  classification [57]. The parameters were obtained from wavelet  analysis, as well as from amplitude and time-of-flight (ToF) analysis of the interface echo between the Si die and bump. The  derived parameters were the ToF shift of the interface pulse, the  signal energy of that pulse, and the distribution of the wavelet  coefficients obtained by continuous wavelet transformation  using a Gaussian mother wavelet.  Wherever all parameters  reached the threshold observed for a non-defective pixel in a FC  bump, the resulting pixel was marked green in the parametric  image superimposed on the acoustic image (left image in Fig. 52). In a separate analysis, all pixels corresponding to bumps  not meeting the conditions for an intact bump were marked red. All other pixels in the image were left out of the matrix, as they  were not recognized to belong to a bump. For evaluation  purposes, the device was extensively inspected by 2-D X-Ray  imaging at locations of the indicated defects. Finally, the  sample was physically cross-sectioned and imaged by SEM. Wherever the automated acoustic algorithm detected a defect, the bump was marked by a yellow dot as shown in the center  image in Fig. 52. In cases where this defect was confirmed by  X-Ray, the bump contains a red marking. Bump-defects  discovered by SEM imaging of the cross section are indicated  by a white circle in Fig. 52. From the center image in Fig. 52 it  is evident that not all defects found by the acoustic method and  verified by SEM were confirmed by X-Ray, even though the


locations have been explicitly pointed out. This demonstrates  the high sensitivity of acoustic waves towards even small  alterations in the physical structure of the inspected specimen. A detailed description of the approach can be found elsewhere


[57].  Figure 53 shows the electron micrographs of the bumps  corresponding to the numbering in the center image of Fig. 52.

### Extending Package Inspection Capability with Acoustic Ghz-Microscopy:  Potential, Application and Challenges


wafer pair reaching almost half way around the circumference. In the lower image, the contrast is changed by moving the  imaging gate from the compressional wave echo to a signal  originating from a transverse wave that was excited at the  surface of the wafer, and partially converted at the bonding  interface into a compressional wave that propagated back to the  transducer where it was captured and used for image formation. During propagation of the transverse wave, the stress field is  directed perpendicular to the direction of propagation which  results in an increased sensitivity to small cracks in the top  wafer. These cracks were not found by optical inspection but  are clearly revealed in transverse-wave acoustic imaging. The  criteria for exciting a transverse mode in this sample was  sufficiently fulfilled by defocusing the transducer from the  surface to the interface. The surface of the sample was then in  the near field of the acoustic lens where the wave fronts are  curved, allowing to reach the critical angle for exciting the  transverse mode by an incident compressional wave.


Extending Package Inspection Capability with Acoustic  Ghz-Microscopy:  Potential, Application and Challenges


Conventional acoustic microscopy operates in the frequency  band 5 - 350 MHz and sufficiently addresses many nondestructive inspection tasks. However, when it comes to novel  microelectronic integration architectures, containing  substantially decreasing feature dimensions, the required  resolution capabilities of conventional SAM may be  insufficient. The resolution of an imaging technique is  inevitably connected to the wavelength of the sensing signals. The wavelength


is related to the velocity


of the wave and


its frequency


according to equation 16:


[16]


This relationship shows that the wavelength decreases with  increasing frequency of the wave. Thus, when the frequency of  the acoustic wave increases, the lateral resolution capabilities  should as well. Acoustic GHz-microscopy employs ultrasonic  signals in the low GHz band, enabling imaging resolution in the  1 µm regime. However, acoustic attenuation increases  exponentially with frequency, requiring adapting the inspection  equipment accordingly. At the frequency of 1 GHz the coupling  fluid water seriously attenuates the signal. Therefore, the focal  length is shortened to 40 µm – 80 µm to keep the propagation  path short. In combination with a strongly focused acoustic lens  with an aperture angle of 100°, this technique allows for surface  and sub-surface imaging with high sensitivity and resolution. Due to the strongly focused sound field and the phenomena  described above, even slightly defocusing the sample surface  leads to angular incidence of the incoming wave front and thus, to inevitable excitation of additional wave modes like  transverse waves or Rayleigh waves.  These can be used not  only to improve imaging detail and contrast, but also to pave  the way for quantitative parameter estimation.

Even though the signal amplitudes in GHz-SAM are rather low, the application of lock-in techniques combined with spatial  oversampling and analogue pre-processing of the signals allows  for rapid image acquisition. A more detailed description of the  working principle can be found [48].


The current section illuminates the potential of acoustic GHzmicroscopy for applications where the sensitivity, sub-surface  sensitivity and/ or the lateral resolution capabilities of  conventional SAM do not suffice.


• layout-aware diagnosis [4, 5],


• cell-internal diagnosis [6-9],


• scan chain diagnosis [10-20],


• at-speed diagnosis [21], and


• iterative diagnosis [22].


An advanced tool is capable of diagnosing defects  down to a logic net segment and physical polygon, and it can differentiate between defects internal to  the cells vs. defects in the interconnect. Newer tools  can also accurately classify a wide range of defect  types. In addition, iterative diagnosis can be used to  increase the initial diagnosis resolution.


Diagnosis can now be used in conjunction with


• on-chip compression [23-25] and


• logic built-in-self-test (BIST) [26].


These advances have significantly improved the  value of diagnosis for failure analysis. Current  diagnosis tools produce results directly applicable to  the failure analysis task at hand. They represent the  results for example in terms of physical location, including the x/y/layer coordinates of a possible  defect location. They also consume production test  patterns even for designs using embedded pattern  compression techniques, no longer requiring special ‘diagnosis only’ test patterns bypassing the  compression circuitry. In the remainder of this  article, we will review many of advances in more  detail and discuss their merits for the failure analysis  engineer.


Beyond the immediate needs of the failure analysis  engineer, diagnosis advances have also paved the  way for using this technology in other areas like yield


loss analysis and subsequent yield improvements [4, 27-29] or test quality improvements [21, 30]. ([28] can be found in this edition of the desk reference  manual.) The key here is the low cost of diagnosis  and the significantly faster time to root cause  compared to traditional yield improvement  methods.


In the following, we use terms and methods from  scan testing. Please see test overview article “IC  Testing: Background and Directions” [31] of this  edition of the desk reference manual for an  explanation of the terms and methods.


2. How Diagnosis Works


Scan diagnosis leverages some of the same  technology that is used in automatic test pattern  generation (ATPG). Most scan diagnosis tools can  only diagnose failures in ATPG or BIST patterns that  leverage internal scan chains or scan-based DFT such  as logic BIST. A typical diagnosis system requires a  gate level representation of the design, ATPG test  patterns, and fail data from the tester. In addition to  scan ATPG tests, functional tests may be used for  screening manufacturing defects. A snap-shot of  observable scan cells or scan-dump can be captured  at a give cycle of a functional test, and analysis of  faults around the window of failing cycles can be  used effectively to diagnosis silicon defects [32].


Each failing pin/cycle on the tester corresponds to a  failure captured in a scan cell for a particular scan  pattern. The first step in the diagnosis process is to  trace the design backwards from the failing scan cell  then to identify which suspects that could cause  these failures. A suspect is typically a particular fault  type (such as stuck-at, bridge, or open) in a  particular location (net). An example suspect would  be “stuck-at-0 fault on the A input of the OR gate /design/module/inst023.” The suspect lists are then  compared across multiple failures (multiple scan  patterns, multiple scan cells), and this process helps  narrow down the suspect list. Simulation is also  performed to see if any of the suspects would cause  any additional failures other than those observed on  the tester.


Suspects are then ranked and scored based on how  well the suspect explains the failures. For instance, suspect /design/module/inst023/A stuck-at-0 might  explain 8 out of the 10 failures on the testers, and  would cause 3 additional patterns to fail. This  suspect would receive a lower score than a suspect  that explains all the 10 failures and would not cause  any additional failures. Since the suspects are based  on fault models and not the actual defects, it is  common to observe less-than-perfect diagnosis  results.


The two most common metrics in measuring  diagnosis results are accuracy and resolution.  Accuracy is a measurement of how well the  diagnosis tool has identified the true defective net(s) and the true defect type. For a given list of  candidates, accuracy is a binary decision: Is the true  candidate on the list, yes or no. Resolution measures  the area of the defective location captured by a  suspect, that is, the bounding box of a defect. For  logic-based diagnosis tools, the resolution equals the  combined area of all reported nets. Logic-based  diagnosis tools do not know where two nets  potentially bridge or where an open on a net might  be located; thus, the whole net must be searched to  find the defect. Layout-aware diagnosis with its  access to the polygon level easily finds and reports, for example, the bridge location in x/y/layer terms, or the few polygons on a net, where an open defect  might be.


3. A Typical Diagnosis Flow


A typical diagnosis flow requires three sets of inputs: A gate level description (i.e. model) of the design, the test stimuli applied on the tester and the failures  recorded by the tester (a.k.a. datalogs) when these  stimuli are applied.


Diagnosis flow starts by processing the datalogs. The  datalogs record failures in terms of pin names and  test cycle numbers which are dependent on the  specific tester that is being used. By analyzing the  DFT architecture of the design, these failures are  mapped to scan operation ID numbers that have  failed, and particular scan cells or primary output


signals in the design where the faulty behavior was  observed. In the end, a list of failures in terms of test  stimuli and design signals, which are independent of  the tester architecture, is obtained.


Diagnosis execution starts by consuming the list of  failures produced by datalog processing step. The  tool identifies the cone of logic that supports the  observed failures and reasons that the defect  location must be contained in that cone. It  enumerates candidate locations, simulates each  candidate using the test stimuli and ranks them by  comparing the simulated behavior to actual faulty  behavior.  In the end, a list of candidate locations is  reported by decreasing likelihood of containing the  actual defect.


4. Making Diagnosis Work in your


Workflow


In this section we described the various  requirements and other considerations that typically  need to be taken into account to set up a full  working scan diagnosis system.

Scan test content is applied on the tester along with  the other manufacturing test content which includes  cache tests, functional tests, IO tests, and parametric  tests. Failures can be captured in-line during  production tests by setting up a fail flow which is  exercised on failing parts (dice at wafer sort or  packaged parts). However, in order to minimize  overall test time budgets, the increase in test-time  due to fail data collection needs to be limited  relative to the total test-time. A test flow to collect  fail data is illustrated in Figure 1. The scan test  content includes a scan-system test to determine if  scan-system is functional. After the scan-system test, scan chain shift tests and scan ATPG capture tests  are applied.


Usually just the production tests can be used for fail  data collection. In addition some other tests are  usually added with negligible impact to tester  memory. In addition to the traditional (1100) repeat  scan chain pattern which detects stuck at and all  transition fault types, some additional chain tests are


added. If the transition defects cause delays longer  than one bit, then shift out value of this traditional  chain test pattern will be a constant 0 or constant 1, which will be incorrectly interpreted as stuck-at-0 or  stuck-at-1. To avoid this pitfall, (0) repeat and (1) repeat chain patterns are also included. These two  patterns will not cause any failures for transition  type defects. Also a slow changing pattern, 16 zeros  followed by 16 ones repeat pattern are added. This  pattern can detect large delay defects. Table 1  shows these patterns and the type of defects they  detect including stuck-at (SA), slow-to-rise/fall (STR/F) and fast-to-rise/fall (FTR/F).


Table 1: Scan Chain Tests


Since failing data collection requires additional test  time, a trade-off needs to be done to ensure  adequate data collection while minimizing costs. To  maintain diagnosis quality and resolution, we need  to collect adequate failure information from failing  scan test. However, too many failures collected can  result in wasted test time with minimal additional  benefit.


The data logging the first 100 failing scan operations  are usually adequate for diagnosis of logic failures.  Diagnosis of scan chain defects require capture tests
