where ∆x is the pixel size in the magnetic ﬁeld image, and∆B is the rms magnetic ﬁeld noise in each pixel. For a hard cut-oﬀ ﬁlter, a = 2.873, with the parameter a varying depending on the ﬁlter used. Equation 3 is an implicit function of z/s, which means that the spatial resolution depends linearly on the sensor-sample separation. Numerical solutions of 3 show that all other parameters only enter logarithmically, reaﬃrming the fact that the most important parameter impacting resolution is separation distance,z.


From an experimental/practical approach, an excellent example was presented in the paper by M. Hechtl [7] in which he studied how distance impacts current detectability, resolution and failure detectability in a very graphical way on a real failing device. Figure 4 shows current density images from identical scans from the back side of a ﬂip-chip mounted integrated circuit. The die was thinned down from 200µm to 5µm while all other scanning conditions were kept identical. Obviously, the thinner the die, the closer the sensor-to-current distance.


Figure 4: Current density image from backside scanning decreasing the separation distance from 200µm to 5µm. Images courtesy of M. Hechtl, Inﬁneon.


At about 75µm, the rectangular shape of the on die current paths are distinct enough, a clear sign of resolution


improvement. It is remarkable that the image reveals not only on-die currents but also interposer current paths that are further away.


A second important parameter is current, as many times the device or failure type limits it. The eﬀect of current into the resulting images acquired with MFI was also studied by Hechtl in the same paper [7] on the same failing device. Figure 5 shows current density images of identical scans were all parameters were identical except for varying the current for each scan from 1mA to 25µA. The impact of reducing the current on the sharpness, resolution and clarity of the images is evident but clearly less than the eﬀect of distance.


Figure 5: Current density image from backside scanning decreasing the current from 1mA to 25µA for a 5µm thinned down die. Images courtesy of M. Hechtl, Inﬁneon.


The actual defect location, a defective MIM capacitor that was shorted, is clearly visible in all images as the brightest signal on the center right area of the images. Two things are worth noticing: ﬁrst, the GMR sensor has enough sensitivity to locate the defect when applying just 25µA of current to the device. The intensity of the current in the failure area indicates that even lower current could have been used and the defect could have still been detected.


Although details on the circuit parts that carry less current are vanishing progressively as the current decreases,1mA of current is enough to reveal many details of the circuitry. Second, sensitivity and resolution are linked together. The lower the current, the less details of the circuit can be obtained. This is a direct consequence of the Standard Inverse as shown in equation 3 [18].


Space Domain Reﬂectometry for Opens


Open failures do not allow, by deﬁnition, the passing of current. DC and low frequency signals, normally used in electrical probing of integrated circuits (IC), carry no net current through the defective trace because of the open boundary , and thus, a diﬀerent technique needs to be used to localize them. If the probing signal is brought into radio-frequency (RF) or microwave range, the defective trace can be viewed as a transmission line terminated with an open circuit formed by the open defect. The injection of (RF) signals allows signals to propagate through the circuit, similar to time domain reﬂectometry (TDR)


[19] or Electro-Optic Terahertz Pulse Reﬂectometry [20]up to the failure point, that act as a reﬂection boundary to the RF signal, at which point, the signal reﬂects back.


When a continuous wave signal is injected into an open trace from one end, the open boundary reﬂects back nearly all the incident power, similarly to TDR, while no RF power is transmitted through the open (Fig. 6). This is because at RF frequencies the open impedance (≈MΩ)is much greater than the trace characteristic impedance(≈ 50Ω). The superposition of the incident and reﬂectedsignals creates a standing wave [21, 22], where the zeros(nodes) and extrema (antinodes) of the standing wave remain at the same ﬁxed positions, and the resulting wave mostly disappears in the vicinity of the open.


Figure 6: Representation of the current standing-wave (red)formed in a transmission line due to the superposition of the signals incident onto (blue), and reﬂected from (green) the open boundary. N and AN indicate the nodes and antinodes, respectively.


By modeling the open as a parallel circuit with resistance R and capacitance C, we can obtain for its impedance


Zopen =R1 + (ωRC)2+ iωR2C1 + (ωRC)2


(4)


where ω is the angular frequency of the RF probing signal.


For the reﬂection, Γ, and transmission, T , coeﬃcients of the incident probing wave one obtains


Γ =Zopen−Z0Zopen+Z0≈ 1− 2Z0Zopen≈ 1T = 1− Γ ≈ 0


(5)


Where the approximation is due to Z0  Zopen. Fromthis, it is easy to see how the open reﬂects nearly all this, it is easy to see how the open reflects nearly all thethe incident RF power back to the feed-line, while no power is transmitted past the open.


Numerical simulations with ﬁnite elements forward simulation conﬁrmed that for a typical trace the RF current vanishes at the open location (see Fig. 7). Note how the signal amplitude decays towards zero in the proximity of the open.


The amplitude of the standing wave current along the trace can be found as follows


I = 2PI=2√Z0sin(γx) ≈VzoPZ0γx ∝√Pωx


(6)


where P is the power of the RF probing signal, γ =1/2/c = 2π/λ is the propagation constant of the e1/2/c = 2π/λ is the propagation constant of the tracetrace transmission line with  the eﬀective dielectric constant, transmission line with e the effective dielectric constant, cc the speed of light, λ the wavelength, and x is the position along the trace. In a loss-less trace, which is an excellent approximation for the package wiring, the standing wave amplitude , Isw, varies in space as Isw = 2I0 sin(βx), where I0 is the incident (or reﬂected) wave amplitude, β = 2π/λ is the wave-number with λ the wavelength of the probing signal, and x is the position along the trace. Since typical trace dimensions are much smaller than λ (≈ 1m for RFsignals), there is no phase variation within the trace making λx 1. Therefore, in the vicinity of the open, the RFsignal intensity varies linearly due to sin(βx) ≈ signal intensity varies linearly due to sin(βx) ≈βx.βx.Detecting the location where signal intensity vanishes is the basis for open detection using magnetic ﬁeld imaging.


Figure 7: Theoretically calculated magnetic ﬁeld amplitude near the open location, marked by the red arrow.


Recent advances expanding the bandwidth of operation of SQUID and GMR sensors have allowed the localization of


open circuit failures by detecting the RF magnetic ﬁelds associated with the injected signals. The basic method for acquisition is identical to that for current imaging explained above, but in this case we will detect RF magneticﬁelds, which required modiﬁcations to the electronics and sensor mode of operation to increase the bandwidth [23].


Unlike in TDR, where the spatial resolution is deﬁned by the pulse electrical length and by precise knowledge of the velocity factor of the sample, the spatial resolution in space domain reﬂectometry (SDR) is determined by the SQUID sensor size and/or SQUID-sample separation, similarly to the current imaging case. This is due to a near-ﬁeld nature of interaction between the sample and SQUID sensor [24]. An estimate shows that 1mW of RF power injected at 100MHz into the open-circuited 50Ω transmission line creates a standing wave where the current amplitude drops below the SQUID sensitivity limit at about 20µm ”in front“ of the open.


The SDR localization method is based on following the signal spatially in the acquired image up to the point where it disappears, location that should coincide with the physical location of the failure. As we are following the signal in space, rather that analyzing timing associated with the signal as is the case for TDR, the technique is named space domain reﬂectometry.


Failure analysis for modern electronic devices and systems,due to industry requirements and the device characteristics(size, structure, composition, etc.) impose serious requirements and constraints to the sensors and scanning platform at the core of this technology. There are three main requirements that are linked: Need of high resolution, high magnetic ﬁeld sensitivity (and thus, low noise ﬁgures) and the geometry of the sensor itself. We will review these and focus speciﬁcally on two of the most common and successfully used sensors: SQUID and GMR as they ﬁt these requirements.


The diﬀerences in magnetic ﬁeld explained above are small and therefore require a very careful analysis between the good and failing parts.


This requires improvements over conventional technology in two areas. First, the instrumentation for current imaging requires more precise automated control of the sample setup and data acquisition. The scan conditions must be as similar as possible between the good and failing parts, so that an eﬀective comparison can be made. Secondly, even with careful sample setup and data acquisition, there will still be misalignment between the two images, and potential signal diﬀerences due to diﬀerent working distances, or even part deformations (e.g. warping). These diﬀerences need to be sorted out from those due to the high resistance


defect. For this, advances have been made in image diﬀerence analysis (IDA) to assist in the identiﬁcation of failing defects.


The following example, extracted from [48], is a ﬂip-chip bump failure. TDR was used to determine that the failure was likely in the interconnect since the signal in the failing part did not get far beyond the substrate, as shown in Figure 22.


Figure 22: TDR results indicate a resistive open that is close to, but beyond the package substrate.


This failure was between power and ground for which there were several bumps. TDR did not deﬁnitively indicate that the problem was in the bumps nor did it identify which bump had the problem. Magnetic current imaging was used to further isolate the problem. Figure 23 shows the region of interest from the IDA image overlaid on the CAD for the particular structure involved.


Figure 23: (Left) IDA results corresponding to the HR ﬂipchip bump damage overlaid on the CAD. (Right) Zoomed-in 3D rendering of the IDA results presented at left.


The defect was isolated with an accuracy of ≈ 30µm andveriﬁed by PFA as shown in Figure 24.


IDA on magnetic ﬁeld images has successfully localized high resistance defects to this same level of accuracy on a variety of defects, including cracked traces and delaminated vias. This 30µm localization by IDA is entirely nondestructive and represents about an order of magnitude improvement over TDR.


Figure 24: Optical image of cross-sectioned failing bump. Nonwet part of bump is circled.


Open Failure


Open failure detection using SDR relies in ﬁnding the location where the resulting RF standing wave decays to zero. It is important that we can isolate this decay associated with the open from others that could be associated to the presence of interconnects, for example. In ref. [49],the authors examined two ﬂip-chip devices with identical structure: a good device and a defective sample with a open failure due to cracking of a C4 bump. RF signal was injected in both cases through the same solder ball in the package using a single probe. The probe signal wire (center of coax conductor) was connected to the solder ball with a needle while the rest of the device was left ﬂoating. Both samples were then successively imaged with a magneticﬁeld imaging system with SDR capability. The resulting RF magnetic images were then converted into RF density signal using the standard inverse technique. Fig. Figure shows a comparison of the results obtained on the good device (top images) and the failing device (bottom row).


Leftmost images are B/W optical images of the scan area and used to register features in the magnetic or signal density images to their physical location in the samples.


Red/blue images are false color images of the measured RF ﬁeld spatial distribution. Images to their right are two diﬀerent color scheme rendering of the RF signal density distribution calculated form the RF magnetic data using the standard inversion technique. Rightmost images show the signal density amplitude proﬁle along the trace conducing to the C4 bump (yellow line in the optical image and thin blue line in the signal density images).


One can clearly see a diﬀerence between the signal propagation in the two samples. While in both cases the signal abruptly stops at the location marked with the yellow arrow, the location where signal gets into the C4 and is thus conduced vertically into the sample, the way the signal disappears is diﬀerent. In the good sample, signal amplitude is constant right up to the C4 bump, conﬁrming the absence of an impedance mismatch between package and die.


Such behavior is expected since SDR operates at frequencies native to integrated circuits, at which the impedance mismatch is minimal by design. In the defective sample,


Figure 25: Comparison of non-defective (upper row) and defective (bottom row) results. From left to right: optical image of the samples; magnetic ﬁeld image at 190MHz; RF signal density; same RF signal density using a rainbow color scheme ,and signal intensity proﬁle along the yellow line in the optical image.


however, the open C4 bump causes gradual reduction in the intensity of the signal towards the open, where it ﬁnally vanishes. It must be noticed also that this decay follows the expected linear decay of the standing wave, as described before.


Short Circuit in Three-Die TSV Sample


The sample investigated in this work is a triple-layer stack,in which two layers of a 50µm thick test chip (Chip 1 and Chip 2 in Fig. Figure) were assembled on a 200µm thick bottom chip (Chip 0 in Fig. 26). The test chips were manufactured by IMEC using its standard 65nm CMOS backend-of-line (BEOL) process, 5 × 50µm via-middle TSVtechnology. Further details of the test vehicle can be found in Ref. [42].


Figure 26: Cross-sectional sketch of the three-die TSVconnected device.


There are TSV daisy chains between all the stacked


chips. A group of interwoven daisy chains, named a1 and a2, connect the bottom chip (Chip 0) and the ﬁrst stacked top chip (Chip 1). A second set of daisy chains, b1 and b2,connect the middle chip (Chip 1) to the top chip (Chip 2).


The a1 and a2 chains should not be electrically connected.


Similarly, none of the a chains should be electrically connected to any of the b chains. Figure 27 shows a top view of the device with the probe area (yellow box) and the scan area (blue box) where we identify the a1, a2, (orange) b1, and b2 (green) daisy chains. Electrical testing,however, showed electrical connection between the a1 and a2 chains, pointing to a short that needed to be localized.


The role of the b1 and b2 daisy chains will be explained later. MFI was used to locate the defect position. This information was then passed for physical validation using FIB [50].


Figure 27: Top view of the device. The yellow area shows the probing area and the blue area the scanning area.


The signal was injected into the respective daisy chains by probing the two V + to V − on the bottom chip. To send a signal between daisy chain a1 and a2 one could probe a1V − to a2V −, a1V + to a2V + or the other four combinations. To reduce the number of scans, four combinations were used, resulting in a total of four scans: a1V + to a1V −to identify the a1 daisy chain circuit, a2V + to a2V − to identify the a2 daisy chain circuit, a1V − to a2V −, and a1V + to a2V +. The last two scans should pass current through the failure. The four MR sensor scans are shown in Fig. 28.


The bright yellow current seen in Fig. 28 is from surface current at the top of Chip 2, meaning that in these speciﬁc locations, the current is coming up to the top surface of the chip stack. However, from the layout, no current should be traveling in this TSV layer. Therefore we can make a preconclusion that there has to be at least one or more shorts where the signal reaches the top surface (Chip 2)seen on the left of the data scans in Fig. 28. We see that the b1− b2 daisy chains also have current, something thatshould not happen as these daisy chains are not connected to a1− a2 daisy chains, indicating an additional short.For better understanding of the failure, high-resolution


Figure 28: Current density images from the four acquired scans overlaid with the optical device images showing abnormal current patterns. Bright yellow current color means the current is closer to the top surface, while darker orange color means current is farther away from the surface.


scans were compared directly with the layout (Fig. 29).


Figure 29: High resolution scans overlaid on optical image.


Bottom image is top view of the CAD layout used for reference.


TSV pairs 18, 23, and 28 (counting from right as shown in Fig.


28) seems to be the shorted TSV pairs.


From Fig. 29 one can see that the current enters the top layer (Chip 2) at TSV 18 and goes back down again to Chip 1 at TSV 28. We expect to ﬁnd at least two shorts at these two locations when using plasma FIB. In addition it was found that daisy chains b also conducted current,indicating a short between chains a and b.


As FIB results show in Fig. 30, a short was found between the two BEOL layers of Chip 1, causing the current to leak into Chip 2. This result indicates a potential issue in the BEOL process of the test wafers used in this work. It may be related to a too thin metal layer which resulted in a local etching of the low-k material and consequent ﬁlling with Cu in the subsequent process step. The result also suggests that the short measured at this location is not


caused by the assembly of this triple layer stack.


Figure 30: Plasma FIB large-volume removal of the three-stack TSV sample with short. Left top inset is zoom-in into the Chip 1/Chip 2 area. Top right inset is further magniﬁcation into the shorted structures, as indicated by red arrows.


3D Fault Isolation using 3D Solver


Magnetic ﬁeld imaging 3D fault isolation capability has been proven, as mentioned before, in a series of cases. Here we present a diﬃcult case of a low resistance short in a complex 2.5D packaged device combining High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and an ASIC with a Si interposer (Fig.


31)and was found to have a signal pin short failure. Full details can be found in Ref. [11].


Figure 31: Complex packaged device comprised of two HBM stacks and an ASIC on a Si interposer.


The device was scanned in a commercial magnetic ﬁeld imaging system with a SQUID sensor. BGAs connecting a failing signal pin and electrical ground were identiﬁed and connected using probes from the bottom to allow the top


of the Si devices to be raster scanned under the SQUID Sensor.


The resulting images are shown in Fig. 32. Left image shows the optical image of a scan of the whole device.


Center image shows the magnetic ﬁeld measured while the right image shows the current density image computed from the magnetic ﬁeld. Note that all images are registered to each other, so anomalies or regions of interest in the current density can be readily identiﬁed with their physical location in the device. Note the presence of a sharp current density peak (bright yellow) marked by the green cursor. The presence of a large signal spreading over the device, associated with the large network in the failure, is also noticeable.


Figure 32: MFI scan results: left, optical; center, magneticﬁeld and right current density image.


For shorts, as the defect is commonly smaller in size than the circuits involved, he current density is expected to increase at the failure location. This is shown as a bright peak in the current density image. Although there could be other natural occurrences of current density increase,the defect normally presents itself as an abnormally sharp peak which makes it easily recognizable. In other situations, a good device, or knowledge about the circuits involved can help to identify the actual defect.


One other way to verify that the peak of interest is indeed associated with the defect is to access it using diﬀerent pin combinations. As the defect is common to all of them,regardless of how we connect, the identifying peak in the current density should show up in all the diﬀerent scans. In order to improve localization accuracy, we acquired higher resolution scans on the region of interest (ROI). Taking advantage of the large network associated with the defect can be accessed from multiple BGAs, we acquired diﬀerent scans using diﬀerent BGAs. These additional scans can also help compensate for undesirable eﬀects on the peak introduced by the surrounding active circuits.


Figure 33 shows the resulting localization image on the ROI. Left image shows the optical image of the ROI along with peak position (green cursor) and a reference ﬁducial selected at the corner of an on-board capacitor (pink cursors). The distance between these cursors is used as coordinates to designate the failure location. This provides lateral (XY) localization of the defect and these coordinates were used as guidance when using the 3D XRM for validation.


Figure 33: MFI scan results: left, optical; center, magneticﬁeld and right current density image.


Once the XY location is obtained, we proceeded to determine the vertical (Z) location of the failure. This is done using the 3D solver approach [8, 6, 10] and uses only the magnetic ﬁeld data. After an initial current path is determined (from the magnetic data itself or from the current density computed before), the 3D solver modiﬁes the current path in the three dimensions optimizing the ﬁt to the measured magnetic ﬁeld. In the process, we obtain critical geometrical information such as distance to the sensor and vertical separation between currents. This provides the desired vertical localization of the defect.


Results are shown in Figure 34. Left image (a) shows a 3D rendering of part of the current path calculated by the 3D solver. Right image (b) shows a top view. The red segment corresponds to the short. Vertical distances are in microns.


Actual distance below the surface of the ASIC is calculated(after compensating for device surface-to-sensor values) to be 1193µm from the sensor. Only some of the currents paths are shown for the sake of clarity.


Figure 34: Left, frontal view of some of the paths computed by the 3D solver. Red segment corresponds to the short.


Right,cross-section sketch of the device showing vertical location of the defect relative to the SQUID sensor. 3D solver provides 1193µm while actual physical location as found by 3D XRM is 1130µm, resulting in ∆z = 63µm.


The XYZ coordinates for the suspected failure location from the 3D MFI tool were passed to a commercial 3D


XRM system for fault validation. Scan on the ROI with 1mm/voxel resolution on a 1× 1× 1mm3 volume (80keVenergy beam, 4 hour scanning) quickly revealed the failure,as shown in Figure 35.


Figure 35: 3D XRM image (device in-plane view) showing the defect. Material can be seen bridging two C4 bump landing pads.


The material clearly bridges the C4 bump landing pads on the interposer, at the TSV/C4 bump interface. Virtual cross-section and selective plane image capability allows to also isolate the defect vertically (Fig. 36). In addition, 3D XRM reveals valuable information about the geometry of the defect (shape, dimensions and thickness), as shown in Fig. 36.


Figure 36: 3D XRM can provide additional details about the defect, such as shape, dimensions and thickness, The 3D reconstruction shows a planar view of the defect, total length of≈ 180µm by ≈ 45µm (≈ 5µm at the narrowest point). Thisview also reveals the relative position of the ROI within the 3D structure of the sample, which can guide cross-section analysis.


3D XRM conﬁrmed the XYZ location of the defect predicted by 3D magnetic ﬁeld imaging.


Summary and Future Directions


The examples presented here demonstrate that magnetic current imaging can be a very eﬀective means of fault isolation in die, packages and assemblies. One of the factors making this technology unique is its ability to image current, regardless of voltage or power dissipation, in an integrated circuit or package in a non-contact, nondestructive way. Since low frequency magnetic ﬁelds are not aﬀected by any of the materials in an integrated circuit assembly,this technique is especially beneﬁcial in situations where the defect is buried under layers of metal, silicon, or encapsulation materials where other techniques are very limited.


Many defects can be imaged for coarse localization without any deprocessing of the sample at all using the high sensitivity of a SQUID sensor.


High resolution scans with a magnetoresistive sensor may require deprocessing, but submicron resolution can be achieved when the sensor is close to the source. The capability of SQUIDs to work at large distances due to their sensitivity makes them ideally suited for isolating defects in packaged devices. They can be used to isolate defects between package, die and interconnect. This high sensitivity allows them to detect currents in the 100’s of nanoamps even in packaged assemblies, and enables the detection of subtle diﬀerences in current paths between good and failing devices. The latter capability enables isolation of high resistance defects like cracked ﬂip-chip bumps and delaminated vias in packages. After physical analysis reveals the defect, magnetic current- imaging by SQUIDs or magnetoresistive sensors can be used to uniquely verify the exact current path and validate the electrical fault.


Incorporation of RF ﬁeld detection capability for both sensors allowed for the detection of open failures using Space Domain Reﬂectometry. This additional bandwidth of operation for the sensors can open the door to high-speed data acquisition for waveform extraction which could provide a means of probing switching currents rather than voltages. 3D capability, achieved by the use of the 3D solver also provides invaluable information to the analyst,allowing to obtain location of the failure laterally and vertically. In addition, the 3D solver allows to map currents in 3D. Quantitative current measurements on test structures could provide valuable data to designers for improving models that would ultimately speed new circuit design.


With the combination of SQUID and magnetoresistive sensors; high-bandwidth and Space Domain Reﬂectometry to localize opens, and 3D fault isolation capability provided by the 3D solver approach, magnetic current imaging has the capability to meet the fault isolation needs of today’s complex structures, including stacked die packaging, and densely populated die with numerous levels of metal. Coupling this technology with advancements in other techniques will provide the failure analyst with a complementary set of tools to isolate the defects of today and tomorrow.

Fault isolation using Time Domain Reflectometry, Electro Optical Terahertz Pulse  Reflectometry and Time Domain Transmissometry


Hemachandar Tanukonda Devarajulu1, Deepak Goyal1


1Intel Corporation, 5000 W Chandler Boulevard, Chandler, Arizona, United States 85226


hemachandar.tanukonda.devarajulu@intel.com,  deepak.goyal@intel.com


Mayue Xie2


Microsoft Corp, One Microsoft Way, Redmond, WA 98052


mayue.xie@microsoft.com


Time-domain based characterization methods, mainly timedomain reflectometry (TDR) and time-domain transmissometry (TDT), have been used to locate faults in twisted cables, telegraph lines and connectors in the electrical and  telecommunication industry since the industry’s early days. They were successfully adopted to electronics industry for  transmission line of printed circuit board (PCB) and  interconnectors between package and PCB [1, 2]. Fundamentally, both methods directly characterize the  electrical path impedance by analyzing the received signal as a  function of time as incident electrical signals are continuously  injected onto the conductor. Hence they are very effective in  finding the defect and locating its location. The incident signals  are usually discrete low voltage step or pulse, which make them  safe for fragile defects without causing recovery as faced by  many thermal methods. They are also the most efficient fault  isolation methods as electrical signal travels along the  conductor at the speed close to light and a curve can be obtained  almost instantly once connection is made.


The main challenge of applying TDR/TDT to high-density  substrate, first-level interconnect and advanced packages is its  resolution relative to signal trace length [3]. A Traditional TDR  can hardly resolve the start and end of a package trace in many  of newest packages, not to mention features in-between. Two  things have been introduced to address these challenges: one is  to use higher frequency signal close to 100GHz, the second is  to use impulse signal vs step. These two improvements are  equally important in dramatically improving fault isolation  accuracy, essentially bringing traditional TDR to high  resolution EOTPR and TDR/TDT.


In this paper, first we will provide a brief review of traditional  TDR and their application limitations to advanced packages in  today’s semiconductor industry. Then the paper will introduce  EOTPR and discuss how its improvements of using high  frequency impulse signal addressed those application  challenges and quickly made it a well-adopted tool in the  industry during the past ten years. EOTPR is a time-domain  reflectometry tool and is very effective for most failures. There  are a few challenges remaining to be resolved, which include  long and branched circuits with short failure. The third part of  this paper introduces a new method which combines impulse


signal and TDT concept. By combining the resolution benefit  from the impulse signal and longer distance from TDT due to  one-way only signal detection, this method was shown to be  every effective in addressing long trace defects in large or  stacked 2.5D or 3D packages. The paper further shows that it  will cover a much wider failures using combo TDR and TDT  method. Cases studies and application notes will be shared and  discussed for each technique. Lastly, application benefits and  limitations of these techniques (TDR, EOTPR and combo  TDR/TDT) will be summarized and compared. As packaging  technology becomes a key product enabler and technology  integrator, the industry is seeing more variations of packages  and at the same time, those packages are becoming more  complex for fault isolation. The main objective of the paper is  to help failure analysis engineers understand the working  principle of these techniques, their pros and cons, and learn  from examples on how to apply the right time-based fault  isolation technique for fault isolation. On the other hand, timedomain based electrical fault isolation methods are  indispensable tools for the electronics and semiconductor  failure analysis community. The second objective of the paper  is to update the industry their current capability status and bring  more interest to these techniques, so that the community can  further advance their techniques and applications.


I. Time Domain Reflectometry


TDR is a measurement technique to characterize a transmission  line based on its reflected waveform   of an injected step signal. An electrical discontinuity represented by impedance change of  the transmission line induces a reflection signature on the time  domain reflection waveform at the impedance transition point. By analyzing the magnitude, time of flight and shape of the  reflected waveform signature, the nature of the impedance  variation in a transmission line can be determined [4]. It is a  popular method for design optimization of high-speed  interconnects, packaging, and devices by minimizing the signal  reflection caused by the interconnect discontinuities resulting  from bends, steps, vias, etc. TDR can also be used for FI of  packages, interconnects, and circuits. When a defect in the  circuit causes an electrical failure, this failure is an electrical  discontinuity by nature, and can be identified by TDR based on  its reflected waveform analysis. Furthermore, because a failure  or defect is also an “abnormal” point deviating from a “known  good” unit waveform, additional techniques for analyzing  waveforms were developed unique to failure analysis


applications. For example, by comparing the failure unit  waveform with the good unit waveform, the failure location can  be determined more accurately to detect small variation due to  marginal failures [2].


Figure 1: TDR instruments from Agilent and Tektronix[6]


TDR tools shown in Figure 1 have been used for finding gross  defects like OPEN and SHORTs in semiconductor packages  over a decade. More details on TDR are described in the paper


[6] by D Smolyansky. There are three most important  specification parameters for TDR tools. The first one is the rise  time, trise, of the reflected signal from the end of the highfrequency probe. Rise time is measured as the time of signal to  rise from 10% to 90% of its maximum value for a step signal. A  related and commonly used term for an impulse signal is fullwidth at half-maximum (FWHM), which refers to the signal  waveform FWHM of its peak value for an impulse signal. For  clean signals approximating a Gaussian shape without much  ringing, the difference between signal rise time and FWHM is  negligible. Signal rise time is related to signal bandwidth by the  equation below [9]


                ℎ =0.35              (1)


Spatial resolution is the minimum distance between two known  features that can result in appreciable difference in reflected  signal waveform. The measurement spatial resolution of the  TDR tool is directly related to signal rise time by


   =             2√        


where c is the speed of light in air, about 3.0 × 108 m/s, eeff is the  dielectric constant of the circuit which is about 4 for most of the  plastic packages. This implies that two small discontinuities, such as two vias in a substrate, can still be resolved as two  separate ones, as long as they are separated by at least ½ the rise  time. Of the incident TDR signal at that location. Otherwise they  will be shown as a single discontinuity in the reflected  waveform and the two discontinuities are not distinguishable


[9].


The second important tool specification parameter of  a TDR is its time-based jitter. Jitter defines how precisely and  repeatedly a signal can be generated and is often in relation to a  reference clock source. It defines the time accuracy of a TDR  tool for obtaining the defect location and is critical for FI  application. The fault detection accuracy is defined as the  difference between the actual defect location and its measured  location. For TDR it is mainly determined by the time-based  jitter of the system under the same measurement bandwidth.  The third important tool specification parameter is  SNR as it directly relates to tool sensitivity along with rise time  and jitter. SNR is defined as 20 log10(s/s). Here, s is the  maximum amplitude of the averaged time domain signal. s is an  estimate of the noise remaining in the average time domain


signal. Sensitivity of TDR determines how much impedance  difference of a failure or design discontinuity needs to be for  the tool to distinguish it from tool noise. A higher SNR allows  the tool to distinguish fine and subtle design elements or  marginal failures from noise. It is important to note that tool  accuracy, resolution, and sensitivity are often characterized  using simple test structures, for example, planar strip lines or  microstrip lines. These test structures are “ideal” for tool  characterization because:


• They have matched impedance profile and very low signal  loss, thus allowing the signal to propagate a very long  distance without too much waveform distortion.


• The effective dielectric constant can be estimated  accurately and does not vary much from location to  location.


In actual packaged devices, however, nets are designed for  lower frequency applications compared to the TDR bandwidth. Thus much of the high-frequency signal may be filtered out  after a certain distance, resulting in reduced actual resolution  and sensitivity. Defect location measurement accuracy will be  affected as well because signal travels through the net bends, transitions, and interconnects with various velocity. Calculating  distance with a single velocity factor will inevitably introduce  calculation error. This is particularly true for 3D packages, where the net will go through various material layers with many  turns and horizontal-vertical- horizontal transitions [9].


When the injecting signal pulse is generated  electrically (e.g., by a diode as in conventional TDR), there are  certain fundamental challenges that limit tool performances. Currently the best commercial tools using a standard diode can  achieve a rise time of less than 10 ps, time-based jitter of less  than 500 femtoseconds, and SNR of 45 dB or better [3]. This  technology can reach an FI accuracy of 75 µm and resolution of  750 µm for an ideal test structure. Tool with such level of  resolution and accuracy is inadequate for most of thin and small  3D packages where the substrate itself may be thinner than 750 µm and interconnects is less than 20 µm. For those package TDR  is not enough to distinguish between the FLI from second-level  interconnect (SLI) because they are closely spaced and show as  a single signature on the reflected waveform [9].


II. Electro Optical Terahertz Pulse Reflectometry


To meet above mentioned challenges, EOTPR has been  developed and further improved to isolate faults in advanced  3D IC packages. It is a unique method of combining electrooptics with improved accuracy and sensitivity [8] and TDR into  EOTPR for its attributes of low time-based jitter, high  resolution, and high sensitivity. The basic idea is to use ultrafast  laser to excite photoconductive switch and generate a highspeed electrical pulse which propagates into device under test (DUT), and after being reflected it is sampled by  photoconductive switch (PCS). Figure 2 illustrates the basic  components involved in the EOTPR system [3]. It contains an  ultrafast laser source, a transceiver module, a high-speed probe, a light detection and modulation module, and a readout and  display instrument. The ultrafast laser source emits a high-speed  optical pulse signal, and is then transmitted to the transceiver  through an umbilical cord. The transceiver box converts the


high-speed optical pulse into an electrical impulse signal which  is then injected into a test structure of the DUT through a highspeed probe. The electrical signal will be reflected back and be  sampled by the transceiver itself to form a reflection waveform.


Figure 2 Terahertz emission and photoconductive switch (PCS) detection [9].


The reflected waveform is thus a representation of the  impedance distribution of the electrical structure under test. The  transceiver box consists of two PCSs, one with the emitter to  produce a high-speed electrical test pulse, and the other with the  receiver to measure the returning electrical signal as a highspeed sampling gate. The electrical waveform is sampled by  varying the delay between the two pulses using the linear stage  and rapid scan delay line, thus achieving a jitter-free equivalent  time sampling. The two switches are integrated together to form  the transceiver module which is coupled to a high- frequency (110 GHz) probe. The emitter PCS is biased with a voltage to  achieve high quality signal generation [9].


The newest system has achieved tool specs of 5.7 ps rise time, 64 dB SNR, and 150 mm testing range. This system has some  distinct advantages over conventional fully electronic sampling  TDR system as summarized by Table .1. This tool has achieved  10 µm accuracy on test measurements following the test  procedures described in Ref. [3]. The results are plotted  qualitatively in Figure. 3 showing a linear relationship between  the maximum peak position in each of the reflected signals (repeated 10 times for each point) and the micrometer position. Statistics analysis of the peak positions shows that the level of  confidence for the reflection waveform shift to a different  position when the probe is moved by 10 µm is larger than the  six-sigma value of 99.99%. These improvements are necessary  for the feature-based FI for 3D packages [9].


Traditionally, the method of applying TDR/EOTPR for FI is  through waveform comparison—the reflected waveform of  failed electrical structure is evaluated against that of a knowngood unit to identify the failure mode as well as the failing  location within the circuit. There are two challenges for this  methodology: First, it requires multiple waveform collections  and good alignment between units. Secondly the distance  measurement with this method starts from the probe contact  point to the defect location.

The velocity factor through this distance is often not a constant  and varies by location. This is particularly true for 3D packages  when a net goes through multiple vertical interconnects and  different material layers. Both of these will bring measurement  error to the defect localization and diminish the accuracy that  the tool is capable of [9].


To minimize this estimation error due to waveform analysis,     a  feature-based FI method is developed with EOTPR by taking  advantage of its improved resolution and sensitivity. First of  all. modeling is used to correlate the waveform design features


to the design elements of a typical package. These recognizable  features on the waveform include the SLI, the plated-through  hole (PTH), and the FLI, as illustrated by Figure. 4. Then the  correlation is confirmed with experimental data demonstrating  the validity of the feature- based FI method. When the  measurement to the defect location is based on these  recognizable features, effect of unit-to-unit variation and signal  velocity variation on measurement accuracy can be minimized


Figure 4. Key design elements of flip-chip package: these  design elements will provide unique and recognizable features  on the EOTPR waveform [9]


The conventional TDR waveform usually does not show any of  these signatures other than FLI due to tool limitations on  resolution and sensitivity. One TDR case study is shown in  Figure. 5 where the FLI can be determined as the separation  point between the TDR waveforms of the bare substrate and  good reference units. It is indicated that the failure location is  past the FLI point where the failure unit waveform deviates  from that of the reference good unit. But it is very difficult to  pinpoint the failure location in terms of distance to the end  points of the trace or distance to the FLI. Feature- based FI  expands tool capability by correlating EOTPR waveform  signatures to design elements. This becomes possible because  the improvements on EOTPR tool resolution and sensitivity  allow it to pick up the subtle design waveform signatures, such  as trace bends, vias, and interconnects of a typical flip-chip  package. A lower rise time is needed to resolve closely spaced  design elements like vias and trace turns, while a higher SNR is  needed for the tool to pick up the very subtle discontinuity of  these designs. The EOTPR waveforms of the same case are  shown in Figure. 6. Here not only the FLI is clearly identified as  the peak of the bare substrate waveform, additional substrate  design elements including the PTH and vias can be identified  and correlated to the waveform features. This correlation can be  established based on distance comparison between database  design and waveform measurement. Another more accurate  way to confirm the correlation is through modeling using finite  difference time domain method as described in Ref [8].
 Once  these features are identified and correlated to the design, failure  location can be measured from any one of these known features  with more accuracy within a few icro meters. For this case the  failure is at the C4 location as identified by the waveform  comparison and confirmed by the cross section [9].


The feature-based FI method is an important application to  quickly disposition failure to memory, interconnect, or logic die  of an advanced 3D package as these components or processes are  often owned by different identities.


Figure 5 TDR waveform of a typical flip-chip package only  identifies the first-level interconnect based on waveform  comparison between known-good and bare-substrate reference  units [9]


Key design elements can be identified and correlated to  waveform features based on reference waveform analysis or net  characterization. Barbeau et al. [10] demonstrated this  application for a typical stacked die flip-chip 3D package. Consider the 3D package with a cross section previously shown     in Figure. 7a. First, the bulk silicon and metal layers of the top  die were removed to expose the top layer of the µC4 bump. An  EOTPR waveform was then collected (blue curve) and its peak  defines the location of the top of the µC4 bump. This process  was then repeated to define the bottom of the µC4 bump, TSV, FLI, and substrate PTH sequentially. The design and waveform  feature correlation is shown in Figure.7b with key design  elements being identified at the stacked die region. When a unit  failed and its waveform is compared with those known features, defect location can then be obtained by measuring from these  known features, thus quickly identifying the failure component  of the stack to memory, logic die, interposer or substrate of the  stacked package. Further, more accurate failure location can be  obtained based on the distance measurement from the nearest  know features, thus making next step failure analysis easier and  quicker [9].

III. Time Domain Transmissometry


TDR is powerful, non-contact and non-destructive techniques  that have been successfully applied for electrical fault isolation  of 2D packages. Yet it had limited success in 3D packages  particularly for dead open and shorts deeply buried inside. As  for TDR based methods, they send a high frequency electrical


pulse or impulse signal into the trace, and detect the defect  location based on the time-of-flight of the signal to and from the  defect location. It is very effective in for dead open (defect  resistance more than 100K ohms) and dead short (defect  resistance less than 1 ohm) when the defects are close to the  signal input port. Great progress has been made during the past  few years to increase signal frequency and resolution. However, experience shows that as signal frequency increases, signal loss  increases exponentially which limits the tool application for  long trace failure fault isolation required by 3D packages [15]. As a result, the conflicting demands of high resolution and long  signal travel distance bring a well-known dilemma between  resolution and signal propagation faced by the industry that  current tools and techniques can’t address effectively. As for  thermal emission based methods, they do not work for open  failure because low frequency signal can’t be applied to the  failure net. They are most effective for resistive defect when  defect resistance density (resistance/volume) is comparably  higher than that of trace conductor. For most package and Si  backend applications, this means the ideal defect resistance  within the range of 1 ohm and 100K ohms. It is not effective for  dead short where the defect resistance density is the same as  that of trace conductor because the thermal signal generated by  the defect is either minimum or non-distinguishable from that  generated by the trace itself. In summary, fault isolation of dead  open and dead short of long chains remain as the biggest  challenges faced by the 2.5D and 3D packages.
 Failure analysis  has so far largely relied on destructive method and electrical  probing, so called “polishing and probing”, which has low  success rate and is time-consuming [11].


A new method is introduced based on Time Domain  Transmissometry (TDT), and discussed on how it can be  applied to address the challenge mentioned above when TDR  and thermal emission based method fail. First, it discusses the  fundamental limitation of TDR when it is applied to long and  lossy chains of 3D packages with simulation of signal loss in  various transmission lines. Based on this understanding, the  second part of the paper proposes to use TDT to increase signal  detection length for short fault isolation by taking advantage of  the fact that signals can be collected at additional input-output  ports. It discusses how to optimize TDR and TDT data  collection, and introduces equations to achieve significant  improvement of signal detection length while preserving its  high resolution. The third section of the paper discusses the tool  and implementation of the methods. Finally case studies will be  discussed to demonstrate the effectiveness of this new method  in terms of significant improvement in signal detection and fault  isolation accuracy compared to traditional method. The  learning and techniques discussed in this paper aim to drive  industry-wide tool developments to advance long chain fault  isolation capability, and benefit the failure analysis technique  advancement and 3D package development [11].


a. Limitations of TDR for Fault Isolation


Time domain reflectometry (TDR) sends a high frequency radio  frequency signal to the device under test (DUT) and observes  the reflection to obtain the information about the DUT [12]. The  TDR instrument is a very wide bandwidth equivalent sampling


oscilloscope with an internal step generator, which is connected  to the DUT via cables, probes, and fixtures, and delivers a fast  rise time to the DUT, as shown in Figure 8. The superposition  of the incident waveform Vi and the reflected waveform Vr is  acquired by the TDR sampling module and is shown in the TDR  output waveform [13]. Since the TDR signal takes a round-trip  to arrive at the TDR receiver, the emergence of Vr is delayed by  twice the delay time of the cable td[11].


Figure 8: Working principle of TDR and its measurement


setup [11].


There are three factors affecting the fault isolation detection  length: signal path loss, return loss and reflection loss. Path loss  is usually expressed in dB. In its simplest form, the path loss  can be calculated using the formula L=10*log10(4d/) where  L is the path loss in decibels,  is the wavelength and d is the  transmitter-receiver distance in the same units as the  wavelength. Plotting of this signal path loss in Figure 9 shows  that the signal degrades exponentially along the transmission  length, and only 20% of original signal strength remains after  eight times of wavelength.


Magnetic current imaging is always used after electrical test as with most other fault isolation techniques. It can be used to isolate any electrical defect involving any anomalous current. This can be measured as a leakage or a resistance change in the device. For a resistance change, it can be either higher or lower than normal. At the time of this writing, magnetic current imaging is only applicable to static defects (i.e. those that can be held in their failing state). It is also possible to use this technique to image current in a good device for the purpose of verifying a design. This review, however, will focus on fault isolation only.


The particular situation to address will inﬂuence which sensor type to use. This choice is made based on allow121


able working distance and how much current the circuit or defect will tolerate. If the device is packaged, the working distance between the sensor and the current is usually larger than 100µm. In this situation, the sensitivity of the SQUID will produce the best results and require the least amount of deprocessing (potentially none at all). Starting with the SQUID can also be helpful in preserving a defect that might be lost through any deprocessing. If the device is not packaged or the front side of the chip is accessible,then a magnetoresistive sensor can be used to obtain higher resolution. The higher resolution is accomplished by the smaller sensor size and the closer working distance. It is always important to remember that for a near-ﬁeld scanning technique like this, the resolution is limited by the sensor size or the working distance, whichever is larger.


The sensitivity for magnetoresistive sensors is lower, but since they are used much closer to the source current, images of currents as small as 25µA have been obtained [7].


This capability is still improving.


In the most general case of a fully assembled device with a short, the SQUID would be the chosen sensor and used initially to isolate the defective component. Once the defective component is isolated and the location is determined to be in the die, interconnect, or packaging, the part would be partially deprocessed to enable imaging closer to the defect.


The SQUID sensor or a magnetoresistive sensor would then be used to obtain a higher resolution image and more precise localization. At this point there may be enough information to move directly to cross-sectioning or parallel deprocessing. Alternatively, other fault isolation techniques may be used to get complementary information before ﬁnal physical failure analysis.


After physical failure analysis, there may be situations that require further proof that the observed defect is actually causing the electrical failure. If the defect is still electrically intact, magnetic current imaging can be used on the cross-sectioned or parallel deprocessed part to verify that current is actually present in the defect. This can be very useful in situations where various parties are in dispute over ownership of the defect or when there is some liability involved for the defect. The last example will show this, with a more detailed discussion found elsewhere in this book.


One of the primary advantages of magnetic current imaging over other physical fault isolation methods is that the analysis can begin on a fully packaged/assembled device without any deprocessing, which can minimize any risk of losing the defect and simplify the initial analysis. It is applicable to advanced packaging like stacked die. Also, one gets information that was previously not available, that is,a direct image of current in the device.


Isolating a Defective Component


One of the ﬁrst challenges in the isolation of a defect is to determine whether it is in the packaging, the die, or


the interconnect. Magnetic imaging with a SQUID can be very useful for this due to its high sensitivity and ability to image through packaging materials without deprocessing.


There are diﬀerent ways to determine the defective component. The ﬁrst involves recognizing the current distribution associated with the die, interconnect or package.


Figure 17 shows three examples of shorts in a ﬂip-chip device with the short in a) the die, b) the interconnect, and c) the package. For the short in the die, the current can be seen clearly distributed on the die (even die edges can be seen in current distribution) and concentrated at the point of the short. In the interconnect example, the current can be seen concentrated at the short location, but there is no current distributed throughout the die.


Figure 17: Current density images of shorts in a ﬂip-chip device at (a) the die, (b) the interconnect, and (c) the package.


Also, there is no current seen in the package because the short in the interconnect is much closer to the SQUID sensor and thus dominates the image at the chosen gain setting. In the package short example, current is seen in the package without any signiﬁcant intensity variation between the short location and the current in the package


[46]. This indicates that the short is in the package. This kind of analysis can be taken a step further and compared to CAD for the package or die to get more precise localization. A second approach involves calculating the depth of the current in the device from the shape of the magneticﬁeld. Modern 3D Solver analysis would be the selected way and some examples will be presented later (3D Solver was not available at the time this study was done, back in 2001).


A third approach can also be used. For this technique a good device is also imaged under the exact same conditions as the bad device. The signal-to-noise ratio can then be calculated for both images. Since the current level is the same in both measurements, the signal-to-noise ratio can be used to determine which current is closer to the SQUID sensor. Depth changes can make noticeable changes in the signal-to-noise. This can then be used to estimate if one current distribution is in the package or die.


Isolating Low Resistance shorts


While magnetic current imaging can be applicable to all types of shorts, low resistance shorts can be diﬃcult or impossible to isolate by many techniques due to the low


power that they dissipate. For magnetic current imaging,only current is needed. The actual power that is generated by a defect is irrelevant, making this technique the only option in some cases for low resistance shorts. To demonstrate this capability, two results have been included from work published elsewhere in more detail [47].


The ﬁrst example is a SRAM standby current failure and the second is an ASIC power short. The 4 MB SRAM is a 0.4µm device with 4 levels of metal. It was ﬂip-chip mounted on a ceramic ball grid array (CBGA) and thinned to approximately 70µm of silicon. The part was biased with 130mVAC peak-to-peak and drew 100µA of current(DC average power Peff = 6.4µW ). Figure 18 shows the current image obtained through the backside overlaid on the CAD layout, with the defect location marked by the red arrow. This matches the defect location found after physical analysis and agrees with the results from other techniques like Thermally Induced Voltage Alteration (TIVA),liquid crystal, and Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM),but acquired with more than 2 orders of magnitude less power.


Figure 18: Backside current image of a standby current failure on a SRAM. The defect is indicated by the arrow and the whole image is overlaid on a CAD layout.


The second example is a 0.1µm ASIC product with 6 levels of metal, which had a power supply short. The device wasﬂip-chip mounted on a CBGA substrate. It was biased with 250mVAC peak-to-peak and drew 6.5mA of current(DC average power Peff = 800µW ).


Figure 19(left) shows the current image overlaid on a backside optical image with a close-up of this region and current direction shown in Figure 19(right). The four lobes in the current image indicate current coming together on one layer and shorting in the middle to another layer where the current separates into opposite directions.This constitutes a plane-to-plane short at the center of the region where the current seems to have disappeared, indicated by the cross


in Figure 19(right).


Figure 19: (Left) Backside current image of ASIC power short overlaid on backside optical image. (Right) Close-up of defect location. White arrows show current converging from top and bottom and diverging from left and right with plane-to-plane short at the center of this current cross.


The current is missing here because it is moving vertically between the layers, which is a magnetically silent direction for the SQUID. The location agrees with the data obtained with a Schleiren Thermal Mapper, which required about two orders of magnitude more current, also shown at the center in Figure 11(b). The resulting deprocessing at this location showed considerable shorting damage, as shown in Figure 20.


Figure 20: SEM cross-sectional image of shorting site identiﬁed in Fig. 19.


Isolating High Resistance Defects (Resistive Opens)


Typically, a high resistance defect is the result of a geometrical change in some circuit element such as a delamination process, crack, void, etc. These deﬀects are normally not detected as static failures, because the resistance change associated with the geometrical changes falls


normally within acceptable levels. their importance is that they normally introduce time delays, which aﬀect functionality of the device. this way, high resistance (also known as resistive opens failures) are detected during functional testing.


Historically, the main approach for localizing these defects has been time domain reﬂectometry. TDR sends a short electrical pulse into the device and monitors the time to receive reﬂections. These reﬂections can correspond to shorts, opens, bends in a wire, normal interfaces between devices, or high resistance defects. Ultimately anything that produces an electrical impedance change will produce a TDR response. These signals are compared to a good part and require time consuming layer-by-layer deprocessing and comparison to a standard part. When complete,the localization is typically at best to within 200 microns.


Clearly, the geometrical variation in the conducting elements will produce a change in the current distribution as compared to a good one, as sketched in Fig. 21 for aﬂip-chip bump situation, and such current alterations will result in a correspondingly variation in the magnetic ﬁeld distribution.


Figure 21: Illustration of current distribution in a good and a delaminated (failing) ﬂip-chip bump.


In this situation, one expects to see a small change in the magnetic ﬁeld distribution around the defect as compared with that in a good part. The localization of high resistance defects through current imaging is accomplished through a detailed comparison of good and failing parts.


Figure 9. Signal path loss over transmission length (plotted


from path loss equation (L=10*log10(4d/)) 


Signal path loss is also related signal frequency. As signal  frequency increases, the propagation distance decreases. Figure  10 shows the simulation of the correlation between the signal  frequency (i.e., bandwidth) and propagation distance in mm


[14], due to the loss and dispersion of the signal when it travels  through a metallic trace with a pre-defined resistance. As a  result, terahertz signal can travel through a substrate for  hundreds of millimeters because substrate traces have


resistance around 1 ohm/mm range. For a typical Si trace with  resistance of 10 ohm/mm or more, signal can only travel around  tens of millimeters. In a typical test vehicle the structure is  routed between the substrate and die over long distances. This  leads to one of the major limitations of RF-based fault isolation  approaches [11].


Figure 10: Effect of increased frequency on the propagation of the  signal [14].


The second loss is due to the fact that the TDR or EOTPR signal  has to go through a round-trip for fault isolation by using  reflected signal for failure detection. As illustrated by Figure 8  of the TDR work principle, the signal splits a least twice. As a  result, its detection length is only one quarter the maximum  signal travel distance. Different from TDR, TDT sends a signal  at one port and detects the transmitted signal at another port as  illustrated by Figure 11. TDT only involves a one-way trip of  the signal and therefore avoids signal splitting and reflecting. It  allows for the most signal into the DUT and can fully utilize the  tool sensitivity, and naturally increases the defect detection  length by four times over that of the TDR method.


Figure 11: Working principle of TDT and its measurement  setup [11].


The third factor is the multiple reflections of the TDR signal  which leads to signal loss. Based on the mechanism of TDR, any impedance discontinuity along the signal propagation path  results in a reflection of the signal, which diverts signal into the  trace for defect detection, and interfering with waveform  formation. When the failure location is deep inside the trace and  far from the TDR probing point, multiple impedance changes  present in between and reflection can also lead to interpretation  of the waveform and determination of the failure location  difficult. The signal loss and dispersion when the signal travels  through the trace would even exacerbate the situation.


The fourth factor in getting more accurate fault isolation is  incident signal shape. Conventional TDR uses a step voltage  signal generated from electrical diodes with internal impedance


of 50 ohms. Generating high frequency impulse signal with  minimum jittering suitable for TDR/TDT applications has been  an active research area with both hardware and algorithm  innovations. EOTPR is one example using photoconductive  switches triggered by femtosecond laser pulses. Recently, silicon-based picosecond pulse radiators were used to produce  high-power broadband pulses in the THz regime without using  any laser source [16]. A detailed review on this topic is beyond  the scope of this paper other than highlighting that an impulse  signal provides detailed point-by-point impedance change, thus  is best for time-domain based fault isolation methods.


To illustrate such situations, Figure 12 shows an example of the  application of impulse signal to TDR and impulse TDT   on the  same DUT, in which ports 1 and 2 are the two ends of a trace, and node 3 is a high resistance point located at the midpoint of  trace 1-2. Figure 12b shows the TDR waveform obtained at port  1 with port 2 open ended, and Figure 12c shows the TDT  waveform by sending the RF signal into port 1 and receiving  the signal at port 2. Due to the presence of high-resistance node  3, the reflected TDR signal will first show a large peak at t = 2 *t1-3, well before the emergence of the major peak resulting  from the open end at port 2. As shown in Figure 12c, however, no matter what and how many impedance changes exist inside  trace 1-2, the first major peak observed in the TDT waveform  always correlates with the trace length. The reason for this is  that TDT signal always takes the minimal time and distance to  arrive at receiving port. Therefore, the TDT method provides a  more reliable and consistent way of measuring trace lengths, especially for traces with rich geometrical features and/or a  complex structure (e.g., branching) [11].

An experiment is designed to further compare the TDR and  TDT methods in terms of signal propagation and degradation. A short failure was created 30.3 mm (Package trace = 7.8 mm, Package die trace = 22.5 mm) from Port 2 as shown in Figure  13a. EOTPR waveform collected on Port 2 shows a very weak


negative peak (at 1600 ps) as shown by Figure 13b. Here the


signal needs to travel (30.3 mm) to the short failure location and


then comes back to the source (total= 60.6 mm) to be detected


by the transceiver. This round-trip travel of the signal degrades


the amplitude of the signal and makes it weak and


indistinguishable [11].


Figure 13: (a) Structure routing in the package. (b) TDR  waveform obtained at Port 2 [11].


Now a similar structure is chosen for TDT analysis. Structure is  routed to the package and die as shown in Figure 14a. Total  structure length is about 81.5 mm connecting Port 5 and Port 6 (Package trace = 10.5 mm, Package die trace = 71 mm). Transmitting signal is launched on Port 5 and TDT signal is  detected at Port 6 at 2246 ps. The observed TDT waveform is  relatively less noisy compared to conventional TDR waveforms


which are susceptible to reflections from the structure. From  this study it has become clear that TDT has capability to detect  signal over larger distance than what conventionally TDR can  by minimizing signal path loss, splitting loss and refection loss. Next section will show the implementation of TDT and  different methods to calculate defection location of long-chain  short failure [11].

c. Implementation of TDT and Case Study


In the previous section, we discussed the two TDT methods  which can be used to isolate defect location of short failure  between two long chains. In this section, implementation of the  TDT will be discussed. A new tool called Advantest TS9000  system was developed for TDR and TDT measurement and  used for data collection of this study. There are two  configurations for signal generation (transmitting) and  sampling (receiving): Configuration one uses Photoconductive  switch (PCS) for both transmitter and receiver; while  configuration two uses photo-diode (PD) for transmitter and  PCS for receiver. Configuration two offers advantages such as  better signal quality and ability to select PD bandwidth for  specific rise time and is the selected configuration for this study. To collect TDR and TDT waveforms with a single probing, each prober is integrated with both transmitter and receiver. The  tool is equipped with two such probes to enable TDT with each  one being able to transmit and receive signal. To demonstrate  the methods discussed above, both TDR and TDT are  performed on a known structure and the signal propagation  distance in compared in both cases. In this case study, a failure  unit is chosen with short failure between two structures. For the  first TDT only method, only TDT waveforms are collected to  calculate the failure location. For the second COMBO  TDR/TDT method, both TDT and TDR waveforms are  collected to provide more accurate failure location. The paper outlines how time-domain based electrical fault  isolation methods have evolved from conventional TDR to  EOTPR and then TDR/TDT to meet the needs of smaller and  more complex package technologies. It illustrates each


technique’s application advantages with real case studies. Specifically, conventional TDR uses step voltage as incident  signal and collects reflected signal as a function of time to  provide failure location based on waveform deviation location. EOTPR as one form of TDR demonstrated this new technique  high accuracy and has gained industry adoption quickly during  the last ten years. TDR/TDT uses an impulse incident signal  that effectively addresses some limitations faced by  conventional TDR and improves fault isolation location  accuracy. Impulse signal allows EOTPR and TDR/TDT to  record reflected signal at each time step, hence it directly  captures the electrical path impedance deviation with peaks for  high impedance and valleys for low impedance.  These features  are very useful to distinguish trace features and help users to  quickly identify SHORT and OPEN and their location. When  comparing waveforms between conventional TDR, the impulse  waveform features from EOTPR and TDR/TDT can be used as  a reference to align waveforms from different parts or collected  at different times or by different users, thus help improve fault  isolation accuracy by reducing noise caused by jittering, unitto-unit variation or other factors. Finally, TDT is introduced for  fault isolation of electrical shorts. It uses two ports with one port  to transmit signal and other to receive, thus doubles signal  detection length by eliminating signal return path. Combo  TDR/TDT method goes a step further to provide additional  benefit for short fault isolation of long and branch structures  when design or signal travel speed can’t be accurately  characterized.


TDT is targeted towards fault isolation of short  structures in test chips (with resistive structures only), as in  OPEN failures, the transmitted signal will not be propagating to  the receiver port due to the presence of OPEN. Application of  TDT to product could be potential application for IO to IO  SHORTs which requires further work to make it effective but  do not have technical gap today as IO-IO SHORTs can be  covered by other FI tools. Comparing long chain TDT to  Scanning Squid Microscopy (SSM), SSM is easier to interpret  with current flowing through the failing circuit whereas TDT  has a disadvantage that it will have limitation for signal  propagation through long structure.


In summary, as 2.5D and 3D packages become a key  enabler to have more computational power in a smaller size, packages have become more complex and more difficult to  perform fault isolation. It is hence critical for failure analyst to  understand the pros and cons of each technique and utilize the  right method to solve the problem effectively.

Frontside Sample Preparation


FA Instruments, Inc.


This tutorial will assist the analyst in making decisions on  frontside access both in package or System in Package (SIP) and multi-chip module (MCM) using mechanical milling, laser  decap, plasma or wet etch methods.  How to endpoint while  protecting the circuit and limitations of the techniques will be  addressed.


Access to a select component embedded in epoxy requires  forethought as to the desired outcome.  The materials involved  dictate the best course of action for access usually with 2 or  more deprocessing methods.  Typically a faster mechanical  milling or an ablation laser approach is used to remove the  majority of material and form a pocket.  Then a chemical or  plasma means is used to expose the embedded device. Sometimes the defect is removed when exposing the device  obfuscating the analysis or the electrical connections do not  withstand the removal techniques.


The package plays heavily in the best chosen approach for  access depending on a cavity down or up orientation and  location of interconnects such as bumps on a flip chip or wirebonds where the wire-loops must be avoided.  Methodologies  for the preparation may require in-situ board level or system  module analysis, die repackaging or limited pocket access. Stacked die requires strategies to determine which die are  sacrificially removed as the target die is approached for  analysis and/or deprocessing.


Background


Package sample preparation has moved into the mainstream of  FA in the last 5-10 years.  While Moore‟s law is concluding at  the die level, the package engineering world continues to forge  ahead and so do the increasingly stringent requirements for  sample prep.  Numerous package options with single or multi  component designs internal to a single package are common. [1-3].


Topside access can be accomplished by flat lapping, pocket  machining, laser etching, RIE (Reactive Ion Etching), chemical etching, or a combination of these.


Flat Lap


Assuming the surface is conducive to flat lapping, this is a  quick method to thin the epoxy filler material over the entire


package surface.  A large area flat platen is typically used with  400 or 600 grit paper to quickly thin close to the internal  bonds.  Since the entire device surface is in contact with a  large area, wear-out of the lapping material is distributed over  a large area.  A chemical or plasma etch is then used to  remove the remaining epoxy and expose the target  components.


Advantages:


1. Simple thinning process to remove the bulk of the epoxy.


2. Shortens chemical etch times as there is less epoxy to remove.


Disadvantages:


1. Must mount to flat lap and may not be possible with board mounted devices.


2. Thinning globally will reduce the package height complicating electrical test with clamp type sockets.


Spacers will be needed to compensate for some socket types.


3. Chemical etch may spill over and corrode the leads as there is no pre-defined pocket unless gaskets are used.


Chemical Decapsulation


Die and bonds can be exposed using wet chemistries to etch  the epoxy encapsulant.  The type of epoxy used and the  composition of the die and bonds determine the best etchant. Typically, injection molded devices are etched with yellow or  red fuming nitric acid.  Yellow fuming or 90% nitric is used to  expose the wire loops then red fuming nitric is used to finish  the etch exposing the die.  The extremely low moisture content  of the red fuming nitric inhibits corrosion of aluminum bond  pads and aluminum wires but is only used on a hot plate due to  rapid vaporization at the etch temperature of 70°C.  The bonds  and pads must not be copper based for nitric etch methods.


Jet etch machines use yellow fuming nitric and/or fuming  sulfuric acid.  The acid is pre heated and injected onto the die  using shaped Viton rubber gaskets to form a seal for the  desired opening.  Glob top encapsulated epoxies require  fuming sulfuric or a mix of fuming sulfuric and fuming nitric  to remove the encapsulant.  Copper based wires with  aluminum pads require a mixture of fuming nitric and fuming  sulfuric optimized as a compromise etch to minimally attack  both the copper and aluminum.


Figures 1 and 2 demonstrate the challenge with small outline  packages.  The part is encapsulated in a potting epoxy and the  top surface etched on a hot plate with red fuming nitric to


expose the die.  The potting epoxy etches more slowly than the  package providing protection for the leads.  The 4 connections  can be probed or wires soldered to continue the analysis per  figure 2.
