Figure 2:  Close up view of TSOP style package cavity down.  Distance between the leads is 2.54mm.  Potting epoxy protects  the package and leadframe.


1. Highly selective etch for exposing aluminum/gold  connections.


2. Etch chemistries can be adjusted for improved  selectivity.


3. Fast process usually < 1 minute to expose die.


1. Mixed metallization system with copper requires  compromise etch mixture of nitric and sulfuric.


2. Corrosive process exacerbated by moisture.


3. Chemical etch may spill over and corrode adjacent  components.


4. Cannot etch burned or carbonized plastic material.


5. Undercut and etch beyond edges of die requires a  careful time endpoint.


6. Non uniform formation of pocket depth.


Laser Ablation


Pulsed solid state lasers typically operating at 1064nm can be  used to ablate the package material over the die.  The area to  be opened is easily and precisely defined.  Ablation typically  removes 25 to 100m of material per scan with each scan  taking about 1 second.  Pulse duration is kept short using qswitched methods to vaporize the plastic composite material.  The die surface must be avoided as the laser will damage the  active die if the package is thinned below 100 µm.  Figure 3  shows a typical laser ablated package with exposed wire loops.  The die must be subsequently exposed by chemical or plasma  means.


Figure 3: Laser ablated BGA package with copper wires. The  ablation process was run until the top of the bond wires were  exposed (left side top of package, right side BGA bottom of  package). At this point, a finishing step needs to be performed  to expose the die surface. [4]

It  can be shown that the lens failure increases with the  numerical aperture of the objective lens and the thickness  of the Si substrate. To ensure a good image quality even  for large magnifications it is therefore recommended to  thin the die.”

A large area platen is  used with various lapping or polishing films to establish a  smooth surface. The observed problem with  deep pocket milling is the high crack risk from the  sidewalls of the deep pockets and thermal power  management of large area thin substrates.  Successful  pocket milling methodologies are discussed later in this  paper.

It is important to note the flat lap method can be  simulated on a modern Computer Numerical Control (CNC) mill with larger 12 mm diameter diamond mylar  film tools.  The large diameter tool greatly accelerates the  removal process over a large area with much less tip  dwell time to wear out the mylar film.  The in line  interferometer and precision tilt control greatly simplify  the process for targeted or flat lapping compared to older  CNC mill systems.


Laser Assisted Chemical Etch


Laser chemical etch methods use a scanning laser to etch  precision pockets for localized backside access.  See  Figure 11.  The sample is typically already thinned using  a mechanical removal method.  Newer techniques use a  pulsed laser referred to as Pulsed Laser Assisted  Chemical Etch (PLACE) to reduce substrate heating.  The technique is useful for small pocket access < 500 µm  x 500 µm and more typically on the order of 50 µm x 50 µm.  Surface finish is on the order of 30 nm RMS with a  spot size on the order of 1 µm.  Z depth control can be  submicron with an Optical Beam Induced Current (OBIC) feedback system.  PLACE is several orders of  magnitude faster than FIB but not as precise.  PLACE  can laser deposit oxide and traces.  PLACE requires


interlock controlled environment with hazardous gases  and is limited to >10um RST work.  Developments in this  area combine PLACE to reach 3 µm, then use plasma  etch to approach 1 µm [15].


Figure 11.  From D. Barton, et al. “FLIP-Chip and “Backside” Sample Preparation Techniques”


Plasma Reactive Ion Etch


The RIE using CF4/O2, SF6 or some form of fluorine will  allow the silicon to be etched.  Unfortunately, the nonuniformity of the etch will quickly manifest after more  than a few microns are removed as seen in figure 12.  Contrast this with Laser MicroChemical (LMC) etching, the laser creates a local zone of reactive silicon only  where the beam is in focus.  A high numeric aperture will  make the system highly selective with focus.  With RIE, the bombardment is perpendicular to the surface and like  the FIB, will generate a reasonable cross section due to  the directional nature of the field [16,17].


1. Dry process to remove Si


2. Can remove 1 or 2 microns with minimal  surface distortion for final target approach.


1. Beyond a 1 or 2 microns of removal, the  surface will quickly form pits.


2. Heating of the sample must be carefully  avoided in a vacuum chamber.


3. Ultraviolet light is created which may  begin to erase NVM memory <2um.


4. Electrostatic fields and ion implantation on  the surface may alter the device with ultrathin silicon for certain technologies.


Figure 12.  AFM image of etched silicon surface after  SF6 RIE plasma etch [18].


CNC based milling and polishing


Pocket milling and polishing allows a select area of a  wafer, board, module, or package to be prepared.  This is  accomplished with a small diameter tip rastered within a  specified region to create an opening.  Different types of  tips are exchanged in the tool collet depending on the  type of material to be removed and the desired finish.  Diamond impregnated tools are usually used to grind  ceramic, glass or silicon surfaces.  Milling tools are  typically used to mill metals, or plastics.  Polishing tools  are used with a diamond suspension or a colloidal silica  suspension to remove surface damage from the silicon  thinning steps.    These machines were originally high  speed CNC mills that have been modified for FA.  The  high speed spindle had to be slowed for final polishing  and coolant is required to reduce the heat generated by  the 60,000 rpm rotating diamond bit.  Ultrasonic  vibration from the spindle can fracture ultra-thin silicon  so speed control is important.


Modern CNC‟s may use annular hollow tools to  dispense coolant, have a small standing bath of coolant or  dispense a small bead of liquid at the tip with suction.  The trend has been to integrate the CNC machines with  measurement capabilities analogous to the evolution of  photon emission tools with thermal and laser capabilities.  Options on a pocket milling machine can now  incorporate a dual band interferometer, microscope, multiple view and alignment cameras for target and  machine vision monitoring with overlay for X-ray  images, electronic and optical endpoint determination, coolant dispense and suction, thermal stage control, interactive loading force sensors, 5-axis control of the  stage, bit exchangers, and so on (Figures 13-16).  The  trend is  to move towards automation of the sample  preparation process but be aware that not only does the  promise of automation come with longer setup time costs  for the first unit it also comes with the complexities of  machine reliability challenges.  If the plan is to do


multiples of the same part in an assembly line fashion  then automation is worthy of consideration, however, experience dictates there will be too much package  variability with too small a sample size to benefit.  The  need for precise targeted interactive surgery on boards or  modules is the main driver of backside preparation  technology.

TIP CONVOLUTION and 3-axis vs. 5-axis CNC mill  considerations


Flip chip style BGA packages typically have a warp  curvature that changes as the die is thinned.  Sometimes it  relaxes as is shown in Figure 17.  Some devices exhibit  the opposite behavior and warp further as they are  thinned.  Adaptive thinning methods are required to  compensate during thinning in order to maintain a  reasonable RST [19].


Figure 17.  Surface profile of one die as it is thinned. The  sag relaxes a total of ~ 45 µm, from 65 µm at 200 µm to  25 µm at 11.5 µm RST.


Refer to Figure 18 through 20 and note the concern with  a 3-axis mill wherein the  tool bit is normal to the tilt  table rather than the part, which will generate steps in the  silicon based on the step pattern.  If the pattern is a nonrolling stepped spiral or raster with an inadequate number  of discrete steps per axis then this will indeed be a  problem as the edge of the milling or grinding bit on the  high side of the curve will create a step effect in the  silicon.  This then requires a lengthy polish to knock  down the high spots.  While the 5-axis method will  more  closely follow the curve model, it too will need to  observe the step resolution to avoid generating steps in  the silicon, though they will be less severe per Figure 20.  It is important to also remember the milling or grinding   bit of a 5-axis mill is intended to keep the midline of the  tool normal to the part‟s surface.  The edges of the  milling bit do not play into the removal of the silicon  unless the removal is aggressive, if the tool has a flat  bottom.  The center will wear faster than the edges as this  is where the majority of the removal to define shape is  occurring.  The 5-axis challenge is in maintaining a  proper Z distance with submicron control while changing  X,Y,Z and tip XY angle.  There is no major concern with  tip edge diameter since the small center area under the tip  ultimately defines the shape.  An annulus bit will cut with  the inside edge on convex shaped die and with the outer  edge on concave shaped die in 5 axis mode.  This all  seems straightforward when assuming there is a convex  curve contour model to follow.  Since the part curvature  typically follows a radius squared model, concave parts  will not necessarily follow the tip centric concept of 5-axis.  Irregular contour or flat parts (not having either  only convex or only concave curvature) such as stacked  die or DRR4 style parts will not benefit further from the  5-axis approach and still require small diameter and/or  rounded tools for minimal tip convolution effects.


Figure 18.  Comparison of 3-axis vs. 5-axis grinding. (Top) In 3-axis the contact angle is invariant and cannot  follow the shape of a curved die, producing “saw teeth” that are several microns in size. (Bottom) 5-axis control  changes the contact angle to follow the curved shape and  yields a well-blended smooth and continuous surface  profile [20].


Figure 19.  Illustration of milling bit to sample interaction  for A: 5-axis mode on convex surface. B: 3-axis mode on  convex surface.  C: 5-axis mode on concave surface. D: 3-axis mode on concave surface.


Figure 20.  Illustration of step created with 5-axis (E) and  3-axis (F) methods.  The step size for both is related to  the milling bit diameter and step spacing.


The 3-axis approach is actually a 5-axis system with 2


axes being predetermined in tilt and fixed during


processing.  Typically, the table the part is mounted on is  precision tilt corrected to the edges of the area to be


thinned.  The tip face does not change angle and removes  material as the X and Y table rasters.  The problem is not  just with the sawtooth cut pattern but also with tip


convolution since the center area of the thinning tip is


cutting in the center of a convex part and transitions to


the perimeter of the tool tip as the tool moves to the


edges.  The complexity of maintaining a smooth surface  is actually a simple solution.  The machine needs the tool  diameter and the RST map from the last thinning


iteration.  The model is automatically generated and


displayed when the RST transmit to mesh is requested as  follows:


1. The area under the tool tip is automatically  calculated based on radius and used to


adjust the measured RST contour map.


This convolution correction mitigates the


problem of matching subsequent adaptive


RST maps to the surface during thinning


and polishing.


2. The RST generated map is cubic fit from a  10 x 10  or higher matrix into a high


resolution matrix of 100 x 100  data points  or better at the CNC mill.  Individual data  points are typically in microns.


3. The tool pattern is based on millions of


rapid data point calculations to move Z as a  function of any RST mesh fed into the


system.


4. The interferometer is part of the machine


eliminating errors with plate reattachment at  each step.


The Importance of Chemical Mechanical Polishing (CMP)


Regardless of the removal method, PLACE, FIB, Plasma, and so on.  The preferred method to smooth and remove  lattice damage from either mechanical or ion  implantation damage is CMP.  FIB assisted Scanning  Capacitive Microscopy (SCM) demonstrates the enabling  importance of CMP [21].


Final polishing can be done in contour mode or simply  with a constant loading force.  The soft nature of the  polish tip reduces the concern over curvature and tip  convolution.


Both the 3-axis and 5-axis milling methods use select  polish methods with colloidal silica to address the last  micron or 2 of height variance from desired final target  RST.  For complex contour parts where the curve  switches from convex to concave, the polishing bit  diameter selection is paramount, however, the smaller  diameter polishing bit for the tight contours means less  dwell time per surface area and therefore rapidly  increasing preparation times.  A decrease in polishing bit


diameter, from 5 mm to 1 mm, is an approximate 25x  increase in preparation time.


The Immersion Lens


Until just a few short years ago, sample preparation and  SIL or Numerically Increasing Aperture Lens (NAIL) were used with a targeted thickness of silicon as per the  lens design requirements from 100 µm down to 30 µm  RST.  The SIL is constructed to match the index of  refraction of silicon (3.4) to a spherical or aspherical lens  element pressed against or etched into the polished  silicon surface.  The RST and surface finish is required to  be within the manufacturers specification for the lens, on  the order of +/- 5 µm of the specified thickness.  The lens  must fit within the confines of the cavity as shown in  Figures 21 and 22.


Figure 21.  The geometry of the objective lens, and the  small working distance necessitate custom configured  sockets, clamps and board for tester stimulus [22].


Figure 22.   SIL in contact with backside thinned silicon


[23].


A good treatise of general optical microscopy concepts, including immersion lenses, can be referenced in the  section on Optical Microscopy by John McDonald in this  Desk Reference.  The SIL is designed to collect light as  shown in Figures 23 and 24.  By using a high index  material in contact with the silicon substrate the useful  magnification is greatly increased over air spaced  objectives.  The increase is shown in Figure 25 for both  the Rayleigh and Sparrow criteria.  The relationship  clearly shows increasing resolution as wavelength  decreases and/or Numerical Aperture (NA) increases.


Figure 23. SIL in optical contact with the wafer gives a  huge benefit in resolution for backside inspection. Note  the hemisphere continues virtually, but not actually into  the wafer [24].


Figure 24.  Diagram showing how increasing the NA of  an immersion lens reduces the depth of field putting  higher demand on surface preparation to enable these  advanced techniques [25].


Figure 25.  Relationship of resolution as a function of  wavelength and NA for 2 commonly used standards.  D is  the resolvable distance between points [26].


Mid-visible, green light, is about .5 micron wavelength


and for an air immersed lens the NA is limited to 1, so


using the Sparrow Criteria, typical Failure Analysis (FA) lab microscopes working in air must be limited to, at


best, about a 0.5 micron resolution.


If the SIL desired position is known, a SIL can be etched  into the substrate using the FIB to create a Fresnel lens as  shown in Figure 26.  Conventional air spaced Near


Infrared (NIR) objectives image the now magnified


image formed with this lens [27].


Figure 26. Zachariasse et. al. ISTFA 2005 Etched Fresnel  SIL lens using FIB.


It should be noted the SIL is designed to work with  thicker silicon substrates in the NIR domain.  The  usefulness of the silicon based SIL will wane as more  analyses push for ultra-thin silicon (< 10 µm RST).


SIL for Ultra-Thin Silicon


Oil or water immersion lenses improve the NA from a  theoretical 1.0 (best case in air) up to around 1.5. The  improvement in resolution coupled with the shorter  visible wavelengths of light possible with ultra-thin  silicon makes the resolving power comparable to the  traditional silicon based SIL.


The liquid immersion lens can also provide refractive  coupling and thermal management if the fluid is free of  air bubbles and excessive turbulence.  This is important  since the ability to dissipate heat during testing is  effectively eliminated.  Obviously SIL based lenses can  be used in conjunction with active liquid cooling.


Since silicon based SILs are limited to operation well into  the NIR they are not useful for ultra-thin silicon.


Further resolution enhancements are possible with a   Gallium Phosphide (GaP) SIL, which has one of the  highest refractive indices in the visible spectrum n=3.45 @ 550 nm and still above n=3.05 @ 1600 nm [28,29].


Some additional resources for GaP SIL follow:


Contactless Fault Isolation for FinFET Technologies   with Visible Light and GaP SI [30].


Visible Laser Probing (VLP) with GaP Solid Immersion  Lens Demonstrating 110 nm Resolution in Common  Laser Probing Applications [31].


The ability to map current at high resolution is enabled  by reducing the distance between the detector and the  source of the magnetic field created by the current flow. This is a form of optics wherein a magnetic field is  mapped by rastering a sensor over the area of interest at a  set distance to form an image.  The sensors are either  Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) or Giant-Magnetoresistive (GMR) [32,33].  SQUID, while the most sensitive, lacks resolution due to the  distance required to keep the sensor cryogenically cooled.  GMR sensors are less sensitive but gain signal in direct  contact with the surface allowing for high resolution  mapping of microscopic fields as shown in Figure 27. This technique can extend to modules where bulk  material can be removed to reduce the unwanted spacing  of the GMR sensor.


Figure 27.  GMR-based MCI image of power supply  short current density from 5 µm ultra-thin silicon surface


[34].


Anti-Reflective Coatings (ARC)


ARC coatings can greatly improve the transmission of  light and are commonly used on a variety of lenses to  reduce glare.  A good reference paper for ARC is by  Brennan Davis[35].  The maximum transmission through  a silicon substrate with a perpendicular beam is shown by  Equation 3,


where T equals the percentage of  light transmitted, and R  equals the percentage of light reflected [36]. The  reflection can be found from Equation 4.


Backside Current Mapping with Magnetic Current  Imaging (MCI)


The refractive index of the typical silicon substrate is nsub = 3.5, and the refractive index of air is nair = 1.0. Combining equations 1 and 2 with these refractive index  values gives the maximum transmission through a silicon  substrate [37].


The refractive index of silicon increases with the  application of ARC, therefor they are quite beneficial for  backside imaging and analysis. About 70% of coaxial  illumination is scattered and 30% of emission  microscopy sensitivity is lost without an ARC (Fig. 8). Backside image quality rivals frontside when ARC is  used on lightly dope smooth surfaced substrates. Today, ARC can be vacuum deposited or spun on. A quick  method of ARC deposition allows silicon polished  substrates to be coated using a spin-on coating process at  ambient temperature in Figure 28 [38].


Figure 28.  Spin on ARC coating.  The RPM and  viscosity of the liquid define the film thickness and  therefor the desired index match.  Typically a gold to  light blue color film gives optimum results for NIR work.


The coating is easily removed with solvents and  reapplied as needed. The thickness of the coating is  controlled by the spin speed (RPM) and viscosity to


allow for optimum waveband thickness.  When ARC is  applied to thin silicon, high magnification backside  images of the circuitry is possible.  These images rival  frontside images as shown in Figure 29.

Surface Quality and Contour Measurement


Examine the 4 images in Figure 31.  The surface  roughness is indicated in rms (root mean square.) How  are the scratches affecting the rms value?  What about the  surface digs or pits?  Defined surface finish standards can  vary, and if not specified correctly, can result in a no-bid  contract for the work, due to the extreme difficulty  imposed, or work not completed to customer satisfaction. Figure 30 shows various surface finish types.  Grinding  steps create a non-flat rough surface while polishing steps  generate a flat but rough surface which will become  smooth as the polishing steps reach the the bottom of the  scratches or pits.  A contoured device may be smooth but  not flat, allowing for the desired uniformity in RST.  In  other words, the top and bottom silicon surfaces are  parallel and similiar to a thin film.


Figure 30.  Surface Types  [39].


Figure 31.  from Ed Cole et al, ISTFA „18 - Flip-Chip  and Backside Techniques. [40]


Surface Measurement Parameters


There are many types of surface roughness  measurements, including visual and measured.  Figure 32  shows a visual standard for surface finish comparisons.  The most common surface roughness measurement, Roughness Average (Ra), is the average calculated from  the measured peaks and valleys. Another roughness  measurement, Root Mean Square (RMS), is calculated  from the measured peaks and valleys that deviate from a  mean line within a defined length or area.  Both use the  same individual height measurements of the surfaces  peaks and valleys, but use different formula as described  in ASME B46.1. Note that RMS values are more  sensitive to single surface flaws than Ra.  Optics typically  use Scratch/dig standards.  Scratch is a subjective visual  comparison to a reference plate with darkfield  illumination.  The resulting brightness is compared to a  standard.  Dig is the diameter of a pit measured as 1 dig = 1/100 mm. [41]


Referring back to Figure 31, RMS or Ra values are useful  to define a fairly flat surface of repeating peaks and  valleys, but they are not revealing as to the profile of  surface being measured.  The area being measured must  be clearly defined.  Disparities such as scratches or pits  are anomalies in the surface and should be identified as  such.  Rt is a measure of the total surface profile height  from peak to valley [42,43].  This measurement is  especially important for ultra-thin silicon.  A single  scratch or pit 1 µm deep on 1 µm RST silicon can kill the  device even though the Ra values across the large area  are very good.  Conversely the RMS could be high due to  a scratch even though the surface is otherwise quite  smooth and acceptable for imaging.  Preferred parameters  for surface measurement should include a thickness map  of the defined RST surface, the max Rt value allowable  for functionality, and the surface finish exclusive of pits  or scratches in RMS or Ra.  Additionally, the local area


to be analyzed or imaged may require a higher standard  of finish.  This is typically the local polished pocket.


Figure 32.  Rubert Composite pocket set standard No. 30-695-1.


Figure 33.  Side camera 45° view of in process polishing.  Locally edges are flat but rough, center is smooth and  flat.  Corners sit 60 µm lower than the center due to  natural convex warpage of this particular BGA package.


Figure 34.  In line interferometer microscope view of top  edge from Figure 33 showing a rough surface with flat  tops from the polish.


The desired final surface finish should be defined  including the level of polish required and the number of  blemishes (scratches and pits) allowable in the area of  interest.  Device edges are typically more difficult to  polish as the underfill contains filler that can release into  the polish step causing scratches.  The rough nature of the  filler also contributes to polishing pad wear.  The polish  pattern and type of polishing pad used will minimize if  not eliminate this problem for most cases.  A surface  finish value should accompany a definition of the number  of allowable scratches and pits in the area of interest.  Only for thicker films will the scratch be well outside the  focus plane and therefore of minimal concern [44,45].


Measurement of Silicon Thickness


There are several ways to determine the RST value nondestructively.


Focal point method:


The thickness of the remaining silicon shall be  determined from Equation 6 [46].


Based on this equation, the focal distance from the  polished surface to the metallization multiplied by 3.434 = thickness of the remaining silicon at a wavelength of  1064  nm.[47]  This is the basis for determining tilt as  well as thickness of the remaining silicon.  Calibrating  for error is done with the chosen microscope objective (100X NIR) and a sample of known thickness.  The index  of refraction with the error factor combined is calculated  for this focus mechanism by dividing the known  thickness of a sample by the focus distance from surface  to circuit.  It is important to note the error in precision is  compounded by the 3.4 index multiplier, making precise  focal point measurements tedious.


Interpretation of Interference Patterns for Thickness  Profile


The interference patterns seen with monochromatic  illumination allow an immediate view of the silicon  thickness variance as shown in figure 35.  Calculation of  the film thickness variance is shown in Equation 7 [48].


t = (*OPD)/(2*n)


n = index of refraction = 3.434 for silicon


t = change in silicon depth.


 = wavelength of light.


OPD = number of observed fringes.


Referring to figure 35, there are 36 fringes from the 30 µm label on the left to the lower right corner of the die.  This corresponds to a change in thickness of


1.064*36/(2*3.434) = 5.6 µm.  Focus measurements are  used to determine the slope.  In this case, the edge is  thicker by 5.6 µm [49].


Figure 35.  Image taken with 1064 nm laser illumination.  The monochromatic light reveals Newton‟s rings based  on thickness variation.


1. Chemical free rapid ablation of various  encapsulants.


2. Sample does not need to be mounted in a holding  fixture.


3. Excellent selectivity to clear encapsulant from  bonds or lead fingers.


4. Copper bonds and lead fingers easily exposed for  inspection.


5. Can remove carbonized or burned plastic from  bond wires or leadframe.


6. Anisotropic ablation leaves minimal undercut.


7. Pocket depth can be somewhat controlled by focal  depth of the laser.


1. Cannot expose die without damage requiring an  alternative method to clear die.


2. Discretes such as ceramic capacitors can be  damaged if exposed.


3. Creates electrostatic charge during ablation.


4. Cracks or voids in the encapsulant can allow the  laser to reach and damage the die.


Plasma Reactive Ion Etch (RIE)


The RIE is typically a parallel plate system with an RF field  driven to excite plasma.  The lower plate contains the part to  be etched.  The resulting plasma is anisotropic using O2 or  some form of Fluorine mixed with O2 to accelerate the etch.  Figure 4 is an overview of a microwave based plasma system  with advantages of lower processing temperatures and reduced  sputtering effects over a standard parallel plate system.  Figure  5 shows typical results using microwave injected Plasma.


Figure 4: Overview of the microwave decapsulation system.  The faraday cage is the key to lowering the process  temperature and preventing heat absorption and metallization  sputtering. [5]


Figure 5: Decapsulation of laser-ablated PBGA microcircuit  using downstream microwave plasma. This takes about two  hours on an older 300-watt system, and less than 20 minutes  on the newer 500-watt systems. [6]


Referring to Figure 6, analysis of units containing 1 mil  copper bond wires that had been stressed to end-of-life


conditions were found to have wires which fell off during the  fuming acid mixture decapsulation process.


Figure 6: Corner copper bond wires which fall off during acid  decapsulation likely contain slip plane fractures like those  seen here on a unit that was decapsulated using Microwave  plasma. [7]


When those units were decapsulated with microwave plasma,


the corner wires remained intact. FE-SEM inspection of those


wires found that they contained slip plane fractures  that would


likely etch rapidly in the presence of nitric acid and cause the


wire to weaken before the sulfate coating could be fully


developed. Analysis of any future copper wire field return


units with open circuit conditions on the corner bond wires


will require the use of plasma decapsulation to safely identify


the nature of the wire break. [8]


1. Dry process to remove residual package material


2. Excellent selectivity to allow copper wires to be  exposed.


3. Package does not need to be mounted in a holding  fixture.


1. Ash forms and will impede the etch process after a  few microns of removal requiring frequent clean


steps.


2. Heating of the sample must be carefully avoided in a  vacuum chamber.


3. Ultraviolet light is created with fluorine which may  begin to erase NVM memory.


4. Very slow removal process.


5. Package masking may be required to prevent etch  outside of target zone.


6. Silver can react and contaminate the surface with  fluorine based plasma.


7. Surface passivation can be etched by fluorine bearing  gasses.


8. Surface bombardment can reduce selectivity  especially with heavier gasses such as argon.


9. Pocket depth can become non-uniform.


Pocket milling and polishing allows a select area of the  product in wafer, board, module or package form to be  prepared with a small diameter tip rastered in the opening.    Modern tools have either a small standing bath of coolant or  use a small bead of liquid at the tip to minimize the mess.  The  trend has been to integrate the tools together.  A typical   pocket polishing machine now incorporates a dual band  interferometer, microscope, multiple view and alignment  cameras for target and machine vision monitoring with overlay  for X-ray images, electronic and optical endpoint  determination, coolant dispense and suction, thermal stage  control, interactive loading force sensors, 5-axis control of the  stage, tool changers and so on.  The need for precise targeted  interactive surgery on boards or modules is the main driver of  mechanical milling prep technology.


1. Precise control of pocket depth irrespective of cracks, voids or dissimilar materials.


2. Side walls can be milled and approached precisely  without undercut.


3. Endpoint detection both electronic and visual.


4. Can dry mill or wet mill.


5. No chemical requirements.


1. Requires a holding fixture to mount the device.


2. Cannot expose bond wires.


3. Cannot expose die surface.


4. Radius of corners limited to tool diameter.


5. Dust and heat created if dry milling.


6. Resulting slurry can contaminate balls or bumps.


Case History


CNC milling to isolate MCM leakage failure


This failure resulted in variant 1k to 10K typical leakage  across Vdd in standby.  All attempts to decap the MCM  module resulted in recovery both with laser and chemical  decap.  The leakage was time variant showing 1/f noise and  jumps in leakage as a function of temperature.  A process of  elimination was used to isolate the leakage to a particular X7R  ceramic capacitor by maintaining electrical connection to Vdd  versus Vss while removing the material.  Figure 7 is a diagram  of the MCM module.  The leakage was originally suspected  associated with Vdd on the die from suspected transient  damage in pre-qual.  Severing the bonds to the die confirmed  the leakage was elsewhere.


Figure 7:  Diagram of MCM module.  Capacitor leakage site  is identified with arrow on side facing the die.


Electrical contact was maintained with a wire harness  integrated with the part mounted on the CNC mill.  A dry ring  was cut around the capacitor at 2000 RPM using a frame  pattern and the frame was successively reduced.  The tip  position of the diamond grinding tool was tracked and noted  the greatest disturb to the leakage was when the tip passed on  the left side (Side facing die) of the capacitor as seen in Figure


8.


Figure 8: Noted Area of the capacitor that exhibited greatest  disturbance during electrically monitored mechanical  decapsulation.


The leakage IV curve varied wildly jumping to brief intervals  of high impedance.  This gave increased confidence the  leakage was likely associated with the sidewall rather than the  base of the capacitor.  The thinning was done in 20 m  increments and reduced to just a few microns per pass in  figure 9, as the leakage became increasingly chaotic.  With  about 10m of remaining plastic, the thinning was halted and  EDX analysis performed in the SEM.  See figure 10.  Silver  was found on the ceramic body of the capacitor sidewall.


Figure 9: Thinned capacitor location of greatest disturb to the  monitored leakage and the correct position to move to SEM  with EDX analysis.


Figure 10: SEM image of residue on sidewall of capacitor


with identified silver responsible for the leakage.


No liquids were used in this thinning process to preserve the  integrity of the contaminants.  On another unit the sidewall  was thinned then snapped off with a tungsten probe to expose  the sidewall.  The silver residue was confirmed and corrective  action ensued.


CNC removal of Stacked Die


Multi-Chip Package (MCP) stacking technology is used with  BGA chips to greatly increase memory capacity.  20 die stacks  with each die only 30m thick is commonplace.  Through  Silicon Via (TSV) allow manufacturing a high density stack of  dies without bond wires enhancing speed and further reducing  package size.  The complexities of access require either  interactive visual endpoint methods or contour mapping to  target each layer.  The challenges with delayering stacked die  are exacerbated by the changing nature of the surface  deformation for each successive die in the stack.


Figures 11-14 show a portion of the process for approaching a  die using interactive visual means.  The device to be delayered  contains an 8 layer stack of 40m die with 10m thick attach  between each die.  The package encapsulant is injection  molded and is approximately 150m from the top die.  The  package is thinned close to the top die either mechanically or  with laser ablation then the remaining encapsulant is removed  by dry or wet etch to expose the topmost die surface.  The  exposed surface is tilt aligned to the CNC mill and thinned as  shown in Figure 11.  The amount of removal is monitored with  5m slices for each pass.  Figure 12 reveals a corner clearing  in the upper left.


Figure 11: Exposed die is thinned with a fine diamond  grinding bit.  The die surface is removed as the tool traverses  the surface.  Water is dispensed and suctioned simultaneously  to keep a clear view of the process.


Figure 12: Stacked die with upper left corner clearing first.  This area is avoided and an additional 5 m is successively  removed from the rest of the die.


Once there is evidence of clearing of the silicon anywhere, this  area is avoided and the remaining area is targeted for another  5m off.  This process continues until most of the residual  substrate is removed as shown in Figure 13.  Using a manual  process, the spin knobs for X, Y, and Z allow quick  positioning.  This process took <2 minutes to complete.


Figure 13: The tip is moved in X and Y over the remaining  islands of residual silicon to clear most of them.


The remaining silicon residue is easily removed with a drop of  acetone and a cotton swab.  The 10m die adhesive is still  intact protecting the exposed die as shown in Figure 14.  Further etch or solvents would be used as needed to remove  the die adhesive.


The die layers can also be removed by thinning partially into  the silicon die and using an interferometer to map the  remaining silicon thickness (RST) variation.  This map is then  applied to correct the irregular contour of the die and can be  added accumulative to each subsequent die layer enabling  adaptive correction.  Please refer to the “Backside Preparation  and Optics” section of this desk reference.  If the warp  deformation exceeds the thickness of the die, the RST method  is not applicable and either the manual method must be used  or a surface interferometry map must be obtained of a properly  exposed die.


Figure 14: Bottom die #8 in the stack exposed and intact after  removal of 7 dies.  The 10m adhesive layer is intact and  ready for removal to expose the die surface.


Electrical Endpoint Detection on CNC


Interactive electrical endpoint detection when thinning  conductive and capacitive materials opens the door to  approaching a suspect site in an IC without relying on the  traditional iterative approach.  Controlled approach of  embedded conductors in insulators (packages) as well as  controlled die thinning with submicron control allows safe  approach to the desired feature without overshoot. [9,10]


Creating access points in an IC has traditionally required  iterative guesswork to reach the target.  Currently, ~1m  control using capacitive detection through the package or  insulator is possible.


The milling spindle drives a coupled 3.3V pulse signal to the  milling/polishing tip.  The mount plate is the lower  capacitance plate and tied to the input of an analog amplifier  as shown in figure 15.


Figure 15:  Image of 208 PQFP mounted to test plate.  At  least one of the leads needs to be in contact with the mounting  plate to the die.  Note: the water stays in the cavity due to  surface tension, defining the upper plate of the capacitor.


Since distance is inversely proportional to capacitance for a  parallel plate capacitor, equation 1, the endpoint reading  accuracy drastically improves as the target endpoint is  approached.  A capacitive response yields a square wave based  on the ratio of charge transferred to the lower sensor plate per  equation 2 [11,12].    Since DI water has resistivities of 20  M-cm or less it will appear as a short circuit in endpoint.


[13].  Mineral oil and crystal bond wax (hot wax) are covalent  and therefore non-conductive. Both can serve as masking  materials for exposed areas, opening the door for various  access techniques.


Any crack or breach in the insulator will show conductively, depending on the chosen fluid, providing a safe early halt to  the process.  A crack causing early endpoint detection can be  masked with mineral oil or crystalbond, then DI or distilled  water reapplied to continue the process until reaching bonds or  any other desired endpoint.


C= *Eo*A/D, where  Eo= 8.854x10-12


(Equation 1)


 = dielectric constant of the material


A = overlapping surface area of the plates


D = distance between the plates


C = capacitance


Or for 2 differing dielectric materials:


i=C dv/dt


(Equation 2)


Endpoint Detection Example


The part is attached to the plate using hot wax with one or  more leads in contact to form the lower plate.  The desired  area to open and tool are selected or loaded from a previous


recipe.  Tilt is corrected, and then a preliminary pocket 100μm


deep is cut.  The surface is wiped clean and DI water is added  only in the pocket.  Surface tension holds the water in the  pocket forming the upper plate of the capacitor.  The milling  process proceeds and capacitance is observed to increase until  the endpoint jumps with a reduced resistance value due to  water contact with the top of the wire loop.  Figures 16 and 17  are optical images of the cavity at endpoint over the bond wire  loops.  The device is now ready for chemical or plasma decap.


Figure 16: Note visible wire loops embedded in the remaining  thin plastic layer.  DI water enhances the image contrast.  Crystalbond wax can be used for capacitive endpoint thinning


inside the wire loops, leaving 10μm or more of remaining


plastic over the die, if desired.


Figure 17: 100X objective used to image wire prior to crystal  bond application, confirming wires are still embedded in  plastic.  Remaining thickness ~ 5m.


Masking the Resistive Endpoint:


If an endpoint is obtained due to an unwanted area, such as a  lead finger, crack or exceptionally high wire loop being  exposed, the pocket can be rinsed out, dried and coated with a  thin layer of mineral oil to isolate the endpoint signal.  The  area is retargeted and DI water added.  The disturbed areas  from milling will wet with all other areas remaining isolated.  Endpoint will occur on approach of next feature related to  milling area.


Potential Issues:


1. Dry milling resistive endpoint requires the tool to  physically contact the wire resulting in excessive  damage.  Additionally tribo-charging of the material  during removal causes wild DC swings on the  endpoint.  Use an ionic solution.


2. False early endpoint can occur if package leads or  surface caps couple to the cavity due to residue or  splashing.  Masking methods can be used if needed.


3. Capacitance data can be erroneous due to die coat, tilt or delamination issues.  A resistive endpoint is  typical for delamination or cracks to prevent die  damage since the liquid will enter and wet a bond  underneath.


Board level CNC endpoint is accomplished in the same  manner with the board ground tied to the lower mount plate.  Thinning proceeds until the endpoint threshold is reached and  the process stops as shown in figures 18-20.


Figure 18:  Water used to establish the upper capacitor plate  for endpoint detection over the lead dress.  The process is set  for automatic stop when the endpoint signal exceeds the set  threshold.


Figure 19:  Capacitance EndP signal increasing as the plastic  is thinned from Figure 16.


Figure 20:  Capacitance EndP signal reached 75 then jumped  to 851 the moment any of the bonds came in contact with the  water during thinning from Figure 18.

Backside Preparation and Optics


Christopher Colvin  FA Instruments, Inc.


This tutorial will assist the analyst in making decisions on  backside thinning and polishing requirements and  hopefully dispel many of the associated myths and  assumptions.  Many have heard Analysts and Scientists in  our field refer to sample preparation as “Black Magic” stemming from a lack of understanding for the  complexities of sample preparation.  Leading to an  oversight of the nearly infinite combinations of modules, packages, die sizes, and material compositions combining  metal alloys, epoxy with fillers, glass, die attach, glass  fibers, ceramic, silicone and so on.  This is further  complicated by Coefficient of Thermal Expansion (CTE) mismatch of the layers and the need to polish dissimilar  interfaces with the same expected surface finish. Removing a significant portion of the die substrate will  usually affect the stability of the package.  Proper  planning of the entire backside analysis strategy is a  requirement that is frequently trivialized at the peril of  the project, as will be shown in subsequent sections.


A request is received as follows:  How much will it cost  to thin a BGA flat to 30 µm +/-5 µm with a mirror polish  finish to < 5 nm RMS roughness?  These types of  requests lead to a great deal of miscommunication and  grief for all involved due to the great volume of omitted  expectations and data.


What is meant by “flat”?  Does the package have  sufficient area beyond the die to allow mounting, if not  what are the options to mount for preparation? Information is required for numerous critical parameters  such as: The starting die thickness, initial flatness of the  die (curvature), cavity up or down orientation for access, exposed die or metal lid, composition of lid, type of die  attach used, composition of Ball Grid Array (BGA) (ceramic or glass/epoxy laminate), package dimensions, bondwires or bumps, silicon die dopant level, power  dissipation requiring a diamond window heat spreader, type of underfill, thickness of package substrate under  die, mounted to motherboard or individual BGA, distance  of decoupling capacitors from die edges, profile of  created pocket edges to allow Solid Immersion Lens (SIL) access or gas assisted etch in Focused Ion Beam (FIB).  Rework removal of the part from the motherboard  or test card for preparation should be considered


carefully.  Once thinned, will the part survive the strain  of reflow or test sockets?  Will all the balls still make  electrical contact in the socket after thinning due to added  warpage of the package?  A little time spent discussing  the objectives will not just identify weaknesses in the  initial assumptions but will allow a best approach to be  explored before the work begins, maximizing the  probability of a successful analysis.  Think through the  project all the way to final delayering and Transmission  Electron Microscope (TEM), Scanning Electron  Microscope (SEM), or FIB work.  Will the preparation  methods such as an epoxy mount complicate subsequent  removal and potential topside delayering once the defect  is identified with photon emission or laser stimulus  methods from the backside?


So why bother with backside preparation?  We do  backside thinning mainly due to inaccessibility of the  features of interest.  This is typically the active region of  the device buried under multiple layers of metal from the  front side creating the need for backside access.  The  package plays heavily in the best chosen approach for  access depending on a cavity down or up orientation and  location of interconnects such as bumps on a flip chip or  wire-bonds of which the wire-loops must be avoided  during access/thinning.  Methodologies for the  preparation may require in-situ board level or system  module analysis, die repackaging or limited pocket  access.  Stacked die require strategies to determine which  die are sacrificially removed as the target die is  approached for analysis and/or deprocessing.


Backside thinning allows for further analysis using SIL, Photon Emission, FIB edit, 3D X-ray, Magnetic mapping, Laser Stimulus, and so on.


Backside sample preparation for through the silicon  analysis has moved into the mainstream of FA in the last  5-10 years.  While Moore‟s law is concluding at the die level, the package engineering world continues to forge ahead and so do the increasingly stringent requirements for sample preparation.  The reader needs to be aware of numerous die and package options for dimension and pin count.  Package options vary from Flip Chip BGA‟s to a vast multitude of System in Package (SiP) configurations.


[1,2,3].


Thinning of the substrates can be accomplished by flat  lapping, pocket machining, laser etching, ion beam


milling, RIE (Reactive Ion Etching), chemical etching, or  a combination of these [4].


Basics for Silicon optical properties


Thinning of the Silicon substrate to a specified thickness  allows matching of desired optical properties to a lens  designed to operate through the specified thickness such  as SILs.  Thinning also reduces the scatter and absorption  of light especially at shorter wavelengths as shown in  figure 1 allowing higher resolution imaging and detection  of higher energy photons.  Dopants in the bulk Si also  necessitate thinner substrates due to increased free carrier  absorption.


Figure 1.  Transmission of light as a function of varying  Si thickness [5].


A detailed excerpt is provided below from “FLIP-Chip  and “Backside” Sample Preparation Techniques” [6].


“ If light of intensity I0 is incident on a piece of bulk Si, the light intensity is attenuated dependent on the  thickness dSi, wavelength λ, and doping concentration of  the substrate [7]. The variation of the transmitted light  intensity IT is given by the so-called Lambert-Beer  absorption law [7]:


The absorption coefficient α consists of two major  contributions: the band-gap related absorption and the  free carrier absorption [7]. Band-gap related absorption  which is also called interband absorption is given by the  bandstructure of Si (Fig. 2) [8].


Figure 2.  Bandstructure of Si [8].


An incident photon can only be absorbed if its energy can  excite an electron from the valence band to the  conduction band, i.e. if its energy is greater than or equal  to the band-gap energy, Egap, of Si (1.12 eV  corresponding to 1.1 μm at 300 K). In Fig. 3(a) the  transmission of undoped Si is shown. Si acts as a lowpass  filter absorbing all photons with energy greater than the  band gap energy and being transparent for photons with  energy less than Egap. By contrast, free carrier (intraband) absorption induces a transition within the  same band. The mechanism for free-carrier absorption is  shown in Fig. 4 for an n-doped substrate. The absorbed  photon [loses] its energy to an electron in the conduction  band that is excited to higher energy within the same  band. To conserve momentum a phonon has to be  involved. Once excited to higher energy, the electron  relaxes via phonon interaction to the conduction band  minimum. Within the scope of a semi-classical model, the absorption coefficient increases linearly with the  doping concentration, n, of the substrate and  quadratically to the light wavelength [9]:


with m* the effective mass, μ the mobility, and n the  doping concentration of the substrate.  In Fig. 3, the light  transmission as a function of doping of the substrate is  shown. The higher the doping concentration is, the lower  the transmission due to free carrier absorption, especially  in the infrared, i.e. transparent wavelength range.  According to formula (1), light attenuation drops  exponentially with decreasing substrate thickness. Thinning the substrate can minimize light attenuation  above the band-gap.


Not only is the transmission dependent on the thickness  and nature of the substrate but also the quality of the  illuminated image taken from the backside of the die. To  minimize diffuse light scattering (caused by scratches and  irregularities at the surface of the die that deteriorate  image quality) a mean surface roughness of less than 5  nm is recommended [10]. Even if the surface quality  requirements are fulfilled, IR light has to be used for  illumination due to the transmission characteristic of Si. As a result, the lateral resolution is reduced compared to  standard frontside illumination. In addition, a lens failure,


Interferometer Thickness Measurement


The Interferometer uses a broad band light source  microscope with a spectrometer to map in the frequency  domain the constructive and destructive patterns in the  specified waveband.  The resulting sinusoidal pattern is  Fourier Transformed to a resulting impulse representative  of the film thickness.  Calibration coupled with the index  of refraction is used to give repeatable results into the  nanometer range.  The quality of the measurement is a  parameter called GOF or goodness of fit [50].  This  parameter relates to the specified thickness calculated  versus measured.  A rough surface will degrade the GOF  value since additional harmonics appear in the spectrum.  It is important to define a narrow measurement range for  the acceptable values to minimize false and unwanted  outliers.  A die knowingly thinned to 30 µm and surveyed  as being no thinner than 25 µm nor thicker than 40 µm  should not have a defined range of 0 to 100 µm.  The  interferometer can be stand alone with mapping  capability or built into a milling machine.  When  integrated, the need to remove the sample and inspect  offline is eliminated.  The ability to generate higher  resolution 3D and contour maps calibrated directly to the  mechanical spindle location greatly improves the  alignment of the contour map to the sample in process.  The interferometer microscope serves additionally as an  inspect tool when in camera mode [51].  Referring back  to Figures 33 and 34, the surface is incompletely polished  and will be used to demonstrate the usage of the  interferometer.  The interferometer coupled with its  microscope allows a quick approximation of surface  quality during the thinning process.  Figure 36 shows the  thickness measured with almost no harmonics in the  spectrum at 118.18 µm in the polished center.  The  surface is around 15 nm RMS roughness.


Examination of the edge area from Figure 34 reveals  polished flat tops on a still rough surface.  The ground  surface has local values of Pv = 6 µm which is roughly  800 nm RMS per Figure 37.  Note the harmonics  blending into the signal with 2 peaks.  A small change in  position will cause the interferometer to hop to nearby  values as a function of peaks and valleys on the silicon  surface.


Final polish with 0.05 µm colloidal silica will easily yield  a smooth surface of 2.5 nm RMS or better.  The  challenge with surface formation is contaminants from  the package may break off and scratch the surface during  the final polish process.

Curvature Modeling and Thermal Relaxation


In the days of primarily injection molded packages, backside thinning was fairly trivial.  The die remained  relatively flat and the fillers used were very compatible  with cross-sectioning as well as backside preparation, additionally, the thinning requirements were much less  stringent.


Due to higher CTE mismatch of composites and silicon, a  strain layer forms and warps the package and die, especially with flip chip type devices.  The compatibility  of the layers involved must not be neglected especially  when repackaging or potting cavities with epoxy for  continued front-side delayering after backside analysis.


If a device shows a concave or convex warpage at room  temperature, it is important to measure the surface  curvature both at ambient and at a higher temperature  such as 70 °C to determine the change in warpage as a  function of stress and to be aware of a crack risk potential  when thinning.  A die under a uniform compressive strain  will warp predictably with a r2 surface characteristic [52].  With the die bent under compressive stress, a scratch can  propagate a crack along the Si lattice similar to scribing  and breaking with wafers.  Please note, devices which do


not exhibit a “relaxation” behavior as a function of


temperature are typically not candidates for this method


[53].  Figure 39 is an interferometer view of an area scan  over a crack.  The limit values rail at 150 µm and 125 µm. The crack risk reduces as the die is thinned below  approximately 150 µm RST for > 60e-8 r2 values.


Figure 39.  Interferometer representation of a crack in the  silicon during grind on a high warp strain part.


The die can be held at a higher temperature to relax the  stress during thinning and/or a very fine grind/polish  based process can be used to thin to the < 150 µm target.  This is common and expected since these are devices  which were underfill snap cured at typically 150 °C and  see subsequent reflow temperatures > 240 °C.   Some


devices require these extra management steps if identified  as high strain candidates.  Figures 40 and 41 illustrate the  strain seen before any deprocessing on the native 750 µm  thick die.  The pattern is a set of parallels imaged off of  the native silicon mirrored surface.


Figure 40.  Image at ambient showing typical convex  warp curvature in the mirrored surface of the silicon die.


Figure 41.  Image at 110 °C at which the surface is flat.  Increasing the temperature further will force the surface  concave.


Deep pocket formation on silicon regardless of how it is  accomplished should be avoided to minimize crack risk.  Figures 42 through 44 show 2 pockets prepared on a  globally thinned substrate without any curve correction.  The substrate should be globally thinned and medium  polished (~30 nm RMS) to < 200 µm RST, then the  desired pocket areas thinned further to target.  Curvature


can be used from the beginning or adaptively as the  silicon is thinned by adjusting the curve model in x and y  for best fit during the thinning and surface shaping  process.  By having shallow pockets and a less brittle thin  substrate, the package will be more tolerant of strain such  as when clamped in a socket, greatly reducing the risk of  crack propagation associated with the high aspect pocket.  The shallow pockets also reduce the issues of sidewall  lens clearance or issues with imaging and gas distribution  in a deep FIB pocket.  It is likely the placement location  of the pockets is initially unknown so having a globally  thinned and polished die allows preliminary analysis with  normal air spaced microscope objectives to identify and  plan for the SIL target zone(s) or FIB edit areas.


Figure 42.  Flat thin and polish with 2 pockets and no  curve correction.


Figure 43.  Contour mesh model with cubic best fit  functions showing RST of a 50 x 50 sized interferometer  measurement array.  The x curvature and y curvature  values can be adjusted to minimize the corrected z range  value.  The map will update and upon approval then be  implemented on the CNC mill with curve correction.


Figure 44.  3D wire mesh model of 50 x 50  interferometer map of RST.


Orange Peel Effect with Ultra-Thin Silicon < 10 µm


Silicon Mechanical properties


Commercially, there is a need for flexible thin products < 50 µm.  These are referred to, in the industry, as UTC (Ultra-Thin Chips).  The same Sub Surface Damage (SSD) problems arise when back grinding creating  potential for stress fractures as seen in FA preparation as  well as commercial thinning.  Likewise, etch pits  produced during thinning by wet etching contribute to  localized stress.


The physical parameters which are measure of strength of  bulk silicon such as Young‟s modulus (E) also change  with thinning. The Young‟s modulus, which normally has  a constant value, becomes thickness dependent especially  when the thickness hits the nanometer regime. After a  certain thickness, hb, the dependence of Young‟s modulus  on the thickness can be described as: [54]


   = 54.872∗ℎb0.226


For Si, the hb is about 80 nm and this value depends on  parameters such as in-plane strain and Poisson‟s ratio.


The mechanical strength of UTCs is also influenced by  thickness and the stress generated during the bending. Mathematically this is expressed as:


  s   = (  ∗ℎ) / (2  )


where h is thickness of UTC and R is the bending radius  of curvature. Under bending conditions, the stress is  directly proportional to the thickness of UTCs and


inversely proportional to the radius of curvature. The  ultimate breaking strength of silicon is 7 GPa [55]. In a  packaged structure with thin silicon over a flexible  substrate, Stoney‟s formula could be used to determine  the stress level. In the most common form, it is written  as:


     = (        2 ) / (6(1 −   )      )


(10)


where ts , tf are substrate and film thickness, and ν is  Poisson‟s ratio. The stress experienced by the top surface  of UTCs is proportional to Young‟s modulus for the  substrate and its respective thickness.


Electrical Behavior


UTC‟s and the supporting flexible mount substrate can  affect the piezo-resistive nature and band structure  causing a variation in the electrical response of the  devices.  The change in mobility is seen to increase with  bending stress in n-type MOSFET‟s whereas p-type are  stress direction dependent [56].


As discussed in the paper “Thermal Exposure Effects of  Backside Thinned Flip-Chip Device on Visible Light  Probing” temperature impacts the geometry of the silicon  surface [57].  Thermal management is very important  with ultra-thin silicon.  Ultra-thin silicon is elastic and  therefore will conform to the underlying surface.  Where  it is beneficial and sometimes required to use temperature  to relax strain on r2 curve warped BGA type packages, the irregular stress seen on stacked die generally does not  relax or benefit thermally.  Temperature control becomes  critical through the entire process from prep to test to  deprocess once the silicon is < 10 µm.  This includes  heating to demount the sample from the wax mount and  obviously any local heat generated during test will  change the shape of the silicon film and possibly the  parameters leading to 2nd breakdown or EOS.  As noted  previously, the silicon per Young‟s modulus is elastic and  will readily stretch to the contour of the underfill and  bumps.  Moisture trapped in the epoxy composite (water  weight gain) can wreak havoc if the temperature is not  maintained closer to ambient.  A lot of preparation work  can quickly come to an end due to failure to manage  temperature through the entire process including the  frictional grinding and polishing steps.  High speed (> 10K RPM) CNC processing can mean likely death to  ultra-thin silicon due to the ease with which frictional  heating can transmit to the underfill without adequate  cooling.  Figures 45 through 47 illustrate the dominance  of the solder bumps and underfill vs. temperature to the  surface flatness.  The resulting bumps resemble the  surface of an orange “orange peel”.  The change of  surface contour is evident as the temperature is changed.  The surface permanently changes with a brief excursion  to 120 °C and back to ambient as shown in Figure 47


demonstrating the danger.   Liquid cooling while testing  with or without a SIL lens is likely to be required.  A  local region can easily climb to 120 °C or more without  cooling and at the least, shift the electrical parameters.  A  successfully completed sample thinned below 1 µm is  shown in Figure 48.


Figure 45. Optical brightfield image of “orange peel” effect associated with 400 µm pitch solder bumps prior to  final polish.  RST = 4.7 µm  @ 20 °C.


Figure 46. Optical brightfield image of “orange peel” effect associated with 400 µm pitch solder bumps prior to  final polish.  RST = 4.7 µm @ 80 °C


Figure 47. Optical brightfield image of “orange peel” effect post 120 °C back to 20 °C cycle prior to final  polish for mount wax removal.  RST = 4.7 µm at 20 °C.


Figure 48.  CMP polished ultra-thin optical image ready  for test.  Thermal management is required.


Wire to Wire Bonding (Repackaging)


This technique is typically used when the package is not  conducive to backside preparation such as a cavity up  BGA where the ball side would have to be milled through  for access severing the inter-connects.  It should be noted  the package layout must be examined carefully as it may  be possible to mill an access pocket if the center balls are  part of a ground plane and the goal is FIB edit for  verification work.  Otherwise, the package is sanded or


ground down by lapping or CNC to remove most of the  package leaving a small section with die and clipped  bond wires embedded.  Since the silicon die is still  embedded in the original package, the package acts as a  carrier for the die.  Depending on the nature of the  package and die, the leadframe will be intact, partially  milled or completely milled away.  If the leadframe is  intact, a probe card or socket can be used to establish  electrical contact to the die through the remaining  leadframe or with wire-bonding.  If the leadframe is  gone, the wires which are bonded to the die will be  visible embedded in the plastic at the polished surface.  Mechanical probes can be used to contact the embedded  wires; however, the number of pins is usually a limiting  factor to probes [58].


Wafers can also be prepared for backside by dicing the  wafer and wire-bonding the die conventionally into an  open leadframe or package.  If an open leadframe is used  it can be encapsulated with room temperature epoxy prior  to backside preparation.


Sizing the Chip


Polish the excess plastic material from the edges and thin  the top if necessary being careful not to disturb the wire  loops embedded in the plastic package.  The polished  chip embedded in the remaining epoxy can now be  treated as an integrated circuit die.  The embedded wires  at the surface serve as bond pads and the polished  backside is now considered the top surface as shown in  figure 49.


Die Attach and Wire bond


The resulting part is attached to a new wireframe package  and wire bonded to create electrical connections between  the die and new leadframe.  Figure 50 shows the die in  place on the new package prior to wire bonding.  Figure   51 shows a section of the finished product with wire to  wire bonds [59,60,61].  The new pinout is implemented  on the loadboard or a socket wiring adapter is used with  the existing loadboard.


Figure 49.  Original package after leadframe removal and  polishing.


Figure 50.  Plastic package (containing die without  leadframe) attached with room temperature epoxy to a  132 lead ceramic pin grid array and ready for wire  bonding.


Figure 51.  Wire to wire bonds around the periphery of  the package.  The polished die surface is to the left.


Case #1 Ceramic Cavity Devices (CCD)


Due to the hardness of ceramic, higher milling speeds  and a more aggressive force are required to mill a pocket  in the ceramic.  Cooling and lubrication also becomes a  concern from the frictional forces of the grind.  Either a  submersion approach or a spray approach are  recommended for both cooling and clearing of the  ceramic particles.


A CCD sensor in a ceramic package is shown in figure


52.  On the frontside, the sensor window was removed  and the wire bonded cavity filled with a low stress epoxy  filler encapsulant.  The part was then affixed with  adhesive tape to a ceramic plate and a pocket was milled  through the backside with a diamond grinding bit at  9,000 RPM in a bath.  Once the die was reached, normal  thinning and CMP polishing ensued to the target of 30 µm.  This part has a spin on antireflective coating.


Figure 52.  Ceramic package cavity prefilled from the top  with low stress encapsulant and milled through the  backside to 30 µm RST.  Note the leadframe began to  expose at 50 µm RST.


Case #2 Injection Molded Parts


Refer to Figure 53.  The initial pocket is milled down  until the leadframe is exposed.  A second smaller pocket  is milled inside the first pocket, with consideration as to  the bond wire proximity per prior x-ray inspection.  Thinning and polishing then continues to the desired  endpoint.  No curvature correction is needed due to the  flat nature typical of injection molded devices.


Figure 53.  Double pocket milled device to provide  maximum SIL lens clearance on a 304 PQFP device.


Case #3 BGA with Contour Preparation


There are several options which may be used  independently or supplementally when preparing a part  with a known r2 model curvature.


1. Flat lap with an angular head.


2. A curve model can be applied to anticipate the  resulting top surface needed at the target  thickness.


3. Temperature can be applied to the part to relax  stress during prep.


4. After partial thinning the data points obtained  from the interferometer for RST can be used as a  mesh overlay model iteratively to generate a  best match of uniform RST.


Note:  For pocket polishing in the recent past, a few data  points such as a 20 x 20 array was used to generate a 3D  model on the offline interferometer.  Since the model was  low resolution with steps, the surface had edge step  issues that were resolved by constant force soft polishing  to round off the edges.  This works but is very operator  dependent.  The sample removal and replacement for  measurements coupled with the need to polish to the  target by dwelling in the higher areas of the device were  tedious but allowed somewhat repeatable thinning to the  limits of the device especially for smaller areas.  Proper  adaptive surface shape definition prior to final polish will  reduce the tedious nature of manual selective polish  methods.


Mounting the sample and stability


The sample can be held with dual stick Kapton tape, thermal release wax (Crystalbond), epoxy, or a  mechanical clamp method.  Considerations for stability  of the mount are important.  Thermal release wax slowly  creeps at room temp and is soluble in acetone.  Tapes are  compressible and may not hold for the duration of the


preparation.  Mechanical mounts may strain the package  or crush the balls complicating subsequent testing.  The  mount or device may have too much flexure due to thin  supporting structures or distant mount points.  This is  more a concern with board/standoff mount methods or  DDR4 type devices without fully populated balls.  Once  mounted, the tilt is corrected and the curve is ascertained  along with the rigidity of the surface to be thinned.  Figure 54 shows the flexure of a standoff mounted PC  board with the upper right mount point furthest from the  die.  The resulting deflection is greater on the upper right  corner and should be reinforced if possible before  preparation.  The 9 posted numbers are the actual surface  values used to calculate the curve.


Figure 54.  Deflection test and curvature measurement to  validate mount stability.  Color represents flex from 0 to  5 µm and posts the drop distance measured with color to  represent the amount of deflection at 40 grams loading  force.  In this case the top right edge has mount standoffs  further from the die correlating to the increased flexure  values in red.


Once the tilt is automatically corrected, a reference point  is set for the milling bit outside the area to be thinned.  This allows tools to be changed and referenced to a  known height so during thinning an accurate  determination of the material removed is maintained.  The measured surface profile, if significantly curved, is  negated with a matching curve profile.  During thinning  this step approximates the actual natural curve at  completion and can be adjusted to predict the final curve  based on a similar set of samples.  Although this step is  not required, if a good surface mesh model is available, it  has some clear advantages:


1. The curve model calculates a smooth radius  square model for all possible XYZ positions  for every submicron step in XY space.


2. The curve model is not restricted to the area  of mesh and extends past the edges.


3. A coarse mesh model can be used to adjust  the offset to the curve model locally giving  similar results to a high resolution mesh.


By locally adjusting the curve model with mesh, the local  extrapolation of the curve is optimized and the required  mesh has less Z height correction between data points  reducing the step error significantly.  In other words, a  mesh minimally correcting a surface already defined by  curve requires fewer iterative corrections to achieve a  uniform RST.  Please note this is only true with a  reasonably uniform convex or concave curvature as is  typically seen with Flip Chip BGA types.


The majority of the silicon is removed without any  curvature correction and measured in Figure 55.  The few  microns of remaining RST error can be compensated out  on the next iterations of surface shaping and polishing  with mesh alone or curve combined with mesh.  It is  important to fully shape (grind/polish) the surface before  repeating measurement of the RST and adding the  corrections to the existing mesh set.


Figure 55.  X and Y curve correction to be applied for  correction of the major component of package warp.  650 µm of silicon was removed without curvature leaving this  RST measured map on the left and the convolution  correction map predicted for a 3 mm tool on the right.


A force map must show uniform force everywhere on the  target area before proceeding.  Figure 56 is a force map  showing the surface is not yet shaped to match the  required mesh+curve model.  The force map is obtained  during thinning to target so progress may be observed.  If  no force map is available then be sure to remove enough  material to guarantee the surface has been shaped to the  mesh.  The adaptive model assumes the new surface  measurements are added only after the shape has been  completely defined by the last loaded model.  Failure to  do this will result in erroneous corrections summed into  the adaptive model.  Figure 57 is the RST contour map  after applying the mesh + curve model thinned and  polished to 30 µm +/- 2.1 µm from center.


Figure 56.  Force map obtained during thinning to ensure  contour.  Thinning continues until the force is equal.


Figure 57.  Mesh contour map of the surface after first of  several adaptive iterations of thinning showing the  remaining error to be corrected.


Ideally, the target thickness should be thick enough to  validate the shape, since silicon cannot be replaced once  removed.  Please note there are many options to this  approach including using a final mesh and/or curve from  a similar device and skipping this measurement step for  optimization of the process time.  The first part typically  takes the longest, as added time is needed to understand   the nature of how the part changes shape during thinning.  This deformation can affect the package and the tool  reference point resulting in over or undershooting the  desired target thickness.  When working with parts that  are moving targets, characterization is important via an  iterative (adaptive) thinning process.  Selective CMP  polish can continue to address the thicker regions as the  target thickness is approached over the region of interest  or for the whole die.  If desired, adding in another  adaptive mesh correction to the data stack will further  assist the thinning.  A final 3D interferometer map is then  obtained to validate the thickness and variance with a  final inspection to confirm the desired surface quality is  achieved.  See Figure 58.


Figure 58.  Final CMP polish result with polish to target  methods used.  All units are in µm and represent final  RST.


Electronic Endpoint Thinning of Silicon


By monitoring the electrical parameters of a conductive  polishing tip with the substrate, it is possible to monitor  the breakdown observed and correlate it with the RST if a  standard correlation exists between breakdown and RST


[62].  Since the elbow of the curve is being mapped as an  endpoint threshold in figures 64 and 65, the varying  resistance of the tip in contact is not dominating the  endpoint determination.  The clear advantage of this  technique is the polish step is also an endpoint step.  The  opaque polishing paste need not be removed as each pass  of polish shows a correlating thickness signal real time to  the tip.  I-V curves into the 100 kΩ range or less for tip  scan measurements are typical for the conductive tip.


Characterization and Calibration of Silicon Endpoint


The part can be mounted while on the board or  individually as shown in figures 59 and 60 [63].   Nonuniform RST due to curvature allows characterization of  the endpoint method.  The surface was globally polished  to 50 µm  RST, then pocket polished further with a 2 mm  diameter Xylem tool using the traditional iterative  method.  Once an open area in the silicon was observed, the process was halted.  Figure 61 is the result. A scan  line at 0,-690 to -1000,-690 µm was chosen based on 0,0  origin in the center of the pocket.


Figure 59.  Graphics card mounted and electrically  connected to floating endpoint sensor plate.


Figure 60.  BGA mounted and electrically connected to  the floating endpoint sensor plate.  Nylon screws provide  a constant gentle down pressure to hold the balls in  contact with the plate while a recessed cavity is designed  to securely hold the part in a BGA or Land Grid Array (LGA) capable mount fixture.  The pocket accommodates  the underlying surface capacitors. These fixtures can be  machined independently or on the same machine used to  thin and polish the part.


Putting in the constants (n and λ) for silicon at 1064 nm  in Equation 11 below:


t = OPD*0.155


The fringes are counted to precisely represent the  thickness at each coordinate allowing characterization of  the relationship between threshold and thickness.


Figure 61.  Laser Scan Microscope (LSM) image at 1064  nm of fringes in a 4 mm pocket.  Scale bar is matched  over region of X-axis line scan from the portion 0,-690 µm to -1000,-690 µm.


A 150 µm soft carbon scan tip was used in Figure 62 to  profile the electrical characteristics of the substrate with a  loading force of 5 grams for the general area in X and Y  to identify the relationship between thickness and  resistance.  Note:  Soft metal tips can also be used.  The  resulting scan line plot is shown in Figure 63.  Figures 64  and 65 show the shift in reverse bias substrate breakdown  at 2 coordinates on each end of the scan line from x = -500 to x = -1000 µm .  The breakdown moves to lower  voltages as the active p-n junctions are approached.  Figure 66 shows the resulting curve of thickness vs. diode threshold.
