A new 4 x 4 pocket was thinned using a modified Xylem  tip with a soft metal conductive core insert.  Endpoint  detection was used and the process stopped when any  portion of the scan showed a moving breakdown below


3.3 V.  Figure 67 is the laser LSM showing fringe  minima on the lower left.  Tip scan conductivity confirms  the minima at 4.7 µm of remaining silicon correlating to  the LSM image.


Figure 67.  Another 4 x 4 mm area thinned on a  deliberate tilt to confirm endpoint capability.  Spot is  thinnest at 4.7 µm RST.  ASAP-IPS machine XY  position map corresponds to fringe bullseye pattern.


Substrate thinning of epitaxial or degenerate substrates is  accomplished with similar methods except the substrate


leakage would change from low ohmic to a diode as the  active area below the doped substrate is exposed.  Characterization is recommended on a sacrificial unit to  identify the expected electrical characteristic versus  thickness for a given process technology.  Note this  method depends on identifying a relationship between  RST and I-V curve characteristics.


It should be clear the system has been reconfigured as a  Scanning Probe Microscope (SPM) since this meets the 3  requirements of an SPM to be able to profile with a  scanning tip in 3 dimensions with force feedback.  This  combination with milling and polishing capabilities  eliminates the need to go between different tools and  opens the door to automated characterization and  endpoint detection based on a desired thickness.


Backside access and imaging is a rapidly growing field  from repackaging to pocket access methods.  With  forethought on the choice of methods and tools the  seemingly daunting task of access is fairly  straightforward even with ultra-thin silicon.

Photon Emission in Silicon Based Integrated Circuits


Christian Boit, Anne Beyreuther, Norbert Herfurth


Technische Universität Berlin, Germany


christian.boit@tu-berlin.de, phone +49 30 314 25520


Abstract - In A Nutshell


Photon emission (PE) is one of the major optical techniques for  contactless isolation of functional faults (CFI) in Integrated  Circuits (ICs) in full electrical operation. Optical CFI is  performed in Near Infra Red (NIR) as the typical signal access  is through chip backside. Complementary optical CFI  techniques use scanning external light emitters and detect either  signal stimulation in the IC or electro-optical modulation of the  reflected light. The specific characteristic of PE is  electroluminescence [2], the optical interaction just by  electrical operation. There is no external light stimulus that may  produce unwanted artefacts.


In ICs, the typical PE phenomenon is an intraband effect of  carriers gaining kinetic energy in electrical fields and scatter  accompanied by light emission of a broad spectrum. The typical  CMOS logic sends no PE signal in static mode. Switching  inverters emit light, so dynamic measurements in picosecond  resolution are used for circuit and delay analysis. Failing FETs  and circuit failures show PE patterns. Also, parasitic bipolar  events like latch up and I/O or ESD (electro-static discharge) related problems can be well detected with PE.


PE is the major CFI technique for IC technologies down to circa  1V supply voltage and 20nm nodes. Smaller nodes and lower  voltages require further steps of development. PE of low power  technologies shifts further into the IR regime, so proper  detectors are necessary. Laser based CFI techniques can  improve their image resolution into FinFET dimensions by  expanding towards visible range. Although PE is limited to  NIR, it contains interesting complementary information, especially if time resolved, because it is free of artefacts.


1) Introduction


Photon Emission – The General Phenomenon


F. Destriau reported Electroluminescence (EL) in 1936 [7]. He applied an electrical field to specific materials and observed electrically stimulated light emission. This phenomenon was mostly understood as recombination of electrons and holes, an interband and bipolar effect. In the world of optoelectronic devices, EL is the term dealing with fundamentals of LED’s(light emitting diode) with bipolar injection.


When A.G. Chynoweth and K.G. Mc Kay [5] published light emission of avalanche breakdown in silicon, they introduced the term “Photon Emission” (PE). They distinguished this phenomenon from EL because of its wide spectral distribution that they could only describe by taking into account intraband kinetic energy exchange relaxation processes, not necessarily


connected to interband recombination, which usually shows  discrete energy levels related to band gap or defect levels.


The term “Photon Emission” has also been established in the


Failure Analysis (FA) of Integrated Circuits (ICs) for the faint  light that could be observed in electronic operation when night  vision detectors, typically vidicon electron tubes with Near  Infra Red (NIR) spectral range, were applied.


At that time, contactless fault isolation in ICs was mostly done  using change of polarization properties of liquid crystals (LCs) at a critical temperature Tc. LC solutions were deposited on the  IC surface, the microscope lamp was equipped with a polarizer  and the IC was heated up to a temperature right below Tc. A  thermal hot spot with a local temperature higher than Tc could  be identified with an analyzer filter. This technique was  inexpensive and not very complicated but reproducibility was  limited and homogeneous thickness of the deposition was  problematic. With the transition to signal access through chip  backside, this technique became a niche application.


PE is directly related to the active device and much more  reproducible in everyday FA life. It has prevailed as one of the  reference techniques for contactless fault isolation (CFI). With  Near Infra Red (NIR) spectral range [1], PE has become one of  the leading CFI techniques that were used for signal acquisition  through chip backside. However, the strong dependence of the  PE signal intensity on supply voltage is problematic with low  power technologies, but a shift of the detected spectrum further  into the IR may solve this problem.


2) Fundamental Mechanism


2.1) Electronic Material Properties and Light Emission


Electronic devices can emit light correlated to electronic  operation. As for all electronic processes in solid state  materials, the energy band model and application of Fermi  statistics are the keys to understanding and categorizing the  effects.


In order to detect light, two basic conditions need to be met: A  release of electronic energy in the range of 0.5 – 1eV to create  photons in visible or near infrared regime plus a generation rate  that overcomes the noise level of the detector, both are  necessary to detect an emission signal.


Good conductors like metals usually do not show light  emission. The reason is the position of the Fermi level right  inside the conduction band(s). The density of occupied states is  close to the atomic density of the lattice. All these electrons can


be shifted into a conduction condition by room temperature  thermal energy. This means, no interaction with other bands  occurs, and carrier transport takes only a very small additional  kinetic energy.


During scattering and relaxation, this small excess energy will  produce phonons (in other words: heat) rather than photons. Heat would produce only atomic optical interaction (absorption  and emission) like black body radiation that follows BoseEinstein statistics. For temperatures that electronic devices  operate in, the respective photonic energies are usually much  lower in the far infra red. This effect is commonly used in LockIn Thermography [9].


Good dielectric materials usually never show light emission. The field is high, but the current is extremely low. The PE event  rate would not be detectable.


So, passive electronic devices are only emitting photons in  visible or NIR range except in special cases of leaky dielectrics  when they break down or highly resistive conductors that heat  up to 500K and higher.


However, semiconductor operation is different in two ways: In  pure condition (i.e. 0K), the conduction band contains no  electrons, the valence band is below the Fermi level and has no  free states. It is an insulator. Even room temperature would not  modify the conductivity to a range necessary for electronic  operation. Only lattice disorder creates conductivity. This is  technically achieved by doping with material that creates  energy levels very close to the energy bands. But the density of  carriers is usually much lower than in metals: In conduction  mode, the required kinetic energy is under some circumstances  high enough to create photons that we can detect as photon  emission. This is an intraband effect. In parallel, electrons in  semiconductors also have a complex relation to interband  effects. In non-equilibrium condition, excess minority carriers  enhance band-band recombination which may create photon  emission as well, although quantities depend very much on the  detailed band structure. Silicon, as an indirect semiconductor, shows very little photon emission intensity during  recombination activity.


2.2) Interband Relaxation - The Bipolar Mechanism (Recombination Related PE = R-PE)


In physics and engineering, the first idea of photon interaction  with semiconductors is the radiative recombination of an  electron in the conduction band and a hole in the valence band – the classical bipolar (negative electrons and positive holes involved) case in minority carrier injection mode like a forward biased pn junction. The spectrum of emitted light is a narrow Gaussian distribution around the band gap energy Egap.


Commercial Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) principally utilize such a phenomenon. The ideal condition is minority carrier injection in pn junctions of forward bias operating mode.


Several more specific cases occur using trap states in the band gap. This is especially important for indirect semiconductors where the electron must change its momentum when relaxing from the conduction to the valence band.


The momentum, in classical mechanics defined as p = mv, is in quantum mechanics the multiplication of the wave vector k withħ (ħ = h/2π, h…Planck constant), p = ħk. In band diagrams,


momentum coordinates are usually set up with the momentum  variable k. With the Heisenberg uncertainty relation


     ⋅      ≥ ħ ,


sharply localized impurities (Δx small) have a large uncertainty  in the momentum space (Δp large). This way, in indirect  semiconductors (different momentum coordinates of the  conduction band minimum and the valence band maximum) recombination via traps is much more probable than direct band –band recombination which would require a third reaction partner, a phonon with small energy but large momentum. Fig 1 illustrates how such a trap assisted process can be constructed in the electronic band diagram with momentum coordinates.


This means that a recombination process at a trap site gives the electron a chance to change momentum while it occupies the trap state, enabling the indirect recombination with momentum conservation. Mostly, these trap assisted recombination processes happen without radiation. In indirect semiconductor materials like silicon, only a very small portion of recombination is radiative. So, LEDs are usually made of other(direct) semiconductor materials. Yet, with sensitive detectors,even the indirect light emission can be monitored for device analysis purposes. It is a contactless way to characterize the operating mode of electronic devices.


2.3) Intraband Relaxation - The Unipolar Mechanism (EField Assisted PE = F-PE)


The vast majority of electronic devices today are FETs which  operate unipolarly (bipolar operation in FETs is only parasitic  and usually very well suppressed). All intended electronic  activity is happening in one band alone. Also in this case, detectable faint light emission occurs. So, electron relaxation  that causes light emission can also happen within one single

band. The carriers pick up kinetic energy in electric fields and  relax by scattering with phonons, crystal defects and charged  coulomb centers. The energy quantum per impact varies and the  impact probability decreases exponentially with increasing  energy. These scattering processes result in light emission with  a broad spectral distribution in the visible to near IR region. This behaviour is correlated to the statistical occupation of  states within one band (holes in valence band or electrons in  conduction band) which follows Fermi statistics. The Fermi  equation can be approximated by the much simpler exponential  law of Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics if the Fermi level is at  least 3kBT off the respective bands, where kB is the Boltzmann  constant and T is the temperature


2.4) The Elementary pn Junction and Photon Emission


Now, the photon mission phenomena of a very principal active  element that can be found in almost each electronic device in  silicon, a pn junction, will be presented and classified.


The basic operating modes of this element will show specific  PE characteristics that allow identification of the respective  operating modes only through PE detection.


There are 4 different operating modes (see Fig. 2). In forward  bias, a low-ohmic on-state is produced by a minority carrier  injection. In reverse, the layer depleted of carriers (space charge  layer SCL) is growing with increasing reverse voltage that  provides a high electric field. This is accompanied by a very  faint reverse current that is amost independent of voltage, representing a high ohmic “off” state. A degraded or poorly  produced pn junction can show an increased reverse current. However, the further increase of the reverse voltage leads to the  breakdown. Where a very sharp increase of current occurs at a  critical voltage.


(1) Forward Bias


In forward bias, the junction injects minority carriers, the density increasing exponentially with voltage. This injection releases a recombination activity proportional to the excess carrier density. A small proportion of this recombination will occur as interband relaxation releasing R-PE. As the probability of band-band recombination is proportional to excess minority carrier density multiplied with majority carrier density,emission intensity is more a monitor of minority carrier density than recombination time constants (see Fig. 3). Emission


profiles of R-PE are images of minority carrier profiles. The  spectrum of this emission signal is a gaussian shape around the  bandgap of the semiconductor.


(2) Reverse Bias


A reverse biased junction raises the pn-energy barrier and creates a large space charge region (SCR) which accelerates the few passing carriers. They lose their gained energy by scattering via phonons, crystal defects and charged coulomb centers. Scattering via charged coulomb centers results in a light emission with a broad spectral distribution in the visible to near IR region. The energy quantum per impact varies and the impact probability decreases exponentially with increasing energy. Fig. 2 shows that the emission intensity is usually below detection limit of PEM unless avalanche condition is approached. In reverse bias, the high electric field in the space charge layer (SCL) would produce F-PE as displayed in Fig. 4.

In pure pn junctions, the low current is producing too little rate  of emission events so emission intensity is usually below  detection limit. This holds only for a good junction.


(3) Leaky pn junction


A leaky junction (Fig. 2) still builds up a considerable electrical field and mostly offers a current density well above PEM detection limit (exception: large area devices like well-substrate junctions in ICs: if a current is leaking all over their large area,PE event density per detector pixel may never overcome noise level, in which case it can be useful to lower the magnification or group pixels).


Leakage currents in silicon are one of the classic PEM applications in failure analysis. They produce emission spots when passing through or created in an SCR (F-PE). Highly localized junctions allow detection even in pA range.


(4) Avalanche Breakdown


When avalanche condition is approached, the carriers that pick up more kinetic energy while passing the SCL than band gap energy is increasing drastically, so the relaxation is accompanied by massive electron hole pair generation, an almost unlimited multiplication of carriers. This is accompanied by strong unstable current conditions and eventually device breakdown which may be destructive if not controlled carefully. Fig. 5 shows how strong light emission of the type F-PE occurs, plus some occasional R-PE events.


Breakdowns of highly doped pn junctions may not always have an avalanche character since the breakdown can be tunnelling related (Zener-effect). Tunneling breakdowns in bulk Si based devices are usually not accompanied by strong PE as carriers pass the SCL without much gain of kinetic energy.


3) Photon Emission in Integrated Circuits


FET Operating Modes


As discussed in the introduction, light emission phenomena are  very unlikely in commercial passive devices built from  conductor and insulator materials like resistors or capacitors. Active devices with nonlinear current-voltage characteristics  are the predominant photon emission candidates. This section  presents the opportunities of contactless characterization for the  most important electronic device, the MOS - Field Effect  Transistor, the heart of integrated circuits and their basic digital  element, the CMOS inverter. We use simple device models to  explain the principal effects.


3.1) FET Function


A MOS Field Effect Transistor (FET) modulates conductivity  in a semiconductor interface to a capacitive dielectric and gate  electrode. The source (S) and drain (D) of the load circuit are  built as pn junctions next to the capacitative structure, both are  zero or negatively biased for a highly resistive off condition. The capacitive structure in between that is built of silicon as the  bottom electrode and a top electrode of metal or poly-silicon  called the gate (G) with a thin dielectric stacked between them. The gate capacitor is never conductive in steady state but if the  gate voltage (VGS) is high enough (higher than threshold voltage  VT), it can bend the bands of silicon into strong inversion so a  conductive channel can connect the two junctions in a low  ohmic manner, sub-VT is treated as off in this article. The  channel conductivity is driven by the gate voltage and this is the  transistor effect: a very small control signal drives a strong load  between the source and drain, the two highly doped parts of the  junctions. This is an unipolar case, no excess minority carrier  injection is happening. PE only occurs if an additional effect is  happening. This is either breakdown of the junction in reverse  voltage condition or the so called pinch-off of the conductive  channel close to the drain when drain voltage VDS reaches or  even overcompensates the effective gate voltage: VDS ≥ VG,eff  with VG,eff = VGS - VT (see Fig. 6).


This is the operating mode condition of FETs in saturation or “pinch off”.


3.2) FET Saturation


Saturation is the FET operating condition of VDS > VGS-VT or  VG eff > 0. When this condition is met, the conduction channel  is not maintained close to the drain. Instead, a high field space  charge layer builds up close to the drain, the carriers passing  through that region gain kinetic energy and the full load current  must pass through this high field zone, which is a very good  condition for producing photon emission.


These energetic carriers generate electron hole pairs in the SCL (below avalanche multiplication though) creating a surplus  reverse current at the drain – body junction. Hence, intensity of  light emission is proportional to the body/substrate current (Fig.7).


Some of the carriers generated in the pinch off region scatter  into the gate dielectric and become hot carriers (Fig.6). Light  emission in an FET can also be used as an indicator of hot  electron injection. A look at the I-V curve (Fig. 7) tells that,

with VDS fixed, VDsat is decreasing with increasing VGS. The  drain voltage that exceeds the pinch off point VDsat (VDsat = VDS


- VGeff) adds more kinetic energy to the carriers and increases the PE signal. For a strong PE signal, many carriers are needed that release this increased kinetic energy by scattering. At low gate voltages, the number of carriers in the channel is relatively small, at high gate voltages the pinch off region is decreasing.


Consequentially, there is a PE intensity maximum correlating to substrate current maximum (which is based on the same effect) occurring at gate voltages well below drain voltages. In static operation, this condition can only be achieved in analog applications like amplifier circuits or individual FET’s. In most cases emission spots are indicating unwanted or failing cases,i.e. with floating pins or incomplete power-down mode. In dynamic operation, FETs will pass saturation while switching.


Consequently, time resolved PE opens up a whole further world of IC signal tracking. In silicon material, pFETs emit much less light than nFETs. Holes in valence band have quite different scattering probabilities than electrons in conduction band. For


more details, see [19]. In modern technologies, pFET channels  often consist of Ge enhanced material that improves PE  intensity a lot. For that reason, the pFET / nFET difference of  PE intensity will not be subject of the following chapters of this  article. Especially for CMOS, the contribution of the two types  of FETs to the composed PE signal is more complicated in real  devices.


3.3) CMOS Logic PE


Inverters are the basic digital elements of digital circuits. They  are composed of a series of complementary (C-) MOS  transistors as shown in Fig. 8. It is important to take into  account, that in real inverters the different signal intensity of pund n-FET may have an influence when the PE contribution of  the nFET and when the pFET is dominant. In high as well as  low condition, only the off current is flowing in the inverter and  in nominal supply voltage ranges, no PE occurs. In this moment, the voltage is between low and  high and the saturation condition makes the FETs emit light (see Fig. 9). So, the dynamic PE measurement is not giving a  waveform of the logical signal pattern but produces a series of  peaks in time when the transistors switch (See Fig. 9). Hence, a  clock and switching transistors can be tracked node by node. For tracking down a logical signal and resolving the delay of  the nodes, it is necessary to resolve the FET delay with the PE  detector. For single device delay measurement, the Time  Resolved Emission (TRE) needs to be captured in the single  picosecond range (Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis  PICA).


3.4) Integrated Circuit / Backside Access


Today, most Integrated Circuits (ICs) are built on silicon wafers  that are a little less than 1mm thick. In the common 2D concept, the active devices like FETs and CMOS logic are processed on  the top 2-5µm below the surface. The interconnects are on top  of the active levels. The number of the levels varies with the  complexity of the circuit from 2 to more than 10. Such a  structure is shown in Fig. 10. As the metal interconnects are  embedded in a transparent dielectric, PE may be detected  through the structured IC frontside. When die interconnect level  number is increasing much over 3, there is almost no path for  the light to transmit through the dielectrics anymore. But silicon  is rather transparent in the near infra red (NIR), as Fig. 11 is  showing (at least in the regular case that the wafer is not highly  doped). The spectral range of PE is well matched for covering  the transparent range of silicon. So there is the chance to detect  PE also through chip backside. Backside PE analysis is well  established for years and is today the standard approach. Even  if frontside access is possible, there is a very important  advantage of backside PE measurements over frontside results: The frontside result varies quantitatively from device to device.


The interconnects are shadowing the light path from device to  microscope in an individual manner for each site. A quantitative  comparison of PE from the devices requires backside access. This is essential for several investigations, i.e. reading out  memories or comparing CMOS nodes in time resolved PE.

4) Detection of Photon Emission


This section discusses the specification and selection of  detectors for proper PE applications. The main topics are image  resolution, sensitivity and spectral range of the detectors. A  further section discusses the value and application of spectral  information in the PE signal. For TRE or PICA, time resolution  is an additional requirement.


4.1) Detector Sensitivity


The spectral range of PE is in the Near Infra Red (NIR). Fig. 12  shows typical spectral detector sensitivities. For the effective  sensitivity, noise is a very critical phenomenon. The further  detectors expand their range towards the lower end of photon  energies, the noisier is the detector. Cooling reduces the noise; however, powerful cooling may be problematic as it may be  accompanied by freezing, dew and vibration.


Si detectors are the least noisy ones for PE. Standard Peltier  cooling is sufficient and there is no practical limit for the  integration time. On the other hand, Fig. 12 shows that they cut  off around 1.1µm which corresponds to the silicon bandgap at


1.13eV. The spectral response has only a very small overlap  with the silicon transparency. For backside access with Si  detectors, thickness and doping of the Si bulk play an important  role. Another problem is low IC supply voltage (see chapter


5.1). In general: IC technologies of 100nm nodes and below  need other detector solutions.


The InGaAs detector shows a very good spectral overlap with  silicon transparency for backside signal acquisition. As the  detection range expands to smaller photon energies, noise and  cooling become even more relevant issues. The noise signal  alone will charge up the detector pixels, so integration time is  limited. The photon emission sensitivity is reduced by the noise  level.


Another detector type is MCT, Mercury Cadmium Telluride or  HgCdTe. The spectral range expands to about 2.5µm. This  detector needs liquid nitrogen cooling and still is quite noisy, so  to date it was used only for special applications.


4.2) Time Resolution


All detectors that have been presented in this chapter are based  on CCD technology. Charging of the cells and read out of the  array take time, typically in the ms regime, so time resolution  of the clock speed in the circuit is not possible. The technical  realization of TRE or PICA started using vacuum tube based  detector systems with either micro channel plates (MCP) or  optical apertures to realize (limited) image resolution. Today, mostly avalanche photo diodes (APDs) are used as time  resolving detectors. Those solutions allow for picosecond  resolution, good enough for switching delays of single FETs. Time resolving PE systems are quite expensive and noise is also  problematic for those applications. A new time resolving  detector concept, Superconductiong single photon detector (SSPD), will be available soon, with many advantages like  drastically reduced jitter, much lower noise and spectral range  expanding a bit further into IR (good for low power  technologies, see 5.1). Because of laser based alternatives for  contactless fault isolation of dynamic fails, time resolved PE is  a niche market.


4.3) Image resolution


Fault isolation requires a microscopical imaging of the


structures. Miniaturization of IC devices has followed Moore’s


law for such a long time that image resolution is a critical topic  for optical CFI and PE in particular. The general approach of  diffraction limited image resolution R in optical microscopy is  Abbe’s law


   =


  λ    


(eq.1)


with the wavelength , NA the numerical aperture of the  objective and the Rayleigh criterion r = 0.61. For air gap  objectives, NA is the sine of the objective opening angle, necessarily a little smaller than 1. A rough approximation of R  is /2 as used by Abbe’s law. If the mean wavelength is 1µm, max R would be about 0.5µm. Microelectronic devices today  have typically much smaller feature sizes than that. But  contactless fault isolation (CFI) in ICs does not have to identify  the smallest geometry. It just requires the electrical function of  the circuit to be active in order to identify the device that the  fail is correlated to. The physical device problem can be  analyzed later with preparation and particle beam techniques. So, PE and other CFI techniques have image resolution  requirements relaxed about an order of magnitude. Fig. 13 and  Table 1 show that it is rather the device pitch than the minimum  feature size that matters. In addition, FETs are not too densely  packed, and some circuit simulation and layout helps to identify  the suspect device fault locale. All over, such CFI systems can  be applied successfully to IC technology generations of 90nm  nodes and often still work for 40nm nodes [36]. This is all based  on backside access. The problem of decreasing PE signal  intensity with reduction of supply voltage has already been  mentioned. Technologies of nodes smaller than 40nm require  better image resolution and an increased PE signal.

4.4) Solid Immersion Lens


Immersion is a way to improve both signal intensity and image  resolution. The diffraction angle between the object and the  objective is determined by the difference of the index of  refraction of the object material and the environmental material. As Fig. 14 indicates, the NA of eq. 1 is valid for the  environmental air. At the silicon/air interface though, the  silicon index of refraction (n = 3.5) for NIR makes all emission  angles higher than 17° to the surface normal suffer from total  internal reflection. So an environment with n >1 will increase


NA by exactly the factor of n. This factor n will improve both  the signal intensity and the resolution R. In the case of a solid  immersion material, an immersion lens can be built with a  hemispherical shape of the same material as the object and then  the rays exit normal to the hemispherical surface without  deviation, and no total reflection occurs. For such a system, NA  is improved maximum by the silicon index of refraction. Models of aplanatic shapes of SILs have been published [40] that promise an even higher NA improvement. With SILs, the  effective thickness of silicon increases a lot, so silicon detectors  are not suitable for this approach.


4.5) Evaluation of PE spectra


Electron Temperature and Band Gap Engineering


The spectral information of PE has only rarely been of interest. A faint signal divided up into spectral increments is much more  exposed to noise. If a silicon detector is used, the evaluation is  still quite straightforward because of the little noise this detector  is producing. A number of such investigations were published  in the 1980s and 1990s. After the millennium, when InGaAs  detectors and the backside approach became more important, the much higher noise and sets of optical filters that were not  easy to comprehend complicated the evaluation of spectral PE  results. There were only a few publications i.e. [12], [45]. Most  of the results were not confirming the publications of the silicon  detector results and were controversial to each other. Very  meticulous investigations ([41], [43], [45], [46]) confirm the  spectral continuity of MCT, InGaAs and Si detector spectra and  evaluate the spectra properly.


Two major effects contribute to PE spectra:


(1) In forward bias pn junctions, it is a Gaussian shape around the band gap as the maximum. The width of this shape is an indicator of the phonon interaction with the recombination process. At full width of half maximum (FWHM), an exponential curve can be fitted to the high photon energy slope of the spectrum. This curve is reciprocally proportional to the environmental temperature following the exponent:


  (−


    ℎ      )


(2) Spectra of FETs in saturation all follow the same characteristic: In the spectral range that the commercial PE detectors operate in, there is no maximum. The intensity decreases exponentially with increasing photon energy like the FWHM case in forward bias, but the temperature is not correlating to the environment. Equation 2 describes the spectra of FETs in saturation. The electron temperature Te is usually much higher than thermal conditions of the IC. Te represents the increased kinetic energy that the electrons pick up by passing through the high field zone of the pinched off channel thus producing hot electrons or impact ionization. The electron distribution in the high field zone is obviously similar to a fermi distribution that again can be approximated by an exponential function with increased temperature as a parameter. The other parameter that contributes to Te is a technology parameter, the mean free path between photon generating scattering events. It is very likely correlated to mobility parameters like strain or scattering probabilities with phonons or crystal impurities.

4.6) PE Signal Intensity and Device Supply Voltage


There is plenty of evidence that PE intensity decreases when  supply voltage is shrinking. The quantitative correlation is not  easy to describe. Electron temperature Te as discussed in section


4.5 is a key to linking voltage and PE. Three voltage related  factors influence the correlation:


1) in a given device, voltage variation influences VDsat, an important factor as described in section 3.2.


2) in a given device, voltage variation influences the FET current.


3) As Te is a function of the E-field, also the PE spectrum is changing with device voltage.


Empirical studies that measured PE of FETs with a variation of  VD and a fixed VG [55] show an exponential behaviour very  similar to eq. (2) with

This empirical equation can be correlated to the spectral PE of  FETs in eq. For a PE measurement of the integral spectrum  of the detector, eq. (2) needs to be integrated over Eph in the  spectral range of the detector. 5) Photon Emission in State of the Art IC


Technologies


State of the art IC technologies are FinFETs with 10nm or even  7nm nodes.  The roadmap is not fully following traditional  Moore’s law anymore. Geometries will shrink further to 5 or 3  nm, but more and more functionality per area will be realized  with not only shrinking geometry but also 3D and other options. Still, the Internet of Things (IoT) with the huge data rates will  demand further integration and higher clock frequencies. Vertical Gates all around the FETs may end up in stacked active  layers. For those technologies, the optical approach for CFI  techniques will be challenged. The high data rates for IoT can  only be realized with ultra low power technologies of 0.5V  supply voltage and below. Channel mobility management will  play an important role in devices that have less and less atoms  in the channel volume. Doping and strain will see a wider  statistical variation, so band gap engineering may vary from  device to device. For that reason, a contactless characterization  of channel band gap is a very useful application of forward bias  PE.


5.1) Low Power Technologies


Electro optical probing is the CFI technique that is well  established for low power technologies. But there are some  disadvantages (signal composed from many FETs in the laser  spot, signal intensity may vary because of local interferences, induced delay variations etc), so a second CFI technique would  be desirable. PE would be a good candidate because there is no  stimulation necessary on top of the electrical IC operation. But: the PE signal intensity decreases drastically with supply  voltage. Investigations [46] have shown though, that this  decrease is reduced when the spectral range of PE detectors  expands further into infrared (see Fig. 16). Si detectors show a  very drastic signal decrease with voltage, for InGaAs it is much  less, and with MCT detectors it is possible to detect voltages of


0.5V and lower. The reason for this behaviour is the decrease  of the electron temperature Te with the decrease of supply  voltage. In Fig. 17, the PE spectra for FETs with different  supply voltages are compared. It can easily be seen how the  signal intensity is shifted further to infrared when the Te  decreases. For 0.8V, Te is only 470K, and even the InGaAs  spectral range is not appropriate anymore. PE of low power  technologies will require detectors that are sensitive up to 2µm  optical wavelength or even higher. MCTs could be the solution  but have a high noise level. Superconducting single photon  detectors (SSPD) may be the better solution, also for time  resolved techniques based on PE, but these detectors will be  quite expensive and need a very intricate cryo-cooling system.


5.2) FinFET 10nm and smaller


A SIL system at average wavelength of 1.3µm is still good  enough for CFI of 14/16nm FinFET technology [62]. Laser- or  LED-based CFI techniques have a degree of freedom in the


wavelength selection. Shorter wavelengths improve image  resolution (se eq. 1), and with GaP as SIL material, down to 


= 550nm is within reach [59-61]. But, the light absorption in  silicon is very high, devices must be thinned to a few µm  remaining Si thickness and photocurrents are induced that may  influence the device delay [58]. E Beam Probing has reoccurred as a CFI technique through the chip backside but for  that application bulk silicon must be another order of magnitude  thinner [76,77]. PE, especially looking at section 4.1, relies on  wavelengths 1.3µm and higher. This sounds not competitive, but the probing techniques always capture waveform signals  from all the devices in the spot size with many interferences  involved, whereas PE only receives signals from the switching  moments that can be correlated to the devices of interest. So, PE is viable as a second optical CFI approach when the spectral  range is expanded further towards the infrared in order to gain  back a stronger signal good enough for time resolution. An  option for the future may be near field optics as well, especially  when thinning of the substrate down to around 100nm (as  required for backside E Beam probing) is explored.


5.3) Band Gap Engineering  Strain and Channel Mobility


FETs have parasitic bipolar devices, the junctions of  Source/Drain to body. If they are forward biased, R-PE occurs  and their spectra can be evaluated for band gap detection. This  way, the average bandgap can be determined contactless in the  operated device without any further preparation as long as the  parasitic can be turned on in the circuit. Fig. 18 shows such  spectra and the correlated average bandgaps for FinFET  technologies. Especially the pFETs are subject to drastic  bandgap engineering. With a Germanium (Ge) content of 30%, pFET mobility is almost on nFET level, so the inverter design  can use identical dimensions for both. PE spectra of parasitic  bipolar junctions can tell the average Ge content (Fig. 18) of the  analysed region and allows to contactless identify whether  devices with a performance problem suffer from wrong  bandgap engineering.

6) Special Devices


There is a huge range of application for PE in the world of  electronic devices. The focus of this article is Integrated  Circuits. However, in addition we discuss I/O devices, integrated bipolar transistors in BiCMOS technologies and  parasitic bipolar effects like latch up that is discussed in this  section.  Also, discrete devices spread over a huge range of  technologies and applications from high power to photovoltaic  applications and are often made of semiconductor materials  other than silicon; nonetheless, PE of those devices is not the  subject of this work.


6.1) Bipolar Transistors


Bipolar transistors (BTs) use minority carrier injection to  modulate the on resistance of a load circuit between Emitter (E)


and Collector (C). The injection is controlled by the forward  bias of a pn junction, so between E and C there is a very thin  Base (B). In good BTs, the control signal is two orders of


magnitude smaller than the load signal. BTs always have a little  higher loss than FETs on the control side, on the other hand they  can reach higher operating frequencies, especially if they have  a SiGe phase and are called Hetero-BT (HBT). BTs in ICs are  designed vertically (Fig. 19), so the 2 junctions are hard to  separate as PE sources. But the 2 major operating conditions,


active and saturation (note that ‘saturation’ in BT is a very  different operating mode from ‘saturation’ in an FET) are


correlated to very different conditions of the B-C junction and  can in most cases be distinguished by the PE image.


Bipolar Transistor in Saturation Mode


The E-B junction is always in forward bias, and in saturation  the E-C junction is forward bias as well. In this case, minority  carrier injection occurs from both sides and a huge  recombination activity is released, mostly accompanied by a  strong PE signal. In that operation, no high electric fields are  present and only R-PE can be observed. In a pure silicon BT, minority carrier diffusion is visible outside the structures of the  device.


PE images then show an exponential signal decrease in distance  x, hence a quantitative evaluation of a semiconductor  parameter, the minority carrier diffusion length, is possible:


As minority carriers diffuse from the injection or generation  area into the semiconductor material, the recombination activity  A decreases with the distance from the source x by:


A =  A0 ⋅ e− xL


(eq. 5)


A: Recomb. Activity, A0: A at junction. with L = D


L: diffusion length, D: diffusion coefficient, : carrier lifetime  x: distance from emission source


A0 is the activity at the source and L the diffusion length as the  square root of the product of the diffusion coefficient D and the  carrier lifetime . The excess carrier concentration of a pn  junction produces R-PE at the pn junction with an intensity that  decreases exponentially with distance to the junction. The  decrease allows for determination of the minority carrier  diffusion length following equation (4). Fig. 20 shows a PE  Collector

The PE spectrum of a BT in saturation shows the Gaussian  distribution discussed in section 3.5 (forward bias). In a pure  silicon BT, the peak will show the Si bandgap and the slope is  a function of junction temperature. In case of a HBT, built-in  fields may produce a different PE profile. The spectrum is  broadened by the local Ge content and an evaluation for the  temperature is complex.


Bipolar Transistor in Active Mode


In active mode, the B-C junction is in reverse bias. The  electrical field is pulling the injected carriers from base to  collector. This is the amplification mode, the load circuit has  almost no loss and unwanted recombination is minimized. The  PE signal is usually weaker than in saturation. The carrier  diffusion into the semiconductor is reduced, and the PE signal  is more limited to the real BT geometry. The PE signal tells  contactlessly about the BT operating mode.


6.2) I/O Devices


Input and output of ICs have to drive higher signal levels than  internal logical patterns. They are little power devices inside the  ICs, so several effects occur that also are common in power  electronics. The high current levels may cause internal voltage  drops to turn on parasitic bipolar devices like a BT. If the  internal voltage drop between Source and Body exceeds ca.


0.5V, Source serves as Emitter and Drain as Collector, and the


body works like a Base. It is a transistor parallel to the FET but  can’t be turned off by the gate. PE can identify the parasitic  bipolar operation. If the I/O device is large enough to separate  S and D in the micrograph PE for the parasitic BT, then it would  show on the Source side. But even without optical separation of  S and D, the spectrum helps to identify R-PE [15].


Also, ESD (electro-static discharge) protection devices located  in the I/O area. These devices need to become very low resistive  when the voltage increases well above supply level. Typically, specially designed large area gate-grounded FETs are used. Also, derivatives of BTs like thyristors can be selected as ESD  protection. PE is a very good technique to obtain information of  proper operation in off state or find the failed location after it  has degraded [69].


6.3) Latch up


Latch up is a parasitic bipolar operation of a CMOS inverter  that creates a low resistive short between well and substrate. It  spreads widely and typically destroys the chip. Between two  neighbouring n and p type FETs, the lower doped well and  substrate are like the two inner layers of a thyristor or silicon  controlled rectifier. Such a structure acts like two intertwined  BTs as shown in Fig. 21. The well and the substrate are the 2  bases to the respective BTs. If the current amplification factors  of the two BTs increase over 1, the parasitic thyristor gets  triggered and can switch off only when the supply is turned off. So there is a critical design distance between n and p type FETs  which keeps the IC from latching up within the operational

7) Perspective


Photon Emission in IC Detection Today and Future


PE is one of the most prominent CFI techniques for IC  technologies down to ca. 1V supply voltage and 20nm nodes. Smaller nodes and lower voltage require further steps of  development. PE of low power technologies shifts further into  the IR regime, so proper detectors are necessary. Image  resolution may be easier to compromise with if PE is used as a  complementary CFI technique for FinFET technologies that can  provide artefact-free time resolution in the picosecond range. The spectrum of the emission is determined by supply voltage  and device design. The CFI techniques that use external light  sources have the freedom to choose the optical wavelength. If  shorter wavelengths are selected, image resolution can be  improved. But the signal response is much more complicated to  interpret because all the devices inside the illuminated spot  contribute to the responding signal [75]. Plus, parasitic optically  induced effects like photocurrents or heat may interfere with the  original device performance and perturb electrical performance. Time resolved PE based techniques with expanded IR  sensitivity could become a valuable complimentary technique  to the external light source techniques that provide better image  resolution.


8) Conclusion


Photon emission (PE) is a very powerful optical techniques for  CFI. Technologies for supply voltages of 1V and higher, it is  one of the major CFI approaches, performed in NIR as the  signal must typically be accessed through chip backside. The  specific characteristic of PE is electroluminescence, the optical  interaction just by electrical operation. There is no external  optical stimulus that may produce artefacts.


In ICs, the typical PE phenomenon is an intraband effect of  carriers gaining kinetic energy in electrical fields and scatter  accompanied by light emission of a broad spectrum. CMOS  logic sends no PE signal in static mode. Switching inverters  emit light, so time resolved techniques based on PE like TRE  and PICA are used for circuit and delay analysis. Failing FETs  and circuit failures show PE patterns. Also parasitic bipolar  events like latch up and I/O or ESD related problems can well  be detected with PE. Photon emission proves to be one of the  most universal and prominent techniques to track signals or  identify locations of specific electronic (mal-)functions in ICs  for debug during product development and failure analysis in  general. The observation that pFETs emit much less light than  nFETs may change with the use of Si enriched with other


materials like Ge in the pFET channel. Resolution is limited to  ca 200nm by the spectral range of the emission, serving  technologies with nodes down to 14/16nm. Low power  technologies require spectral sensitivities up to 2µm  wavelength, further increases the resolution gap. Still, if a TRE  system can be equipped with such a detector, i.e. SSPD, it may  be a complementary technique for all the external light based  CFI techniques because the signal is free of artefacts and  externally introduced delay.

Physics of Laser-Based Failure Analysis


Felix Beaudoin and *Edward Cole Jr,


Globalfoundries, Malta, New York and *Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, New Mexico  coleei@sandia.gov, phone 505-844-1421


The basic physics behind active photon injection for  local photocurrent generation and thermal laser  heating are reviewed along with standard scanning  optical microscopy failure analysis (FA) tools.  The  goals of the article are to arm analysts with an  understanding of how the tools function and provide  the tenants that will assist in determining how best to  employ a given approach for a given situation.  All of  the methods described can be performed on a standard  SOM (scanning optical microscope) using the proper  laser wavelengths.


Multiple scanning optical microscopy methods for  integrated circuit (IC) FA have become essential tools  to locate and diagnose defects and failure sites.  The  popularity of laser-based approaches stems from their  relatively straight forward application, information


delivered, silicon’s relative transparency to infrared


wavelengths, and their applicability to backside FA.


Active laser-based approaches take advantage of  direct IC interactions with focused, localized light. With illumination using shorter wavelengths/higher  energies than the silicon indirect bandgap, the  interactions are primarily photocurrent based using  electron-hole pair production.  Using longer  wavelengths/lower energies than the indirect silicon  bandgap result in local heating of the target sample. While there are multiple stimulus variations and


detection “schemes”, the basic interactions of local


leakage current generation and heating form the  genesis of active laser FA. For both cases, understanding the interaction physics can be used for  efficient FA.


This article will start by briefly reviewing the physics  behind photocurrent generation in silicon and thermal  laser stimulation (TLS).  The discussion will include  several models for understanding the local thermal  effects on metallic lines, junctions, and complete  devices.  The article will conclude with a description  and case study examples of multiple photocurrent and  thermal injection techniques.  The photocurrent  examples are based on OBIC [1] and LIVA [2].  The


thermal stimulus examples are OBIRCH/TIVA [3, 4] and SEI [4].  Lastly, we discuss the application of solid  immersion lenses (SILs) to improve spatial resolution. Additional active stimulus methods incorporating  electrical testing for detection are described in other  chapters in this Desk Reference.  Passive laser-based  methods using reflected light variations through  photo-electric interactions as well as passive light  emission techniques are also explored in detail in their  respective chapters.


Photocurrent Generation in Silicon


Active photon probing takes advantage of the  interactions of a scanned photon beam with an IC.  For  photon energies greater than the indirect band gap of  silicon (> 1.1eV or wavelength < 1100nm) electronhole pairs are generated in silicon.  Normally the  electron-hole pairs will randomly recombine and there  is essentially no net effect.  However, when electronhole pairs are generated near the interface between  differently doped regions in an unbiased IC, the charge  carriers are separated by the built-in potentials  between areas with different Fermi levels as shown in  Figure 1.  Biasing an IC alters the Fermi levels and  hence alters the magnitude of electron-hole pair  separation or photocurrent. In contrast to passive  photon probing techniques, the detector in active  photon probing is the IC itself.  The relative  transparency of silicon to near-infrared (NIR) wavelengths allows photocurrent generation from  either side of the silicon, so the techniques can be  applied for backside FA.


The photon beam source for active probing is usually  a SOM, sometimes referred to as a laser scanning  microscope (LSM).  The basic SOM consists of a  focused light spot that is scanned over the sample in a  raster fashion. The light source is typically a laser. While dependent upon the particulars of the optics  used, spot sizes on the order of 0.7X the laser  wavelength used in air can be achieved and ~0.2X the  wavelength achieved with an SIL (solid immersion  lens).  The spatial resolution of electrical effects on the  device is limited by carrier diffusion lengths and  carrier lifetimes, thermal conduction, device structure  as well as spot size.  By using different laser  wavelengths and intensities, variations in the amount


of photocurrent can be obtained and backside photon  probing performed.


Photocurrent generation near defects will alter the  power demands of the test device and this can be used  to localize structure and defects.


Figure 1.  Photocurrent generation from photon  produced electron hole pairs.


Thermal Gradient Generation and  Physical Effects


TLS uses an NIR laser beam to thermally stimulate  ICs. The laser energy is chosen below the silicon  indirect bandgap energy (1.1eV) to avoid generation  of photocurrents that could mask thermal effects [5]. As with photocurrent generation, the silicon substrate  is relatively transparent at NIR wavelengths. Laser  beam absorption depends on the doping type and level [6,7], but in general TLS is applicable to front and  backside FA. For heavily-doped silicon substrates, the  die backside may be thinned (e.g. 100m) to minimize  laser power losses due to absorption for thermal or  photocurrent analyses [8,9].


A small portion of the absorbed NIR laser beam  principally heats IC metallic elements, and to a lesser  extent, polysilicon elements and highly doped  substrate areas. The laser modifies the electrical  properties of the heated medium, namely its  resistivity. This change of resistivity alters the current  when using a constant voltage source, or the voltage  when using a constant current source. These electrical  changes inside the device may be monitored at the  power supply nodes. Correlating IC power  consumption changes with the laser spot location  provides precise localization of thermally sensitive  areas such as resistive defects.


TLS induced IC power consumption variations can


be classified as follows:


i) resistance variation (OBIRCH, TIVA)


ii) thermoelectric energy conversion or Seebeck effect (SEI)


Resistance variation


A temperature increase in the heated elements induces  a resistivity variation, modeled as follows:


 = 0TCR(T-T0)


where  is the resistivity, TCR is the thermal  coefficient of resistance, and T is the temperature  variation.


When the IC is biased, the thermally-induced


resistance variation is monitored through the device  voltage or current consumption depending on the  biasing method. This is illustrated by the following

Seebeck effect


The Seebeck effect is based on the generation of an  electromotive force by temperature gradients at  junctions composed of two different materials (e.g. aluminum-tungsten) [10]. The Seebeck voltage  induced when one side of a thermocouple is heated is  given by:


where Q1, Q2 are the respective thermoelectric power  of materials and Q1-2 the relative thermoelectric power  difference of the two materials.


When no bias is applied to the IC, the measured  voltage variation is directly related to the Seebeck  effect. This effect is also present when the IC is biased, but its contribution is often negligible compared to the  TLS signal due to the resistance variation and  transistor amplification [4].


Thermal Models


We present several models aimed at understanding the  TLS signal when the NIR laser beam is scanned over  a single metallic line.


Thermal simulation model


To gain insight into the heating dynamics, a 3D finite  element model of a 1m x 0.5m aluminum line  embedded in silicon dioxide was studied. A schematic


diagram of the modeled structure is shown in Figure 2. The material properties of thin film Al, bulk SiO2 and  Si, given in Table 1, were assumed to be temperature  independent. A detailed description of the model is  given in [11].


The TLS effect was dynamically modeled for the two  following cases:


(1) Longitudinal case when the laser beam is scanned  perpendicular to the metal line.


(2) Transversal case when the laser beam is scanned  parallel to the metal line.


Thermal simulations were performed for a laser beam  power of 100mW, a laser beam radius of 0.65m and  an initial temperature of 25oC. Both transversal and  longitudinal cases were resolved for a fast scanning  speed of 1.23m/s and slow scanning speed of


0.00768m/s. These respectively correspond to a  1024x1024 frame scanning time of 2s when a 5x  objective is used and to a scanning time of 16s when  an objective of 100x is used.


Figure 2. Schematic diagram of the modeled


structure.


The model confirmed that the metal line reaches the  permanent regime at the slowest scanning speed. The  temperature profile for the longitudinal case is shown  in Figure 3. The peak temperature is obtained in less  than 10s.


The temperature profile along the metal line at the  hottest spot for all cases is given in Figure 4. A  permanent regime temperature of 79.9oC was  obtained. However, this maximum temperature was  not reached for the fastest scanning speed. At low  magnification, defects may be undetected if the  scanning speed is not sufficiently slow. For instance, a  1024x1024 frame scanning time higher than 4s is  required when a 5x objective is used.

Localized heating can also be used to locate open  conductor sites from the front and backside of an IC.  Open conductor sites are identified through the use of  the Seebeck effect. As shown above, thermal gradients  in conductors generate electrical potential gradients  with typical values on the order of mV/K.  This  thermoelectric power or Seebeck Effect refers to the  work of Thomas Johann Seebeck (1770-1831).  The  most common application of thermoelectric power is  the thermocouple, which uses the difference in  thermoelectric voltages of two different metals to  measure temperature. If an IC conductor is electrically  intact and has no opens, the potential gradient  produced by localized heating is readily compensated  for by the transistor or power bus electrically driving  the conductor and essentially no signal is produced.  However, if the conductor is electrically isolated from  a driving transistor or power bus, the Seebeck Effect  will change the potential of the conductor.  As  described in the modeling section, this change in  conductor potential will change the bias condition of  transistors whose gates are connected to the


electrically open conductor, changing the transistors’


saturation condition and power dissipation.  An image  of the changing IC power demands (via constant  current biasing) displays the location of electrically  floating conductors. For the laser and SOMs used to  date a maximum temperature gradient of about 30oC  has been achieved, with most work producing  temperature changes of 10oC or less.  The resulting  small changes in open conductor potential need the


sensitive constant current biasing approach for defect  detection.  Figure 17a shows a backside SEI image of  a FIB-opened conductor.  Figure 17b is a reflected  light image for registration.  The open conductor can  be seen as well as strong contrast at the metalpolysilicon interconnections.  The enhanced contrast  results from the thermopower difference in the two  different materials (polysilicon and the metal  conductor).

Improving Spatial Resolution


One persistent challenge with laser-based approaches  to FA is spatial resolution.  Using 1m laser  wavelengths to examine 45nm node technologies and


below produces serious limits to defect localization.  Two approaches have been successfully demonstrated  to improve backside spatial resolution, solid  immersion lenses and substrate ultra-thinning.


Figure 17.  Backside SEI image (a) showing an open  conductor resulting from an FIB cut and a reflected  light image (b) for registration.


Solid Immersion Lenses (SILs)


SILs essentially increase the light collection efficiency  of the optical system, increasing the numerical  aperture (NA) which is inversely proportional to the  spatial resolution.


The most popular SIL approach is the NAIL (NA  increasing lens) [24]. An example of a NAIL is shown  in Figure 18.  The curvature of the NAIL lens, usually  Si or GaAs, increases the NA of the optical system.  The NAIL/sample interface must be very flat and  clean, and the sample thickness tailored to the NAIL  specifications, usually 100m, + 20m.  The NAIL  can be moved from location to location as needed.  Figure 19 shows a TLS image on a 90nm sample with  better than 200nm resolution using a SIL with a  1340nm laser.


Two other SIL approaches have been described.  One  uses a machined hemisphere on the back of the silicon  substrate to form a FOSSIL (forming substrate into  SIL) [25]. A second approach uses a machined  diffraction or Fresnel lens [26].  Both the FOSSIL and  Fresnel approaches have no interface problems  because the SIL is part of the substrate, but neither are  movable like the NAIL.


More improved spatial resolution is possible using an  aperture to block the central axis of the SIL.  The


evanescent or “darkfield” approach may produce


images with resolutions approaching 70nm with 1m  light. [27]

Ultra-Thinning the Silicon Substrate


Recent advances in sample preparation have enabled  ultra-thinning of the silicon substrate while keeping  the sample under test functional. [28] While silicon is  highly absorptive and scattering to visible  wavelengths, it is not completely opaque.  If the silicon  is thin enough, < 5m for example, shorter wavelength  visible light can be used for active laser probing from  the backside of the sample, yielding an increase in  spatial resolution.  SILs can also be applied to ultrathinned samples to further improve spatial resolution, with analysis of ~ 30nm node devices reported  possible. [29]


A description of ultra-thinning techniques and results  of their application are described in other sections of  the Desk Reference.


We have described the basic physics behind active  laser-based FA methods.  Both localized photocurrent  and thermal generation were explored through models  and case studies.


Photocurrent-based (OBIC/LIVA) and TLS (OBIRCH/TIVA/SEI) methods can rapidly and  precisely localize diffusion related defects and shortcircuit defects and current paths. Laser methods are  applicable from the frontside of ICs as well as from the  backside.


With proper sample preparation for optical access, laser-based FA methods can require only a few  minutes to a few hours to localize defects. A better  understanding of the generation physics makes it  possible to gain insight into the physical nature of the  located defect.


Because of their great effectiveness and future  potential, photon probing methods will continue to be  mainstays in IC FA for the foreseeable future and  topics for development and improvement.

Many defects generate excessive heat during operation; this is  due to the power dissipation associated with the excess current  flow at the defect site. There are several thermal detection  techniques for failure analysis including liquid-crystal imaging, fluorescent microthermal imaging (FMI), and infrared (IR) thermography.   Both liquid-crystal imaging and FMI rely on  the presence of a thermal sensing film placed on the sample to  provide an indication of thermal activity. Infrared  thermography is a non-contact thermal mapping technique.


IR thermography [1-4] is the most popular technique for  thermal detection; it detects an object's temperature from its





infrared emission based on blackbody radiation physics [5]. The  fundamental of blackbody radiation is described in detail in the  next section.


IR thermography with lock-in detection is the focus of this  article.  Liquid-crystal imaging and FMI technique for thermal  detection are also briefly described in this article.


Basics of IR Imaging Based on  Blackbody Radiation


Blackbody radiation physics describes the process by which all  heated objects emit radiation to their surroundings. All the

The connection between the peak radiation wavelength and  temperature forms the basis for infrared (IR) temperature  measurement.  Physicists in the late 19th century knew the  relationship between the temperature of a blackbody (a body  that absorbs all of the radiation incident upon it) and the peak  wavelength of the radiation being given off by that body, but  could not describe that relationship mathematically.  The most


important observation was that all blackbodies at the same  temperature emitted radiation with the same spectral  distribution, regardless of their composition.  The spectral  distribution of the radiation emitted by a blackbody is known as  the spectral radiancy, RT (ν), where ν is the frequency of the  radiation.  The quantity RT (ν) is defined so that RT (ν)dv is the  energy emitted per unit time in the frequency range ν to ν + dν  from a unit area on a surface at temperature T.


The integral of the spectral radiancy RT(ν) over all frequencies  is known as the radiancy, RT, or

Classically, a small hole in a cavity is the best approximation of  a blackbody.  From this approximation, we can easily find the  number of modes present in the cavity and assign an energy to  each of these modes which should describe blackbody  radiation.  The spectral radiancy of a blackbody (R(ν)) is


directly proportional to that of a cavity.  Using the equalpartition of energy theory where each mode of the cavity is  assigned an energy,  = kT, we end up with the Raleigh-Jeans  formula for blackbody radiation,

This formula proved to be accurate at low frequencies, but  failed miserably at high frequencies in the ultraviolet end of the  spectrum.  This theory was ultimately known as the ultraviolet  catastrophe.  The reason for the failure of this theory is simple.  The equal-partition theorem is only valid for a continuous  distribution of energies.  However, the energy of an  electromagnetic wave is quantized in units of h.  The theory  of energy quantization led Max Planck to the correct equation  to describe the blackbody radiation spectrum

In most applications, the object under examination will not be  a perfect blackbody.  As such, the radiancy will have to be  corrected for the emissivity of the material.  The emissivity, e, is defined through Stephan's Law which relates the radiancy to  temperature,

In fact, the majority of the information relating  to the object's temperature is well into the infrared region of the  electromagnetic spectrum.  In the semiconductor industry, there  are few devices that operate at such high temperatures.  If we  expand the scale shown in Figure 1 to temperatures around  room temperature, we begin to understand the difficulties in  performing high spatial resolution thermal imaging on  semiconductor devices. It is clear  from this curve, that very little energy is emitted at wavelengths  less than about 3 µm and most of the energy is emitted at  wavelengths greater than 5 µm.  In order to collect the infrared  radiation information from objects near room temperature, a  detector sensitive well into the infrared range is needed.

Infrared Thermography


It is evident from Figure 2 that IR detectors is required for  analysis of devices that emit radiation in 3 um to 12 um range.  Most IR thermography systems use one of two types of  detectors; indium antimonide or mercury cadmium telluride.  Indium antimonide (InSb) detectors are sensitive in the  wavelength range of 1.5 µm to 5.5 µm.  Mercury cadmium  telluride (HgCdTe) detectors are sensitive over the range of 8 µm to 12 µm.  Both detectors offer similar temperature  sensitivities and ranges, but InSb operates at shorter  wavelengths and should have somewhat better spatial  resolution.


IR thermal imaging systems have excellent potential for  temperature resolution but they suffer from a fundamental  limitation on spatial resolution.  In general, the spatial  resolution of a microscope is limited by the wavelength of light.  The relationship between resolution and wavelength as given  by Lord Rayleigh's criteria can be written [6]


N . A.


where λ is the wavelength of light being imaged and N.A. is the  numerical aperture of the microscope.  This result provides a  good estimate of the resolving power of a microscope system. This relation shows that IR thermal systems that gather  radiation in the 1.5 µm to 12 µm range will not be able to  resolve sub-micron structures that are found on modern  integrated circuit (IC) technologies.


IR thermal systems rely on directly sensing the emitted infrared  radiation from objects to measure their temperature.  In general, there are several ways to accomplish this measurement.  The  simplest method is measure the radiance and, if the emissivity  of the material is known, directly compute the temperature of  the sample.  Systems of this type use a very simple  photovoltaic-type detector that is sensitive to IR wavelengths.  Cooled InSb photovoltaics are perhaps the most common.  These detectors are generally sensitive in the 1.5 µm to 5.5 µm  range.  To directly measure the temperature of a sample, the  radiance is measured first. The radiance from a sample at a  given temperature is related to the radiance that would be  collected from a blackbody at the same temperature by the  emissivity, or


T e TBB=


where RT is the radiance from the sample, e is the sample's  emissivity, and RTBB is the radiance of a blackbody at the same  temperature.  Ideally, if the sample's emissivity is known, its  temperature can be calculated if the relationship between the  radiance collected by a given system from a blackbody and its  temperature is known.


In order to increase the accuracy of the temperature  measurement, the radiance that is reflected by the sample must  be accounted for.  Thus, the total radiance collected by a system  from a sample would be

Figure 3 shows a series of example images of an integrated  circuit test structure taken with an IR thermal imaging system.  The structure is an electro-migration test structure that has 4 m  wide aluminum lines separated by 4.5 m.  The lines are 3470 m long yielding a total resistance of about 30 Ω.  The images  in Figure 3 show that IR systems can easily sense hot areas on  integrated circuits at relatively low power densities but will  have difficulty resolving features less than about 5 m.  The  image in Figure 3c was taken after the surface of the chip was  painted with a black non-conductive paint with an emissivity  value of 0.96.  With the growing use of flip chip packaging  technology, the need for backside localization of thermal  features may create a resurgence in the use of IR thermal  analysis for defect localization within integrated circuits.  Regardless, IR systems will continue to be used in areas such  as multi-chip modules, circuit boards, and IC packaging issues  as they have been for years where absolute, non-contact  measurements are essential and sub-micron spatial resolution is  not needed.
