LADA and SDL: Powerful Techniques for Marginal Failures


NXP Semiconductors, Austin, Texas, USA


Diagnosing the root cause of a failure is particularly challenging  if the symptom of the failure is not consistently observable. Many of the global fault isolation techniques such as light  emission microscopy or OBIRCH can be ineffective, and  probing techniques such as laser voltage probing are very time  consuming.


In 2001, Cole et al. [1] published the seminal paper on Resistive  Interconnect Localization, later [2] generalized to Soft Defect  Localization (SDL).  The SDL technique takes advantage of the  marginality of failures to localize the circuit causing the failure. SDL uses a focused ~1300nm laser to locally heat transistors  and interconnect.


In 2003, Rowlette et al. [3] published the first description of  Laser Assisted Device Alteration (LADA).  Similar in setup to  SDL, LADA employs a 1064nm laser to induce local currents  in p-n junctions.


Both techniques have the same core characteristics:


1. SDL and LADA are applied to marginal failures, also known as soft failures, which fail at one bias condition and pass at a different bias condition.  Often, the supply voltage and input clock frequency are the bias conditions that modulate the fail state.


2. The device under test (DUT) is repeatedly looping a marginally failing test.


3. The failing test is biased near the pass/fail boundary


4. Using a laser scanning microscope (LSM), a focused laser is rastered over the back side of the DUT,dwelling at each pixel for one test loop.


5. Each pixel is assigned a color based on the outcome of the test loop as the laser illuminates the site.  A failing loop colors the pixel white, and a passing loop colors the pixel black.


6. This process is repeated with multiple frames,averaging to a grey scale fail rate at each pixel.


7. In the final image, darker sites indicate areas where the laser perturbation pushes the device towards passing.


Lighter sites indicate areas where the laser pushes the device towards failure.  Both types of sites aid in localization of the cause of failure.


Because of the similarity in the techniques, in this paper we will  refer to them as LADA/SDL when differentiation is  unnecessary.  LADA/SDL are now incorporated into  commercially available LSM-based fault isolation tools, from  Checkpoint Technologies, Hamamatsu Photonics, Semicaps, and Thermo Fisher Scientific.  These LSM tools include other  techniques such as laser voltage probing, OBIRCH, and light  emission microscopy.  Other marketing terms for LADA/SDL  include Dynamic Laser Stimulation (DLS) and Dynamic


Analysis by Laser Stimulation (DALS).  An example LADA  image is shown in Figure 1.


Figure 1.  A low magnification LADA overlay image.  The  background is the reflected laser scanned image of the die.  The  false color overlay are the LADA sites.  Green sites indicate  where the laser pushes the DUT towards passing, and red sites  indicate where the laser pushed the DUT towards failing.


Types of Failures Appropriate for LADA/SDL


LADA/SDL is a global fault isolation technique.  It is not  necessary to start with detailed knowledge of the circuit, a fault  tree analysis, or a hypothesis of the root cause.  The only  necessary deliverables are the failing DUT, the test that  demonstrates the failure, and the voltage, frequency or other  bias conditions that modulate the failure.  The bias conditions  are available as a Shmoo plot [4].


LADA/SDL is especially useful on digital circuits.  The effect  of the laser will induce ~10ps of timing or ~10mV of Vt shift. This small perturbation is not enough to disturb the behavior of  a properly functioning CMOS digital circuit, which may require  an order of magnitude more perturbation.  But when biased at  the pass/fail boundary of the shmoo plot, the circuit responsible  for the failure is operating within a few picoseconds or  millivolts of the boundary, so the small effect of the laser pushes  the DUT towards passing or failing.  LADA/SDL will find the  circuit responsible for the failure within hours.


An analog circuit, however, may be naturally sensitive to ~10ps  of timing or ~10mV of Vt shift.    So, the laser will affect  properly functioning circuits as well as the circuit responsible  for the failure.  Understanding the results on analog circuits can  take days or weeks.


Setup for LADA/SDL


A schematic view of the setup for LADA/SDL is shown in  Figure 2.  A tester (or applications board) exercises the DUT  and simultaneously provides a fail flag signal and a loop trigger  signal to the LSM.  The LSM rasters the DUT with either a  1064nm laser (for LADA) or a ~1300nm laser (for SDL), and  creates an overlay image.   The background of the overlay, often  called the pattern image, is the reflected image of the DUT from  the back side.  The foreground is a false color image, where  green indicates sites where the laser perturbation induces the  DUT to pass, and red indicates sites that are induced to fail.  The  image may also be a simple greyscale without the overlay, where white indicates failing and black indicates passing.


LADA/SDL analysis setup requires three steps:


1. Create the test loop with the fail flag and loop trigger,


2. Select the laser dwell time, and


3. Select the shmoo bias point


Figure 2.  A schematic view of the tool setup for LADA/SDL.


Setup Step 1: Create the Test Loop


Reducing the Loop Length.  LADA/SDL requires a short test  loop because the acquisition time is directly proportional to the  loop length.   In a 512x512 image, one frame of data with a 1ms  loop requires 4.4 minutes.  This is a reasonable loop length – in  one hour, 14 frames can be averaged for a good first look at the  data.


Longer loops are possible but will require overnight averaging.  A 20ms loop requires 80 minutes per frame.  A 100ms loop is  impossible, requiring 7.3 hours per frame.


One possibility is to reduce the scan resolution, which reduces  the number of pixels.  However, high resolution data will  eventually be required so effort must be taken to reduce the loop  length.  The end of the loop should not extend beyond the first  failing vector [5].   Most often the loop will start at the first  vector of the pattern, but in some cases, it might be possible to  start the loop at a later vector.    For example, scan patterns can


be looped back across two capture cycles from the first failing


vector – just prior to the capture cycle that starts the loading of  the failing pattern.  Other types of patterns can be much more  challenging to find an appropriate place to loop back.  It is  important that the loop passes on a non-failing DUT, and that  the expected failing vector is observed while looping the failing  DUT.


Creating the Loop Trigger and Fail Flag.  The loop trigger and  fail flag signals, which are sent to the LSM, are generated by  the test pattern.  Two digital tester channels are dedicated for  the LSM signals.  As shown in Figure 3, the loadboard is  modified to connect these two tester channels to BNCs for  connection to the LSM.


Figure 3.  Example of a modified loadboard used in the authors’ lab to route dedicated tester channels for the loop trigger and  the fail flag to the LSM.


The test pattern as used in the production test program must be  modified to create the loop trigger and the fail flag.  These two  signals must be defined in the tester program pin configuration  and added to the failing pattern.  A high-level view of the  required pattern is shown in Figure 4.  At the beginning of the  loop, the loop trigger is generated by setting the loop trigger  signal high for one vector, then low for the rest of the pattern.  At the end of the loop, the fail flag is generated by using a “Jump On Fail” test pattern instruction that controls which  vector gets executed.  The last vector of the loop is duplicated.  One copy of the last vector has the fail flag signal set high, and  the other is set low.  The Jump On Fail instruction executes the  Fail Flag=1 vector if the loop failed, the Fail Flag=0 vector if  the loop did not fail.  In this way, the LSM can immediately  detect the failing status of the loop for imaging.  Variations on  this test pattern editing methodology are possible [6].


Other techniques to generate the fail flag are possible, including  the use of the test method programming that controls the test  flow and the execution of tests.  However, because the tester  must interact with the tester’s computer, using the test method  programming adds a significant delay to the loop length (up to  several milliseconds) which will increase the acquisition time  of an averaged frame.  Therefore, it is best to modify the actual  test pattern with the “Jump On Fail” opcode.


Figure 4.  High-level view of the test pattern modifications  necessary for LADA/SDL.  At the beginning of the loop is the  trigger vector, which generates the loop trigger.  At the end of


the loop is the fail flag vector, using the “jump on fail”


instruction that chooses between the two states of the fail flag.


Connecting the Loop Trigger and Fail Flag.  The Loop Trigger  signal is a straightforward connection to the LSM.   On some


LSM tools, the input is labelled “Pixel Clock In”.  The LSM can


be configured to use the Loop Trigger to control the laser dwell  time.


The Fail Flag should be connected to the digital fail input, rather  than the analog input that would be used for OBIRCH.  This


input may be labelled “DLS In” or “Tester Signal”.  The


advantage of choosing a digital input is shown in Figure 5.  The  analog input will integrate the fail signal, so the duty cycle of  the fail signal affects the contrast.  The contrast should only  depend on the average fail rate.  Using the digital input on the  LSM provides better contrast and a more representative value  of the fail rate.  However, it is possible that the fail signal might  have to be conditioned to be compatible with the LSM [5].


Figure 5.  Using the analog input, which displays a greyscale  pixel based on the integrated value of the fail flag signal, does  not truly reflect the pass/fail status of the test loop.  The digital  input presents a white pixel if the fail flag is high, regardless of  the integrated value.


Setup Step 2: Choosing the Laser Dwell Time


The laser dwell time at each pixel should be approximately one  test loop.  During LADA/SDL, the engineer likely does not  know when during the test the laser will interact with the failing  signal, so illumination of the pixel during the entire loop is  important to achieve the necessary interaction.


More importantly, the fail flag is emitted by the tester once each  loop.  Since the fail flag colors the pixel, the LSM must not  advance to the next pixel until it can assign a color to the current  pixel.  Choosing a shorter dwell time when confronted with a  long loop length will increase the acquisition time and reduce  the localization resolution, as shown in Figure 6.  The pixel  coloring from the fail flag will smear in the scan direction, enlarging the LADA/SDL site and reducing the contrast.


In [7], the authors demonstrated a method of resolving the time  of a LADA interaction by measuring the shift of the LADA site  when a dwell time much shorter than the loop length is used.


Figure 6.  A magnified LADA image acquired with a dwell time  that is faster than the test loop.  The data is smeared in the  horizontal scan direction, and the background is averaged into  the LADA site data reducing its contrast.


Two methods can be employed to set the laser dwell time.  First, the loop trigger can be used as an external control to step the  laser from pixel to pixel.  This synchronous method guarantees  that the LADA/SDL data will not be smeared and is a  straightforward approach.   However, if the loop trigger rate is  too fast for the LSM, the dwell will be longer than the loop  length.  The dwell time is fast, but the fail rate data will be  incorrect.  For example, if the dwell time is 10 times the loop  length, then a single fail in one of those 10 loops will record as  a white pixel, when it really would be a 10% grey pixel in a  frame average.


At least one LSM manufacturer offers a “counting mode” fail


flag input, which can be used when the dwell time is longer than  the loop length.  In counting mode, a pixel is assigned a grey  level based on the number of assertions of the fail flag during  the pixel dwell.


The second method to set the laser dwell time is to select one of  the internal LSM dwell time choices.   In most cases, these  choices are presented as a time per frame rather than as a dwell  time.  The dwell time can be approximated by dividing the


selected time per frame by the number of pixels in the image.  For example, a 120 second 512x512 frame is approximately a  120/(512x512) = 458 microsecond dwell time.  This  approximation will always overestimate the dwell time because  it does not account for the retrace time – the time for the scanner  to move from the end of a line to the beginning of the next line.  A more precise measurement of the dwell time can be made by  measuring the period of the pixel clock if it is available as an  output from the LSM.


Setup Step 3: Choosing the Shmoo Bias Point


Setting the 50 percent background fail rate. Due to intrinsic and  extrinsic noise, the timing and voltage level of signals in the  DUT exhibit jitter.   As shown in Figure 7, when the DUT is  biased at the shmoo boundary between pass and fail, the  probability of a failure is 50% due to the jitter.   In [8], the  authors mathematically demonstrate that the ideal bias point for  reducing the acquisition time of LADA/SDL is at the 50% fail  rate, precisely centered on the shmoo boundary.  The 50% fail  rate is the best starting point for LADA/SDL.  If the signals are  strong, the engineer may then move the fail rate away from  50%.


Figure 7.  When biased at the shmoo boundary, the DUT has a  50% probability of failure due to the gaussian jitter.


To set the shmoo bias point, the engineer must first select a  point near the pass/fail boundary, and then start the test loop. To precisely choose the 50% fail rate, the bias must be adjusted  while monitoring the fail rate during the test loop.  Most testers  allow the power supply voltage to be changed while running a  test pattern in a loop.  Timing changes may not be possible.  The  shmoo bias point may also be set by adjusting other parameters, such as the temperature of the DUT.  Air cooling can be used to  reduce the self-heating, or a heated chuck can be used to bias a  temperature sensitive failure.


One method to monitor the fail rate is to observe the fail flag on  an oscilloscope that is triggered by loop trigger.   In standard  acquisition mode, the fail flag will flicker, as the device  sometimes fails.  But in averaging mode, the averaged  amplitude of the displayed fail signal will be proportional to the  fail rate.  For example, when the fail rate is at 50%, a 1V fail  flag will display as 0.5V on the oscilloscope.


Another method to monitor the fail rate is described in [7].  DXGlue is an FPGA-based connection between the tester fail  flag and loop trigger and the LSM is used to measure the fail  rate and forward the information to display software running on  a PC.  The user continuously monitors the fail rate and other  statistics from the software.  At least one vendor has added a  similar fail rate monitoring feature to the LSM software.


During the analysis, continuous monitoring and adjustment to  keep the background fail rate approximately 50% is necessary.  The fail rate may move, as the shmoo boundary moves, for  several reasons:


1. The DUT may self-heat during the test loop.  Air or  water cooling may be necessary to stabilize the DUT  temperature.


2. Landing the solid immersion lens (SIL) will locally  cool the device, because the SIL acts as a heat sink.


3. The lab environment may cause the fail rate to creep.


4. Large LADA/SDL sites that dominate the frame will  affect the fail rate.  Adjustment should not be made in  this case, because it is the background fail rate that is  important for reduced acquisition time.  The user can  stop the scan to observe the background fail rate in the  presence of large LADA/SDL sites.


Removing large noise sources.  The intrinsic and extrinsic noise  that cause timing jitter can create different types of histograms, as shown in Figure 8.  The ideal situation is shown Figure 8(a), where a modest spread in the jitter is smaller than the timing  delta induced by the laser, so the entire distribution can be  moved from 50% to the pass (or fail) region.  A larger jitter  spread caused by random noise sources (Figure 8(b)), prevents  the laser from significantly affecting the fail rate, and hence  reduces the contrast between the background and the  LADA/SDL site.   Periodic noise sources can create a bimodal  jitter distribution (Figure 8(c)), which may not be possible for  the laser to shift into the pass or fail region.


The distribution can be seen by observing the behavior of the  fail rate while biased at 50 percent.  A very stable fail rate  indicates that the intrinsic noise has little effect on the fail rate, and therefore the laser will also have little effect.  A fail rate  that is noisy but averaged at 50% is the best condition for  LADA/SDL, because it indicates that the fail rate can be easily  modulated.


Figure 8.  Three types of jitter histograms biased at the 50% fail rate, showing how the distribution moves with the laser  illumination. (a) A well-behaved jitter histogram with a modest  variance can be completely moved into the pass region by the  laser for a 0% fail rate.  (b)  A large random noise source will  spread the jitter histogram and the laser will not have a large  effect on the fail rate.  (c)  A periodic noise source can cause a  bimodal jitter and the laser will have no effect on the fail rate.


A fail rate strip chart, as described for DXGlue in [9], is a  straightforward method to observe the noise in the background  fail rate.  DXGlue also presents a Fourier transform of the fail  rate. The spectrum should be flat, with no periodic noise.  Any  peaks in the fail rate spectrum indicate the presence of a  periodic noise source.  A peak that is synchronous with the test  loop period may indicate that the DUT is not in the same state  each loop and that the choice of beginning or end of the loop  may not be valid.


Where to bias in typical shmoos.  The most common type of  shmoo is shown in Figure 9(a), which shows a typical speedvoltage curve: the DUT can run faster at higher power supply  voltage.   The best area to bias is at low voltage, on the slope of  the pass/fail boundary [10].  At this point, transistors are  sensitive to perturbation.  At a lower voltage, where the curve  is flat, there are fewer mechanisms for perturbation.


Figure 9(b) illustrates a shmoo finger, which is an abnormal  failing region surrounded by passing regions.  It is useful to bias  on both sides of the finger because different portions of the  circuit may be active on either side.  Narrow fingers can be hard  to bias if the width of the finger is greater than the system jitter.


Closely related to the shmoo finger is the striped shmoo, shown  in Figure 9(c).  The striped shmoo is typically the result of a  design flaw across an asynchronous clock boundary in the  DUT.  The stripes can be narrow but may become wider and  easier to bias at slow clock speed.


Finally, the speckled shmoo shown in Figure 9(d) is particularly  challenging because the speckled width likely exceeds the  width of the jitter.  Without an abrupt boundary between pass  and fail, the laser-induced timing perturbation cannot move the


jitter distribution completely into pass or fail.  It is best to focus  on finding an unstable fail rate, rather than a 50% fail rate, because an unstable fail rate indicates that the laser will be able  to influence the fail rate.


Figure 9.  Examples of various types of shmoos.  (a) A typical  voltage/speed shmoo.  (b) A shmoo finger.  (c) A striped shmoo.


(d) A speckled shmoo.  Green areas indicate passing; red or  other colors indicate the device is failing.  The colors indicate  the first failing vector.


LADA/SDL With an Applications Board Instead of a Tester


The setup described thus far has assumed the use of a standard  semiconductor tester to create the test loop.  Sometimes, it may  be necessary to exercise the DUT in its application  environment, with a board that was not designed for  characterizing or testing the device.


LADA/SDL with an applications board can be challenging. Plotting the shmoo is a manual process, so it is likely that only  a few points will be measured to estimate the pass/fail  boundary.  Controlling the bias point to achieve a 50% fail rate  is also not straightforward – the system clock is often set with a  crystal, and the voltage supply may not be readily adjusted to  millivolts because of on-board regulators.  Finally, the DUT  socket is likely not compatible with backside access, especially  if the technology node requires SIL imaging.   The engineer  must look for solutions to all these problems prior to starting  the LADA/SDL analysis.  It is likely that the solutions will not  lead to the ideal setup, so the engineer should attempt to find a  tester-based solution.


Creating a test loop on an applications board will often require  that code be written to induce the failure.  To generate the loop  trigger and the fail flag, additional code must be added to toggle  the state of pins on the DUT.  An example test loop code is  shown in Figure 10.  The code should also try to balance the  execution time between pass and fail, especially if a loop trigger  is not used to step the laser from pixel to pixel.


Applications board have been used especially for performing  SDL on analog or mixed signal devices.  Although not  discussed in this paper, closely related to LADA/SDL are  techniques that use the variation of an analog output from the  DUT instead of the fail flag for imaging [11-13].


Figure 10.  Example C code for a LADA/SDL loop using an  applications board. The code must create the loop trigger and  the fail flag, in addition to exercising the failure.


The LADA/SDL Workflow


After the setup is complete, successful LADA/SDL depends on  using a thorough, iterative and increasingly focused search.  The steps include


1. Acquire low magnification images over the entire  DUT, averaging for perhaps 100 frames.


2. Overlay the low magnification images with the CAD  and evaluate the best areas to focus on.  Ignore the PLL  and analog areas, especially if a digital issue is  suspected.


3. Acquire high magnification images (with the solid  immersion lens) on the areas chosen in step 2.


4. Overlay the high magnification images with the CAD  and extract the schematic of the implicated circuit  elements.


5. Pursue additional fault isolation such as laser voltage  probing, followed by physical failure analysis if  necessary.


Low Magnification LADA/SDL


The engineer will quickly discover during low magnification  imaging that the necessary laser power for a LADA/SDL  response will change with the choice of objective.  LSMs  display the power setting of the laser.  However, the  LADA/SDL response and the laser damage threshold are  related more directly to the irradiance.  Irradiance is the laser  power per unit area at the DUT and depends on the numerical  aperture (NA) of the objective.


Irradiance, denoted Ee, can be estimated as

Figure 11 illustrates how the laser power must be reduced for  higher NA lenses to maintain a constant irradiance.  The laser  power must be reduced by a factor of 100 when switching from  a typical low NA, low magnification lens to the SIL.


Figure 11.  A plot of the laser power necessary at various  numerical apertures to maintain a constant 10mW/µm2  irradiance.  Typical NAs are indicated: a low magnification

Based on the authors’ experience, a known damage threshold is  100 mW/µm2.  However, it is critical to stay well below that,


perhaps at no more than 10 mW/µm2.  The damage threshold  depend on many factors, including the process technology, circuit voltage, the sample preparation, the laser wavelength, and the DUT temperature.


Aligning with the CAD


Refer to the CAD navigation chapter of this Desk Reference for  more information about alignment and overlay of FA images  with the layout.   A critical step to add value is to map onto the  schematic the affected circuit elements for further study.  Pinpointing the transistor in the layout that is responsible for a  LADA/SDL site can be challenging at small geometry process  nodes.  As shown in Figure 12, when multiple LADA/SDL sites  are present, it is likely that the sites are from interconnected  transistors.  By highlighting all the routing that goes through  each site, it is possible to reduce the set of nets to only those  that traverse through all the sites.


Figure 12.  LADA sites with the aligned CAD overlay.  The sites  may be large relative to the transistors, but it is possible to  deduce the affected transistor by looking for an interconnected  path.  Only the green shaded nets traverse all 3 sites; the  purples nets intersect only some of the sites.


Exact Fail Imaging


LADA/SDL pass sites always implicate a circuit associated  with the failure.  Pass sites can be analyzed with a high  confidence.  Fail sites, however, can be the result of shifting to  the failing boundary of the shmoo, or they can be the result of  interacting with a different circuit that causes the DUT to fail in  a way different than the shmoo.  For that reason, fail sites are  considered with less confidence that they may be associated  with the failing circuit.


Exact fail imaging can be used to distinguish fail sites  associated with the shmoo from “red herring” sites that indicate  a failure that is different than the shmoo.  To perform exact fail  imaging, bias the DUT on the failing side of the shmoo  boundary.  Then invert any failing compare strobes on the test  pattern such that the test now passes.  Move the bias back to the  50% fail rate and perform LADA/SDL.  Any sites that were  originally fail sites and are now black sites are exact fails – these  sites indicate that the fail exactly matches the shmoo and these  sites can be associated with the failing circuit with a high  confidence.  Any fail sites that don’t invert are red herrings and  should be ignored.


Although masking test pattern failures that are not associated  with the shmoo failure can reduce red herrings, they may not be  eliminated because the vectors associated with the shmoo  failure may also be associated with red herrings.


Presenting the LADA/SDL Results


LADA/SDL data should be presented and analyzed in both  image form and in schematic form.  In image form, Figure 13  illustrates the importance of using the grey scale image (which  should be overlaid with the CAD).  Figure 13(a) shows a detail  in the grey scale image that is not shown in the false color image  in Figure 13(b).  Once the images are understood, the green/red  false color image can be used for the report if it sufficiently  describes the issue.


An example of annotating the schematic in the region of the  LADA/SDL sites is shown in Figure 14.  In this case, red is  indicated on a logic gate for failing sites, and green for passing  sites.  The location of the red or green dot near the logic gate  indicates if the site is on the PMOS or on the NMOS of the gate.  Additional fault isolation information, such as photoemission, can be indicated on this schematic to give a clear picture of all  the data gathered during analysis.  This schematic serves as a  tool for determining the next failure analysis steps.

Time-Resolved LADA


LADA/SDL identifies the spatial location of the circuit  associated with a shmoo failure.  Time-resolved LADA (TRLADA) identifies the interaction time, the critical time at which  the circuit is causing the shmoo fail.  In some cases, TR-LADA  also improves the localization resolution.  At the time of this  writing, none of the LSM vendors have announced a TR-LADA  feature.  We limit the discussion here to TR-LADA because  there have been no publications on time-resolved SDL.


TR-LADA employs a modulated or pulsed 1064nm laser, synchronized with the test loop.  The interaction time is  determined by turning the laser on during a selected period of  the test loop and observing the results.  A TR-LADA site is only  present if the laser illuminates the location of the circuit during  the time of the activity that causes the shmoo fail.


TR-LADA can be categorized by the order of magnitude of the  pulse width of the laser. Microsecond TR-LADA is  implemented with a modulated continuous wave laser [10,14] and is useful for determining the interaction time within tens of  microseconds but offers no localization resolution  improvement over standard LADA. Nanosecond TR-LADA


[15] offers some localization improvement for pulse width < 33ns and can determine the interaction time down to 1-2 tester  cycles.  Picosecond TR-LADA [16-19] provides significant  localization resolution improvement (see Figure 15) because of  the ability to time the pulse to interact with the transistor and  avoid the effects of well interaction.  Picosecond TR-LADA  also allows interaction time resolution to sub-nanosecond.  Femtosecond TR-LADA, employing two-photon absorption [20] offers no advantages over picosecond TR-LADA.


Figure 15.  A comparison of LADA and TR-LADA with a 0.9NA  air gap lens, showing the spatial improvement of TR-LADA.   The laser pulse arrives just before the electrical activity at the  leftmost site, interacting only with the transistors.  The laser  pulse is early for the two other sites causing more interaction  with the well and increasing the size of the site.


With two spatial dimensions plus the time dimension, there are  two useful TR-LADA modes.  First, with time held constant, an  image can be made as in conventional LADA.  A sequence of  these images can be made at successive times to create a “movie”.  Second, with the laser parked at a specific LADA  site, a TR-LADA waveform can be created by sweeping time  as shown in Figure 16.    The waveform is useful when  searching for the interaction time or measuring propagation  delays [16].


Figure 16.  Example of TR-LADA waveforms.  The Y axis is fail  rate and the X axis is time.   This example is a waveform of a  passing LADA site.


Picosecond TR-LADA can directly image defect locations, as  shown in Figure 17.  By making a movie, the engineer can look  for any anomalous point sites that may be present indicating an  interaction with a defect.


Figure 17.  An example finding a point site, which looks larger  and more complex in conventional LADA.  The point site at  t0+200ps is the location of a defective gate contact. [17]


Laser Interaction Physics Introduction


LADA/SDL offer a great deal of value to the failure analysis  lab, without the engineer having to thoroughly understand the  physics of the photon interaction with the silicon.   But to make  the best interpretation of the results, it is important to have a  working understanding of the interaction mechanisms.


There are two dominant absorption mechanisms that will occur  between the laser and the IC.   The first mechanism is free  carrier absorption (FCA) in metal layers and heavily doped  silicon.  FCA is proportional to the square of the wavelength, so it 1.6X greater in SDL (~1300nm wavelength) than in LADA (1064nm).


The second dominant mechanism is specific to LADA: electron-hole (e-h) absorption in the silicon. [21] : Generated  photocurrents affect the bias at the transistor.  Electron-hole


absorption is possible with SDL as a non-linear two-photon  effect.  However, with a continuous wave (CW) laser the  induced current is 2-3 orders of magnitude lower than the single  photon e-h absorption of LADA [22].


SDL Laser Interaction Physics


Free carrier absorption results in heating of the free carriers in  metal, silicides, and the highly doped silicon layers.  The SDL  technique using the ~1300nm laser interacts in this way at a rate  that is 1.6X greater than the 1064nm laser.  Because the CW  1300nm laser produces almost no photocurrents, a good starting  point for understanding SDL is to assume all interaction are  based on thermal perturbation.


The local heating of SDL has different circuit effects depending  on material:


1. Defects: Various effects depending on the defect  composition and form


2. Transistors: Opposing effects lower mobility [2] and  lower Vt; dependence on bias and on normal and  reverse temperature regions.


3. Metal interconnect:  Resistance is increased [1].


4. Adjacent dissimilar conductors:  The Seebeck effect  can change current flow, which is not discussed in this  article. For further details, see [23]


In the next sections, examples are given for the first 3  interactions and then transistor interactions are covered in more  detail.


SDL Example: Interaction at the Defect Site


Since every defect will have its own characteristics and  interaction mechanisms a general summary of interaction  cannot be made.  However, an SDL site in an area that is  inconsistent with the CAD layout shapes is an indication of the  defect.  The interaction of the laser with the defect itself changes  the electrical characteristics of the defect and modulates the fail  rate of the test loop.


Figure 18 illustrates an example of an SDL site at a defect.  A  large failing interaction site is located at a hollowed-out metal  route, and this is the only site.  In this case the likely physical  explanation is that the thin conductor is being heated and hence  increasing in resistance.  But because this is a defect, another  plausible explanation is that an interface is separating one  portion of the routing from the remainder and the heat is flexing  the surrounding materials enough to open or close the electrical  connection. Regardless of the explanation, this highly localized  point site indicates a defect and an accurate model of the  interaction physics is not required.


Figure 18. (a) SDL point site that is inconsistent with the layout  shapes, indicating a likely defect.  (b) The cross-section  micrograph shows a hollowed-out metal route in which there  are multiple plausible explanations for how it interacts with the  laser.  But more important than the explanation is that the  defect has been found.


SDL Example: Interaction at a Transistor with a Floating  Gate


When the ~1300nm laser interacts with a MOSFET transistor  there will be two opposing device level effects.  The heated  transistor will have lower Vt and lower mobility.  In Figure 19, where the defect causes a floating gate, the dominating effect is  the Vt perturbation.  Fig 19(a) shows SDL images of the passing  and failing regions identified on a buffer circuit consisting of  two invertors (Figure 19(b)).  A passing site is seen on the  pMOS of the first invertor while a fail site is seen on the nMOS.   The effect of lowering the Vt is shown in the simplified  simulated waveforms of Figure 19(c).  The lowering of the Vt  modulates the size of the pulse through the invertor and hence  modulates the failure rate.


(a) SDL Image           (b) Schematic and Layout


(c) Signal analysis of SDL site


Figure 19.  (a) Pass and fail SDL sites.  (b) The SDL sites  overlaid with the CAD show that it is at an inverter.  The defect, later identified, caused the gates to float. In (c) the signal  analysis shows a qualitative explanation of how the laser effect


of lowering the Vt will cause a change in the invertor output and  therefore a change in the failure rate of the test.


SDL Example: Interaction with Metal Routing


When metal or silicide is heated the resistance of the metal  increases.  The example shown in Figure 20(a) shows a case  where two inverters driving opposite logic levels are connected  through a low resistance bridging defect.  The resulting effect  will be a midlevel at the next inverter gate.  Because the SDL  bias point is set such that the fail rate is 50%, this midlevel is  poised at the switching threshold of the inverter.  Any small  change in the midlevel will therefore change the failure rate.


The SDL image in Figure 20(b) contains a green vertical stripe  which is passing region, and a red, failing vertical stripe.  The  two stripes correspond to the metal routing of the inverter  outputs that are bridged. The voltage divider between the  correct driver and that of the bridged driver will change based  on which metal routing is heated.  When the routing to the  correct driver is heated, it will lose control of the voltage divider  and therefore the device will fail the test more often.  The  opposite occurs when the interconnect to the bridged driver is  heated.   Because there are lower metal layers blocking the path  of this laser to the upper metal layers associated with this  routing, the exact location of the defect is not evident.  Deprocessing of the device revealed clear bridge between the  metal routing, shown in Figure 20(c).

Further Discussion on SDL Sites at Transistors


In the discussion above we have noted that there are two  competing effects when the laser heats a transistor.  The  consequences of these two effects are illustrated in Figure 21. Illuminating and heating the device will lower the threshold  voltage and speed up the transistor.  But the mobility  simultaneously decreases, which will slow down the transistor.  Which effect dominates depends on two factors that are  discussed here:  the reverse temperature effect [24] and the  spatial characteristics of the laser spot.


Figure 21.  Inverter schematics of illuminated nMOS and  pMOS along with the list of competing mechanisms associated  with the heating effects on transistors.  The resulting effects of  signal propagation speed through the invertor will depend on  circuit bias, illumination spot size and the temperature of the  device.


Reverse Temperature Effects and SDL. While a thorough  explanation of temperature effects is beyond the scope of this  article, it is worth outlining the main points that are important  to understanding this topic and how to interpret SDL results.  Refer to [24 - 27] for more details.


CMOS circuits have 2 regions of operation with respect to  temperature [24].  Region 1, at high Vdd, is the region of


“normal” temperature effects.  In region 1, the transistor


saturation current limits the circuit speed; threshold voltage is  less important.  The circuit slows down as temperature  increases and mobility decreases.


Region 2, at lower Vdd, is the region of “reverse” temperature  effects.  The threshold voltage is more important than the lower  drain voltage, and the circuits speeds up as temperature  increases and Vt decreases.


Between Region 1 and 2 there is a voltage (Vit) at which the  circuit speed is insensitive to temperature.


By obtaining shmoo plots at two or more temperatures one can  observe Regions 1 and 2.   In Figure 22 a shmoo plot is shown  at room and hot temperature. Using these shmoo plots one can  quickly determine which region the circuit is operating in. The  in this technology, the shmoos show that Vit=1V.


A summary of the temperature effects on several different  technologies is shown in Figure 23.  The x-intercept on this  graph is the Vit value for each technology.  Older technologies  had nominal supply voltages significantly higher than Vit so that  devices would slow down as they were heated.  In more modern  technologies the Vit is close to the nominal supply voltage and  it is important to understand which region the device is  operating in so that accurate interpretations of the SDL sites can  be made.


Figure 22.  Shmoo plots showing reverse temperature effects.


(a) image showing room temperature shmoo plot of the Vdd  voltage vs latching clock edge.  (b) Hot temperature shmoo plot  where the blue dashed line shows room temperature reference  behavior.  At approximately one volt the circuit has no change  in speed.  At lower voltages the device operates in the reverse  temperature region and speeds up at higher temperatures.


For success with SDL, the engineer should verify that the  device is not biased in the insensitive area between region 1 and


2.   Acquiring a shmoo plot at two different temperatures can  be used to help interpret the SDL sites at transistors, and to  select an appropriate bias point.  Once the Vit is understood, the  engineer will also be able to interpret the effect of the laser heat  on the propagation delay of CMOS circuits.


Figure 23.  Plot showing the temperature effects on several  technologies.  More modern technologies have nominal  operating voltages that are below the Vit and therefore will  show reverse temperature effects.  Note the temperature  insensitive voltage, Vit, is at the horizontal axis intercept.  Data  is taken from [24, 25].


Effects of the Spatial Characteristics of the Laser.  If the spatial  spot size of the laser is such that it illuminates both the source  and drain nodes of the transistor then the transistor heating is  approximately uniform.  Spatial effects can be ignored and only  the reverse temperature effects must be considered when  analyzing an SDL site.


In the case where the laser spot size is small enough to heat the  source node separately from the drain node then the analysis  must consider how independent source or drain heating will  affect the transistor.  Experiments detailed in [28, 22] have  shown the effect of non-uniform heating of the transistor.  Figure 24 shows current mapping images of a nMOS test  structure where the drain and source nodes are illuminated  separately with a high spatial resolution solid immersion lens (SIL).  Two biases where chosen to accentuate the effect of the  laser heating.  When biased in saturation where the carrier  mobility dominates, only the heating at the drain decreases the  current.  When biased near the threshold voltage, only the  heating at the source increases the current.  The consequence of  these current modulations is that source node heating will lower  Vt and speed the device while drain node heating will lower the  saturation current and slow the device speed.


Through independent heating of source/drain regions using a  SIL, transistor level features can be observed and used to  modulate failure rates using the ~1300nm laser.  These  transistor interactions are quite different from the more  traditional defect related SDL interactions, and more closely  related to LADA.  We have applied the term Free Carrier  LADA (FCLADA) [22] to the use of the ~1300nm laser for  analysis of design flaws such as speed paths, where the  transistor interaction creates the image

The bright site at the source indicates a current  increase.  (c) Current mapping of the device when biased in  saturation shows a dark region of reduced current when the  drain is heated. LADA Laser Interaction Physics


The interaction physics of the 1064nm LADA laser with the  silicon is through two mechanisms.  First, heating will occur as  in SDL, but the shorter wavelength reduces the free carrier  absorption to about 60% of its value at 1340nm.  Second, absorption of photons by valence electrons create electron-hole  pairs.  This absorption creates optical beam induced currents (OBIC) at all junctions that the laser passes through [3].  And  because the diffusion lengths of carriers in the silicon are quite  large, even junctions within several microns of the laser will be  affected by OBIC.  In many technologies the OBIC interaction  will dominate and the thermal effects of the 1064nm laser can  be ignored. As shown above in Figure 25, in more recent  process nodes the free carrier absorption and resulting thermal  perturbation of the 1064nm laser is comparable to the OBIC  interactions and both need to be considered.  The remainder of  this section will focus on the OBIC interaction and its effect on  the CMOS circuit.


The LADA interactions will be covered in four sections:


1. Cross-sectional views of the OBIC current sources in  an inverter are presented.


2. Examples of well-based OBIC are shown.


3. The drift and diffusion components of OBIC are  explained.


4. Guidelines for interpreting results on speed path  analysis are given.


Cross-Sectional View of OBIC Sources


Figure 26 shows a simplified figure of the p-n junctions found  in a CMOS process.  Two positions of a laser source are shown  on this figure so that nMOS and pMOS cases can be illustrated.  Note that in each case the laser passes through the depletion  region at the junction between its source/drain and its well.  Also, the laser will pass through the depletion region at the  Nwell and P substrate junction.  All along the path of the laser, electron-hole pairs will be created.


Carriers created within the depletion regions are acted on by the  electric field and are therefore a drift current.  This current is  fast: on the order of several picoseconds [22]. Carriers  generated near but outside of the junction are not acted on by  electric field but go through a diffusion process. Those that  happen to diffuse toward a depletion region will then be acted  on by the electric field.  This diffusion process is comparatively  slow   The diffusion process creates an unexpected OBIC  source at the Nwell/Pwell junction when the nMOS is  illuminated because the minority carrier diffusion length is  large enough so that some carriers will diffuse laterally towards  the Nwell/Pwell junction.


Figure 26.  LADA laser interactions shown on a simplified  cross-sectional view of the CMOS structures with two examples  of laser illumination (on the left the laser is illuminating a  pMOS drain and on the right the laser is illuminating the nMOS  drain.) with major interactions and effects listed.


The OBIC sources of LADA are shown in more detail Figure


27.   Note that the OBIC that occurs at the drain of a transistor  directly adds to the transistor current.  OBIC at the Pwell/Nwell  junction locally decreases the threshold voltages of both  inverter transistors by increasing the voltage on the Pwell and  lowering the voltage of the Nwell.   The well OBIC dominates


the LADA response because of its larger area, and always  speeds up the inverter due to the lower Vt.  OBIC at the drain  either speeds up or slows down the inverter, depending on the  polarity of the output transition and which transistor drain is  being illuminated.  More details are presented later.


One final comment on the cross-sectional view is that it is  similar to many latch up cross-sectional schematics.   Depending on the source drain area and laser irradiance, OBIC  currents at the wells can typically be in the microamp range [3] and so latch up sometimes does occur on circuits that are prone  to latch up.  In the authors’ experience across several process  technologies most are fairly tolerant to 1064nm laser  illumination.  However, some technologies, including those  without highly doped substrates, may be less tolerant.  Evaluating whether correlation units latch up during 1064nm  scanning can be done prior to performing LADA on a failing  device to reduce the risk of damaging a failing device.


Figure 27. Cross-sectional view of the CMOS inverter with  OBIC sources shown as dependent current sources.  This model  captures how Nwell to Pwell currents lower the Vt of both  nMOS and pMOS transistors.  The dependent current sources  at the output of the invertor will add to (or subtract from) the  normal current conduction of the invertor output.  The well  effects will dominate the LADA response.


Examples of Well OBIC Sources in LADA Images


The Nwell/Pwell OBIC will be the largest in magnitude and  have a large effect on Vt and speed of the transistors.  These  effects are shown in Figure 28, a LADA image of a typical race  between a fast clock and a slow data path.  When the data path  is sped up with the test will pass.  The green passing sites in this  figure align to the horizontally oriented Nwell/Pwells.  OBIC at  these wells speeds up the data path and the test passes.  When  the clock transistors are illuminated failing sites are identified  because the clock speeds up and the data loses the race.


The higher magnification image Figure 28(b) illustrates that the  actual transistors of the data path are not in the center of the  large Nwell/Pwell passing LADA sites.  The actual shape of the  LADA site is determined by the well straps and not the  transistors themselves.  Using a solid immersion lens can  improve the localization, but as shown in Figure 29 there are  cases where the transistor cannot be identified.


These images illustrate both a benefit and disadvantage of  LADA.  The large interactions of the well structures are  straightforward to identify at low magnification with a large


field of view.   However, the well structures interfere with  identifying the actual transistors of the LADA site.


Figure 28. This LADA image shows the data path transistors (green sites) in a race versus the clock path transistors (red  sites).  (a) is a lower magnification showing the entire race.  (b) shows the higher magnification (air gap lens) of several data  path interaction sites. Note that the data path transistors are  not in the center of the larger N/Pwell interaction sites

The Drift (fast) and Diffusion (slow) Components of OBIC


To understand the two types of OBIC it is helpful to look at  OBIC generated at a p-n junction with a picosecond pulsed laser  source, as is used in time resolved LADA. Figure 30 shows the


two components of the OBIC and reveals that the drift current


is fast with a response time approximately equal to the laser  pulse width.  The drift current consists of carriers created in the  electric field of the depletion region that are quickly collected. The slower diffusion current, created nearby and diffusing into  the depletion region, continues for 500ps.  For larger area  Nwell/Pwells the time constant is tens of nanoseconds [17,18].


Figure 30.  For a 10ps laser pulse into a p-n junction there are  two components of OBIC.  Data for graph taken [29].


Figure 31(a) shows a schematic of an inverter in the data path  of a set-up time failure.  When the data signal is sped up by the  laser pulse the test will pass.  The laser interaction with the well  of this invertor will consist primarily of the slow diffusion  currents at the Nwell/Pwell structure, additionally slowed by  the capacitance of the well.


As discussed in the Time Resolved LADA section above, the  pulsed laser can be positioned at the interaction time, the time  at which it interacts with a critical data transition that  determines whether the test passes or fails. Figure 31(b) shows  three pulse times: just prior to the critical transition, at the  critical transition, and after the interaction time.


The resulting LADA images in Figure 31(c) show a large dark  passing site for the nWell/pWell shape when the pulse occurs  prior to the interaction time, which gives the diffusion current  sufficient time to be collected at the wells and then lower the Vt  of the invertor transistors.  The lower Vt speeds up the edge and  causes the test to pass. When the laser pulse is at the interaction  time, only the drift component is fast enough to have an effect  on the data edge, so that the LADA site localizes to the actual  inverter.  The slower well interactions do not have time to affect  the data signal.    When the pulse is after the interaction time, there can be no effect.


Figure 31. LADA interactions with respect to time. (a) Schematic of inverter in a hold time data path.  (b) Three pulsed  laser timing cases: Blue pulse is before critical data transition, Green pulse is coincident with the data transition, and the  orange pulse occurs after the interaction time and has no effect  on test result.  (c) The resulting TRLADA images for the blue  and green cases showing the reduction of the well response.


Next, we compare the results of LADA with a continuous wave (CW) laser to that of an optimally timed TRLADA pulse in  Figure 32.  This image shows that the LADA results have less  ability for localization due to the large diffusion component of  the LADA site.  The TRLADA result of this figure shows  localization capability that matches the optical spot size of the  laser itself, because only the fast drift components at the  inverter output create image.  One additional feature shown in  this image is that the effect of the laser on the output signal now  shows a different polarity depending on whether the nMOS is  illuminated (producing a failing site) or the pMOS is  illuminated (producing a passing site).  This ability to produce  different effects at each transistor type will be discussed in more  detail next.

LADA Laser Interaction Summary


The LADA interactions discussed here show the clear presence  of the two OBIC interaction currents.  The drift component that  is as fast as the transistors themselves and is local to the  illuminated laser spot.  The diffusion components are relatively  large and while helpful to identify the signal paths involved in  the failing test, they are not helpful for achieving the best  possible localization.  SIL based LADA imaging can sometimes  localize transistors within the well.  Optimally timed TRLADA  can pinpoint the transistor and serves as a useful demonstration

Oscilloscope vs. Digitizer


Most conventional LVP tools employ a high-speed  oscilloscope for waveform acquisition. This provides the  highest measurement bandwidth possible. Obviously, high  bandwidth is required when measuring fast clock signals, but  it is also important when high edge-placement accuracy (EPA) is needed for precise determination of switching times. For a  given SNR waveform, EPA is improved as edge rise-time is  reduced (rise-time is proportional to 1/bandwidth). It should be  noted that measured rise-times are impacted by device jitter  due to the averaging required to extract a useable waveform.


As hinted at earlier, Textronix oscilloscopes are usually used  because of their DPO mode of operation. This mode provides  the highest throughput for most use cases, greatly reducing the  time needed to acquire a waveform. However, a major  restriction of DPO mode is the limited number of data points  that can be collected within a given acquisition window – also  known as the record length. The record length is fixed at 1000  samples per waveform. This is a significant restriction, especially when functional debug may necessitate the  interrogation of test patterns spanning several microseconds  with GHz/ns resolution.


Some oscilloscope-based LVP tools can enter a custom state  known as High Sample Rate Mode which offers up to 50k time  bins per waveform. This relaxes the record length restriction of  DPO mode but does so at the expense of added acquisition time  and reduced efficiency. In DPO mode, a waveform is captured  after every trigger received with almost 100% efficiency in  most cases (depending on loop length); however, with a 50k  record length in High Sample Rate Mode, a waveform may  only be captured after every 5th trigger signal on average (also  dependent on loop lengths used).


There is a balance between record length, acquisition window, and acquisition efficiency. For long acquisition windows, high  resolution is often not necessary since the analyst is only  interested in observing a snapshot of the functional operation. As a result, a low bandwidth detector is commonly selected. The benefit of a low bandwidth detector is that it has lower  noise factor in its amplifier stage that can result in a significant  improvement in SNR, therefore significantly reducing the time  it takes to acquire a usable waveform. Having a tool that can  switch between low- and high- bandwidth operation enables  the analysts to operate in both acquisition domains. Common  dual-bandwidth LVP platforms offer approx. 10kHz - 100MHz  operation for low-bandwidth and approx. 50MHz - 7GHz for  high-bandwidth operation.


To improve acquisition efficiency, LVP tool vendors are  beginning to replace oscilloscopes with state-of-the-art  digitizers. By increasing the number of time bins available but  reducing the sampling rate (and therefore measurement  bandwidth) digitizers are capable of acquiring moderate


bandwidth waveforms that span the entire length of the test  pattern. This enables the analyst to screen failing test patterns  with a single waveform that spans the full range of interest  while still providing enough timing resolution to reveal fine  details. The sampling rate for such high-speed digitizers is  currently ~4GS/s – which equates to a waveform being  sampled every 250ps; however, record length can scale to  approx. 512,000 samples (128µs time span). The digitizer  approach is certainly an attractive option for FA labs and is  something which has the capability to add even more value to  LVP and its extended applications. An example of which is  depicted in Fig. 8 where a timing glitch is observed using a  digitizer-based system but is hidden by the bandwidth vs. acquisition time span trade-off of oscilloscope-based probing.


Regarding the FA flow however, the two systems form a  complimentary pair. The oscilloscope approach is excellent for  high-resolution timing extraction whereas the digitizer solution  enables rapid isolation and debug of anomalous logic behavior  over longer acquisition periods (albeit with reduced  bandwidth). For FA labs entertaining a wide variety of failing  modes, it is valuable to have access to both LVP acquisition  modes since they complement each other, driving root cause  identification with efficiency and accuracy. Outside of the  technological offerings, two additional parameters drive  customer interest and those are price point and ease-of-use. Oscilloscope-based LVP systems offer the highest possible  bandwidths but are more expensive and limited in their ability  to capture large dataset waveforms with high timing resolution  over wide time spans. Digitizer-based LVP systems, on the  other hand, are less expensive and can efficiently capture large  dataset waveforms, but trade-off ultimate bandwidth. Furthermore, a system’s ease-of-use is also critical to tool  selection if FA cycle time is important.


Figure 8: Oscilloscope- vs. digitizer-based LVP.


Thermal Management


In some cases, a DUT can generate a tremendous amount of  heat during functional operation due to power consumption (>100W). Graphics processors for example are classic  examples. This not only creates problems on the test floor in  fabrication environments during device qualification, it also  challenges the ability for LVP tools to aid the FA process since  the thermal load on a typically thinned and backside exposed  device (~100um) must be managed. One solution comes in the  form of a diamond [20] or sapphire heat spreader. These heat  spreaders are essentially transparent windows on which the  device is situated and is positioned between the imaging  objective and the exposed silicon. During operation and  testing, heat that emanates from the DUT is dissipated through  the diamond/sapphire. The window ‘spreads’ the heat out to a  heat exchanger which then transfers the heat into some  temperature-controlled coolant (e.g. air, water, etc.). Another  solution is through air-water cooling. A radial spray jet can be  situated around the imaging objective and directed towards the  DUT. The water-based solution can also be employed in a nonSIL-based geometry (i.e. with low magnification air-gap lenses (so as there is a suitable cone and window fixture included that  prevents water from disrupting the optical path – the use of  water in an optoelectronic probing platform must be carefully  managed for obvious reasons. In addition, turbulent water flow  between the objective lens and the DUT will restrict the optical  resolution performance.


Optical Resolution


Optical resolution performance is a key differentiator between  equipment providers in the arena of electrical fault isolation. To address this requirement, LVP tool vendors furnish their  tool-sets with the latest in SIL technology [21-23]. A SIL is  essentially a hemisphere of high-index material whose  aplanatic imaging points are exploited by an air-gap objective  lens. A SIL makes direct contact with the exposed silicon  substrate and enables an increase in optical resolution by  increasing the numerical aperture (NA) of the imaging system. To achieve the best optical performance, the SIL material  should have an index of refraction that closely matches that of  the silicon substrate while also being sufficiently transparent at  the LVP wavelength(s) used. For below bandgap LVP (i.e., >1.1µm) Si SILs can be used. Above bandgap LVP (<1.1µm) however, requires the use of more expensive GaAs SILs. Dual  wavelength systems necessarily employ GaAs SILs. Aplanatic  SILs (ASIL), in which refraction at the air-SIL interface is  exploited, are also available and can deliver even higher NAs. Commercial hemispherical SILs offer NAs of around 3.3, whereas ASILs can offer close to the theoretical limit of


3.48NA; however, the latter has greatly reduced tolerance for  silicon thickness variations and, therefore, more stringent  sample preparation requirements.


Optoelectronic Imaging and Probing


LVP has many derivatives [24]. Beyond the acquisition of a  functional waveform, many alternative fault isolation  technologies have been demonstrated. The main driver for their  development is the limited usefulness of precise single-point  probing/waveform acquisition if the analyst lacks guidance on  where to place the probe. The developed fault isolation  technologies described below allow imaging and mapping of  device functionality over a wide field-of-view (FOV). The  analyst can then identify suspicious electrical and functional  behavior more accurately and efficiently prior to waveform  probing. In many situations, the techniques allow sufficient  localization that waveform probing can even be bypassed. They serve as a key enabler in the FA flow.


Frequency Mapping (FM)


FM (also known as Laser Voltage Imaging (LVI) or  Modulation Mapping) provides a map of the locations within  the LSM FOV that are modulating at a target frequency. The  map can be overlaid on the LSM pattern image to give precise  localization [25]. This technology utilizes the same hardware  as a conventional LVP tool with the main difference being that  instead of the reflected laser signal being directed towards a  high-speed oscilloscope for time-domain analysis, the return  signal is sent to a high-bandwidth spectrum analyzer for  frequency-domain characterization – please see Fig 9. The  spectrum analyzer is used as a narrow-band filter to reject all  frequencies in the return signal, save the target frequency. It  outputs a signal whose strength is proportional to the  modulation strength at the selected frequency. The spectrum  analyzer output is captured at each pixel location as the LSM  raster scans the laser to create a map of the modulation strength  over a ROI. In most systems, the map is captured concurrently  with the LSM pattern image to save time and help ensure  overlay accuracy. It is also usually possible to send the return  laser signal to more than one spectrum analyzer to capture  multiple frequencies simultaneously. An example of FM  images is presented in Fig. 10 in which target frequencies of  6MHz, 12MHz, and 48MHz are overlaid with an LSM pattern  image [26].


Figure 9: Hardware schematic for LVI implementation.


Figure 10: Laser Voltage Imaging [26].


FM is an ideal global fault isolation technique for scan chain  debug [27-29]. Before the combinational logic inside a DUT


can be screened, the structural integrity of the DUT’s numerous


scan chains must be established. To do this, a chain check


pattern is created in which a repeating sequence of 1100… is


shifted through the scan chain inputs and monitored at their  outputs. If the chain outputs receive this chain check pattern  then the chain is functional; however, if the output is static (or  deviates from this strict vector sequence) then the chain has


been compromised and a root cause must be determined. Since  the chain check pattern is periodic (i.e. clock-like), its  frequency can be monitored using FM to interrogate scan  chains. This works by mapping the spatial locations within a  given field-of-view at which the target frequency is present. In


other words, one can spatially interrogate the chain’s latch


locations to determine if their transistors are toggling. By  identifying the latch location at which the target frequency is  no longer present, one can quickly detect where the target  frequency has ceased to propagate. Subsequent analysis  involves implementing LVP to provide further characterization  opportunities. This hybrid FM and LVP methodology has been  used to great effect to successfully isolate the physical location  in which scan chain are defective.


It should be noted that an optimal requirement for FM is that  the target frequency is periodic, and that the duty cycle is set to  50%. Any deviation from 50% will result in a reduction in the  SNR – although this can be exploited in 2nd Harmonic  FM [30, 31].


Aside from scan chain debug, the understanding and  implementation of FM has significantly matured over the years  to enable the interrogation of defects associated with other  types of fail mode. For example, FM has been utilized to isolate  shorts by modulating the power rail at a specific target  frequency and observing where anomalous modulation  occurs [24]. Logic state mapping of memory bit cells has also  been demonstrated by modulating the power rail with a small  periodic change to its DC level (e.g. a 1.2V to 1V modulation  on top of a 1.2V supply) [32]. One thing to note in these  examples is the difficulty of externally modulating the power  rail at a high enough frequency to be within range of the  detectors in a typical system. Even 10kHz frequency can be  difficult to achieve due to supply noise filtering. For laser logic  state mapping, the use of internal power gate features was  adopted to create periodic supply modulations. The flip-side  here is that the SNR of a thermal signal can be very weak at  high frequencies since heat does not have time to spread very  much. This is a key driver to encourage LVP vendors to offer  even lower bandwidth detectors as well as lock-in amplifier  capabilities.


In another example, FM has also been utilized to identify a  level-shifter defect associated with a 14nm SRAM DQ failure  in which the DQ pin was configured to toggle at a target  frequency while its signal input and output propagation path  was monitored [33]. FM has also been extended to acquire and  display phase-based information related to the target frequency  under investigation [34, 35].


These are all powerful examples of identifying defects through  LVP-inspired optoelectronic mapping (i.e. thru free-carrier or  electro-optical effects). It should be noted here that even after  the implementation of such image-based techniques is  complete, LVP is usually still required to fine-tune the


analyst’s understanding of the failure as well as the exact


location of the defect.


Although FM is generally considered a laser-based technique; it is possible to implement FM, and optical probing for that  matter, without the use of a coherent light source. Electro-Optic  Frequency Mapping (EOFM) [36] replicates the  implementation and benefits of conventional laser-based FM  but does so with the use of a super-luminescent diode (SLD) - i.e. an incoherent light source. EOFM competes with LVI in  that it also offers both amplitude- and phase-based spatial maps  of target frequencies. Note here that laser sources are preferred  for high-bandwidth investigations; however, incoherent light  sources can offer better SNR at lower bandwidths due to their  reduced relative intensity noise (RIN) below ~1MHz. This is  highlighted in Fig. 11 in which RIN is plotted against  frequency for a SLD, a laser source (HSL), and a cooled highpower incoherent light source (cHIL) at 1.3um.


Figure 11: Relative Intensity Noise (RIN) vs. frequency for a  super-luminescent diode (SLD), a laser source (HSL), and a  cooled high-power incoherent light source (cHIL). Measurements were acquired at 1.3um. Figure has been  reproduced with kind permission from Hamamatsu Photonics.


Laser Voltage Tracing (LVT)


LVT [37, 38] is a novel laser-based circuit analysis technique  that combines elements of both LVP and LVI. It essentially  performs spatial analysis like LVI, but for specific aperiodic  signals – a capability in which LVI is limited (as discussed  previously). LVT acquires an aperiodic LVP signal with a  high-speed digitizer then processes the data with boxcar  averaging based on two pre-defined parameters: a “gate” (a  temporal window over which a signal of interest is expected) and a “baseline” (a temporal window over which no signal of


interest is expected). The measured LVP signal is then


integrated within the “gate” and the “baseline” sampling


windows. The resulting signal is the difference between their  relative strengths. This measurement procedure is performed at  every pixel within a 2D area to create an optoelectronic map  that highlights spatial locations where the signal of interest  resides.


An example of LVT is given in Fig. 12 [39]. Fig. 11 (a) reveals  the LVP waveform collected from a sub-20nm FinFET buffer. The voltage supplied is 0.9V, the test loop length is 6.4us, and  a single 50ns pulse is injected into the buffer. The LVT gate is  set to match the pulse width of the signal. Note here that this  particular gate positioning provides an optimal example – more  realistic scenarios, where the gate width is increased to allow  for uncertainty in the precise timing of the signal, will offer  more challenging analysis environments. The baseline is set  with the same time width, but in a time window where no  pulse/signal is expected. Figure 12 (b) is the best-attempt at an  LVI image and Fig. 12 (c) is the resulting LVT image. Since  the buffer output duty cycle is <0.0001, LVI returns no signal; however, LVT can clearly discriminate between the buffer’s 4  transistors. The colors represent the polarity of the signal, with  red indicating that the gate has a positive net amplitude and  green indicating it has a negative net amplitude (with respect  to the baseline).


Figure 12: (a) LVP waveform of a single pulse navigating a  sub-20nm FinFET buffer over which the “gate” and “baseline” observation windows are defined. (b) LVI image  does not return any signal. (b) LVT shows the buffer (made of  4 transistors) clearly. The red and green colors represent the  positive and negative change in amplitude of the signal with  respect to the baseline, respectively [39].


Visible Laser Probing (VLP) - IR to Visible


As process technology continues to scale, the ability to resolve  spatial features in images acquired through the silicon backside  of the device becomes increasingly challenging. The spatial  resolution of an optical system can be determined by the  Rayleigh criterion:


Δ  ,    =


0.61  


where Δ  ,    is the minimum resolvable lateral distance,  is the  wavelength of the laser, and NA is the numerical aperture of the  optical system. This shows that in addition to increasing the NA (which is already achieved through advanced SIL optics) a  shorter wavelength will also yield a higher spatial resolution  for both imaging and signal extraction; however, the utilization  of shorter wavelengths for LVP introduces several technical  challenges.


Conventional LVP systems employ CW 1340nm lasers (which  is above 1117nm – the wavelength that corresponds to the  silicon band gap energy). This means that the exposed silicon  backside is mostly transparent to the laser radiation and that  free-carrier effects dominate in influencing the generated the  LVP signal – as described in the Theory section. Yet, to address  the requirements of improved probing resolution, 1064nm  lasers are now commonly employed. The caveat here is that  incident wavelengths shorter than 1117 nm will influence  device performance during LVP acquisitions since locally  generated photo-carriers will modify the switching  characteristics of the transistors whose rise/fall times one  wishes to measure. This effect is well-known and has been used  to the advantage of FA engineers for many years, specifically  through the implementation of Laser-Assisted Device  Alteration (LADA) [40]; however, since LADA is understood (with 10s of picoseconds of perturbation typically observed) it  can be identified and ultimately removed from the  interpretation of the resulting waveforms.


Invasiveness


LVP using 1064nm lasers is not a sufficient solution however; therefore, as the industry advanced towards 14/16nm and  beyond, and the FA community embraces the latest research  and developments, a transition is being made beyond IR  probing and into the exciting domain of visible light probing (VLP – LVP using wavelength in the visible spectrum), with  sub-600nm laser wavelengths being entertained. VLP has  successfully been applied to various process technologies. Some of the first results can be found in [41 - 44].


While sub-600nm wavelengths will help improve spatial  resolution performance there are several things that need to be  considered when determining optical probing performance. As  mentioned earlier, as wavelength is scaled (reduced) beyond


the silicon band edge, the magnitude of laser light absorbed by  the silicon substrate scales (increases) with it. Invasiveness  therefore plays a key role in determining VLP performance. An  example of this is given in Fig 13 in which a 12.5MHz  waveform was acquired using 2mW of laser power from a  1320nm, 1154m, 1064nm, and 785nm probe [45]. This is  further supported in Fig. 14 in which a laser power study was  performed between a conventional 1064nm LVP system and a  785nm VLP system [45]. These results clearly demonstrate that  reduced laser powers are necessary when using VLP systems  to avoid the limiting effects of invasiveness. The authors note  here that although 785nm is technically assigned to the nearinfrared portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, LVP tool  vendors still include it in their suite of VLP wavelength  offerings.


Figure 13: Waveforms collected at 12.5MHz with an optical  power of 2mW from the drain of a two-transistor inverter using (A) 1320nm, (B) 1154nm, (C) 1064nm, and (D) 785nm laser  interrogation.  [45]


Figure 14: Laser power study between 1064nm (left) and  785nm (right) systems. From top to bottom, the power was  increased: 1.5mW, 2mW, 3mW, 4mW, and 5mW. The shape of  the 5mW 1064nm waveform (bottom left) qualitatively matches  the 2mW 785nm (second from the top, right side) waveform.


[45]


In addition to enabling VLP, visible light FM has also been  demonstrated and utilized during various product debug  scenarios. Figure 15 below illustrates how FM employed in this  configuration has the ability not only to return significant SNR  improvements over conventional LVP, it also has the capability  to resolve spatial features separated by only 108nm [46]. This  is made possible through the reduced impact of cross-talk. The  reason for the higher SNR of VLP in this example is that the  signals from adjacent transistors are well separated due to the  smaller spot size. With NIR probing, transistor activity cancels  each other because the beam overlaps multiple transistors that  toggle oppositely.

Sample Preparation


As mentioned previously, the silicon absorption coefficient  increases with decreasing laser wavelengths. This results in a  reduction of the absorption depth and, therefore, a reduction of  the practical silicon substrate thickness. To make matters  worse, laser probing requires the incident laser light to doublepass the silicon substrate which magnifies the problem. Table 1  contains an overview of a range of wavelengths and their  respective absorption depth in silicon. It also contains the  required SIL material and the expected spatial resolution  performance.
