When employing LVP on devices with conventional  1340/1064nm lasers, the silicon bulk is usually thinned and  polished down to ~100m. In order to enable VLP however, the backside of the sample has to be thinned and polished to a  remaining silicon thickness of <10um for 785nm. For 577nm  its <2m – please refer to Fig. 16. This is challenging (even for  the most skilled technician in any FA lab) but remains feasible  with practice and access to the appropriate tool sets. It should  be noted here that there exists a practical limit to how far  wavelength can be scaled for optical probing since employing  a remaining silicon thicknesses in the nanometer range is  simply not an option – as captured in Table 1.


Figure 16: Normalized silicon transmission as a function of  wavelength across different substrate thicknesses [41]


In addition to potentially damaging the sample during thinning, handling and probing, warpage of the sample also plays a  significant role [47]. If sample thickness is not even across the  backside of the device, then optical probing can be close to  impossible. Another challenge with removing silicon bulk  material from the backside is the reduction in heat conduction. Device overheating is an important consideration which, if not  managed appropriately, can lead to the destruction of the  device. As a result, cooling solutions may be required. Deploying a SIL on a sample this thin may also lead to  substrate cracking. This needs to be prevented by carefully  controlling the pressure applied by the SIL. It was also reported  recently that thermal effects observed during the sample  preparation process can lead to underfill shrinkage which can  manifest a surface topography which echoes that of the  subsurface solder bump profile. This leads to challenges in  achieving the required optical contact between the SIL and the  sample for realizing diffraction-limited imaging and probing  performance [48].


VLP Tool Components


To accommodate a scaled wavelength for VLP, tool vendors  must modify the optical components inside their systems. This  includes optical fibers, beam-splitters, and lenses, but most


importantly photodetectors and SIL’s. SIL’s for LVP at


1340nm and 1064nm wavelengths are made of silicon and  GaAs, respectively, to satisfy the requirements of both high  transmission and refractive index matching between SIL and


silicon substrate. For VLP however, Si and GaAs SIL’s are not


an ideal option due to their significant absorption profiles at  shorter wavelengths (the SIL of course needs to be transparent  to the light that is used for probing) as well as their index


mismatches. Instead, Gallium Phosphide (GaP) SIL’s are


utilized due to its favorable optical characteristics in the visible  portion of the spectrum.


In addition to hardware-based modifications that dictate the  transition from LVP to VLP, there are also some interesting  practical considerations which must be pondered also.  Compared to the relatively strong back reflection received  from the exposed silicon surface of the device under test, a  modulated LVP signal, derived from the active areas of the  device, is typically in the parts-per-million range. Therefore, due to the increased absorption occurring at shorter  wavelengths, a modulated VLP signal will be even further  reduced in magnitude. As a result, devices need to be thinned  to have sufficient round-trip transmission. Increased  invasiveness (and lower damage thresholds), which requires  reduced laser power, is also a significant consideration. Furthermore, the reduced responsivity of detectors at shorter  wavelengths must be entertained: for a given laser power, a  shorter wavelength means less photons. Since detectors at best  give 1 electron per photon, this means less electrical signal. As  a result, emphasis must then be placed on photodetector  selection to enable optimized SNR and gain. In addition, since


VLP requires the use of ultra-thin substrates, the plane at which  the signal originates (i.e. the active regions) will be in close  proximity to the exposed back surface of the device. This will  likely prevent practical VLP imaging and probing if the  dominant surface reflection is not confocally suppressed and  good SIL-to-substrate contact maintained. Scratches are also a  problem. A SIL targeted for 50 or 100um silicon thickness can  tolerate a lot of scratches. For ultra-thin silicon however, a  scratch is a bigger fraction of the optical contact area which  means a reduced tolerance for it. Scratches can be on either the  SIL or the sample – preferably the sample due to the cost of  SIL tip replacement.


Common Observations


The acquisition of an LVP waveform is straight-forward and  requires little time. Correctly interpreting the information  contained within the resulting waveform however can be quite  the opposite. Even as the data is being collected and displayed, it is imperative to critically examine the attributes of each  waveform in order to successfully navigate an analysis – otherwise, one can be easily misled. Some common LVP  observations/considerations include the following:


Waveform Inversion:


LVP does not give a direct measure of the polarity of the  device’s electric response. In fact, polarity changes in the  acquired waveforms are readily observed when the focal  position of the laser is swept through the active region [49]. This inversion of the waveform’s logical state is something that  is well-known amongst analysts yet is rarely addressed in the  technical literature. This is most likely due to the complexity  of managing the various optoelectronic phenomena in play as  well as explaining the influence of these effects in the intricate  and diverse environments of modern nanoelectronics systems. At a high-level, consideration must be given to optical  interferometric effects within such structures (i.e. axial  constructive and destructive interference) as well as the  numerous reflections the probe laser experiences after  interacting with the front-end-of-line metallization behind the  active region. Interestingly, such waveform polarity changes  take place when the laser is focused post-active region. Beforehand, the waveform’s logical state remains constant  with only the magnitude increasing as the laser traverses the  silicon substrate on its way to the transistors on interest. A  detailed review of such observations is welcome and, perhaps, overdue.


LVP Waveforms are Averaged!


This is a fundamental aspect of LVP technology and something  that is regularly overlooked or simply forgotten. The process  of averaging provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the  presence of inconsistent temporal characteristics from within a  given signal. For example, if something is intermittently  switching (say 1100 is 1000 half the time) then you will  observe a ‘tri-state’ waveform. Tri-state waveforms can also be


the result of cross-talk. Overall system jitter, when considered  under the umbrella of signal averaging, can also have a  significant influence on measured rise-times and effective  bandwidth.


Cross-Talk:


Technology scaling has placed a tremendous burden on the  accuracy of LVP results, which is ultimately proportional to the  spatial resolution of the system. As a result, limited lateral  spatial resolution reduces efficacy through challenges faced in  CAD alignment, optical probe placement and therefore crosstalk. Although VLP technology has attempted to address such


concerns, not every device can easily navigate VLP’s stringent  requirements – nor does VLP effectively eliminate the concern. As a result, it can be commonplace to misinterpret the presence  of a signal from a given location when it is in fact emanating  from an adjacent node.


Under-sampling:


Without careful consideration for the attributes of the signal of  interest, an analyst may select inappropriate acquisition  conditions. As such, critical signal transitions can be missed. For example, failing to capture the presence of a fast temporal  event (such as the glitch example given above) due to the  selection of a sampling rate that is too low.


AC Coupling:


AC coupling (also known as capacitive coupling) removes the  DC offset in a signal by making use of a DC-blocking capacitor  in series with the signal. AC coupling effectively rejects the  DC component of a signal by normalizing it to a mean of the  baseline. It is crucial for DC noise rejection, as mentioned  earlier; however, it can lead to confusing waveforms under  some conditions. For example, if the signal of interest is a  single transition but the observation window is zoomed out in  time. In this example, the resulting waveform will capture a  fast initial transition followed by a slow decay.


Waveform Displays:


Nowadays, LVP waveforms are displayed in terms of absolute  modulation instead of ppm. That means a weak modulation (low ppm) on a strong background can give a waveform (or  map) that is similar to that from an active node (which usually  has a strong modulation but a darker background). Also note  that waveform amplitude will vary with laser power.


the effects of the two different OBIC components and their  effects on localization.


Although not discussed in detail, process technology may affect  the LADA response.  Grounded bottom gated well SOI will not  show the large well sites, so sites will be more localized than on  bulk technology.  Back-biased FDSOI is very challenging for  LADA, because any well that shares the same back bias  generator as the transistor that is in the LADA path will show  as a LADA site.  This effect can also be eliminated by using  TRLADA or SDL.

Laser Voltage Probing of Integrated Circuits: Implementation and Impact


Keith A. Serrels


NXP Semiconductors, 6501 West William Cannon Drive, Austin, TX 78735, USA  Email: keith.serrels@nxp.com


Ulrike Ganesh


Robert Bosch GmbH, Reutlingen, Germany


Email: ulrike.ganesh@de.bosch.com


This article discusses the state-of-the-art in commercially  available Laser Voltage Probing (LVP) technology for the  purpose of integrated-circuit failure analysis. An overview of  LVP history, theory, system architecture, and application  extensions will be reviewed. Current limitations and future  work will also be considered. The purpose of this article is to  establish a clear technical foundation and evolutionary timeline  while detailing how LVP is utilized in a practical setting. This  review should be considered an entry point into LVP  technology and a guide towards future learning.


Introduction/Background


Electrical fault isolation is an essential process in the failure  analysis (FA) workflow. The ability to efficiently and  accurately localize anomalous circuit activity with nanometric  precision enables analysts to better interpret failing electrical  signatures before definitive physical analysis methodologies  can be applied to successfully determine root cause. Fault  isolation techniques have continually evolved to match the  progressive developments implemented by innovative design, test, and process engineers as device performance and  functionality regularly re-establish the state-of-the-art in  product offerings. A powerful fault isolation technique that has  equally matured over time is Laser Voltage Probing (LVP) [1-13]. Originally developed to address the limitations  of electron beam probing, LVP has transitioned into a wellestablished and essential analytical optical technique that is  utilized for observing circuit functionality at internal nodes  interrogated through an exposed silicon substrate. It has  enabled the fault isolation of contemporary integrated circuits (IC) for many decades and plays a pivotal role in the FA  workflow.


The primary objective of the FA workflow is to establish the  root cause of a detected failure as efficiently as possible so as  to reduce the product development lifecycle, reduce time-tomarket and, consequently, maximize profitability. A crucial  step in analyzing a failure is to monitor device functionality.


Non-contact optical probing techniques serve as a key enabling  technology in silicon-level design verification and product  debug. Historically, electrical micro-probing and electron  beam probing were utilized to observe device activity through  an acquired waveform from the front-side; however, due to the  implementation of modern flip-chip packaging architectures as  well as the use of ten or more back-end metallization levels  serving as interconnect to route internal signals to different  areas across the die, these previously indispensable probing  methods are now seldom considered. Accordingly, as the  semiconductor industry proliferates higher speed and  integration density, the FA community had to circumvent these  front-side access limitations by introducing a path to probe  electrical signals from the back-side of the die (i.e. through the  silicon substrate). Electron beam and mechanical probers are  intrusive and require direct access to metal lines to perform  waveform extraction; therefore, unless invasive circuit edit  modifications are employed and micro-cavities created through  multiple metallization layers (which may disrupt ideal device  operation), these technologies offer no value. Conversely, LVP  is a non-invasive optical platform that does not make direct  contact with the device but can measure its electrical activity  by accessing the active layer through an exposed silicon  substrate.


LVP as a practice has developed over many years to add  tremendous value in the FA of contemporary microelectronic  devices. Not only has there been application extensions (some  of which will be discussed later in this article), system  configurations are also regularly upgraded to enable improved  capabilities and ease-of-use. Examples of which include  enhanced detector arrangements (e.g. integrated high- and lowfrequency modules), resolution improvements (both spatial  and temporal), and user-friendly software environments. This  has provided a vehicle for the FA analyst to efficiently and  accurately address a wide variety of fail modes across various  technology nodes: from a routine 28nm scan chain analysis  where an analyst can quickly isolate flip-flops or buffers in  which signal propagation is inhibited, to more advanced failing  signatures in which complex device functionality must be  examined within 14nm logic blocks. Optoelectronic probing  and imaging of silicon ICs is an invaluable capability for fault


localization and one, as we will see as we navigate this article, which is entrenched in the FA workflow.


LVP Theory


LVP is made possible through the detection of optical intensity  and/or phase modulation using high-speed, high-sensitivity  photodetectors. These parts-per-million variations are detected  after a focused laser, which has navigated the imaging optics  of a laser scanning microscope, has interacted with the active  layer of a device. Many light-matter interactions take place  within the focal volume of the probe beam; however, for LVP  there are specific optoelectronic phenomena that dominate. These are split into electro-optical effects and free-carrier  effects:


Electro-Optical Effects:


Electro-optical effects in silicon describe the change in both the  absorption coefficient and the index of refraction as a function  of an applied electric-field. Some examples of electro-optical  effects are given below:


Electro-Absorption


Electro-absorption, also known as the Franz-Keldysh  effect [14], is the change of a material’s bandgap energy due to  the application of an electric-field. The electric-field variations  introduced by the time-dependent voltages applied to a metaloxide semiconductor field effect transistor (MOSFET) disrupt  the local space charge distributions which, in turn, alter the  semiconductor’s band structure. This bandgap modification  results in an increased overlap between the valence and  conduction energy bands which increase the opportunity for  electrons and holes to interact. The higher the degree of band  structure overlap, the greater the level of absorption. More  specifically, this absorption mechanism takes place as a result  of photon-assisted tunneling through a modified energy  barrier [15]. The change in the absorption coefficient for  silicon as a function of photon energy at various electric-fields  is presented in Fig. 1 [16].


Electro-Refraction


Band structure distortion through electro-absorption also has  an influence on the refractive index of the material. This is  known as electro-refraction. When an electromagnetic wave  enters the active region of a device, its phase velocity will  change due to the presence of an internal electric-field.  This  light-matter interaction causes the local space charge profile to  vibrate within the silicon lattice which in turn disturbs the  phase velocity of the original incident wave. In other words, the physical properties of the silicon change with a fluctuating  electric-field which amends the speed at which the incident  laser frequency can travel; hence, a modified refractive index


(the refractive index is defined as the ratio between the speed  of light and the phase velocity). This refractive index change is  wavelength-dependent and has been calculated by Soref and  Bennett using the data from Fig.1 – please see Fig. 2 [17]. Note  that the refractive index change is positive for wavelengths >1050nm and negative for wavelengths <1050nm.


Figure 1: Electro-absorption spectrum of silicon for various  electric-fields [16].


Figure 2: Electro-refraction spectrum in silicon [17].


The Kerr Effect


Another effect that describes a change in the refractive index of  a material in response to an applied electric-field is the Kerr  Effect [18]. Here, the applied electric-field results in the  material becoming birefringent, with different indices of  refraction being observed for light that is polarized parallel to, or perpendicular to, the applied field. The Kerr Effect is also  known as the quadratic electro-optic effect since its response is  proportional to the square of the applied electric-field.


The Pockels Effect


The Pockels effect also describes the manifested birefringence  in crystals caused by an electric-field; however, instead of  displaying a quadratic dependency, the effect is linearly  proportional with respect to the applied electric-field. This  effect is rarely discussed for silicon since it is observed only in  materials that do not have a centro-symmetrical crystal  structure (e.g. Gallium-Arsenide). As a result, since silicon has  a centro-symmetric crystal structure the Pockels Effect, and it’s  influence on LVP, is negligible but is included here for  completeness.


Free Carrier Effects:


Free carrier effects in silicon describe the change in both the  absorption coefficient and the index of refraction as a function  of the density of free carriers. Note here that in addition to the  free carriers that are available in a static semiconductor device, free carriers can also be injected depending on the voltage that  is applied to the device. An example for the presence of free  carriers in a FET is the inversion channel. Some examples of  free carrier effects are given below:


Free Carrier Absorption


As a general rule, when the incident photon has energy below  the silicon bandgap energy (i.e. <1.1eV; >1100nm), the  absorbed radiation conserves energy and generates lattice  vibrations in the form of heat (phonons); however, if the  incident radiation is above the bandgap (i.e. >1.1eV; <1100nm), the absorbed radiation generates localized  photocarriers [19]. These carriers are promoted from the  valance band to the conduction band (i.e. from an initially  dormant electronic state); however, excitation can also take  place from an already excited state. The former describes interband absorption and the latter free carrier absorption – since  the carriers are “free” to move within the energy level it  originated.


Soref and Bennett investigated the role of free carrier effects in  silicon (free carrier absorption and refraction) where they  collected absorption spectra data based on free carrier effects  from the literature and presented the combined absorption


spectra from 0.001eV (1.24mm) up to 2.8 eV (443nm) for free  electrons and holes - please see Fig. 3 and 4 [17]).


Figure 3: Optical absorption spectra of silicon showing the  influence of various concentrations of free electrons [17].


Figure 4: Optical absorption spectra of silicon showing the  influence of various concentrations of free holes [17].


Free Carrier Refraction


By considering the free carrier absorption data collated by  Soref and Bennett in [17], the resulting dependency of the  index of refraction on the charge carrier density for free


electrons and holes was determined. The results for 1300nm  are shown in Fig. 5.


Figure 5: Free carrier refraction as a function of free carrier  concentration [17].


Three carrier effects are typically considered for LVP: 1) traditional free-carrier absorption, 2) Burstein-Moss bandfilling (this shifts the silicon absorption spectrum to shorter  wavelengths – a blue shift), and 3) Coulombic interaction of  carriers with impurities (an effect that shifts the spectrum to  longer wavelengths – a red shift). These 3 effects act  simultaneously; however, what is practically observed is a  dominant red shift; therefore, Coulombic effects are stronger  than band-filling in silicon.


Commercial LVP Systems


Heinrich et al. were the first to demonstrate the value of both  continuous wave (CW) and pulsed LVP systems [3]. In their  initial CW work, a 1340nm laser interrogated a flip-chip  packaged silicon bipolar device using a fast photodiode and  real-time oscilloscope to acquire a propagating waveform. A  dual-beam interferometer scheme was employed to detect the  phase-modulations induced on the laser beam reflected from  the active region of the device. A system bandwidth of  200MHz was claimed. As was mentioned earlier, due to the  increasing adoption of flip-chip technology, particularly by  Intel at the 250nm node, as well as the growing number of  metallization layers being implemented, e-beam probing, the  primary technology at the time, was now much more difficult  to use (requiring FIB probe point creation). The early LVP  work of Heinrich et al., at both Stanford University and IBM  was investigated by researchers at Intel (most notably, Bob Rao


and Mario Paniccia) as a potential solution to this problem. Once they saw the potential on CMOS in their lab, they  engaged with Schlumberger (around 1996) to build a system  for them. Many others were also moving, or had moved, to flipchip and were also looking for a solution.


The result was the development of the first commercial LVP  solution (the IDS2000). Instead of a CW 1340nm laser, a  mode-locked 35ps 1064nm laser was used to achieve high  bandwidth (up to 10GHz in the IDS2000). In addition, the  complicated phase-sensing dual-beam interferometer  arrangement employed by Heinrich et al. was replaced by a  single beam amplitude sensing scheme.  It was thought that  1064nm excitation would primarily exploit the Franz-Keldysh  effect and return stronger amplitude modulation by operating  near the silicon bandgap. The resolution improvement from  using the shorter wavelength was also, no doubt, considered an  advantage.


As LVP technology matured, an interferometer was added to  the second generation system (IDS2500) after experience with  the original system pointed to the existance of a strong phase  component in the signal (e.g. from observed waveform  inversion – this will be addressed later in the article). A  Michelson interferometer arrangement was selected due to the  simplified probe placement (i.e. no need to find a suitable  reference point location, as required in the arrangement of  Heinrich et al.). The increased vibration sensitivity that  resulted from the integration of the Michelson interferometer  into the Laser Scanning Microscopes (LSM) in the IDS2500  required the implementation of active measures - i.e. tracking  device vibrations by moving the reference arm mirror - to bring  the added noise under control and improve signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Later systems replaced the Michelson interferometer  with a greatly simplified polarization-based, common path   interferometer (PDP scheme) which was significantly easier to  set up and use and did not require active noise cancellation.


Incorporating an interferometer into the system allowed the  measurement of both amplitude and phase perturbations during  data acquisition. Phase measurements minimize some of the  disadvantages of acquiring intensity-only waveforms. For  example, under intensity-based operation, optimal waveform  acquisition is dependent on both the laser’s axial (focal) position and lateral probe point within the diffusion region - which is extracted through trial and error. In phased-based  mode, this dependency is reduced which improves the  probability for the analyst to efficiently obtain a usable  waveform. Phase-based measurements are still available on  modern LVP platforms, although the method to extract such  information is very different- more on this later.


The concept of CW LVP was resurrected around 2004 at  Optonics and NPTest (now parts of Thermo-Fisher Scientific) when it was realized by researchers there that detector and realtime sampling oscilloscope technology had matured to the  point that useful levels of bandwidth and reasonable


acquisition times could be achieved. Modulation mapping was  developed shortly after (first results in 2005). The technology  was widely disseminated after research results were published  by Kindereit et al. in 2006 and 2007. The first commercial CW  LVP system was offered for sale around 2008 by Semicaps. Currently, CW LVP systems are available from at least 4  equipment providers.


Pulsed laser-based LVP systems are not currently offered by  equipment providers; however, it is important to understand the  relative advantages and disadvantages of this mode of  operation as it may be resurrected in the future to address the  primary limitation of CW operation: bandwidth. Pulsed laser  systems provide the highest measurement bandwidth: The last  system produced, introduced in 2006, still has an unmatch >20GHz bandwidth (depending on device jitter). There are  legacy systems in the field kept around for corner-case  situations requiring such high performance. Usable bandwidth  for CW systems, on the other hand, has not increase beyond 6-7GHz, even after 10+ years of development. CW bandwidth  has even regressed as lower-bandwidth detectors have gained  in popularity due to their lower noise floors– this will be  addressed later in the article- and as next generation 577nm  visible light probing systems, with their 1-2GHz bandwidth (limited by visible light detector technology) begin to be  deployed.


Despite their bandwidth limits, CW techniques have proven to  be much more successful than pulsed-laser techniques for a  number of reasons. One is their far superior ease-of-use that  results from their natural DC noise rejection (through AC  coupling of the signal). The commercially produced pulsed  laser-based systems acquires signals at DC which results in the  accumulation of associated noise caused primarily by device  under test (DUT) vibrations and drift. This noise then has to be  removed by dividing the pulsed-laser measurement with a (nearly) simulatenously-acquired reference laser measurement. Non-linear effects of the 10ps laser pulses (vs CW reference  laser) degrades the noise rejection to <10:1, which is orders of  magnitude worse that for a CW based system. As a result, CW  measurements are more stable and reliable. With a pulsed  laser-based system, it is usually necessary to acquire multiple  waveforms of the same signal to ensure the trustworthyness of  the measurement.


Another major reason for the success of CW LVP is the ability  to rapidly interrogate a device in 2D by looking at the  modulation levels of a target frequency in real-time using a  spectrum analyzer (this is known as modulation mapping and, again, will be discussed later in the article). This real-time  feedback allows probe placement to be quickly optimized to  provide the highest quality waveform. With pulsed-laser based  systems, optimizing probe placement was a time-consuming  trial-and-error process because the primary indicator of proper  probe placement was the quality of the acquired waveform  itself.


In summary, contemporary LVP tools offer high-throughput  waveform acquisition solutions using CW 1340nm and/or CW  1064nm lasers. 1340nm probing is less invasive (since there is  no localized injection of photocarriers) and more efficient (due  to improved SNR from stronger modulation and higher  detector responsivity). Laser damage threshold is also higher at  1340nm, providing greater margins when setting laser power. The primary advantage to using 1064nm is the improved  spatial resolution. The choice for the FA lab can be addressed  by asking a simple question: can the user get away with the  reduced resolution of 1320/1340nm probing? If yes, it's  probably better in all ways. If no, then the lab will need to cope  with the increased invasiveness and decreased SNR offered by  1064nm wavelength. Interestingly, there is now a 3rd option of  1154nm offered by some vendors, which splits the difference!


Waveform Acquisition Process


An illustration of how LVP is implemented into a confocal  LSM is presented in Fig. 6. A focused CW IR laser beam is  raster scanned over the backside of an exposed die. The  reflected light is sent back to a high-speed photodiode detector  and the reflected light intensity at each pixel position is  processed and mapped to form a 2D image of the observation


area. This forms a “pattern” image of the device. The pattern


image is then used to identify a transistor of interest. This is  typically aided by overlaying Computer Aided Design (CAD) layers to help identify critical physical locations.


Figure 6. Hardware schematic for LVP implementation.


The laser is then positioned, or “parked”, on a space-charge  region from which a waveform is to be acquired – with current  geometries and resolution limitations, the beam usually  overlaps with the source-gate-drain structures of a FET. At this  point, the analyst will enable LVP mode in the tool’s software  environment to establish the desired waveform acquisition  settings. The magnitude of the reflected light at this location is  a function of the silicon thickness due to linear absorption (note  here that the laser light traverses the silicon substrate twice – once on route to the active area and once more on its way back  to the photodetector). It is possible to perform LVP from the  backside through full-thickness silicon (~760µm) as well as  thinned silicon (sub-100µm) depending on the laser  wavelength selected and substrate doping involved.


When a transistor switches state, the local electric-field is  modified which results in a change in the reflected light  intensity due to the change in the absorption coefficient and the  index of refraction. The magnitude of the modulation is in the  100-1000 parts-per-million range; therefore, sensitive multiGHz photodiodes and detection electronics are necessary. In  parallel to identifying the node of interest, the analyst will have  a lab-based tester configured to exercise the DUT with a given  test pattern. The tester will issue a trigger to highlight the start  of each loop and that signal must be delivered to the LVP tool. With the trigger signal identified, the analyst must then define  both the LVP acquisition window (i.e. the acquisition time  span) required and the time relative to the trigger at which the  acquisition will take place (i.e. trigger delay).


With these parameters established, the LVP tool can then  initiate the acquisition process. This typically requires the  accumulation of many thousands of extremely weak  waveforms over the temporal window of interest, so they can  be averaged together to reduce noise. Note here that the  averaging process has implications for the acquired waveforms (e.g. jitter degrades rise-time, intermittent signals can give ‘tristate’ type waveforms, etc.) and single shot measurements are  not possible so there can be no useful jitter measurements. Also, averaging means the trigger needs to be stable relative to  device activity. Standard LVP systems will employ an RF  amplifier to split this detected signal into an RF component and  a DC component. The RF component is first amplified then  sent to a high-speed oscilloscope for waveform acquisition. The DC component is used to form the LSM pattern image.


The oscilloscope is critical in that it dictates the measurement  capabilities of the tool, such as measurement bandwidth and  sample rate. Even more importantly, the oscilloscope has a  significant impact on acquisition time due to trigger efficiency / dead time. Segmented memory (LeCroy) was one of the  crucial initial developments for reducing acquisition times that  made CW LVP feasible. Then Tektronix’s FastAcq/DPO  technology offered a solution to the limitation of data throughput (at least for most use-cases). Finally, an important point to  be noted regarding oscilloscope bandwidth is that minimum  measured rise-times are the result of convolving the rise-times


of the oscilloscope with those of the photodetector and the RF  amplifiers. As noted above, these parameters can vary  depending on the equipment provider and the LVP  requirements of the FA lab. The LVP waveform on the  oscilloscope is then displayed in pseudo-real time as it is being  acquired on the tool’s graphical user interface for  interpretation.


An example of employing LVP in a 28nm design debug  environment is given in Fig. 7 in which an AC scan failure is  interrogated to confirm that a failing vector of interest is bound  between specific launch and capture flip flops (FF). First, a  waveform of sufficient temporal resolution is acquired from a  global clock driver to serve as a time stamp for all subsequent  measurements. Second, waveforms are acquired from the  outputs of the associated launch and capture FF’s in both a  passing and failing state. Since a failure that takes place within  the combinational logic can only be “observed” by a tester at  the capture FF cycle, it is anticipated that both the passing and  failing waveforms from the launch FF will be identical – which  they are. Passing and failing waveforms acquired from the  capture FF however will differ and, in this case, manifest the  incorrect AC speed transition. Subsequent probing will  transition back from the capture FF, into the logic, to isolate  the exact circuit element at which the failure takes place.


Laser Invasiveness:


LVP is made possible through our ability to measure ppm  changes in a laser beam’s amplitude and/or phase after it has  returned from the active region of a device. However, it is not  only the incident laser that is affected by such an interaction. The device itself can also be influenced. This has been  exploited through global fault isolation techniques such as  LADA since the energy from a 1064nm laser can perturb the  switching characteristics of illuminated transistors. Such an  invasive interaction, although positively utilized for LADA,


can lead to unfavorable results for LVP. For example, this can  be observed as “shark-fin” waveforms or by transitioning a  device from a passing state into a failing state (e.g. when  probing soft fails).


Naming Convention:


Another interesting observation, this time related to  nomenclature, is the fact that LVP does not actually measure  voltages. It is a representation of the change in optical power  contained within a beam after it has interacted with a functional  transistor. It can communicate switching characteristics based  on when and how the MOSFET is in operation. These translate


into the resulting waveform’s temporal profile and shape,


respectively. Some vendors refer to LVP as Electro-Optic  Probing (EOP) or the Laser Timing Module/Probe (LTM/P). These naming conventions are equally accepted within the  industry and are understood to represent the same optical  probing application.


Future Work


Like all analytical techniques and toolsets, a common theme  for future work, in addition to enabling extended functionality  on a single toolset, concerns the improvement of resolution and  sensitivity. Tool vendors are under constant pressure to  innovate and invent in order to supplement their current  offerings in order to remain both valuable to the industry and  profitable. This pursuit is no different for LVP and is discussed  below.


Spatial Resolution


As was stated in the Introduction, the value of LVP is derived  from its ability to efficiently and accurately localize anomalous  circuit activity with nanometric precision. This capability  however has been under constant threat as process technology  is scaled below 20nm, where the spatial resolution required for  effective optical probing surpasses that offered by the latest


SIL’s. As a result, the FA industry responded with the


introduction of VLP; yet, even the tight focal geometries  offered by visible light is not enough to eliminate the  debilitating effects of cross-talk where the electrical activity  from neighboring nodes combine into a single optical  waveform due to the lateral distribution of the incident laser’s  point spread function (PSF). Probe placement (i.e. knowing  where to probe) is also important and is limited not only by  spatial resolution but by poor CAD alignment accuracy. An  interesting solution to these two limitations was demonstrated  recently in which electrical waveforms were acquired from a  time-resolved LADA-based system where the propagation  delays of critical paths were extracted via a simple pass/fail  detection scheme [50, 51]. In this work, single event upsets (SEU) were generated in FF’s to serve as an initial CAD  alignment mechanism that offers nanometric precision after  which “waveforms” are acquired from nodes tied to the critical  path. These waveforms were not hindered by cross-talk since


only nodes that are involved in the path can contribute to the  acquired pass/fail signal. This approach, although impressively  innovative, is limited to the interrogation of soft failures and  cannot be applied to the selective probing of an arbitrary node  of interest. Inducing SEU in FF’s however remains an option  for precision CAD alignment in the interrogation of advanced  technology nodes [52].


Furthermore, as noted earlier, the stringent sample preparation  requirements for implementing VLP are not yet commonplace  in today’s FA environment. As a result, interest is now placed  on supporting the fault isolation workflow by developing  improved recipes for efficient data interpretation. An example  of this is in creative test pattern editing where, for example in  scan chain debug, the stimulus for every chain other than the  individual scan chain of interest is turned off in the test pattern  so as to minimize the electrical activity across the die. Another  example may be through the application of sophisticated  autonomous waveform prediction and pattern searching  algorithms [53].


With VLP it is believed that the industry has exhausted the  opportunities in conventional scaling. Incident wavelengths  have been scaled beyond the bandgap energy of silicon (1.1eV,


1.1µm) through aggressive sample preparation down to sub10µm substrate thicknesses and the limits of NA scaling has  been reached with the introduction of central and aplanatic  SIL’s (offering NA’s up to 3.3 – the practical limit). This leaves  the industry to entertain more exotic resolution enhancing  techniques, all of which remain in the research and  development stage for now. Some areas currently under  consideration include the return of e-beam probing. Focused  Ion Beam (FIB) circuit edit techniques can be used to expose  the active region of transistors, which can then be e-beam  probed. In addition, Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) and  Near-field Scanning Optical Microscopy (NSOM)-based  techniques are also generating attention - once analysts get  used to the idea of removing most of the substrate. A major  advantage these near-field techniques have over VLP is that  you don’t need a large flat area to land a SIL, only a relatively  small access hole.


SNR improvements are typically proportional to improvements  in spatial resolution performance; however, there are always  other mechanisms which can be explored. For example, the use  of a lock-in amplifier setup may improve signal sensitivity. This would come at the expense of bandwidth though (~600MHz maximum). Another option is to employ dualphase interferometric back-side imaging and detection [54]. Also, tool vendors could revisit the implementation of  polarization and phase-based effects in an attempt to coax out  improved signal sensitivity by making modifications to the  existing optical column. Though this may be possible, it may


not be practically feasible since the increased complexity  would likely lead to decreased tool usability.


Digitizer-Based LVP


As the industry starts to embrace digitizer-based LVP, it  creates a paradigm shift in which new opportunities for the  failure analyst are created. For example, as discussed  previously, oscilloscope-based LVP may currently offer bestin-class performance when precise timing measurements are  required, digitizer-based LVP, with 32GS/s (~31ps sampling  bins), is not too far behind. In addition, the significant sampling  space offered by a digitizer, enables new spatiotemporal  acquisition options. An example of which is the ability of the  digitizer to mimic the function of LVT; however, instead of  being limited to a restricted temporal observation window, a  digitizer can identify and map the presence of an asynchronous  waveform of interest as it shifts in time across many tens of  microseconds.


As a summary, the key benefits of using a digitizer include:


• Improved trigger collection efficiency with less down  time (i.e. faster waveform averaging)


• 512k samples can be collected every trigger without


trigger collection efficiency penalty (i.e. massive


amounts of real-time collection/on-board processing)


• In some cases, waveforms can be collected over entire  tests (e.g. with the ability to acquire at 32GS/s – which is  31ps per sample – 512k samples will return 18µs of


waveform data in almost real time) - with collection


efficiency faster than a high bandwidth scope


There are some downsides however. These include:


• Sampling rates are currently limited to 32GS/s on stateof-the-art digitizers with a 512k sample width


• Still need oscilloscope averaging for precision timing  applications, e.g. measuring small propagation delays


For logic probing, the best solution available is a digitizer. For  precise delay measurements however, the best solution is an  oscilloscope. Ideally, tool vendors would consider integrating  the best of both worlds into a system that lets you start with  digitizer-based probing for rapid waveform acquisition and  interrogation (over long periods of time) then switch to  oscilloscope-based probing for performing timing  measurements. Having access to both digitizer and  oscilloscope capabilities certainly entices bespoke  development opportunities.


Summary / Conclusion


LVP is a key enabling technology that has matured into a wellestablished and essential analytical optical technique that is  crucial for observing and evaluating internal circuit activity. From the initial transition from electron- to laser-based probing  to the more recent evolution from IR- to visible light-based  interrogation, LVP has transitioned through periods of  continual research and development while overcoming many  challenges to provide an elegant optical probing solution for  the FA community that has spanned >20 years of technology  node scaling. The deployment of LVP will remain at the heart  of silicon device FA for many years to come and so we look  forward to the exciting developments that will likely transpire. It is hoped that this article serves as a valuable technical guide  for both entry-level and established analysts while enticing the  pursuit of more specific and/or detailed LVP material.

CAD Navigation Principles


Arpan Bhattacherjee


Synopsys Inc., Mountain View, California, USA


Martin Parley


Qualcomm Technologies Inc., San Diego, California, USA


Over the revolutionary era of semiconductor technology, Computer-Aided Design (CAD) Navigation tools have played  an increasingly critical role in silicon debug and Failure  Analysis (FA) in efforts to improve manufacturing yield while  reducing time-to-market for integrated circuit (IC) products. This paper covers the key principles and advancements of CAD  Navigation solutions for IC and package FA – including some  of the best-known practices for fast fault localization, accurate  root cause analysis, FA equipment utilization, efficient crossteam collaboration, and database management.


Shrinking technology nodes have continually increased the  need for CAD-based FA techniques to isolate defects in ICs. Electrical Fault Isolation (EFI) becomes more and more  complex with additional levels of interconnects, smaller feature  sizes, and higher transistor densities in modern semiconductor  devices. These challenges increase FA cycle time significantly, as illustrated in Figure 1.


Figure 1: Shrinking technology nodes increase FA cycle time


CAD Navigation (CADNav) plays a vital role in reducing the  overall time to localize IC failures, determine their root causes  and provide feedback to the appropriate team to drive corrective  actions (e.g., Design, Manufacturing). Without CADNav, the  time to isolate and correct the IC would take immeasurably  longer and may not even be possible with traditional analytical  techniques.


In efforts to improve the time to market (TTM) cycle for  semiconductor products (see Figure 2) both fab and fabless  companies rely on FA results to build defect pareto charts and  identify problems that have the most impact to manufacturing  yield ramp.


Figure 2: Typical IC manufacturing time to market cycle


Time to market can be shortened by finding root cause failures  earlier and implementing manufacturing changes faster to  achieve target yields. Shorter TTM for semiconductor products  is business-critical because companies can beat their  competitors to the market and sell their products when prices  are at their highest. Semiconductor companies strive to  maximize their yield as early as possible to net the highest profit  margin (see Figure 3).


Figure 3: Faster fault localization enables faster yield ramp  and helps maximize profit while margins are at their highest


To maximize market profitability, it is imperative to facilitate  FA techniques to isolate root causes of failures as fast as  possible. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the IC design  schematic to identify potential failures (e.g., diagnostic results) and correlate them to their physical location on the IC, as seen  in Figure 4.


Figure 4: Net highlighted in IC schematic and layout


CADNav tools provide the ability to quickly cross-reference  between schematic and layout to investigate IC defects and also  the ability to link to FA equipment in order to position the stage  at the exact location of interest on the failing device under test (DUT).


Even at the accurate location, it is very difficult and sometimes  impossible to see the small areas of interest (e.g., buried tracks) and the structures surrounding it due to tool and technique  limitations. In these cases, CAD layout polygons can be  overlaid onto the live microscope image to visualize all the  circuit features in the area of interest on the DUT. The overlaid  polygons are then used as a guide to accurately position the  equipment stage to perform the next appropriate actions.


CADNav enables EFI to localize the fault area to the smallest  possible region and may be followed by physical failure  analysis (PFA). PFA also utilizes CADNav to analyze device  cross-sections, layer connectivity, electrical signal flow and  other CAD-based attributes to identify and confirm the rootcause of IC failures.


By now, the value of CADNav for FA is apparent as it leverages  a full spectrum of design data to allow quick and seamless  correlation between schematic, layout and FA equipment for  efficient analysis and circuit debug. Therefore, preparing and  maintaining a comprehensive CADNav database plays an  important role in meeting a semiconductor company’s TTM  objectives.


CAD Navigation Database


The key to enabling a fully-functional CADNav system is the  quality and completeness of its input data. By leveraging  various data sources from the IC design flow, CADNav tools  are able to extract and consolidate all the significant IC design  information required for FA, as well as allow custom  configurations of the data to match the actual silicon as closely  as possible, including support for multi-patterning technologies (MPT).


MPT was effectively introduced during the fabrication of 20nm  devices to overcome the lithographic limitations involved in the  IC manufacturing process. Two or more process steps are  required to create MPT layers (e.g., Litho-Etch-Litho-Etch). In  leading-edge technologies (e.g., 7nm), there can be several  mask layers involved to create a single IC layer. CADNav tools  have accommodated for these advancements by ensuring that  the database matches the physical IC, regardless of the number  of mask layers involved in the manufacturing process. A single  CAD layer can be synthesized using the same Boolean  operations as the original photomasks such that it represents the  final layer in CAD, as intended by designers.


The following sections describe the key elements of a complete  CADNav database, as well as some considerations and best  practices to maintain it for optimal results.


Database Inputs


A complete CADNav database integrates design data from  three primary sources, as shown in Figure 5.


Figure 5: CAD Navigation database comprised of layout, netlist and schematic data


i. Layout


An IC layout file contains the geometric shapes for all  mask layers of the chip [1]. Common formats include  GDSII and OASIS, the latter being more efficient due to  smaller data sizes. Along with the layout file, additional  information may be required to describe the name and  purpose of each layer along with any operations required  to reconstruct MPT layers. This information can be  obtained from designers and imported into the CADNav  environment.


ii. Netlist


A netlist file is comprised of the circuit connectivity  information. There are various formats used for this file, however, the most common formats used in the industry  are SPICE and EDIF.


iii. Schematic


The schematic is derived from Layout Versus Schematic (LVS) files that are generated during physical verification  that checks and confirms the consistency between IC  layout and schematic. There are several LVS tools  available in the market, each one having a unique data  conversion flow for a CADNav database.


Considerations and Best Practices


Although the intent of a CADNav database is to make end-user  flows easy, there are certain precautions to consider regarding  database preparation and management. Since time is of the  essence for achieving TTM objectives, it is critical to save time  wherever possible in the overall workflow. The following  sections describe the main challenges and suggest some of the  best-known methodologies to address them.


i. Data Gathering


Gathering the required input data can be a challenge, as


there could be many different design teams or design flows


used within a single company. It is advisable to create a


standardized and streamlined data specification and


process flow that works across various teams within a


company, while emphasizing the importance of the data for


enabling efficient FA and minimizing TTM.


Locating input data after the design has been taped out can


be a challenge because it is common that the designers of


that particular dataset have moved on to other projects and


are not available to regenerate any files.  This is especially


true if an LVS rerun is required since it can be very


complex and time consuming.


Therefore, the best practice is to collect all the necessary


input files and prepare the CADNav database in advance,


before it is needed for FA. Preparing the CADNav


databases early for all designs may be costly in terms of


effort and data storage, but it can save several days of


critical FA time.


ii. Automation and Scale


If there is significant volume and variety of designs, it is


recommended to implement automated processes and tools


for gathering data, configuring standard settings, and


converting the inputs to an organized CADNav database.


iii. Database Administration


Given the importance of CADNav for FA and the


considerations listed above, it is recommended as a best


practice to designate one or more people as the database


administrator (DBA). Having a designated DBA can


significantly mitigate the challenges associated with data  gathering, automation and scale. Other benefits include  efficient data storage and management, database  uniformity, having a single point of contact to collect enduser feedback and drive new features into the CADNav  roadmap.


iv. Protecting Confidential Information


In a fabless environment, the netlist and LVS information  is particularly sensitive and is typically not shared with the  foundry or external FA facilities. This means that the FA  lab of a fabless design company is the only team equipped  to do the most advanced EFI and PFA techniques, such as  nodal analysis with a Laser Voltage Prober (LVP), which  relies heavily on schematic data to understand the expected  circuit behavior versus actual LVP results.


Active Voltage Contrast (AVC)


Sometimes contact chains are not completely open  but have a high resistance far beyond the specification because of a partially open contact. The leaking  current through this faulty contact prevents charging  and its localization with PVC. This is shown in Fig.


12.


Fig 12: The contact chain part left from the faulty  contact can’t be charged because charges can escape through it faster as they were generated by the  primary beam. PVC localization just works on totally open contacts.


With a nanoprober in SEM/FIB as shown in Fig. 13  definite voltages can be applied to definite structures.


Fig. 13: 4-probe nanoprober, mounted on a stage of  a Dualbeam FIB.


With an external voltage applied to such a chain as  shown in Fig. 14 there are sufficient charges in the  left part of the chain and at the faulty contact is a  leap in potential according to Ohm’s law.


Fig. 14: Principle of Active Voltage Contrast. With  an external voltage applied to a high-resistive contact chain different potentials emerge on the two  parts of the chain resulting in a clearly distinguishable Voltage Contrast


Currently there are two basic types of in-chamber  nanoprobing systems available – stage mounted


ones and chamber mounted ones. Both have advantages and disadvantages depending on the purpose  they are to be used for. Chamber mounted system  do not allow any stage movement after the probes  have been lowered. It doesn’t matter for device  characterization purposes where 4, 6 or even 8  probes have to contact structures in very small region.


For AVC sometimes test structures are contacted at  their probe pads because it is easier than to do so at  tiny conducting lines. Probe pads often are several  hundreds of micrometers away from the structure itself. Here a stage mounted system is very helpful, because the pad is placed under the beam first in order to lower the tips under visual control and after  that the stage is moved together with the tips until  the test structure is under the beam in order to  search for AVC.


Stage mounted systems have some restrictions regarding stage moving range and sample size. Some  prober models do not allow the use of the load lock  due to geometrical restrictions. On the other hand, this prober type can easily be used at any other tools  of the same type, just an electrical feedthrough  flange is necessary at each tool. In Table 5 advantages and disadvantages of both prober types are  listed.


Table 5: Advantages and disadvantages of the two  basic nanoprober types.


The number of probe tips for AVC application is  not critical. It can be performed even with a single


tip, two are sufficient whereas a device characterization requires 4, 6 or 8 tips.


Another interesting question is whether one should  use a SEM or FIB for AVC localization issues. A  SEM with 2 kV primary beam voltage can mostly  be used. As an exception, when lines are to be cut, a  FIB is needed. A tool with both SEM and FIB column would be ideal.


The last question to be discussed here is which voltages should be applied to the structures. Since most  of the secondary electrons have energies of 2-4 eV  and below, a probing voltage of +5V is o.k. A general rule for the probing voltage is “the higher the  better” but at voltages above 7V we occasionally  observed irreversible gate oxide damage and the  AVC image changed dramatically preventing any  further localization.


For failure localization Voltage Contrast both in  SEM and in FIB can be used. Both methods have  their advantages and disadvantages.


Knowledge of all facts influencing the VC generation (capacitance, leakage, doping and circuitry) is  very helpful for successful failure localization.


Active Voltage Contrast is more laborious but offers completely new opportunities for failure localization.

Transistor Characterization: Physics and Instrumentation


ANSYS Inc, Beltsville, MD, USA


ashok.alagappan@ansys.com, 301-640-5816


Semiconductor technology has advanced significantly  and has been the key enabler of many state-of-the-art electronic  products and emerging applications. Most credit for such  advancement goes to the continuous scaling of transistors, which are not only the basic building blocks of IC components  but essentially the heart of the components responsible for  pumping out current continuously during the operation of the  product. It becomes imperative to follow certain design  techniques and manufacturing processes to create them and  characterization methods to ensure the devices perform within  specifications.  Proper characterization across design  parameters, manufacturing process variation and operating  conditions is essential to achieve the desired performance  characteristics and lifetime requirements of the product. This  article discusses the device parameters that determine the  design criteria and manufacturing processes, and methodology  to characterize the two common transistor types in CMOS  technology.


Integrated Circuit Design


Product life cycle of an integrated circuit starts with  circuit design which defines the functionality of the component. Digital logic is typically obtained by building logic gates  represented by Boolean algebra. The logic gates make up  functional and control units of the chip. Analog design is  achieved by matching the device characteristics to obtain  desired amplification, filtering and signal integrity. Circuit  design is typically broken down into functional blocks. Each  component will have several functional blocks put together  depending on the complexity of the product.  Other than the  functionality of the circuit, there are several performance  metrics which the design team tries to achieve, among which  timing, speed, device leakage and standby current are some of  the key performance metrics.


These individual performance metrics are typically achieved by  adjusting the transistor characteristics in the critical path.   Desired characteristics of the transistors are obtained by  adjusting the critical dimensions such as channel width and  length of the device and modulating the bias voltage. A typical  product, irrespective of its manufacturing process node and the  type (digital, analog or mixed signal) will have transistors of  different gate lengths and widths. Short channel, long channel  and medium channel devices are integrated into the circuit of  each block in order to achieve the functionality and


performance metrics. Simulation is typically performed at this  stage, often using spice netlist, Verilog or VHDL analysis to  ensure functionality is achieved for the particular block and the  component as a whole. Circuit schematic is then converted into  layout. This is achieved by laying out polygons and rectangular  shapes in electronic design automation (EDA) tool. The shapes  represent different manufacturing processing layers. The layout  is then verified against the schematics to verify the correct  functionality after which simulation is performed at the layout  level. This is where the parasitic effects are modeled to ensure  speed, timing and other performance metrics are met. Circuit  layout is then sent to the mask shop to manufacture lithography  masks using a process called tape out.


Semiconductor Manufacturing


The manufacturing process of a semiconductor product is one  of the most complex, expensive and time-consuming processes. A typical fabrication involves silicon wafers to go through a  sequence of processing steps, wherein layers of material get  deposited, patterned and etched. Transistors are active devices  in a die and the structures are made during the early part of  processing. It is also called front end of line (FEOL).  After the  formation of active devices, contact structures to the active area  of the device and interconnects to route the signals are formed. They are typically called middle of line (MOL) and back end of  line (BEOL) respectively. Details about the two prominent  MOS structures are discussed in the next section.


MOS Device Physics


Planar MOS device


Planar MOS structures were predominantly used as a core  device in digital logic structures until 45nm process node. Formation of transistor involves deposition of a thin layer of  oxide which forms the dielectric of the transistor. A layer of  polysilicon or metal is then deposited on top of the gate oxide, patterned and etched according to the device geometries of the  technology. A source/drain mask defines the region of the  transistor where source and drain regions are formed by doping  either donor or acceptor atoms depending on whether the device  is N or P type. A planar MOSFET structure is shown in figure


1.


Figure 1 – Structure of a planar MOS device


Planar device structures were successfully implemented in  designs from 250nm down to roughly 20nm. The challenge  with planar devices with 20nm gate length and effective gate  oxide thickness of approximately 1A was the on/off  characteristics. In other words, how well the device could be  turned on and off without adverse effects of off-state leakage  current affecting the device performance. As planar device ran  out of steam due to these limitations, the next level of scaling  of planar transistors led to what is known as FinFET devices. Next section discusses the structure of FinFET device in detail.


FinFET device


FinFET structures as shown in figure 2 were developed to  address the challenges of the planar device. Formation of  FinFET device is similar to planar transistors except the masks  and sequence of steps are different. FinFET devices are  essentially 3D devices where the source and drain regions are  raised and the gate with oxide layer surrounding the raised finshaped source drain regions. This type of structure helps the  leakage characteristics by enabling better control of channel on  all three sides instead of one side as in planar device, which is  more effective in blocking the leakage current.


There are additional performance benefits that come with  FinFET devices. With better control over the gate, less voltage  is required to turn on the device resulting in improved power  efficiency compared to a planar device structure [3].


Industry adopted FinFET MOS structures start at approximately  Sub-20nm process nodes.


Figure 2: Structure of a FinFET MOS device


In FinFET structures, charge carriers travel in three dimensions  or surfaces compared to planar which is unidirectional. Higher  charge carriers in relatively smaller gate length result in faster  turn on/off characteristics at the device level and better overall  performance at the full chip level.


Device Properties


The physics of operation of the two device types are similar. However, the characteristics and parameters that define them  are different. The basic parameters that define the transistor are  gate length, width, and junction depth.


With technology scaling, transistor geometries are shrunk. Gate  length becomes smaller and gate oxide thickness gets reduced. The type of gate oxide in older technologies is typically SiO2. The advantage of shrinking the device dimensions from a  technical standpoint is to make the device faster and dissipate  less power. From a business perspective, it makes the  manufacturing process more cost effective. As with any  development process, it comes with challenges and limitations. Reduction in gate oxide thickness increases the gate leakage  due to tunneling of charge carriers into the thin gate oxide. Industry circumvented the problem by introducing a dielectric  layer with a high dielectric constant (K) to increase the effective  oxide capacitance. The process is also known as the high-K  process. Hafnium (HfO2) based dielectric material was a  popular choice starting 45nm process node. Hafnium has a  dielectric constant of 25 compared to 3.9 for SiO2.


Industry adopted high-K metal gate process approximately for  sub-45nm process nodes. Another change in the gate stack  came next which is a natural evolution of high-K gate dielectric  process.


The gate material which has been polysilicon until the adoption  of high-K gate dielectrics, forms a depletion region at the  interface of polysilicon and gate oxide. With device scaling, the  polysilicon depletion width increases effectively reducing gate


oxide capacitance. This results in a degradation of device  performance. It became imperative to not only reduce the gate  oxide thickness but also polysilicon depletion layer thickness. The compatibility of high-K dielectric material and polysilicon  material and the resulting performance also becomes an issue  that cannot be ignored. This led to the introduction of metal gate  to address the challenges of depletion effect and adoption of  high-k dielectric material. What ensued was a marriage between  the two is which is known as high-K metal gate, also known as  HKMG.


As gate lengths keep reducing to increase the speed of operation  and reduce cost, MOS devices start deviating from their ideal  behavior and start exhibiting what is called short-channel  effects. It occurs when the channel length becomes comparable  to depth of source and drain junctions and width of their  depletion layer. A transistor in such a condition is called short  channel transistor and their behavior are short channel effects. Understanding these second order effects and their impact on  device behavior is essential when designing and fabricating  integrated circuits. Second order effects are discussed in the  next session [5].


Drain Induced Barrier Lowering (DIBL)


Under normal conditions (Vds = 0, Vgs = 0), the potential  barrier on the reverse biased source and drain depletion regions  stops the carrier flow from source to drain regions. The applied  gate bias acts to lower the barrier to enable current flow source  to drain. As the channel gets shorter, a large Vd widens the drain  depletion region to a point that reduces the potential barrier  causing current flow even for zero gate bias. This effect is called  drain induced barrier lowering or DIBL [1]. The effect can be  measured by the lateral shift of the transfer curve in the  subthreshold regime as d(Vth) divided by the drain voltage  difference as shown in figure 3.


         =  (    ℎ)  (      )                 (1)


Figure 3. Source transfer characteristics of MOSFET with  drain current plotted in log scale showing DIBL


Threshold voltage (Vt) roll off as a function of short and long  channel lengths are demonstrated in figure 4a and effect of  DIBL on channel length in figure 4b.


Figure 4. Threshold voltage variations


Velocity Saturation


The IV characteristics of a short channel device deviate from  the ideal behavior expressed in equation 1. One of the reasons  for such behavior includes velocity saturation and mobility  degradation effects [2]. Velocity of charge carriers is  proportional to applied electric field for small fields. As the  electric field along the channel gets stronger and reaches a  critical value Esat, the velocity of charge carriers tends to  saturate as shown in figure 5. In other words, above a critical  electric field, the velocity of carriers stabilizes and cannot move  faster. This phenomenon is seen in short channel transistors that  experience higher electric fields [1].


Figure 5. Effect of electric field on electron velocity and  mobility


Hot Carrier Degradation


This is a classic degradation phenomenon in which carriers gain  enough energy to overcome the oxide barrier and get trapped. The trapped charge impacts the transistor performance by  altering the threshold voltage. There is time dependency to this  degradation mechanism, and it results in aging of transistors.


Effects of hot carriers are reduced through manufacturing  techniques such as lightly doped drain (LDD), wherein dopants  are added adjacent to the source and drain terminals. This doped  region effectively reduces the electric field in the channel by  increasing the distance between the source and drain regions  with wider depletion region.


Overall, to reduce short channel effects, channel depletion layer  thickness, junction depletion width (Xj) and oxide layer  thickness under the gate needs to be reduced. Halo and LDD  implants are used by the source and drain terminals to reduce


the electric field.  Location of halo and LDD implants in a  transistor structure is shown in figure 6.


Figure 6. Planar MOSFET structure showing LDD (Extension) and Halo doping regions


Short Channel effects on finFET Devices


Ideally, finFET devices have better performance to short  channel effects than planar MOSFET’s due to gate architecture  providing better control over the channel. Off state leakage  current induced by DIBL and threshold voltage roll off as seen  in planar devices are well under control for finFET’s due to the  inherent structure of the device; three gates over the channel  and ultra-thin body structure.


Factors that make finFET’s less suspectable to short channel  effects are discussed.


Channel doping is low compared to planar FET’s, which  provides better field effect mobility and improvement in on  state current. The main reason for the contribution of off-state  leakage in bulk devices is due to the phenomenon known as  GIDL (Gate Induced Drain Leakage). It is a mechanism which  originates from the region of drain under the gate. The current  flows as substrate current in case of NMOS transistor due to  band to band tunneling [5].


Next section discusses the characterization methodologies for  device structures.


Device Characterization


The fabricated devices can be tested to extract the performance  characteristics of the device with respect to manufacturing  process variation, design or performance at a system level.


The devices are tested at different stages during the  manufacturing process in the wafer form or post packaging by  the manufacturer or in the product form by the end user. During  the manufacturing process, the devices get tested prior to the  completion of all steps. It is called inline testing and they are  done on parametric structures that mimic the device structures  of the actual product. A final test is also done on similar  structures after the completion of the manufacturing process. A  sampling plan that captures the manufacturing variation enables


the manufacturer to test different devices and make  optimizations as needed. Typically, devices across different  regions in the wafer and different wafers in a lot are tested. Devices can be tested post packaging in the product form as  well to determine the performance characteristics. Sometimes  they are done as part of failure analysis or troubleshooting to  determine the root cause of issues such as leakage and timing  delay.


Basic device characteristics and testing methodology are  presented next.


The parameters that define transistor operation are drain voltage (Vd), drain current (Id), gate voltage (Vg), gate current (Ig) and  threshold voltage (Vth).


Characteristics that define the transistor behavior are output (Id  Vs Vds) and transfer (Id Vs Vgs).


Id Vg curve determines the turn on or output characteristic of the  device. It defines when the device starts conducting current. The point at which the device starts conducting current defines  the threshold voltage of the device.


Figure 7: Output characteristcis (Id Vs Vgs) of a MOS device


Id Vds curve defines the transfer characteristic of a test device is  shown in figure 7. It describes the behavior of the device after  the device is turned on and the relationship between drain  current with respect to applied drain bias.


The current voltage relationship of an ideal NMOS transistor is  as shown below

There are three regions of importance on the transfer  characteristics of a device.


Linear or Triode region


The linear region or the triode region is where the drain current  increases gradually with applied drain bias. Transistor behaves  like a voltage controlled resistor in this region. To turn the  device off at this stage, the gate to source voltage (Vgs) has to  be substantially lower than the threshold (Vth) of the device.


Saturation region


Drain current increases gradually with respect to applied drain  bias as when in figure 8 from a test case device and after a  certain voltage, it saturates. This is defined as the saturation  region and the transistor behaves like a voltage controlled  current source in this region.


Figure 8: Transfer Characteristics (Id Vds) of a MOS device


In this region, equation 1 does not hold. The voltage difference  over the channel region remains fixed at Vgs – Vt, and the  current remains constant (saturates). Replacing Vds in equation  1 by Vgs – Vt, gives the drain current for the saturation mode as  shown in equation 4 [1]
