Subthreshold region


As shown in figure 3, drain current (Id) as a function of gate to  source voltage (Vgs) in log scale, current does not drop abruptly  to zero at Vgs = Vt. Device operates in the subthreshold region  at this stage.


Test Methods


This section discussed the test methods involved in making the  measurements. Testing involves the use of Keithley Source  Measurement Unit (SMU), which is typically used because of  their ability to source and measure low currents. Number of  terminals to be tested determines the type and number of  SMU’s. Two channel SMU’s can perform most of the  characterizations on a single transistor.


Figure 9 below shows a set up with two SMU’s in use for IV  characterization of a MOSFET.


In the case where a fabless company needs to outsource FA  jobs to a service lab or foundry, CADNav tools provide the  ability to export select regions of the layout and apply  security measures such as encryption, password protection  and expiry date to protect semiconductor design IP. Figure  6 provides an example of a partially exported CAD layout  comprised of four corners (for equipment stage alignment) and the localized region of interest for external FA.


Figure 6: Partial CAD layout extracted for external FA


FA Equipment Integration


Throughout the lifespan of microelectronics failure analysis, a  wide variety of analytical equipment and techniques have been  innovated in efforts to ensure effective FA. A strong link  between CAD and FA equipment has played a vital role in  advancing FA techniques from traditional approaches and  practices. In modern FA, it is almost always required to link  CAD data to equipment. Common types of FA equipment that  interface to CADNav software include Focused Ion Beams (FIB), Scanning Electron Microscopes (SEM), Photon  Emission Microscopes (PEM), and Laser Voltage Prober (LVP).


Once the CADNav database has been configured, it can  facilitate lab-wide collaboration by connecting various FA  equipment over a shared network (i.e., company server). Figure


7 depicts how a central database simultaneously serves multiple  FA equipment from different vendors within a single lab.


Figure 7: CAD Navigation ecosystem in a typical FA lab


A central CADNav server and software platform in an FA Lab  allows the ability to integrate numerous equipment workflows  into one streamlined process, creating a unified ecosystem for  optimal workflow efficiency. For example, if an EFI engineer  localizes a fault using a PEM, a PFA engineer can immediately  access the same database, along with the fault location and other  relevant information, on a completely different piece of  equipment (e.g., FIB) and prepare for the next appropriate  actions.


CADNav applications have also enabled the ability to add “virtual layers” on the CAD layout. A virtual layer can contain  various user-defined information, as well as external data  sources, that can be overlaid onto the CAD layout and live FA  equipment. The following section highlights this powerful  capability in the EFI workflow of Automated Test Pattern  Generation (ATPG) scan chain integrity, where external  diagnosis tools convert their output into virtual layers in order  to link them to the CAD layout for fault isolation.


CADNav Applications in FA


Laser Voltage Imaging


Alongside the rapidly growing trend of design-for-test (DFT) scan based designs, defects within scan chains have become  increasingly common in ICs [3]. An established technique for  isolating failures along ATPG scan chains is Laser Voltage  Imaging (LVI), also known as Frequency Mapping, along with  CADNav applications.


The typical FA workflow for scan chain integrity failures starts  by using an ATPG diagnostics tool (provided by an EDA  vendor). The diagnosis provides a list of candidates that could  be causing the failure, identified by scan chain name and scan  cell position along the chain, as well as the digital logic  instances, net names and other various attributes to aid analysis (e.g., fault scores and suspected fault type).


Often, diagnosis does not identify a single candidate but rather  multiple positions within the scan chain, or sometimes only the  chain where the failure occurs, with no position along the chain.


Multiple candidates may span long distances, thus necessitating  further EFI techniques.


For a comprehensive analysis approach, it is possible to get the  full scan chain map from DFT tools and convert all the positions  of the scan chain to CAD layout coordinates, as shown in Figure


8. Given the flexibility of the CADNav virtual layer file format (ASCII), it is relatively easy to integrate external coordinatebased data into the CADNav environment and enable vast  possibilities for powerful customizations, depending on the  need.


Figure 8: Scan cell bounding boxes from DFT tools overlaid  with LVI image indicating a break in the scan chain


Having the entire scan chain mapped to CADNav coordinates  is especially useful for Frequency Mapping because it allows  the EFI engineer to identify exactly which scan cells are  operating properly while the device is under test [5]. This  approach is intended to detect where in the chain the data stops  propagating (e.g., where a scan clock or data signal is lost). After locating the non-operational nodes, CADNav tools can  enable the analyst to identify the hierarchical instance name, net  name, and cell type, and do further circuit investigation if  required, such as tracing cones of logic in the schematic and  finding connected sub-circuits that could be related to the fault.


If waveform analysis of the defective node is needed, the LVP  approach can be used to investigate the waveform and compare  it to simulation results [5] in efforts to identify problems such  as race conditions, hold time problems, or signals stuck at logic  high or low.


Diagnosis and FA for ATPG capture patterns is similar to scan  chain integrity but often requires more intensive crossreferencing between CAD layout and schematic, as well as a  cross-domain understanding of IC design behavior and LVP  nodal analysis.


Photon Emission Microscopy


In semiconductor FA, Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM) is a  widely adopted EFI technique to detect the consequential  leakage currents of IC failures. FA engineers use PEM to


capture the emitted light induced by defective transistors and  then utilize CADNav applications to localize the root-cause.


A typical PEM image has a collection of emission sites that  could be initiated by a single defect. Just one defect in silicon is  capable of biasing several electrically-related transistors into  anomalous mode, in which those devices can emit an  observably similar amount of light as the culprit device.


It is important to note that not all emissions are related to  defects. Emissions could also be observed during normal  operation of the device, making it nearly impossible to  distinguish the emissions that are caused by defects. Therefore, diagnostics can play a major role in locating the initial region  of investigation on the DUT.


The goal of the FA engineer is to find the single failing  transistor that is triggering other transistors in its path to emit  photons. Correlating these photon emission sites, or “hot spots”, to their transistor-level circuit schematics is critical in  determining the location of the root-cause failure.


When PEM is used for fault isolation on ATPG failures, CADNav can be an extremely useful addition to the process. The ATPG diagnostics results can be overlaid on the  microscope image to provide a rough starting area for PEM. Any hot spots observed far away from the diagnostic result, or  in a different circuit block, may be quickly and safely ignored. If a single hot spot is observed at or near the diagnostics  location, it can be concluded with relatively high confidence  that this hot spot is associated with the failure and will lead to  the correct area of interest for PFA.


In the case of multiple emission sites, there is an even more  useful application that CADNav tools provide, which allows the  analyst to identify all the nets that pass through a cluster of hot  spots. Once these nets are identified, they are sorted in  descending order by the count of hot spots touching each net, thereby linking all the emission sites to the net(s) with the  greatest probability of being associated with the root cause  defect (see Figure 9).


Figure 9: Common net found to overlap multiple emission sites


Additionally, knowing the logical net name and connected cell  types can be useful to determine the type of failure. For  example, if a clock net with many branches has the most  commonality to the emission sites, CADNav applications make  it easier to understand how a single defect on the clock net can  cause multiple hot spots.


Passive Voltage Contrast


Passive Voltage Contrast (PVC) using an SEM is an FA  technique to locate open vias, shorted gates and single-bit  floating gate memory failures [9]. CADNav tools have provided  the capability of simulating the expected PVC response of a  healthy IC and comparing it with the actual PVC image to  quickly identify discrepancies between the two, thereby  locating the failure (see Figure 10).


Figure 10: CAD-detected failure on PVC image


By simulating the expected PVC result in CAD and correlating  it with the actual SEM image, CADNav tools can immediately  pinpoint failure locations and allow FA engineers to move on  to the next appropriate actions.


Cross-section


After isolating an electrical failure on an IC, the typical next  step is to proceed with destructive PFA techniques to identify  and confirm the root-cause defect. Cross-sectional analysis can  be done to get an informative view of the defect. CADNav tools  provide a useful frame of reference for comparing mechanical  or FIB-based cross-section results to the expected result shown  in CAD (see Figure 11).


Figure 11: 2-D and 3-D cross-sectional view in CADNav


Delayering (Parallel Lapping)


Another PFA technique traditionally used to get a closer look  at the defect is top-down delayering, or parallel lapping. This  technique is also commonly used for preparing samples for  imaging and analysis techniques like SEM, nanoprobing, Electron Beam Absorbed Current (EBAC), and Transmission  Electron Microscopy (TEM). CADNav applications assist the  delayering process by isolating the layout polygons of a traced  net on each individual chip layer, which is used as a reference  during each step (see Figure 12).


Figure 12: Precise IC delayering with CADNav assistance


Circuit Edit


FIB circuit edit is a critical task in semiconductor debug and has  been adopted as an industry-standard practice for new design  bring-up. FIB induced circuit modifications allow the testing of  design related fixes without the need to wait for a new mask  revision, which is extremely expensive and could take several  months, and provides no guarantee that the modification will be  a success.


CADNav is important for all planning and operation of the FIB. In efforts to avoid irreversible errors during FIB circuit edit,


CADNav tools provide the ability to emulate the effects of  circuit modifications by checking the feasibility of the edit  before it is performed. Figure 13 depicts an emulated FIB edit  and the resulting change in electrical signal flow.


Figure 13: Emulation of FIB circuit edits in CAD


Once the CAD emulation is complete and circuit modifications  are confirmed, virtual layers can be used to place 2-D markers  on the layout with specific dimensions, along with annotations  or instructions about the FIB operations to be performed. These  markers can be transferred to the equipment in real-time and  overlaid on the live image for precise circuit edit operations.


CADNav for Package FA


The shrinking size of consumer electronics has driven  innovative changes in semiconductor packaging technology. The modern FA engineer may face complex package designs  with many PCB layers, shrinking geometries, multiple ICs or  packages within a system.


Similar to IC data, package data can be integrated into a  normalized CADNav database and linked to its associated ICs, creating a cohesive CAD representation of a complete system  on chip (SoC). CADNav tools and applications described  earlier for IC failure analysis such as circuit edit, 2-D and 3-D  cross-sectional analysis, and equipment stage navigation also  apply for package-level FA.


In addition to viewing the SoC design layout, CADNav tools  provide the ability to easily visualize the electrical connectivity  between interrelated modules, enabling full-system  visualization and signal traceability of complex package  configurations (see Figure 14).


Figure 14: CADNav layout of an SoC with mounted IC on PCB


Due to the numerous data sources involved in multi-module  packages, good management and organization of databases is  of utmost importance.


This article encompasses the key principles of CAD Navigation  for various aspects of semiconductor failure analysis and its  importance for improved yield and profitability.


An overview of the required input data and formats were  described for both IC and package devices, along with key  considerations and best practices recommended for maintaining  a cohesive database.


Challenges with an FA lab ecosystem were addressed by  providing an integrated database and software platform that  enable design layout and schematic analysis in the FA lab for  quick and accurate navigation and cross-tool collaboration.


The FA workflows presented together with CADNav are  proven methodologies that have been developed and fine-tuned  over many years to achieve faster FA cycle times, leading to  higher product yields, quicker TTM, and ultimately increased  profitability.

Failure Localization with Active and Passive Voltage Contrast in FIB and SEM*

The common Passive Voltage Contrast (VC) localization method is based on brightness  differences of conducting structures in SEM and  FIB images [1-10] and can be used for failure  localization issues. The Active Voltage Contrast  method (AVC) as it was described as Biased  Voltage Contrast by Campbell and Soden [11] and  by the author in [12] offers even more localization  possibilities. Particularly the PVC methods became  widely accepted in the semiconductor FA  community. Nearly all labs make use of it. There  are several Voltage Contrast mechanisms in SEM  and FIB and not all of them are always completely  understood. This paper will give a comprehensive  overview over all phenomena related to this subject. The multiple advantages, possibilities and limits of  VC failure localization are systemized and  discussed.


Passive Voltage Contrast in FIB  Basic principles of PVC localization in FIB


PVC means brightness differences in FIB (or SEM) images of structures having different electrical  properties. The die isn’t connected to any power  supply or signal sources (passive) and is in most  cases partially deprocessed.


Failure localization with PVC is based on the fact, that floating structures are charging up under the influence of the primary beam in FIB and SEM (Fig. 1). They appear dark. In contradiction to that  grounded structure appear bright. In example 1 one  part of a contact chain appears dark because it is  floating due to a contact open. The bright part is  grounded by design. In this context the term “grounded structure” means, that it has any contact  to any substrate region or to a large network in contradiction to the conventional meaning where


“grounded” indicates a resistance to mass potential  of almost zero.


Fig. 1: Insulated structures are charging up positively under the influence of leaving secondary electrons. Immediately after that the majority of produced secondary electrons are prevented from leaving the sample by the electric field. These structures  appear dark in the image. Grounded structures do  not charge and appear bright because of the high  secondary electron yield.


If a structure that usually supposed to be floating  appears bright, then it is in urgent suspicion to be  faulty. On the other hand, if a structure that supposed to be grounded appears dark, it is also a  strong indication for a fault. The first case is not just  limited to structures that are floating a priori because of the design. Structures can be made floating  by deprocessing as it is shown for a gate and its  contact in Fig. 2.


Fig. 2: Structures can be made floating by deprocessing


Another possibility to make structures floating is  cutting conducting lines with a FIB cut as it is  shown in Fig. 3. If such a line is bright instead of  dark, the unwanted substrate short can be found by  cutting the line into pieces (see Example 2). The  remaining bright part is bearing the fault.


Fig. 3: Structures can be made floating by cutting


For other failure localization issues it can be helpful  to ground a structure if it isn’t a priori grounded because of the design. Fig 4 shows, how a short between two adjacent floating structures can be detected by grounding one of them by FIB.


Fig 4: Localization Example: The right structure  was grounded by milling a FIB hole through it followed by a metal deposition. The left structure is  supposed to be dark because it is floating. If it isn’t, there must be a short (red) to the adjacent one.

Advanced mechanisms of PVC generation


If diodes, capacitors and transistors are involved, PVC generation and interpretation is much more  complicated. In the case of substrate contacts the  doping has to be taken into account. When large  structures are investigated, their capacitance plays  an important role. Even transistors can affect the  PVC generation when they are broken. In Fig. 5 the  PVC generation at S/D contacts is shown. The diodes, formed by n-contacts in p-wells are reverse  biased. The charging generated by the leaving secondary electrons can’t flow down to the substrate. These contacts appear dark. The p-diffusions in nwells are forming forward biased diodes. Here the  positive charges can flow easily to ground, such  contacts are bright.


Fig 5: PVC generation at S/D contacts


Contacts connecting the wells (p-diffusion in p-well  and n-diffusion in n-well) always appear bright because there is no diode. In example 3 the different  contrasts of different contact types are to be seen.


Fig 6 shows how the capacitance of a structure can  influence the generation of PVC. If a structure is  very large, e.g. a very long conducting line, then  there are not enough charge carriers produced in order to raise the potential of this structure significantly. It stays bright like a grounded structure or  becomes gradually dark because it is charging  slowly during the image scan like it is seen in example 4.


Fig. 6: Large structures are like big capacitors  which can’t be charged sufficiently during the short  time the ion beam scans over them


Fig. 7 shows an equivalent circuit diagram for a  structure having a certain capacitance C and a certain resistance R to ground. The current source is  the sum of positive ions hitting the structure and of  the secondary electrons leaving it. The solution of  the corresponding differential equation delivers the  voltage Uc which is building up at the structure.


Fig. 7: Equivalent circuit diagram, solution of the  corresponding differential equation and graphical  representation for different structure capacitances


The time tscan is the total time the ion beam scans  over the structure. The larger the capacitance of the  structure the brighter it appears.


The formula for the voltage Uc is also well suited  for studying the influence of the leakage current  from a structure to ground. These leakage currents  can occur due to surface conductivity after deprocessing or due to the circuitry this structure is connected to.


Fig. 8: Influence of leakage resistance to the voltage building up at the structure during ion beam  scan


In Fig. 8 graphical representation of Uc(t) is to be  seen for a fixed capacitance C but different values  of the leakage resistance R. For low values of R the  Voltage Uc can’t build up to an amount which is  necessary to prevent the secondary electrons from  leaving. They can reach the detector resulting in a  bright appearing structure. In our experience Rmedium  is approximately 1 GOhm. Below this order of  magnitude no dark structures can be observed.


At transistors we observed another interesting PVC  phenomenon. The contrast of s/d contacts changed  depending whether the corresponding gate was  grounded or not.


Fig. 9: The s/d contacts of n-MOS transistors are  showing different PVC depending on whether the  gate is opened or closed


The left source contact in the transistor of Fig. 9 is  normally expected to be dark because of the reverse  biased diode under it. In reality it is bright because  the charges can escape through the open transistor  to the drain which is grounded. The gate was  charged positively through the oxide during the ion  beam scan and thus opened. When this gate conductor is grounded by a FIB cut nearby (no metal fill is


necessary) the source contact suddenly turns dark as  it is demonstrated in example 5.

Some experiences to share


Sometimes it is hard to achieve a noticeable PVC in  the Focused Ion Beam. Knowing the mechanisms  behind PVC generation, one can derive some basic  rules to get or to improve the contrast between  charging and floating structures. The goal to be  achieved is either to reduce the leakage currents or  to improve the charge carrier generation.


[1] The first thing one should try is to increase the primary beam current, because it improves the net charging of the structure. It should be noted,however, that there is always a tradeoff between damaging the structure by milling it away and the achievement of good PVC. In case of doubt the influence of a strong ion beam should be tested at an uncritical structure of the same kind.


[2] The next thing one should try is to change the sample orientation. If structures are to be charged that are longer than wider, it is more effective to align their long side horizontally so that the horizontally scanning ion beam is hitting a big portion of the structure abruptly which can overcome possible leakage currents and can increase the chance to charge it up sufficiently. The easiest way to do it is to change the scan direction by software buttons instead of rotating the sample stage.


[3] The scan speed also plays an important role.


Slower scan speeds improve the chance of sufficient charging.


[4] A tilted surface is emitting more secondary electrons than a horizontal one. This improves the charge carrier generation. Therefore stage tilting may help.


[5] When lines are to be FIB cut, one should always use the fluorine GIS because it prevents the redeposition of conducting material on the surface and thus it reduces the leakage currents(see example 6)


[6] Typical beam currents for the most localization issues are 10-50 pA. For low magnifications a current up to 100 pA can be used, for special problems at high magnifications 1-10 pA may be best.


PVC in SEM versus FIB


In table 3 is explained why the charge generation in  FIB is much stronger then in SEM.


Table 3: Comparison of Charging in FIB and SEM. In SEM both negative and positive charging is gettable depending on primary beam energy. In FIB  just positive charging is possible but this is much  stronger.


In SEM, the incoming primary electrons and the  leaving secondary electrons are partially compensating each other resulting in less charging then in  FIB. Because this depends on primary beam current, sample material, sample orientation, magnification and other factors the charging in SEM can be  both positive and negative, which can be an advantage in comparison to the FIB.


The accelerating voltage of the electron beam has  the largest influence on the type of charging as it is  shown in Fig. 10.


Fig. 10: Influence of the beam energy to the emission yield in SEM. The threshold voltages E1 and E2  depend on sample, sample material and SEM configuration like beam current, chuck to ground resistance, vacuum, etc.


The threshold voltage E1 is in our experience approximately 0.5 kV and E2 is around 2 kV. In Example 7 SEM images with two different beam energies show different PVC. Depending on the problem to be solved either FIB PVC or SEM PVC is  the method of choice. In table 4 advantages and disadvantages of both methods are set against each  other.


Table 4: advantages and disadvantages of FIB and  SEM PVC


Inline e-beam inspection


An important application of Passive Voltage Contrast in SEM is the inline e-beam inspection technique. In an inline SEM a retarding field at the  chuck provides low landing energies of electrons  which are necessary for VC localization. The primary energy of the electrons right after having left  the cathode is not affected by the retarding field and


is high as it is necessary for a high SEM resolution. With a charge control plate mounted above the wafer both positive and negative surface charging can  be detected (Fig. 11).


Fig. 11: Both positive and negative charges can be  detected in inline e-beam inspection tools


In examples 8 and 9 is shown that both types of  charging can be helpful for detection of faults at  wafer level.


Figure 9: Device characterization setup using source meter (SMU)


Next section discusses how a curve tracer can be used to  measure and plot DC current voltage characteristics [4]. Test  circuits are required for characterizing the output and transfer  characteristics. A depiction of test circuit is shown in figure 10.


Figure 10: Measurement techniques to generate output and  MOSFET transfer IV curves (Left – output IV curve, Right – Transfer IV curve)


Output Characteristics: Drain voltage is fixed at a desired  voltage and gate voltage is swept over the desired range using  an Arbitrary Waveform Generator, or AWG. AWG2/SMU2 is  set up at 10x faster than AWG1 so that drain current is swept  for each body terminal value. Scope channel is set up to  measure Id on Ch2 and Vgs on Ch1. R1 is chosen to optimize  the desired voltage drop in order to get the current plot. A  typical output characteristic curve is shown in figure 11.


Figure 11: Sweep of output characteristics


Transfer characteristics: Drain voltage is swept for a desired  range for different gate voltages. AWG2/SMU2 has to be set  much faster than AWG1/SMU1 so that drain current is swept  for each gate step voltage. Scope channel probes are set to  measure Id on Ch2 and Vds on Ch1. Resistor R1 is chosen to  limit the voltage drop across R1 to optimize the current plot for  NMOS device. A typical output of sweep characteristics is  shown in figure 12.


Figure 12: Sweep of transfer characteristics


Device Tuning


If the desired performance characteristics are not achieved, adjustments can be made from a design, manufacturing and  system level. Some of the changes are discussed below.


In the Design stage, adjustments are made to the width and  length of the devices to get the desired output and transfer  characteristics. However, design adjustments are not just to get  the desired characteristics of a single transistor but to get the  performance of a desired circuit.


Designing is performed based on models developed from  silicon technology. However, there is no guarantee that the  transistors behave the same way as designed in silicon due to  variations in manufacturing and process changes. The second  level of adjustments to get the devices to target is performed  during device fabrication. At the processing level, implant  doses can be adjusted to get the desired target. Doping  adjustments can be made on the source/drain regions, and  channel regions.


Device characteristics are locked post-manufacturing process. Functional and reliability testing are performed to ensure key  performance indicators are met prior to product delivery.


Transistors are the most important active structure of any  semiconductor component. Performance characteristics of such  devices within the specifications are key to ensuring proper  functionality and long-term reliability of the product is  achieved. In this article, a summary of the semiconductor  technology from design to manufacturing and the  characterization methods have been discussed.

The Fundamentals of Nanoprobe Analysis


Randal Mulder


Silicon Laboratories, Inc.; 400 West Cesar Chavez, Austin, TX 78700


Kent Erington


NXP, Inc.; William Cannon Blvd, Austin, TX 78700


In the late 1990s to early 2000’s, the semiconductor industry  was in the process of transitioning from aluminum  metallization and Boron Phosphorus Silicon Glass (BPSG) inter-level dielectric (ILD) backend wafer technology nodes  to 130nm copper metallization and Low-K dielectric (ILD) backend technology nodes. The 0.18um and older  technology nodes which featured typically three layers (or  less) of metallization with the BPSG as the insulation layers  were relatively easy to microprobe by constructing on the  surface of the die Focused Ion Beam (FIB) deposited  tungsten microprobe pads on which to land microprobe  needles. Microprobing was required in the failure analysis  of defective semiconductor devices to access specific  functional nodes in the device to track down and localize the  point of functional signal failure. Microprobing was also  used to check for metallization shorts, resistive/open Vias (vertical metal to metal connections) metallization, and  transistor probing and characterization. Once micro-probing  and other localization techniques were completed that  diagnosed the location of the failing circuit node, physical  analysis was then performed to determine the physical  mechanism causing device failure.


Microprobe pads on the die surface are created by using a  focus ion beam tool (FIB) to mill through the dielectric  layers of the device to open windows allowing access to  individual metal lines and to then deposit platinum or  tungsten to create the microprobe pads and the connection to  the exposed metal line(s). A microprobe needle is then  landed on the microprobe pad to gain access to the device  metal line to measure functional signals or to make  parametric measurements.


With the introduction of 130nm backend copper  metallization and low-K dielectric for ILD, microprobe pads  became very difficult to construct (Figure 1 and 2). The  number of metal layers increased from three (or less) to six (or greater) with thick top metallization layers used for  routing Ground and VDD while the lower metal layers were  used to route signals. Accessing signal lines required using  the FIB to open smaller windows through many more layers  of metallization and oxide without causing shorts to the  upper metallization layers. Dummy metallization tiling was


also introduced for all metal layers for more uniform wafer  processing results.


Figure 1: With the introduction of copper metallization, the  number of metal layers greatly increased, the spacing  between the metallization has decreased, and Low-K  dielectric replaced BPSG making the construction of microprobe pads for fault isolation very difficult.


Figure 2: FIB cross section image of a 55nm device shows  eight metallization layers. The thick Metal7 and Metal8  layers primarily distribute power and ground throughout  the device and are insulated by traditional oxide. Low K  dielectric is used for the insulator below metal 7 down to  the top of metal 1. BPSG is used as the insulator for the  transistors below metal 1 in most cases.

However, the tiling minimized the open areas of oxide to  access metal lines at lower levels. This require the FIB to  mill through both oxide as well as the dummy copper  metallization. FIB milling through copper metallization is  difficult due to the pronounced grain boundaries of the  copper which results in uneven milling of the copper. Oxide  and copper do not mill at the same rate adding another level  of difficulty for FIB microprobe pad construction when  trying to expose lower layer metallization lines.


In addition to the increased number of metallization layers, the inter-level dielectric was change from BPSG to low-K  dielectric to reduce capacitive coupling. Low-K dielectric is  not as hard as BPSG dielectric and has an almost spongy  physical quality. When its physical structure is disturbed by  FIB milling, it tends to lose its ability to insulate and  becomes leaky to adjacent metal lines making the electrical  isolation of the FIB openings for the deposited tungsten  difficult.


Due to the difficulties of constructing FIB deposited microprobe pads for copper metallization semiconductor  technologies, the ability for failure analysts to perform fault  localization on failing devices became much more difficult. Fortunately, as this was occurring, nanoprobe analysis was  developed and introduced. In 2001, the first atomic force  nanoprober (AFP) was introduced by Andy Erikson, Multiprobe Inc. The AFP was a modified version of the  atomic force microscope (AFM), but instead of one piezo  scanning probe tip/probe-head there where multiple  tips/probe-heads engineered to act in unison to image and  probe. The scanning probe tips could image and probe  transistors at the exposed transistor contact level as well as  image and probe exposed metallization layers. This was a  significant advancement at a time when micro-probing  became much more difficult perform. Later, imaging  techniques such as current contrast imaging and scanning  capacitance imaging were added features to the tool.


Not long after the introduction of AFP technology, an insitu SEM nanoprobing solution was also developed by  Zyvex Inc. where piezo controlled probed tips placed inside  the SEM chamber could probe both transistors and  metallization nodes. In addition to probing, Active Voltage  Contrast, electron beam absorbed current (EBAC), electron  beam induced current (EBIC), and electron beam induced  resistance change (Ebirch) imaging techniques were added  to the tools capabilities.


With the development and integration of nanoprobe  technologies into the failure analysis lab and FA process, nanoprobing has become a permanent fixture in the failure  analysis process flow for most failure analysis labs. Nanoprobing is now an indispensable tool for localizing and  identifying failure mechanisms types resulting in much  higher physical analysis success rates.


Overview and Outline


The purpose of this paper is not to provide a detailed  presentation of the physics/engineering of the nanoprobe  tools or a detailed explanation of how to run these tools. Nanoprobing is now a mature technology platform. How  these systems are constructed and run and perform their  analysis techniques has been well established since the early  2000s in technical papers and articles. The training for the  functional operation of the nanoprobe tools themselves is  provided by the tool vendor or by experienced analysts  already trained and practiced in running the tool. There is no  need to repeat this information in this article.


Instead, the purpose of this paper will be to address the  ancillary issues regarding the nanoprobing and  characterization of transistors, probing copper metallization  layers, and the various imaging techniques. These ancillary  issues and strategies are vital for quickly and successfully  obtaining the require results need to determine device  failure. If these issues are not accommodated properly, achieving any type of meaningful results will be much more  difficult if not impossible.


The outline for the topics discussed in this paper are as  follows:


1. Sample Preparation for Transistor Probing and  Copper Metallization Probing.


2. Transistor Characterization:


a. Four Probe Transistor Characterization


b. Two Probe Transistor Characterization


c. Probing and Characterizing Metallization  Issues


3. AFP: Current Contrast Imaging


4. AFP: Scanning Capacitance Imaging


5. SEM Nanoprobe: EBAC Imaging


6. SEM Nanoprobe: EBIC Imaging


7. SEM Nanoprobe: EBIRCH Imaging


8. SEM Nanoprobe: Active Voltage Contrast Imaging


9. Conclusion


The “Sample Preparation” and “Transistor Characterization”


sections of this paper are applicable to all nanoprobe tool  types. The remaining sections will be specific to AFP or  SEM based tools.


Sample preparation is critical for a successful nanoprobe  analysis. Once an analyst has become proficient in operating  a nanoprobe tool, sample preparation is usually the limiting  factor on which the analysis will be successful or not. Also, in many cases, even if the sample preparation has not been  performed very well, the device characterization may still be  completed successfully but obtaining the results will be  difficult and much more time consuming.


In most cases, sample preparation for nanoprobing requires  the removal of the die from the package. There can be  instances were FIB sample preparation can be performed  with the device in package, but this paper will focus on the  standard option which is performed the vast majority of the  time. The die is removed from the package and then  mechanical polishing is used to remove metallization and  oxide layers until the desired layer is reached for  nanoprobing. For transistor characterization, the desired  level is the top of the contact layer just under Metal 1. Probing of a specific metal layer requires polishing to the  top of the target metal layer.


There are two desired outcomes when the delayering is  completed. The first is good planarity and the second is a  clean conductive surface for either the tungsten contacts or  the copper metallization of the targeted metal layer.


Good planarity is desired because it may be required to  analyze multiple locations on the chip. An example is when  a device has multiple SRAM random bit failures that are  distributed across the memory blocks. If planarity is poor  then one of the failing bit locations will be reached first  while the other locations will still have one to several  additional layers still covering those locations and will not  be available for nanoprobe analysis. Only FIB cross-section  or TEM cross section lift out analysis is available as a  means of physical analysis on the exposed bit without  sacrificing the other failing bit locations. If wet etching was  used to expose the polysilicon, contacts and substrate for the  first bit, then then other bit locations would be sacrificed. If  mechanical polish deprocessing is continued to access the  other bit locations without first performing physical analysis  on the first bit, then the polishing will consume the first bit  and it will not be available later for physical analysis to  determine the failure mechanism. Good planarity results  allow the nanoprobe analysis of multiple fault locations at  the same time which then allows for multiple chances for a  successful physical analysis to identify the failure  mechanism(s).


A second example of a problem caused by poor planarity is  when a circuit area to be analyzed has nodes separated over  large distances. The circuit nodes of interest may be in one  location and the well ties, bit lines, word lines and other  circuit nodes may be on the opposite side of the circuit  block. Poor planarization may mean either one of the  locations is not accessible at the desired layer. Additional  delayering to access the covered location will then result in  the loss of the already exposed circuit area. Good planarity  isn’t always needed in some cases if circuit areas of interest  are small, but as a practice it’s always prudent to keep the  die delayering as planar as possible to make analysis easier. Another issue with poor planarity is the difficulty of  cleaning the die and preventing debris from the other


unprocessed die areas from landing on the circuits of  interest which prevents the probing of the circuit nodes.


How the quality of delayering planarity is achieved is


dependent on the analyst’s ability and available


deprocessing methodologies. In general, a straight polish  through the layers either by finger polishing on a wheel or  delayering on a polisher doesn’t usually result in the best  planarity (Figure 3). Often, a combination of wet etching, RIE plasma etching, and mechanical polishing can be used  to obtain better planarity results [1], [2], [3], [4] (Figure 4). In any case, the analyst should develop a deprocessing  recipe for all semiconductor technology nodes on which  they will be working before they receive actual failing  samples. In most cases, perfect delayering will not be  achievable, but the goal should be to have as much of the  die area be at the same deprocessing level as possible.


Figure 3: Optical microscope image of a 55nm device after  mechanical polish. The deprocessing technique was not  adequate resulting in very poor planarity across the die.


Figure 4: Optical microscope image of a 55nm device  deprocessed to the Metal1 layer. The deprocessing recipe  was optimized to achieve good planarity across the entire  die (See references).


The need for a clean, conductive surface is self-evident. When the tungsten needles of the nanoprobe tool make  contact to either the tungsten transistor contacts or to copper  metallization lines, a small ohmic barrier must be overcome  to establish conductivity even for clean probe needles/die  metallization. If the surface of the die metallization (or the  probe tips) is not clean (particulates, nonconductive residue, oxidation), the establishment of electrical conduction  through the tip and to the sample metallization will be  greatly reduced or will not be possible.


It’s recommended that the last layer to be removed be


removed by finger polishing on a polish wheel with a  standard polishing pad/cloth. The tungsten contacts or  copper metallization will already be slightly higher than the  surrounding oxide when finished (slightly delineated). Additional delineation for nanoprobing will only require a  short exposure to buffered oxide etch (BOE for tungsten  contacts) or reactive ion etch (RIE for copper metallization  lines) to get the contacts/metal lines high enough above the  oxide to land the nanoprobe tips. Do not use diamond  lapping film to remove the final layer. The diamond film  polishing results in the surrounding oxide layer being higher  than either the tungsten contacts or copper metallization. This will then require a significantly longer exposure to the  BOE for tungsten contacts and RIE for copper to get  delineation for landing nanoprobe needles.


Use a 0.05um diamond or aluminum slurry. The diamond  slurry is preferable since the diamond particulates are the  most spherical and will not embed into the tungsten/copper  metallization of the die. Do not use silicate polishing slurry. The silicate particles are jagged and will embed into the  metallization of the die. The silicate is non-conductive so  establishing electrical conduction to the probe tips will be  blocked by the embedded silicate particles.


The following polishing methodology has been developed  to remove the last layer and achieve clean conductive die  surfaces (at the transistor contact or metallization line) for  nanoprobe analysis.


1. Final polish - 0.05um diamond slurry on a final A  pad.


• 200RPM with a finger-polish technique.


• Cleans surface ILD and metal.


2. Polish - Clean pad with just water to remove any  remaining slurry particles.


3. Tungsten Contacts: 10:1 BOE for 5-15 seconds  depending on technology node.  Rinse with  Acetone and blow dry.


4. Copper Metallization: RIE - Leave the sample in  the chamber under vacuum (1e-5 mbar).


• 1 hour.


• Extract as much of the water from the  sample as possible.


• Exposed to an Argon plasma for about 30  seconds.


• Copper topography ~ 10nm.


The copper will stay nicely conductive for several hours. Probe within a few hours after sample preparation. Exposed  copper metallization oxidizes rapidly. If you have to leave  the sample over-night, place it in a dry nitrogen box.


The other variable that has to be paid close attention is the  condition of the nanoprobe needles. Bent, dirty, or oxidized  tungsten probe needles will also make establishing electrical  conductivity to the sample difficult or impossible. Probe tips  that have been on the tool for a while used to probe samples  become worn, bent, oxidized or collect particulates. Even  new probe needles can become oxidized over time even if  stored properly. Methodologies have been developed to  clean and sharpen new and used probe tips. The use of a  focused ion beam (FIB) tool works well for all types of  tungsten probe tips [5]. Once cleaned and well prepared  samples and clean probe tips are obtained, probing of  tungsten contacts or copper metallization should be  relatively easy.


Transistor Probing and Characterization


Transistor probing and characterization techniques are  applicable for both SEM and AFP based nanoprobe  systems. The objective is to get the probe tips on the  transistor contacts with the minimum amount of resistance. The exact probe tip to transistor contact resistance values  are not precisely known (Kelvin measures are typically not  made during transistor characterization) so transistor  characterization is a somewhat qualitative measurement. Therefore, measured results for the failure have to be  compared to a reference or correlation device in some cases  when marginally performing transistors are the cause of the  device failure.


Typically, two types of measurements are performed. Fourprobe measurements identifies the defective transistor(s) in  the failing circuit. However, additional measurements need  to be performed to identify the possible type and location of  the defect within the transistor. Two-probe measurements  identifies type and location of defect within the material  interfaces of the transistor. The type of two-probe  measurements that are performed are Gate to Well, Gate to  Source, Gate to Drain, Source to Well, Drain to Well, and  Drain to Source (Gate off). These additional measurements  give significant information as to the nature of the failure  mechanism (gate oxide defect, poly defect, substrate  dislocation defect, Vt shift defect, etc.). This additional  information indicates the type and location of the physical  analysis that should be performed (cross section TEM, plain  view TEM, sequential FIB cross-sectioning, wet etch  deprocess with SEM inspection, etc.) to greatly enhance the  physical analysis success rate.
